hdb-035.q: What was al-Ḥākim's stated aim in al-Mustadrak?
o: To gather hadith he judged to meet the Ṣaḥīḥayn's terms but which they omitted
To list the errors he found in the chains of al-Bukhārī and Muslim
To collect the weak hadith that the two Shaykhs had rejected
To explain the difficult words in the two Ṣaḥīḥs
hdb-035.e: Al-Ḥākim collected hadith that, in his judgement, met the conditions of al-Bukhārī and Muslim or of one of them, though they had not included them. Later critics found him lenient (mutasāhil) in this judgement.

hdb-036.q: Which scholar abridged al-Mustadrak and commented on many of al-Ḥākim's gradings in his Talkhīṣ?
hdb-036.e: Al-Dhahabī's Talkhīṣ al-Mustadrak summarises the work and often agrees with or corrects al-Ḥākim's claim that a hadith meets the two Shaykhs' conditions.

hdb-037.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Hady al-Sārī, biography of al-Bukhārī
hdb-037.q: In which year is al-Bukhārī commonly said to have died?
hdb-037.e: Al-Bukhārī died in 256 AH near Samarqand. 261 is the year commonly given for Muslim, 241 for Aḥmad and 279 for al-Tirmidhī.

hdb-038.src: al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, biography of al-Nasāʾī
hdb-038.q: Which of the six compilers died last, commonly dated to 303 AH?
hdb-038.e: Aḥmad ibn Shuʿayb al-Nasāʾī is commonly dated to 303 AH, after the other five, who all died in the third century (al-Tirmidhī 279, Abū Dāwūd 275, Ibn Mājah 273).

hdb-039.src: al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, biography of Ibn Mājah
hdb-039.q: Ibn Mājah, compiler of one of the four Sunan, bears which nisba after his home city?
hdb-039.e: Muḥammad ibn Yazīd Ibn Mājah was from Qazwīn in Persia. Al-Sijistānī is the nisba of Abū Dāwūd, al-Naysābūrī that of Muslim.

hdb-040.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Hady al-Sārī, on the arrangement of the Ṣaḥīḥ; al-Nawawī, al-Minhāj, introduction
hdb-040.q: Which statement correctly contrasts the arrangement of the two Ṣaḥīḥs?
o: Muslim gathers a hadith's chains in one place; al-Bukhārī splits and repeats it under chapters
Al-Bukhārī gathers a hadith's chains in one place; Muslim splits and repeats it under chapters
Both arrange their hadith by the narrating Companion rather than by topic
Neither book repeats a hadith; each report appears exactly once
hdb-040.e: Muslim usually brings all chains and wordings of a hadith together in one place. Al-Bukhārī cuts and repeats hadith under different chapter headings to draw legal and other inferences, so his headings (tarājim) show his fiqh.

hdb-041.q: Which description best fits the content of Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn?
o: Hadith on character, worship and conduct, chapters often opening with verses
Hadith on legal rulings with notes on their narrators and gradings
Hadith on creed arranged as a refutation of sects
Hadith on the Prophet's battles arranged by year
hdb-041.e: Al-Nawawī arranged Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn in chapters on sincerity, manners, virtues and worship; many chapters begin with relevant Quranic verses before the hadith. Legal hadith with gradings is the approach of Bulūgh al-Marām.

hdb-042.src: al-Kattānī, al-Risāla al-Mustaṭrafa, section on the muṣannafāt
hdb-042.q: How does a muṣannaf, such as that of ʿAbd al-Razzāq, typically differ from a sunan?
o: It is arranged by topics and contains many Companion and Successor reports
It is arranged by Companions and contains only Prophetic hadith
It is arranged by the compiler's teachers in alphabetical order
It contains only hadith with chains meeting the two Shaykhs' terms
hdb-042.e: Both muṣannaf and sunan are arranged by subject, but a muṣannaf includes a large share of mawqūf and maqṭūʿ reports (statements of Companions and Successors), while a sunan concentrates on marfūʿ hadith on rulings.

hdb-043.src: al-Kattānī, al-Risāla al-Mustaṭrafa, section on the muṣannafāt
hdb-043.q: Which of these works belongs to the muṣannaf genre?
o: the Musnad of Abū Dāwūd al-Ṭayālisī
hdb-043.e: The Muṣannaf of Abū Bakr ibn Abī Shayba, like that of ʿAbd al-Razzāq, is a topical collection rich in Companion and Successor reports. Al-Ṭayālisī's work is a musnad and al-Ṭabarānī's a muʿjam.

hdb-044.src: al-Kattānī, al-Risāla al-Mustaṭrafa, section on the jawāmiʿ
hdb-044.q: What makes a hadith collection a "jāmiʿ" in the technical sense of the compilers?
o: It covers all main subjects: creed, rulings, manners, exegesis, history, trials and virtues
It gathers only the hadith on which the scholars of a city agreed
It combines the chains of two earlier books into one work
It is arranged by the Companions, beginning with the ten promised Paradise
hdb-044.e: A jāmiʿ covers all the main areas of the religion (often listed as eight), such as the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī and the Jāmiʿ of al-Tirmidhī. A sunan focuses on rulings; arrangement by Companions is the musnad.

hdb-045.q: Which Companion narrates the hadith that the lawful is clear, the unlawful is clear, and between them are doubtful matters?
hdb-045.e: This hadith, which also mentions the heart as the piece of flesh on which the body's soundness depends, is narrated by al-Nuʿmān ibn Bashīr and recorded by al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

hdb-046.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Hady al-Sārī, on the reason for compiling the Ṣaḥīḥ
hdb-046.q: According to a well-known report, which teacher's remark about compiling a concise book of only sound hadith moved al-Bukhārī to write his Ṣaḥīḥ?
hdb-046.e: Al-Bukhārī related that he was with Isḥāq ibn Rāhawayh when Isḥāq wished someone would compile a short book of the sound sunna, and this settled in his heart. ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī was another major teacher, but the report names Isḥāq.

hdb-047.q: Which transmission (riwāya) of al-Muwaṭṭaʾ is the most widespread and is usually meant when the book is cited without qualification?
o: That of Yaḥyā ibn Yaḥyā al-Laythī
That of Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Shaybānī
That of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Wahb
hdb-047.e: Al-Muwaṭṭaʾ has several recensions; the Andalusian Yaḥyā ibn Yaḥyā al-Laythī's version became the standard text. Al-Shaybānī's recension is known for adding Ḥanafī comments.

hdb-048.src: al-Bukhārī, al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-ʿIlm, chapter on writing knowledge
hdb-048.q: Abū Hurayra said that one Companion had more hadith than he did because that Companion used to write while he did not. Who was it?
o: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ
hdb-048.e: Al-Bukhārī records this statement of Abū Hurayra about ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, whose written collection is known as al-Ṣaḥīfa al-Ṣādiqa. It shows that hadith were written down already in the Companions' time.

hdb-049.src: Ibn Ṭāhir al-Maqdisī, Shurūṭ al-Aʾimma al-Sitta; Ibn Ḥajar, al-Nukat ʿalā Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ
hdb-049.q: Who is commonly named as the first to count Sunan Ibn Mājah among the six core books?
hdb-049.e: Abū al-Faḍl Ibn Ṭāhir al-Maqdisī is commonly credited with first adding Ibn Mājah to the five in his works on the conditions of the six imams. Ibn al-Athīr, by contrast, counted al-Muwaṭṭaʾ as the sixth book. Al-Mizzī later followed the six-book canon with Ibn Mājah in his indexes.

hdb-050.src: Ibn al-Athīr, Jāmiʿ al-Uṣūl fī Aḥādīth al-Rasūl, introduction
hdb-050.q: Ibn al-Athīr's Jāmiʿ al-Uṣūl combines six books, following Razīn al-Saraqusṭī. Which book does it include in place of Sunan Ibn Mājah?
hdb-050.e: Following Razīn, Ibn al-Athīr counted al-Muwaṭṭaʾ as the sixth book in Jāmiʿ al-Uṣūl. Other scholars proposed Sunan al-Dārimī, while the later majority settled on Ibn Mājah.

hdb-051.src: Ibn Ḥajar, al-Nukat ʿalā Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ; al-Kattānī, al-Risāla al-Mustaṭrafa
hdb-051.q: Which statement correctly describes the scholars' views on the sixth of the six books?
o: Most later scholars count Ibn Mājah; others named al-Muwaṭṭaʾ or al-Dārimī
All scholars agree on Ibn Mājah, and no other book was ever proposed
Most scholars count al-Muwaṭṭaʾ; only Ibn Ḥajar accepted Ibn Mājah
Most scholars count the Musnad of Aḥmad; some suggested al-Mustadrak
hdb-051.e: The later majority, following Ibn Ṭāhir al-Maqdisī and al-Mizzī, count Sunan Ibn Mājah for its many additional hadith. Razīn and Ibn al-Athīr counted al-Muwaṭṭaʾ, and some scholars thought Sunan al-Dārimī more fitting because it has fewer weak reports.

hdb-052.src: Muslim, al-Ṣaḥīḥ, Muqaddima; Ibn Ḥajar, Hady al-Sārī
hdb-052.q: Regarding a narrator who reports from his shaykh with "ʿan", what condition is commonly attributed to al-Bukhārī in contrast to Muslim?
o: Al-Bukhārī required proof that they met at least once; Muslim accepted contemporaneity with possible meeting
Muslim required proof that they met at least once; al-Bukhārī accepted contemporaneity with possible meeting
Al-Bukhārī rejected every ʿan report; Muslim accepted it only from Companions
Both required that the narrator state explicit hearing in every link of the chain
hdb-052.e: Al-Bukhārī is commonly said to have required established meeting (liqāʾ) at least once. Muslim, in the Muqaddima of his Ṣaḥīḥ, defended accepting contemporaneity (muʿāṣara) with the possibility of meeting, provided the narrator is not a mudallis.

hdb-053.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Bulūgh al-Marām, introduction; Majd al-Dīn Ibn Taymiyya, al-Muntaqā min Akhbār al-Muṣṭafā
hdb-053.q: Ibn Ḥajar notes in Bulūgh al-Marām that the author of al-Muntaqā uses "muttafaq ʿalayh" differently. In al-Muntaqā it means narrated by …
hdb-053.e: Majd al-Dīn Ibn Taymiyya uses "muttafaq ʿalayh" in al-Muntaqā for Aḥmad together with al-Bukhārī and Muslim; Ibn Ḥajar, in contrast, uses it for al-Bukhārī and Muslim only. Al-Shawkānī's Nayl al-Awṭār is a commentary on al-Muntaqā.

hdb-054.q: In Bulūgh al-Marām, which compilers are meant by "al-arbaʿa" (the four)?
o: Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah
Aḥmad, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī
al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī
Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad and Abū Ḥanīfa
hdb-054.e: Ibn Ḥajar defines "al-arbaʿa" as the authors of the four Sunan: Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah. "Al-thalātha" is the same without Ibn Mājah, and "al-khamsa" adds Aḥmad to the four.

hdb-055.q: In Bulūgh al-Marām, what does "akhrajahu al-thalātha" (the three narrated it) mean?
o: Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī narrated it
al-Bukhārī, Muslim and Aḥmad narrated it
al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah narrated it
Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah narrated it
hdb-055.e: Ibn Ḥajar uses "al-thalātha" for the authors of the four Sunan except Ibn Mājah: Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and al-Nasāʾī. "Al-sabʿa" means Aḥmad together with the six.

hdb-056.src: al-Sakhāwī, al-Ḍawʾ al-Lāmiʿ, biography of al-ʿAynī; Ḥājjī Khalīfa, Kashf al-Ẓunūn, entry al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaḥīḥ
hdb-056.q: Which Ḥanafī scholar, a contemporary of Ibn Ḥajar, wrote ʿUmdat al-Qārī, a major commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī?
hdb-056.e: Badr al-Dīn al-ʿAynī, a Ḥanafī of Cairo, wrote ʿUmdat al-Qārī alongside Ibn Ḥajar's Fatḥ al-Bārī. Al-Qasṭallānī (Irshād al-Sārī) came later, al-Kirmānī and Ibn Baṭṭāl earlier.

hdb-057.src: Ḥājjī Khalīfa, Kashf al-Ẓunūn; al-Kattānī, al-Risāla al-Mustaṭrafa
hdb-057.q: Which pair of commentary and base book is correctly matched?
o: Maʿālim al-Sunan by al-Khaṭṭābī – Sunan Abī Dāwūd
Tuḥfat al-Aḥwadhī by al-Mubārakfūrī – Sunan al-Nasāʾī
al-Tamhīd by Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr – Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim
Subul al-Salām by al-Ṣanʿānī – Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn
hdb-057.e: Al-Khaṭṭābī's Maʿālim al-Sunan is an early commentary on Abū Dāwūd. Tuḥfat al-Aḥwadhī explains al-Tirmidhī, al-Tamhīd explains al-Muwaṭṭaʾ, and Subul al-Salām explains Bulūgh al-Marām.

hdb-058.src: Muslim, al-Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Īmān, first hadith; al-Nawawī, al-Minhāj
hdb-058.q: In Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, the hadith of Jibrīl is introduced by Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar asking Ibn ʿUmar about a new group. Which group?
o: People in Basra who denied the divine decree (qadar)
The Khawārij who had gathered at Ḥarūrāʾ
Tribes who refused to pay zakāh after the Prophet
People in Kufa who denied the coming of the Hour
hdb-058.e: Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar reports that Maʿbad al-Juhanī was the first in Basra to speak about qadar. He and Ḥumayd met Ibn ʿUmar on ḥajj, who disowned that view and cited his father ʿUmar's hadith of Jibrīl, which includes belief in qadar.

hdb-059.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, first type; al-Nawawī, al-Minhāj, introduction
hdb-059.q: Which statement correctly describes the scholars' views on ranking the two Ṣaḥīḥs?
o: Most prefer al-Bukhārī; Abū ʿAlī al-Naysābūrī and some Maghribīs preferred Muslim
All scholars prefer Muslim, while Abū ʿAlī al-Naysābūrī preferred al-Bukhārī
Most hold them exactly equal, and no scholar preferred either book
Most prefer Muslim; only al-Dāraquṭnī preferred al-Bukhārī
hdb-059.e: The majority rank al-Bukhārī first in soundness. Abū ʿAlī al-Naysābūrī and some scholars of the Maghrib preferred Muslim, which later scholars often explained as referring to its arrangement and the gathering of chains rather than to greater authenticity.

hdb-060.src: al-Bukhārī, al-Jāmiʿ al-Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Tawḥīd, last chapter; Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī
hdb-060.q: With which book (kitāb) does Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī end, closing with the hadith of the two phrases light on the tongue and heavy in the Balance?
hdb-060.e: Al-Bukhārī ends with Kitāb al-Tawḥīd, and its last hadith, from Abū Hurayra, praises two phrases of glorification that are heavy in the Balance. Ibn Ḥajar notes the fitting link between the opening on intention and this ending on the weighing of deeds. Kitāb al-Iʿtiṣām comes just before it.

hdb-061.src: al-Būṣīrī, Miṣbāḥ al-Zujāja fī Zawāʾid Ibn Mājah, introduction
hdb-061.q: What is the subject of al-Būṣīrī's Miṣbāḥ al-Zujāja?
o: The hadith found in Ibn Mājah but not in the other five books
The weak narrators found in the chains of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim
The difficult words in the Sunan of Abū Dāwūd
The hadith of al-Muwaṭṭaʾ missing from al-Bukhārī
hdb-061.e: Miṣbāḥ al-Zujāja fī Zawāʾid Ibn Mājah studies the additional hadith (zawāʾid) of Ibn Mājah beyond the other five books and grades their chains; these additions are why many count his Sunan sixth, and also why it contains more weak reports.

hdb-062.src: al-Kattānī, al-Risāla al-Mustaṭrafa; al-Dhahabī, Siyar, biography of al-Dārimī
hdb-062.q: Which statement about the collection of ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Dārimī is correct?
o: It is arranged by fiqh chapters although it is also called al-Musnad
It is arranged by Companions in the same way as the Musnad of Aḥmad
It was compiled after al-Nasāʾī's al-Mujtabā and depends on it
It contains only hadith on manners and has no chapters on rulings
hdb-062.e: Al-Dārimī (commonly dated to 255 AH) arranged his work by chapters like a sunan, yet it is often called Musnad al-Dārimī, showing that "musnad" was also used in the sense of a book of connected chains. He died long before al-Nasāʾī.

hdt-001.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar, on the definition of the isnād
hdt-001.q: In hadith terminology, what is the sanad?
o: The chain of narrators leading up to the text
The wording of the report itself
The book in which the report is recorded
The explanation of the report's meaning
hdt-001.e: The sanad (or isnād) is the chain of people who transmitted the report, one from another, until it reaches its source. The wording that follows the chain is the matn.

hdt-002.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar, on the matn
hdt-002.q: What is the matn of a hadith?
o: The words at which the chain of narrators ends
The first narrator named at the start of the chain
The list of teachers from whom the narrators heard
The grading given to the report by a later critic
hdt-002.e: The matn is the actual content of the report: the speech or description at which the isnād ends. The isnād is only the route by which that text reached us.

hdt-003.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the marfūʿ
hdt-003.q: A report attributed to the Prophet (peace be upon him), whether a saying, an action or a tacit approval, is called:
hdt-003.e: Marfūʿ means 'raised' to the Prophet. Mawqūf stops at a Companion and maqṭūʿ at a Successor; mursal describes a gap in the chain, not the level of attribution.

hdt-004.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the mawqūf
hdt-004.q: A saying or action attributed to a Companion, without being attributed to the Prophet, is called:
hdt-004.e: Mawqūf means 'stopped': the report stops at the Companion. If it went up to the Prophet it would be marfūʿ; if it stopped at a Successor it would be maqṭūʿ.

hdt-005.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the maqṭūʿ
hdt-005.q: A saying attributed to a Successor (tābiʿī) or someone after him is called:
hdt-005.e: Maqṭūʿ concerns whose words the report contains (a Successor or later). Munqaṭiʿ and muʿḍal, by contrast, describe narrators missing from the chain.

o: A report the Prophet relates from Allah, which is not Quran
A verse of the Quran that the Prophet explained to the Companions
A report that was narrated only in Jerusalem by its scholars
Any hadith that speaks about the virtues of the earlier prophets
hdt-006.e: In a ḥadīth qudsī the Prophet attributes the content to Allah. It is nevertheless not part of the Quran and does not take the Quran's rulings.

hdt-007.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, opening on the division into ṣaḥīḥ, ḥasan and ḍaʿīf
hdt-007.q: Of the three basic grades of hadith, which is the highest?
hdt-007.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ divides hadith into ṣaḥīḥ, ḥasan and ḍaʿīf, with ṣaḥīḥ at the top. Gharīb refers to the number of routes, not to a grade of acceptance.

hdt-008.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the mawḍūʿ
o: A fabricated report falsely ascribed to the Prophet
A report from whose chain exactly one narrator is missing
A report that goes back only to a Companion's own words
A report whose chain includes a slightly weak narrator
hdt-008.e: Mawḍūʿ means invented and falsely ascribed to the Prophet. It is the worst kind of weak report; strictly speaking it is not a hadith at all.

hdt-009.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the definition of the Companion
hdt-009.q: According to the definition preferred by Ibn Ḥajar, who is a Companion (ṣaḥābī)?
o: Someone who met the Prophet as a believer and died as a Muslim
Someone who lived in Medina during the Prophet's lifetime
Someone who accompanied the Prophet for at least a year
Someone who narrated at least one hadith from the Prophet
hdt-009.e: Ibn Ḥajar defines the Companion as one who met the Prophet while believing in him and died in Islam. Long companionship or narrating hadith is not a condition.

hdt-010.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the Successor
o: A Muslim who met a Companion and died as a Muslim
Anyone born after the death of the Prophet
A student of one of the four imams
A Companion who converted after the conquest of Mecca
hdt-010.e: The tābiʿī is defined in relation to the Companions: he met a Companion while Muslim and died in Islam. Being born after the Prophet's death is not enough without such a meeting.

hdt-011.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the mutawātir
o: One narrated at every level by too many to have agreed on a lie
One narrated by exactly two reliable narrators at every level
One narrated by a single trustworthy narrator of excellent memory
One recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim in their two Ṣaḥīḥs
hdt-011.e: Tawātur requires a large number at every stage of the chain such that collusion on falsehood is ruled out by normal experience, ending in sense perception. Being in both Ṣaḥīḥs does not make a report mutawātir.

hdt-012.q: Who wrote Nukhbat al-Fikar, the concise text on hadith terminology?
hdt-012.e: Nukhbat al-Fikar is by Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī, who also wrote its commentary Nuzhat al-Naẓar. Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ wrote the earlier Muqaddima.

hdt-013.q: What kind of work is al-Bayqūniyya?
o: A short teaching poem on the terms of hadith
A commentary on the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī
A biographical dictionary of hadith narrators
A collection of forty hadiths with brief notes
hdt-013.e: Al-Bayqūniyya is a brief poem listing the main types of hadith in verse. Its brevity made it a common first text for students of muṣṭalaḥ.

hdt-014.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the ways of receiving hadith
hdt-014.q: What is samāʿ as a way of receiving hadith?
o: The student hears the teacher narrating the hadith
The student reads the hadith to the teacher
The teacher gives written permission to narrate
The student finds the hadith in a teacher's handwriting
hdt-014.e: In samāʿ the teacher narrates, from memory or from his book, and the student listens. Reading to the teacher is qirāʾa, permission is ijāza and finding a text is wijāda.

hdt-015.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on who is accepted as a narrator
hdt-015.q: In narrator criticism, what does ʿadāla refer to?
o: The number of a narrator's teachers
hdt-015.e: ʿAdāla concerns the narrator's character: being a sane, adult Muslim, free of open sin and of what damages decency. Precision of memory is the separate condition of ḍabṭ.

hdt-016.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar, on ḍabṭ
hdt-016.q: Ibn Ḥajar divides ḍabṭ (precision) into two kinds. What are they?
o: Precision of memory and precision of the written book
Precision of grammar and precision of meaning
Precision in the chain and precision in the text
Precision in youth and precision in old age
hdt-016.e: Ḍabṭ al-ṣadr means the narrator retains what he heard so he can recall it at will; ḍabṭ al-kitāb means he keeps his written copy sound from the time he heard until he narrates from it.

hdt-017.q: What is the subject of the science of muṣṭalaḥ al-ḥadīth?
o: Rules for judging whether a chain and text are accepted
The explanation of rare and difficult words in hadith
The history of the early Islamic conquests and battles
The rulings of worship that are derived from hadith
hdt-017.e: Muṣṭalaḥ al-ḥadīth studies the chain and text in order to judge acceptance or rejection. Explaining words or deriving rulings belong to other disciplines (gharīb al-ḥadīth, fiqh al-ḥadīth).

hdt-018.src: al-Nawawī, al-Taqrīb wa-l-Taysīr, the type on the mawqūf
hdt-018.q: Al-Nawawī notes that the jurists of Khurasan used the word athar for a particular kind of report. Which one?
hdt-018.e: According to al-Nawawī, the Khurasan jurists called the mawqūf athar and the marfūʿ khabar, while the hadith scholars applied athar to both.

hdt-019.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the mashhūr
hdt-019.q: Which report is called mashhūr in Ibn Ḥajar's classification?
o: More than two narrators at every level, short of tawātur
Exactly two narrators at every level of the whole chain
A single narrator at one level, more at the other levels
So many narrators at every level that lying is impossible
hdt-019.e: Ibn Ḥajar defines the mashhūr as an āḥād report with more than two routes, without reaching the conditions of tawātur. Exactly two is ʿazīz, one is gharīb.

hdt-020.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the ʿazīz
hdt-020.q: According to Ibn Ḥajar, a report whose narrators are never fewer than two at any level of the chain is called:
hdt-020.e: Ibn Ḥajar defines the ʿazīz as a report whose narrators do not fall below two at any stage. If one level has only one narrator it is gharīb.

hdt-021.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the gharīb
hdt-021.q: Which statement about a gharīb hadith is correct?
o: It has one narrator at some level and may still be ṣaḥīḥ
It is always weak because it comes through only one route
It is always fabricated because no other narrator knows it
It must contain a rare or unusual word somewhere in its text
hdt-021.e: Gharīb describes the number of routes, not the grade. A gharīb report with a sound chain can be ṣaḥīḥ; the hadith on intentions is a well-known example of a ṣaḥīḥ gharīb report.

hdt-022.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the ṣaḥīḥ
hdt-022.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the five conditions of a ṣaḥīḥ hadith?
o: Being narrated by at least two Companions
Narrators who are upright and precise
Freedom from shudhūdh and hidden defects
hdt-022.e: The five conditions are a connected chain, upright narrators, precise narrators, absence of shudhūdh and absence of ʿilla. A single Companion's narration can be fully ṣaḥīḥ.

hdt-023.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar, on ṣaḥīḥ li-ghayrihi
o: A ḥasan li-dhātihi report raised to ṣaḥīḥ by other routes
A ṣaḥīḥ report narrated from a Successor
A weak report accepted because a scholar acted on it
A ṣaḥīḥ report whose text was later shortened
hdt-023.e: When a report that is ḥasan in itself is supported by further routes of equal or greater strength, the combined support raises it to ṣaḥīḥ, but 'because of something else', not by its own chain.

hdt-024.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the ḥasan li-dhātihi
hdt-024.q: In Ibn Ḥajar's definition, what distinguishes ḥasan li-dhātihi from ṣaḥīḥ li-dhātihi?
o: One of its narrators has somewhat lighter precision
Its chain has one narrator missing
It stops at a Companion instead of the Prophet
It is supported only by a weak route
hdt-024.e: Ibn Ḥajar keeps all conditions of the ṣaḥīḥ for the ḥasan li-dhātihi except that the precision of a narrator is lighter. A missing narrator would make it munqaṭiʿ and weak.

hdt-025.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the ḥasan
o: A mildly weak report strengthened by similar routes
A ṣaḥīḥ report whose text is slightly shorter than usual
A fabricated report that later became famous among people
A report that only a single Successor narrated from a Companion
hdt-025.e: A report whose weakness is not severe (for example a narrator of weak memory, not a liar) can rise to ḥasan li-ghayrihi when it comes through other routes. Severe weakness, such as fabrication, is not repaired by more routes.

hdt-026.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the mursal
hdt-026.q: In the well-known definition, what is a mursal hadith?
o: A Successor attributes a report directly to the Prophet
A Companion attributes a report to another Companion
A compiler drops his own teacher from the chain
A narrator inserts his own words into the text
hdt-026.e: The mursal is a report in which a tābiʿī says 'the Prophet said' without naming the Companion he heard it from. Dropping from the compiler's end is muʿallaq; inserting words is idrāj.

hdt-027.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the muʿallaq
hdt-027.q: A report from whose chain one or more narrators are dropped at the compiler's end is called:
hdt-027.e: Muʿallaq ('suspended') means the omission is at the beginning of the chain, on the side of the author, sometimes up to the whole chain. Al-Bukhārī's ṣaḥīḥ contains such suspended reports in its chapter headings.

hdt-028.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the muʿḍal
o: One with two or more consecutive narrators missing
One with a single narrator missing at the end
One with two narrators missing at separate places
One with a narrator whose identity is unknown
hdt-028.e: Muʿḍal requires two or more narrators dropped in succession. Two dropped at different places, not in succession, is classed as munqaṭiʿ (in more than one place).

hdt-029.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the munqaṭiʿ
hdt-029.q: In Ibn Ḥajar's classification, a chain from which a narrator has dropped in the middle, not in a consecutive pair, is called:
hdt-029.e: Ibn Ḥajar sorts gaps by position: at the compiler's end it is muʿallaq, after the Successor mursal, two in succession muʿḍal, and otherwise munqaṭiʿ.

hdt-030.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the maqṭūʿ
hdt-030.q: What is the difference between maqṭūʿ and munqaṭiʿ?
o: Maqṭūʿ concerns the speaker; munqaṭiʿ a gap in the chain
Both mean a gap in the chain, but in maqṭūʿ the gap is longer
Maqṭūʿ is always accepted, while munqaṭiʿ is always fabricated
Both mean a Successor's saying, but from different regions
hdt-030.e: Maqṭūʿ describes the text: words of a Successor or later. Munqaṭiʿ describes the chain: a narrator is missing. A maqṭūʿ report can have a fully connected chain.

hdt-031.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the shādhdh and the maḥfūẓ
hdt-031.q: According to Ibn Ḥajar, what is a shādhdh report?
o: An acceptable narrator contradicting one more reliable than him
A weak narrator contradicting reliable narrators
A reliable narrator adding a word no one contradicts
A narrator reporting something no one else has narrated
hdt-031.e: Ibn Ḥajar defines shādhdh as the report of an acceptable narrator that opposes someone weightier. When the contradicting narrator is weak, the result is munkar. A mere solitary narration is not shudhūdh by itself.

hdt-032.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the munkar and the maʿrūf
hdt-032.q: In Ibn Ḥajar's terminology, the report of a weak narrator that contradicts reliable narrators is called:
hdt-032.e: Ibn Ḥajar reserves munkar for a weak narrator's contradiction of the reliable; its opposite is called maʿrūf. When an acceptable narrator contradicts a weightier one, it is shādhdh.

hdt-033.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the muʿallal
o: One with a hidden defect, though outwardly it looks sound
One whose narrator is openly known as a liar by everyone
One with an obvious gap at the very start of its chain
One whose text contains a rare word needing explanation
hdt-033.e: The ʿilla is a concealed cause that damages soundness while the chain appears free of it; only expert critics detect it by gathering routes. An openly lying narrator is an apparent, not a hidden, defect.

hdt-034.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on tadlīs
o: Narrating, in vague wording, what he did not hear from a teacher he met
Calling one's teacher by an unfamiliar name in order to hide him
Narrating a report by its meaning instead of its exact wording
Narrating from someone's book without that author's permission
hdt-034.e: In tadlīs al-isnād the narrator uses a phrase such as 'from' or 'he said' that suggests hearing, while he actually got it through someone else. Concealing the teacher with an obscure name is tadlīs al-shuyūkh.

hdt-035.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the ways of receiving hadith, the ijāza
hdt-035.q: As a way of receiving hadith, what is ijāza?
o: The teacher's permission to narrate his reports without hearing them
The student reciting the teacher's reports back to him in a session
The teacher handing a copy of his book to the student in person
The student finding the reports written in his teacher's handwriting
hdt-035.e: Ijāza is permission, spoken or written, to narrate the teacher's material. Reciting to the teacher is qirāʾa, handing over the book is munāwala, and finding a handwritten text is wijāda.

hdt-036.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the ways of receiving hadith, qirāʾa
hdt-036.q: Reading hadith to the teacher while he listens and confirms is also called:
hdt-036.e: Qirāʾa ʿalā al-shaykh is also called ʿarḍ ('presentation'), because the student presents the material to the teacher. Wijāda, iʿlām and waṣiyya are weaker, separate methods.

hdt-037.q: Besides 'the Muqaddima', by what title is Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ's work on hadith terminology known?
hdt-037.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ's work is known as ʿUlūm al-Ḥadīth (also Maʿrifat Anwāʿ ʿIlm al-Ḥadīth). Nuzhat al-Naẓar is by Ibn Ḥajar, al-Kifāya by al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī and Tadrīb al-Rāwī by al-Suyūṭī.

hdt-038.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the mawḍūʿ
hdt-038.q: What is the ruling on narrating a hadith known to be fabricated?
o: Forbidden, except when stating that it is fabricated
Allowed in sermons if the meaning is good
Allowed for virtuous deeds but not for rulings
Allowed if the narrator gives the full chain
hdt-038.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ states that narrating a fabricated report knowingly is not permitted in any subject unless its fabrication is made clear. Unlike some weak reports, it has no place even in virtues and exhortation.

hdt-039.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, on the difference between the Quran and the ḥadīth qudsī
hdt-039.q: Which feature belongs to the Quran but not to the ḥadīth qudsī?
o: Its recitation is worship and valid in the prayer
It is attributed to Allah as its ultimate source
It was conveyed to the people by the Prophet
It contains guidance, promises and exhortation
hdt-039.e: Both are attributed to Allah and conveyed by the Prophet, and both contain guidance. Only the Quran is recited in the prayer as worship and is inimitable in its wording.

hdt-040.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar, on the mutawātir
hdt-040.q: Why does Ibn Ḥajar say the mutawātir is not studied in the science of isnād?
o: It yields certainty without examining its narrators
It is always narrated without any chain of narrators
All of its narrators at every level are Companions
It is limited to reports concerning the Quran's text
hdt-040.e: Because tawātur produces necessary knowledge, there is no need to check the narrators' reliability; the isnād sciences examine reports to decide acceptance, which is the domain of the āḥād.

hdt-041.src: Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Jarḥ wa-l-Taʿdīl, introduction
hdt-041.q: What is the purpose of al-jarḥ wa-l-taʿdīl?
o: Judging narrators as reliable or not, to assess their reports
Explaining the legal rulings contained in individual hadiths
Arranging hadiths according to the chapters of fiqh books
Reconciling hadiths that appear to contradict one another
hdt-041.e: Jarḥ (impugning) and taʿdīl (vouching for) are the critics' judgements on narrators; on them depends whether a chain is accepted. Reconciling apparent contradictions belongs to mukhtalif al-ḥadīth.

hdt-042.src: al-Suyūṭī, Tadrīb al-Rāwī, the type on the mashhūr and mutawātir
hdt-042.q: What is the difference between mutawātir lafẓī and mutawātir maʿnawī?
o: Lafẓī: the wording is mass-transmitted; maʿnawī: only a shared meaning
Lafẓī: the chain is connected; maʿnawī: the chain has gaps in it
Lafẓī: it is from the Prophet; maʿnawī: it is from the Companions
Lafẓī: it yields certainty; maʿnawī: it yields only probability
hdt-042.e: Lafẓī tawātur means the same wording reaches us through mass transmission. Maʿnawī tawātur means many different reports, each perhaps āḥād, share one common meaning, such as the Prophet raising his hands in supplication. Both yield certainty.

hdt-043.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on al-iʿtibār, al-mutābiʿ and al-shāhid
hdt-043.q: In Ibn Ḥajar's usage, how does a shāhid differ from a mutābiʿ?
o: A shāhid is via another Companion; a mutābiʿ via the same one
A shāhid supports the chain; a mutābiʿ supports only the text
A shāhid must be ṣaḥīḥ; a mutābiʿ may even be fabricated
A shāhid is always mawqūf; a mutābiʿ is always marfūʿ
hdt-043.e: Ibn Ḥajar calls a supporting route through the same Companion a mutābiʿ and one through another Companion a shāhid, while noting that the terms are sometimes used interchangeably. The search for both is called iʿtibār.

hdt-044.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the shādhdh and the munkar
hdt-044.q: What is the term for the preferred report that stands against a munkar one?
hdt-044.e: In Ibn Ḥajar's pairs, the preferred report against a shādhdh is maḥfūẓ, and the preferred report against a munkar is maʿrūf. Muḥkam refers to a report free of any opposing report.

hdt-045.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the mudallas and the mursal khafī
hdt-045.q: According to Ibn Ḥajar, what separates tadlīs from mursal khafī?
o: Tadlīs: from one he met; mursal khafī: from a contemporary never met
Tadlīs drops a Companion; mursal khafī drops a Successor from the chain
Tadlīs occurs in the text; mursal khafī occurs only in the chain
Tadlīs is deliberate lying; mursal khafī is an innocent slip of memory
hdt-045.e: Both use an ambiguous phrase suggesting hearing. Ibn Ḥajar distinguishes them by the relationship: if the narrator is known to have met the teacher it is tadlīs; if he was only his contemporary without meeting it is mursal khafī.

hdt-046.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on tadlīs
hdt-046.q: A narrator refers to his teacher by an unfamiliar name, kunya or attribution so that the teacher is not recognised. This is called:
hdt-046.e: In tadlīs al-shuyūkh nothing is dropped from the chain; the teacher is disguised by an unusual description. Its harm is that it makes the teacher hard to identify and evaluate.

hdt-047.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on jahāla
hdt-047.q: In Ibn Ḥajar's terms, what is majhūl al-ʿayn?
o: A named narrator with only one person narrating from him, unvouched
A narrator from whom two narrate but whose reliability is unestablished
A narrator who is not mentioned by name anywhere in the chain
A narrator whose name is known but whose date of death is unknown
hdt-047.e: Majhūl al-ʿayn has a single narrator from him and no vouching. If two or more narrate from him without vouching, he is majhūl al-ḥāl (mastūr). An unnamed narrator is called mubham.

hdt-048.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on who is accepted as a narrator
hdt-048.q: What position does Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ state as correct regarding the reasons for jarḥ and taʿdīl?
o: Taʿdīl is accepted without a reason; jarḥ only with its cause
Both are accepted only when their causes are clearly explained
Jarḥ is accepted without a reason; taʿdīl only with its cause
Neither needs a stated reason if the critic is a known imam
hdt-048.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ reasons that the causes of uprightness are many and hard to list, while people differ over what counts as a defect; so jarḥ needs explanation (mufassar), but taʿdīl does not.

hdt-049.src: Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Jarḥ wa-l-Taʿdīl, introduction on the levels of narrators
hdt-049.q: Which expression of taʿdīl indicates the highest level of reliability among these?
hdt-049.e: Repeating or combining words of firm reliability, as in 'thiqa thabt', ranks above a single term. Ṣadūq and lā baʾsa bihi indicate a lower level, and shaykh lower still.

hdt-050.src: al-Sakhāwī, Fatḥ al-Mughīth, on the levels of jarḥ
hdt-050.q: Which of these expressions represents the most severe level of jarḥ?
hdt-050.e: Describing a narrator as a liar (kadhdhāb) or fabricator is the gravest jarḥ, and his reports are not used even as support. Layyin and fīhi maqāl are among the lightest expressions of weakness.

hdt-051.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the ways of receiving hadith
hdt-051.q: Which of the following is NOT among the eight ways of receiving hadith listed by Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ?
hdt-051.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ lists samāʿ, qirāʾa, ijāza, munāwala, kitāba, iʿlām, waṣiyya and wijāda. Istifāḍa (widespread report) is a term from the law of testimony, not a way of receiving hadith.

hdt-052.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the ways of receiving hadith, wijāda
o: Finding reports in someone's handwriting, without hearing or permission
Hearing reports from a teacher together with many others in a large gathering
Receiving a teacher's books because he bequeathed them in his will
Receiving a letter from a teacher containing reports written for him
hdt-052.e: Wijāda is coming across a text in the known handwriting of a narrator without having heard it from him or received permission. One may say 'I found in the handwriting of so-and-so', but not 'he narrated to me'.

hdt-053.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the ways of receiving hadith, munāwala
hdt-053.q: Which form of munāwala does Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ treat as the highest?
o: Handing over the book together with permission to narrate it
Handing over the book to the student without any permission
Giving permission to narrate without handing over anything
Sending the book in writing to a student in another city
hdt-053.e: The highest munāwala is when the teacher gives the student his original or a checked copy and says it is his narration and he permits him to narrate it. Munāwala without permission is weak according to the sound view.

hdt-054.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the muḍṭarib
hdt-054.q: When is a hadith called muḍṭarib?
o: When its versions conflict, are equally strong, and none can be preferred
When a weak narrator in it contradicts one or more reliable narrators
When one of its versions is clearly stronger than all the other versions
When a narrator adds his own explanation into the text of the report
hdt-054.e: Iḍṭirāb requires conflicting versions of comparable strength with no way to reconcile or prefer. If one version is stronger, it is preferred and the hadith is not called muḍṭarib.

hdt-055.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the mudraj
hdt-055.q: A narrator's own words are joined to the Prophet's words without a separating marker. This is called:
hdt-055.e: Idrāj in the text means words of a narrator are inserted so that they appear to be part of the hadith, often as an explanation. Maqlūb is an inversion of words or names; muṣaḥḥaf is a change of dots or letters.

hdt-056.src: Ibn Ḥajar, al-Iṣāba fī Tamyīz al-Ṣaḥāba, introduction
hdt-056.q: Someone met the Prophet as a believer, then apostatised, then returned to Islam and died a Muslim. According to the view Ibn Ḥajar calls soundest, is he a Companion?
o: Yes, he is counted a Companion
Only if he met the Prophet again after returning
Only if he narrated hadith before apostatising
hdt-056.e: Ibn Ḥajar's definition adds that the person counts as a Companion 'even if apostasy intervened, according to the soundest view', provided he died in Islam. Some scholars made renewed meeting a condition, which is why the issue is discussed.

hdt-057.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the mursal
hdt-057.q: How does the majority treat the mursal of a Companion, such as a young Companion reporting an event he did not witness?
o: As connected proof, since the omitted narrator is presumed a Companion
As weak in the same way as any other mursal from a Successor
As fabricated unless some Successor independently confirms it
As mawqūf on that Companion and not attributed to the Prophet
hdt-057.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ notes that the mursal of a Companion is treated as connected, because Companions mostly narrate from other Companions, and all Companions are upright. So the gap does not harm the report.

hdt-058.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the age and condition for receiving hadith
hdt-058.q: Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim heard the Prophet recite Sūrat al-Ṭūr in the Maghrib prayer before he became Muslim, and narrated it afterwards. What principle does this illustrate?
o: Receiving as a non-Muslim is valid if one narrates after Islam
A non-Muslim's narration is accepted without any conditions at all
Only what is heard after accepting Islam may ever be narrated
A narrator must be an adult both when hearing and when narrating
hdt-058.e: Scholars distinguish taḥammul (receiving) from adāʾ (conveying). Islam and maturity are conditions for conveying, not for receiving, so what Jubayr heard as a non-Muslim was accepted when he narrated it as a Muslim.

hdt-059.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the mursal; al-Shāfiʿī, al-Risāla, on the mursal
hdt-059.q: Which statement correctly describes the classical positions on using the mursal as proof?
o: Most critics: weak; Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfa: accepted; al-Shāfiʿī: accepted if supported
Most critics: accepted; Mālik: rejected; al-Shāfiʿī: accepted without any conditions
All four imams: rejected; only later Ḥanafīs accepted it with conditions
Al-Shāfiʿī: every mursal accepted; Mālik and Abū Ḥanīfa: rejected entirely
hdt-059.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ reports that the hadith critics settled on its weakness, while acceptance is the position of Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa and their followers. Al-Shāfiʿī in al-Risāla accepts the mursal of senior Successors when supported, for example by a connected route or another mursal.

hdt-060.src: Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Muqaddima; Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar, on the muʿanʿan
hdt-060.q: Concerning a chain using 'ʿan' between two non-mudallis narrators, which statement describes the well-known difference?
o: Muslim: contemporaneity with possible meeting suffices; al-Bukhārī (reportedly): one proven meeting
Al-Bukhārī: contemporaneity alone suffices; Muslim: repeated meetings must be proven
Both: the narrator must state explicit hearing in every report, or it is broken
Both: every ʿan-chain is rejected unless that report is also mass-transmitted
hdt-060.e: In the introduction to his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim argued that contemporaneity with the possibility of meeting suffices for a non-mudallis. The stricter requirement of proven meeting is attributed to al-Bukhārī and his teacher ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī.

hdt-061.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the shādhdh
hdt-061.q: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ quotes al-Shāfiʿī's definition of the shādhdh. What is its key point?
o: A reliable narrator contradicting what others narrate
Any report that only one reliable narrator transmits
A weak narrator's report that nobody else transmits
A report whose text contains strange vocabulary
hdt-061.e: Al-Shāfiʿī said the shādhdh is not that a reliable narrator reports what others do not, but that he reports something contrary to what people narrate. This makes contradiction, not solitariness, the decisive element.

hdt-062.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the ṣaḥīḥ; al-Nawawī, al-Taqrīb wa-l-Taysīr, the type on the ṣaḥīḥ
hdt-062.q: Which statement correctly describes the discussion about authenticating hadith in later centuries?
o: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ discouraged independent later grading; al-Nawawī allowed it to the qualified
Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ allowed anyone to grade hadith; al-Nawawī forbade it to all later scholars
Both held that no grading made after the time of al-Bukhārī can be valid at all
Al-Nawawī forbade all later grading; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ required it of every single jurist
hdt-062.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ was cautious about independent taṣḥīḥ in his time and directed students to gradings of earlier imams. Al-Nawawī answered that it is permissible for one who is capable and has strong knowledge, and later scholars generally followed him.

hdt-063.src: al-Suyūṭī, Tadrīb al-Rāwī, the type on tadlīs
hdt-063.q: What is tadlīs al-taswiya, often considered the worst kind of tadlīs?
o: Dropping a weak narrator between two reliable ones
Calling one's own teacher by an obscure, unused kunya
Narrating from a contemporary one never actually met
Shortening a long text without indicating the omission
hdt-063.e: In taswiya the mudallis removes a weak narrator not from his own position but further up, between two reliable narrators who had met, so the whole chain appears reliable. It deceives the critic about a narrator he cannot see.

hdt-064.q: Which work does Ibn Ḥajar name at the head of the earliest writings on hadith terminology?
o: al-Kifāya fī ʿIlm al-Riwāya by al-Khaṭīb
hdt-064.e: In the preface to Nuzhat al-Naẓar, Ibn Ḥajar names among the first to write on the subject al-Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad al-Rāmahurmuzī in al-Muḥaddith al-Fāṣil, though it was not comprehensive. Al-Ḥākim and al-Khaṭīb came after him.

hdt-065.q: Al-Suyūṭī's Tadrīb al-Rāwī is a commentary on which work?
o: Ibn Ḥajar's Nukhbat al-Fikar on hadith terms
Al-ʿIrāqī's verse rendering of Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ
Al-Bayqūnī's short poem on the hadith terms
hdt-065.e: Al-Nawawī abridged Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ's Muqaddima in al-Irshād and then further in al-Taqrīb wa-l-Taysīr; al-Suyūṭī wrote Tadrīb al-Rāwī as its commentary. Ibn Ḥajar himself commented on the Nukhba in Nuzhat al-Naẓar.

hdt-066.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the ḥasan; al-Khaṭṭābī, Maʿālim al-Sunan, introduction
hdt-066.q: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ quotes a definition of ḥasan as a report 'whose source is known and whose narrators are well known'. Whose definition is this?
hdt-066.e: This definition is al-Khaṭṭābī's, from the introduction of Maʿālim al-Sunan. Al-Tirmidhī's description is different: no narrator accused of lying, not shādhdh, and narrated through more than one route.

hdt-067.q: Which set of conditions does al-Tirmidhī give for what he calls ḥasan in his Jāmiʿ?
o: No narrator accused of lying, not shādhdh, more than one route
A connected chain, fully precise narrators, and no hidden defect
Narrated by two Companions, with no mudallis anywhere in the chain
Accepted in practice by the jurists and not contradicting the Quran
hdt-067.e: In al-ʿIlal al-Ṣaghīr at the end of his Jāmiʿ, al-Tirmidhī explains that by ḥasan he means a report without a narrator accused of lying, which is not shādhdh and is narrated through another route as well. This is closer to what later scholars call ḥasan li-ghayrihi.

hdt-068.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the Companions
hdt-068.q: Who is commonly named as the last Companion to die, without exception of region?
o: ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb
hdt-068.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ and others state that Abū al-Ṭufayl was the last Companion to die anywhere. Anas ibn Mālik is named as the last in Basra and Sahl ibn Saʿd among the last in Medina.

hdt-069.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on the ḥasan, remarks on 'ṣaḥīḥ al-isnād'
hdt-069.q: Why does Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ consider the verdict 'ṣaḥīḥ al-isnād' weaker than the verdict 'ṣaḥīḥ'?
o: The chain may be sound while the text is shādhdh or defective
It means that the chain has at least one unknown narrator in it
It is used only for those reports that stop at a Companion
It means the report is mutawātir but its wording is weak
hdt-069.e: 'Ṣaḥīḥ al-isnād' affirms only the conditions of the chain: connection, uprightness and precision. Freedom from shudhūdh and ʿilla in the text is not thereby guaranteed, unless a reliable imam uses the phrase without noting any defect.

hdt-070.src: Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Muqaddima, on the isnād being part of the religion
hdt-070.q: The statement that the isnād is part of the religion, recorded in the introduction of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, is attributed to whom?
hdt-070.e: Muslim records from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak that the isnād is part of the religion, and that without it anyone could say whatever he wished. In the same introduction Muslim records from Ibn Sīrīn that this knowledge is religion, so one should look to whom one takes it from.

hdt-071.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar, on the addition of a reliable narrator
hdt-071.q: According to Ibn Ḥajar's Nukhbat al-Fikar, when is an addition (ziyāda) by a narrator of ṣaḥīḥ or ḥasan reports accepted?
o: As long as it does not conflict with a more reliable report
Only if every other narrator of the report also mentions it
Only if it occurs in the text and not anywhere in the chain
Always, regardless of what the other narrators reported
hdt-071.e: Ibn Ḥajar states that the addition of such a narrator is accepted unless it is incompatible with the report of someone more reliable; if it is, the preferred report is maḥfūẓ and the other shādhdh. He adds that accepting every addition without distinction does not fit the hadith scholars, who require that the ṣaḥīḥ not be shādhdh.

hdt-072.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, the type on reliable narrators who became confused (al-mukhtaliṭūn)
hdt-072.q: A reliable narrator suffers ikhtilāṭ (deterioration of memory) late in life. How are his reports treated?
o: Reports heard before the decline are accepted; later or unclear ones are not
All of his reports are rejected, including those he narrated earlier
All of his reports are accepted, since he was once a reliable narrator
Only the reports heard from him by his own sons are accepted
hdt-072.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ explains that what was taken from a mukhtaliṭ before his confusion is accepted, while what was taken afterwards, or where the timing is unclear, is not. Critics therefore record which students heard from him early.

hs-001.src: Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, on the caliphate of Abū Bakr
hs-001.q: Who became the first caliph after the death of the Prophet?
hs-001.e: Abū Bakr was chosen at the gathering of Banū Sāʿida and the pledge was then given to him publicly in the mosque. He ruled for about two years until his death.

hs-002.src: Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, on the caliphate of ʿUmar
hs-002.q: Who was the second caliph, nominated by Abū Bakr before his death?
hs-002.e: Abū Bakr consulted the leading Companions and nominated ʿUmar, whose caliphate saw the great conquests and the organisation of the state.

hs-003.src: Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, on the caliphate of ʿUthmān
hs-003.q: Who was the third of the rightly-guided caliphs, known as Dhū al-Nūrayn?
hs-003.e: ʿUthmān was given the title Dhū al-Nūrayn (the possessor of two lights) because he married two daughters of the Prophet, one after the other.

hs-004.src: Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, on the caliphate of ʿAlī
hs-004.q: Who was the fourth of the rightly-guided caliphs?
hs-004.e: ʿAlī, the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law, became caliph after the killing of ʿUthmān and moved his capital to Kūfa.

hs-005.src: Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, introduction to the caliphate
hs-005.q: What is the Arabic title given to the first four caliphs?
hs-005.e: The first four caliphs are called al-Khulafāʾ al-Rāshidūn, based on a hadith about the sunna of the rightly-guided caliphs after the Prophet. The other terms describe different groups of Companions.

hs-006.src: Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, on the beginning of the Hijri calendar
hs-006.q: From which event does the Hijri calendar count its years?
o: The Hijra of the Prophet from Makka to Madīna
The first revelation in the cave of Ḥirāʾ
hs-006.e: The Companions under ʿUmar chose the Hijra as the starting point because it marked the founding of the Muslim community in Madīna. The year count begins with the first of Muḥarram of that year.

hs-007.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, on the beginning of the Hijri dating
hs-007.q: Under which caliph was the Hijri calendar introduced as the official system of dating?
hs-007.e: The sources say ʿUmar introduced the dating after a letter without a clear year caused confusion; the Companions agreed on the Hijra as the starting point. The exact year of introduction is variously reported.

hs-008.src: Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, on the Umayyad caliphs
hs-008.q: Which city was the capital of the Umayyad caliphate?
hs-008.e: Muʿāwiya made Damascus the centre of power, and it stayed the Umayyad capital. Baghdad was founded later by the Abbasids; Cairo was founded by the Fatimids.

hs-009.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, on the founding of Baghdad
hs-009.q: Which Abbasid caliph founded the city of Baghdad as his capital?
hs-009.e: Al-Manṣūr founded Baghdad in the year commonly dated 145 AH (762 CE) as the round city of Madīnat al-Salām. Hārūn al-Rashīd and al-Maʾmūn made it a centre of learning later.

hs-010.src: Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, on the year of the community (ʿām al-jamāʿa)
hs-010.q: Who founded the Umayyad dynasty after the year of unity?
hs-010.e: Muʿāwiya, governor of Syria, became sole ruler in 41 AH when al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī handed over the caliphate to unite the community. His descendants and the line of Marwān ruled until 132 AH.

hs-011.src: al-Maqqarī, Nafḥ al-Ṭīb, on the conquest of al-Andalus
hs-011.q: Which commander led the Muslim army across the strait into Spain in 92 AH (711 CE)?
hs-011.e: Ṭāriq ibn Ziyād crossed with his army and defeated the Visigothic king Roderic; the mountain where he landed is named after him, Jabal Ṭāriq. His superior Mūsā ibn Nuṣayr followed.

hs-012.q: Which city became the capital of the Umayyad state in al-Andalus and a centre of learning?
hs-012.e: Cordoba was the capital of the Umayyads of al-Andalus from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I onwards and had a great library and a famous mosque. Granada became the last Muslim capital in Spain.

hs-013.src: Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, events of 583 AH
hs-013.q: Which Muslim ruler recaptured Jerusalem from the Crusaders in 583 AH (1187 CE)?
hs-013.e: After the victory at Ḥaṭṭīn, Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn entered Jerusalem. Nūr al-Dīn had prepared the ground earlier, while Baybars and Qutuz lived in the following century.

hs-014.src: Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, events of 583 AH
hs-014.q: Which battle in 583 AH opened the way to the recapture of Jerusalem by Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn?
hs-014.e: At Ḥaṭṭīn near Tiberias the Crusader army was destroyed, which left the kingdom of Jerusalem undefended. ʿAyn Jālūt was against the Mongols, Yarmūk against Byzantium and Malāzgird against Byzantium again.

hs-015.src: Ibn Iyās, Badāʾiʿ al-Zuhūr; Ottoman chronicles on the conquest of Constantinople
hs-015.q: Which Ottoman sultan conquered Constantinople in 857 AH (1453 CE)?
o: Muḥammad II, known as al-Fātiḥ (the Conqueror)
hs-015.e: Mehmed II, aged about twenty-one, took the Byzantine capital after a siege of about fifty days. The city became Istanbul and the Ottoman capital.

hs-016.src: al-Masʿūdī, Murūj al-Dhahab, on the end of the Umayyads
hs-016.q: Which dynasty replaced the Umayyads as the ruling caliphal house in the East in 132 AH (750 CE)?
hs-016.e: The Abbasids, descendants of the Prophet's uncle al-ʿAbbās, overthrew the Umayyads at the Battle of the Zab and ruled from Iraq. The Fatimids, Ayyubids and Seljuks came later.

hs-017.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, on the wars of apostasy
hs-017.q: What is the name of the wars that Abū Bakr fought against tribes that refused to pay zakāt or abandoned Islam?
hs-017.e: After the Prophet's death several tribes rebelled or refused zakāt, and false prophets appeared. Abū Bakr sent armies against them and re-established unity within about a year.

hs-018.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, on the death of ʿUmar
hs-018.q: Which caliph was stabbed while leading the dawn prayer by Abū Luʾluʾa, a Persian slave?
hs-018.e: ʿUmar was attacked in the mosque at dawn in 23 AH and died of his wounds a few days later. Before dying he appointed a council of six to choose the next caliph.

hs-019.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, on the year 35 AH
hs-019.q: Which caliph was besieged in his house in Madīna and killed by rebels in 35 AH?
hs-019.e: Rebels from several provinces besieged ʿUthmān for weeks and killed him while he was reading the Quran. His death began the first great civil strife (fitna) of the community.

hs-020.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, on the conquest of Bayt al-Maqdis
hs-020.q: Which caliph travelled to receive the surrender of Jerusalem in person?
hs-020.e: The Christian leader of the city asked for a treaty to be concluded with the caliph himself, so ʿUmar came to Jerusalem and agreed terms that guaranteed the safety of the people and their churches.

hs-021.src: al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, biography of Abū Ḥanīfa
hs-021.q: Which scholar is the founder of the Ḥanafī school of law?
hs-021.e: Abū Ḥanīfa (80–150 AH, commonly given), who lived in Kūfa and Baghdad, is the eponym of the Ḥanafī school, which grew through his students Abū Yūsuf and Muḥammad al-Shaybānī.

hs-022.src: al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, biography of Mālik
hs-022.q: Which scholar of Madīna is the founder of the Mālikī school and author of al-Muwaṭṭaʾ?
hs-022.e: Mālik ibn Anas (93–179 AH, commonly given) spent his life in Madīna. His al-Muwaṭṭaʾ is one of the earliest surviving collections of hadith and legal rulings.

hs-023.src: al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, biography of al-Shāfiʿī
hs-023.q: Which scholar, born in Gaza, is the founder of the Shāfiʿī school and author of al-Risāla?
hs-023.e: Al-Shāfiʿī (150–204 AH, commonly given) studied in Makka, Madīna and Iraq and settled in Egypt. His al-Risāla is regarded as the first systematic work on the principles of jurisprudence.

hs-024.src: al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, biography of Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal
hs-024.q: Which scholar of Baghdad, tested during the miḥna, is the namesake of the Ḥanbalī school and author of the Musnad?
hs-024.e: Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal (164–241 AH, commonly given) refused to say that the Quran is created under the caliphs' inquisition, was flogged, and became a symbol of steadfastness.

hs-025.src: Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, events of 656 AH
hs-025.q: Which event in 656 AH (1258 CE) ended the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad?
o: The Mongol sack of Baghdad under Hülegü
hs-025.e: The Mongol army under Hülegü besieged and sacked the city, killed the caliph al-Mustaʿṣim and destroyed much of its libraries and population. An Abbasid line later continued in Cairo under the Mamluks.

hs-026.src: Standard modern histories of Turkey and the late Ottoman Empire (e.g. Lewis, The Emergence of Modern Turkey)
hs-026.q: In which year was the caliphate formally abolished by the Turkish Grand National Assembly?
hs-026.e: The Grand National Assembly in Ankara abolished the caliphate on 3 March 1924 after the sultanate had been abolished in 1922. The other years mark the conquest of Constantinople, the Ottoman conquest of Egypt and the fall of Baghdad.

hs-027.src: al-Maqrīzī, al-Mawāʿiẓ wa-l-Iʿtibār (al-Khiṭaṭ), on the founding of Cairo
hs-027.q: Which dynasty founded the city of Cairo and the mosque of al-Azhar?
hs-027.e: The Fatimid general Jawhar al-Ṣiqillī founded al-Qāhira in 358 AH (969 CE) for the caliph al-Muʿizz; al-Azhar was established in the same period. Its later role as a centre of Sunni learning developed under later dynasties.

hs-028.src: Ibn Khaldūn, Kitāb al-ʿIbar, on the kings of Mali; al-ʿUmarī, Masālik al-Abṣār
hs-028.q: Which ruler of the Mali empire made a famous pilgrimage to Makka in 724 AH (1324 CE) and spread gold along the way?
hs-028.e: Mansa Mūsā travelled across the Sahara to Makka with a huge retinue; his generosity was so great that, according to the reports, the value of gold dropped in Cairo. He later brought scholars and builders back to Mali.

hs-029.q: Which scholar wrote the Muqaddima, an introduction to the study of history and society?
hs-029.e: Ibn Khaldūn (732–808 AH, commonly given) wrote the Muqaddima as the introduction to his universal history, Kitāb al-ʿIbar, discussing the rise and fall of states and the nature of society.

hs-030.src: Ibn al-Nadīm, al-Fihrist; standard histories of Islamic science
hs-030.q: Which scholar of the Abbasid period wrote a famous book on al-jabr and gave algebra its name?
hs-030.e: Al-Khwārizmī wrote al-Kitāb al-Mukhtaṣar fī Ḥisāb al-Jabr wa-l-Muqābala at the court of al-Maʾmūn. The word algebra comes from al-jabr, and ‘algorithm’ from his name.

hs-031.src: Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra al-Nabawiyya, on the events at Saqīfat Banī Sāʿida; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya
hs-031.q: Where did the Anṣār gather after the Prophet's death, which led to the choice of Abū Bakr?
hs-031.e: The Anṣār met at the saqīfa of Banū Sāʿida to choose a leader. Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and Abū ʿUbayda joined them, and after discussion the pledge was given to Abū Bakr.

hs-032.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, on the Battle of al-Yamāma
hs-032.q: Which false prophet was killed at the Battle of al-Yamāma in the wars of apostasy?
hs-032.e: Musaylima of Banū Ḥanīfa was killed at al-Yamāma (12 AH) and many Quran reciters fell in the battle. Al-Aswad was killed in Yemen and Ṭulayḥa and Sajāḥ later repented or retreated.

hs-033.src: Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, biography of Khālid ibn al-Walīd
hs-033.q: Which Companion, nicknamed Sayf Allāh (the sword of God), led the Muslim armies in many early victories?
hs-033.e: The Prophet gave Khālid ibn al-Walīd this title after Mūta. He fought in the wars of apostasy and the conquest of Iraq and Syria, including the battle of Yarmūk.

hs-034.src: al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-Buldān, on the conquest of Iraq
hs-034.q: Against which empire was the Battle of al-Qādisiyya fought under the command of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ?
hs-034.e: Al-Qādisiyya (commonly dated 15 AH) broke the Sasanian army and opened Iraq to the Muslims. The Byzantines were fought at Yarmūk.

hs-035.src: al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-Buldān, on the conquest of Egypt
hs-035.q: Which commander led the conquest of Egypt under ʿUmar and founded the garrison city of al-Fusṭāṭ?
hs-035.e: ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ entered Egypt in about 20 AH and founded al-Fusṭāṭ with the first mosque in Africa, which still bears his name. Later Cairo grew near this site.

hs-036.src: al-Māwardī, al-Aḥkām al-Sulṭāniyya; al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk
hs-036.q: What was the dīwān that ʿUmar established?
o: A register of soldiers and stipends paid from the public treasury
A school for the Companions' children
hs-036.e: ʿUmar created the dīwān to record the fighters and others entitled to stipends from the state treasury (bayt al-māl), ranking them by precedence in Islam. The word later came to mean government bureau.

hs-037.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Ṣaḥāba (the shūrā after ʿUmar); Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya
hs-037.q: ʿUmar named a council of six to choose his successor. Which of these was NOT among them?
hs-037.e: The six were ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, Saʿd and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf. Abū ʿUbayda had already died in the plague of ʿAmwās (18 AH). ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf conducted the consultation that chose ʿUthmān.

hs-038.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, events of 18 AH
hs-038.q: Which disaster struck Syria in 18 AH and killed Abū ʿUbayda and Muʿādh ibn Jabal among many others?
hs-038.e: The plague of ʿAmwās (Emmaus) struck Syria and Palestine in 18 AH. The Year of Ashes famine in the Hijāz fell in the same period but affected Arabia, not Syria.

hs-039.src: al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-Buldān, on the conquest of Cyprus
hs-039.q: Under ʿUthmān, which commander was permitted to build a fleet and raid Cyprus around 28 AH?
hs-039.e: ʿUmar had refused sea expeditions as dangerous, but ʿUthmān allowed Muʿāwiya, governor of Syria, to launch the first Muslim naval campaign, against Cyprus. The Battle of the Masts followed in 34 AH.

hs-040.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, events of 36 AH
hs-040.q: What was the Battle of the Camel (al-Jamal) in 36 AH?
o: A clash near Basra between the army of ʿAlī and the party of ʿĀʾisha, Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr
A battle between ʿAlī and the Khawārij
A battle with the Byzantines in Syria
A battle over the control of Makka
hs-040.e: After ʿUthmān's killing, ʿĀʾisha, Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr went to Basra demanding justice for him; war broke out against their intentions near Basra. ʿAlī won, and both Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr were killed.

hs-041.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, events of 37 AH
hs-041.q: Which battle in 37 AH between the armies of ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya ended with the call to arbitration?
hs-041.e: At Ṣiffīn on the Euphrates the armies fought for weeks until Muʿāwiya's side raised copies of the Quran and called for arbitration. The arbitration split ʿAlī's camp and produced the Khawārij.

o: Those who left ʿAlī's army after the arbitration at Ṣiffīn and then fought him
The followers of Muʿāwiya in Syria
hs-042.e: The Khawārij (‘those who went out’) objected to the arbitration, left ʿAlī's army and were fought by him at Naharwān in 38 AH. ʿAlī was later killed by a man of this movement.

hs-043.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Ṣulḥ (the hadith about al-Ḥasan); al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh
hs-043.q: What did al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī do in 41 AH to end the strife?
o: He handed over the caliphate to Muʿāwiya
He led an army against Muʿāwiya in Syria
He asked the Byzantines for help
hs-043.e: Al-Ḥasan reconciled with Muʿāwiya and surrendered the office in order to save Muslim blood; the year is called ʿām al-jamāʿa. A hadith in al-Bukhārī records the Prophet's words about him as a means to reconcile two groups of Muslims.

hs-044.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, events of 61 AH; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya
hs-044.q: What happened at Karbalāʾ in Muḥarram 61 AH?
o: al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī and his companions were killed by the forces of the Umayyad governor
Makka was besieged by the Umayyads
hs-044.e: Al-Ḥusayn, grandson of the Prophet, set out for Kūfa after being invited and was stopped at Karbalāʾ, where he and a small band were killed on 10 Muḥarram. The event deeply affected the Muslim community.

hs-045.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh; standard histories of Islamic architecture
hs-045.q: Which Umayyad caliph built the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, completed around 72 AH?
hs-045.e: ʿAbd al-Malik ordered the Dome of the Rock, the oldest surviving major Islamic monument. His son al-Walīd later built the Great Mosque of Damascus and renovated al-Aqṣā.

hs-046.src: Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, on ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz
hs-046.q: Which Umayyad caliph, who reigned about two and a half years from 99 AH, is remembered for justice and for ordering the collection of hadith?
hs-046.e: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz (r. 99–101 AH) lifted unjust taxes, stopped the cursing of ʿAlī from pulpits and, according to reports, instructed scholars such as Ibn Shihāb al-Zuhrī to write down the sunna.

hs-047.q: Which Abbasid caliph is especially associated with the Bayt al-Ḥikma (House of Wisdom) and the translation movement in Baghdad?
hs-047.e: Al-Maʾmūn (r. 198–218 AH) supported the translation of Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic and the work of scholars like al-Khwārizmī. The translation activity had begun earlier under al-Manṣūr and Hārūn al-Rashīd.

hs-048.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, on the miḥna
hs-048.q: What was the miḥna that began under al-Maʾmūn in 218 AH?
o: A state inquisition testing scholars on the doctrine that the Quran is created
hs-048.e: Al-Maʾmūn, influenced by Muʿtazilī thinkers, required judges and scholars to affirm that the Quran is created. Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal's refusal made him a symbol, and al-Mutawakkil ended the policy in about 234 AH.

hs-049.src: Ibn Abī Zarʿ, al-Anīs al-Muṭrib bi-Rawḍ al-Qirṭās; standard histories of Fez
hs-049.q: Who founded the al-Qarawiyyīn mosque and school in Fez, around 245 AH (859 CE)?
hs-049.e: Fāṭima al-Fihriyya, who had inherited wealth from her father, financed the mosque and its school, which became a major centre of learning and is often described as one of the oldest continuously operating educational institutions.

hs-050.src: Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, events of 658 AH
hs-050.q: Which Mamluk victory in 658 AH (1260 CE) stopped the Mongol advance towards Egypt?
hs-050.e: At ʿAyn Jālūt in Palestine the Mamluk army under Sultan Qutuz, with Baybars among its commanders, defeated the Mongols. Ḥaṭṭīn was against the Crusaders, Malāzgird against Byzantium and al-Zallāqa in Spain.

hs-051.src: al-Maqqarī, Nafḥ al-Ṭīb, on the end of Muslim rule in Granada
hs-051.q: In which year did Granada, the last Muslim kingdom in Spain, fall?
hs-051.e: Granada, ruled by the Naṣrid dynasty, surrendered to the Catholic monarchs in January 1492. The year 1085 saw Toledo's fall, 1212 the defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa and 1031 the end of the Caliphate of Córdoba.

hs-052.src: Ibn Iyās, Badāʾiʿ al-Zuhūr, on the Ottoman conquest of Egypt
hs-052.q: Which Ottoman sultan conquered Syria and Egypt from the Mamluks in 1516–1517?
hs-052.e: Selim I defeated the Mamluks at Marj Dābiq (1516) and al-Raydāniyya (1517) and took control of the Hijāz, becoming protector of the two holy cities. Later sources link him to the transfer of the caliphal title, a point historians debate.

hs-053.src: Standard histories of the Mughal empire (e.g. Richards, The Mughal Empire)
hs-053.q: Which Mughal emperor commissioned the Taj Mahal in Āgra as a tomb for his wife Mumtāz Maḥal?
hs-053.e: Shāh Jahān built the Taj Mahal, completed in the mid-seventeenth century, after his wife's death in 1631. Bābur founded the dynasty at the First Battle of Pānīpat in 1526.

hs-054.src: Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa, ʿUyūn al-Anbāʾ fī Ṭabaqāt al-Aṭibbāʾ; Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī al-Ṭibb
hs-054.q: Which scholar of Bukhārā wrote al-Qānūn fī al-Ṭibb (The Canon of Medicine), used in medical teaching for centuries?
hs-054.e: Ibn Sīnā (c. 370–428 AH) wrote the Canon, a systematic summary of medical knowledge that was taught in Europe and the Muslim world. Al-Rāzī wrote al-Ḥāwī and Ibn al-Nafīs described the pulmonary circulation.

hs-055.src: Ibn Juzayy (ed.), Riḥlat Ibn Baṭṭūṭa (Tuḥfat al-Nuẓẓār)
hs-055.q: Which traveller from Tangier wrote a famous account of his journeys across Africa, Asia and the Muslim lands in the 8th century AH?
hs-055.e: Ibn Baṭṭūṭa (703–c. 770 AH) travelled for about thirty years and dictated his Riḥla to Ibn Juzayy. Ibn Jubayr, al-Idrīsī and Ibn Ḥawqal are other geographers or travellers of earlier centuries.

hs-056.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, introduction; al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ
hs-056.q: Which scholar wrote the large chronicle Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, as well as a well-known Quran commentary?
hs-056.e: Al-Ṭabarī (224–310 AH, commonly given) wrote both Jāmiʿ al-Bayān in tafsīr and the universal history Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, which records events year by year with chains of transmitters.

hs-057.q: Which work by Ibn Kathīr is a universal history from creation to his own time?
hs-057.e: Ibn Kathīr (701–774 AH, commonly given) wrote al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, a history from the beginning of creation to the events of his time. Al-Kāmil is by Ibn al-Athīr, Siyar by al-Dhahabī and Murūj by al-Masʿūdī.

hs-058.q: Which work by al-Dhahabī gives biographies of scholars and notable figures, arranged by generations?
hs-058.e: Al-Dhahabī (673–748 AH, commonly given) compiled Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ and the larger Tārīkh al-Islām. Wafayāt al-Aʿyān is by Ibn Khallikān and Futūḥ al-Buldān by al-Balādhurī.

hs-059.src: al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, biography of al-Bukhārī
hs-059.q: Where was Imam al-Bukhārī born, in 194 AH?
hs-059.e: Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl al-Bukhārī was born in Bukhārā, travelled for hadith across the Muslim world and died in 256 AH near Samarkand. His Ṣaḥīḥ is the most authoritative collection for most scholars.

hs-060.src: al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, biography of al-Ghazālī; Ibn ʿAsākir, Tabyīn Kadhib al-Muftarī
hs-060.q: Which scholar of Ṭūs (450–505 AH, commonly given) taught at the Niẓāmiyya of Baghdad and wrote Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn?
hs-060.e: Al-Ghazālī became professor at the Niẓāmiyya in Baghdad, left his post in a spiritual crisis and later wrote Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn. Al-Rāzī and Ibn Rushd lived later, and al-Nawawī lived in Syria in the 7th century AH.

hs-061.src: Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa, ʿUyūn al-Anbāʾ; Ibn al-Haytham, Kitāb al-Manāẓir
hs-061.q: Which scientist wrote Kitāb al-Manāẓir (Book of Optics), shaping the study of light and vision?
hs-061.e: Ibn al-Haytham (born in Basra, worked in Cairo, d. c. 430 AH) argued that vision happens when light enters the eye and used experiments. Al-Zahrāwī was a surgeon of Andalus and al-Bīrūnī worked on astronomy and geography.

hs-062.src: Standard histories of the Maghrib and Algeria (e.g. Danziger, Abd al-Qadir and the Algerians)
hs-062.q: Which scholar and emir led the resistance against the French conquest of Algeria from 1832 until 1847?
hs-062.e: ʿAbd al-Qādir, a Sufi scholar, built an organised state in western and central Algeria before surrendering in 1847. ʿUmar al-Mukhtār resisted Italy in Libya; Shāmil resisted Russia in the Caucasus.

hs-063.src: al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-Buldān, on the conquest of Syria; al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh
hs-063.q: What was the main consequence of the Muslim victory at the Yarmūk (15 AH)?
o: Byzantine rule in Syria effectively ended
Spain was opened to Muslim armies
hs-063.e: At Yarmūk the Muslim army under Khālid ibn al-Walīd and Abū ʿUbayda defeated a much larger Byzantine force, after which the remaining Syrian cities fell. Persia was broken at al-Qādisiyya and Nihāvand.

hs-064.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, on Nihāvand
hs-064.q: Which battle (commonly dated 21 AH) is called ‘the victory of victories’ (fatḥ al-futūḥ) because it ended Sasanian resistance in Persia?
hs-064.e: At Nihāvand in the Jibāl region, the Muslim army under al-Nuʿmān ibn Muqarrin defeated the last large Sasanian army. After that, the Persian plateau was gradually opened.

hs-065.src: Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, events of 114 AH
hs-065.q: Which battle in 114 AH (732 CE), in Gaul, ended the northward advance of the army of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ghāfiqī?
hs-065.e: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Ghāfiqī, governor of al-Andalus, was killed in the battle called Balāṭ al-Shuhadāʾ against the Frankish forces of Charles Martel, and the Muslim force withdrew. Wādī Lakka (92 AH) was the battle that opened Spain.

hs-066.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, events of 129–132 AH
hs-066.q: Which leader organised the armies in Khurāsān that brought the Abbasid revolution to power in 129–132 AH?
hs-066.e: Abū Muslim raised the black banners in Khurāsān in 129 AH, and his armies defeated the Umayyads at the Battle of the Zab (132 AH); Marwān II, the last Umayyad caliph, was killed soon after. Al-Manṣūr later had Abū Muslim killed.

hs-067.q: Which Abbasid caliph founded the city of Sāmarrāʾ as a new capital, around 221 AH?
hs-067.e: Al-Muʿtaṣim moved the court from Baghdad to Sāmarrāʾ to keep his Turkish troops away from the population. The city remained the capital for about half a century.

hs-068.src: Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, events of 133 AH
hs-068.q: The Battle of Talas in 133 AH (751 CE) is traditionally linked to the spread of what craft from China to the Muslim world?
hs-068.e: At Talas in Central Asia an Abbasid-allied army met Tang forces. The tradition holds that Chinese prisoners taught papermaking in Samarkand, from where it spread to Baghdad; some historians treat the story with caution and note earlier paper contact.

hs-069.src: al-Maqqarī, Nafḥ al-Ṭīb, on ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Dākhil
hs-069.q: Who founded the Umayyad emirate of al-Andalus after escaping the Abbasid massacre of his family?
o: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān I, known as al-Dākhil (the Entrant)
hs-069.e: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muʿāwiya, a grandson of the caliph Hishām, fled Syria, reached Spain and established his rule in 138 AH (756 CE). ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III declared the caliphate nearly two centuries later.

hs-070.src: al-Maqqarī, Nafḥ al-Ṭīb, on ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Nāṣir
hs-070.q: Which ruler declared the caliphate of Córdoba in 316 AH (929 CE), taking the title al-Nāṣir li-Dīn Allāh?
hs-070.e: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III, facing the rise of the Fatimid caliphate in North Africa, declared himself caliph. His reign is regarded as the peak of Umayyad Andalus; the caliphate collapsed in 422 AH (1031).

hs-071.src: al-Maqqarī, Nafḥ al-Ṭīb, on Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ
hs-071.q: What was Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ, built by ʿAbd al-Raḥmān III?
o: A palace-city near Córdoba that served as the seat of government
A fortress on the Strait of Gibraltar
A port on the Atlantic coast
hs-071.e: Madīnat al-Zahrāʾ was a royal palace-city outside Córdoba, begun around 325 AH (936 CE). It was ruined in the civil war that ended the caliphate and was rediscovered by archaeologists.

hs-072.src: Ibn Abī Zarʿ, Rawḍ al-Qirṭās; al-Maqqarī, Nafḥ al-Ṭīb
hs-072.q: Which victory in 479 AH (1086 CE) did the Almoravid ruler Yūsuf ibn Tāshfīn win after being called to help by the Andalusian princes?
hs-072.e: After the fall of Toledo in 478 AH, the taifa kings, led by al-Muʿtamid of Seville, asked the Almoravids for help. Yūsuf crossed with his army and defeated the Castilian king at al-Zallāqa, delaying the Christian advance.

hs-073.src: Ibn Abī Zarʿ, Rawḍ al-Qirṭās; Ibn Khaldūn, Kitāb al-ʿIbar
hs-073.q: Who was the spiritual founder of the Almohad (al-Muwaḥḥidūn) movement in the Maghrib?
hs-073.e: Ibn Tūmart, a Berber scholar from the Atlas, started the movement against the Almoravids with a reform call based on tawḥīd. His successor ʿAbd al-Muʾmin built the Almohad state.

hs-074.src: al-Maqrīzī, Ittiʿāẓ al-Ḥunafāʾ bi-Akhbār al-Aʾimma al-Fāṭimiyyīn al-Khulafāʾ
hs-074.q: Where was the Fatimid caliphate first established in 297 AH (909 CE)?
hs-074.e: The Fatimid caliphate, an Ismāʿīlī Shīʿī dynasty, was proclaimed by ʿUbayd Allāh al-Mahdī in Ifrīqiya; it moved to Egypt in 358 AH when al-Muʿizz entered the new city of Cairo.

hs-075.src: Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, events of 567 AH
hs-075.q: Who ended the Fatimid caliphate in Egypt in 567 AH (1171 CE) and restored Sunni allegiance to the Abbasids?
