hs-075.e: After the death of the last Fatimid caliph al-ʿĀḍid, Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn had the sermon said in the name of the Abbasid caliph and founded the Ayyubid dynasty. Jawhar was the Fatimid founder of Cairo.

hs-076.src: Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, events of 447 AH
hs-076.q: What happened in 447 AH (1055 CE) when the Seljuk leader Ṭughril Beg entered Baghdad?
o: He ended Buyid domination and became the protector of the Abbasid caliph
He handed Baghdad to the Fatimids
He was defeated by the caliph's army
hs-076.e: The Seljuks, Sunni Turks, replaced the Shīʿī Buyid amirs as the dominant power in Baghdad while keeping the Abbasid caliph as religious head. The caliph gave Ṭughril the title of sultan.

hs-077.src: Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, events of 463 AH
hs-077.q: Which Seljuk sultan defeated and captured the Byzantine emperor Romanos Diogenes at Malāzgird in 463 AH (1071 CE)?
hs-077.e: Alp Arslān's victory at Malāzgird (Manzikert) opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement. His son Malikshāh succeeded him and his vizier Niẓām al-Mulk shaped the state.

hs-078.src: Ibn Khallikān, Wafayāt al-Aʿyān, biography of Niẓām al-Mulk
hs-078.q: What was the main purpose of the Niẓāmiyya madrasas founded by the vizier Niẓām al-Mulk, the first being in Baghdad (459 AH)?
o: State-supported colleges to train jurists and teachers, in the Shāfiʿī school
Military academies for the Seljuk army
hs-078.e: Niẓām al-Mulk endowed a network of colleges in the Seljuk lands that taught Shāfiʿī law and Ashʿarī theology, with salaried professors. Al-Ghazālī and al-Juwaynī taught in them.

hs-079.src: Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, events of 492 AH
hs-079.q: In which year (AH/CE) did the First Crusade capture Jerusalem?
hs-079.e: The Crusaders took Jerusalem in Shaʿbān 492 AH after a siege, and a large part of the population was killed. The other years are the recapture under Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn, ʿAyn Jālūt and the fall of Acre.

hs-080.src: Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, events of 539 AH
hs-080.q: Which Muslim ruler's capture of Edessa (al-Ruhā) in 539 AH (1144 CE) marked the start of the Muslim counter-offensive against the Crusader states?
hs-080.e: ʿImād al-Dīn Zangī of Mosul took Edessa, the first Crusader state to fall, which led to the Second Crusade. His son Nūr al-Dīn continued the effort and brought Egypt into the same camp.

hs-081.src: al-Maqrīzī, al-Sulūk li-Maʿrifat Duwal al-Mulūk, events of 690 AH
hs-081.q: Which Mamluk sultan captured Acre, the last major Crusader stronghold, in 690 AH (1291 CE)?
hs-081.e: After a siege, al-Ashraf Khalīl took Acre in 1291, and the remaining Crusader coastal towns were abandoned soon after. His father Qalāwūn had prepared the campaign.

hs-082.src: al-Maqrīzī, al-Sulūk li-Maʿrifat Duwal al-Mulūk, events of 648 AH
hs-082.q: Who became ruler of Egypt in 648 AH (1250 CE) after the death of the Ayyubid sultan al-Ṣāliḥ, and is counted as the founder of the Mamluk line?
hs-082.e: Shajar al-Durr, widow of al-Ṣāliḥ Ayyūb, concealed his death during the Crusade of Louis IX, then ruled and married the Mamluk commander Aybak. She is a rare example of a woman who held sovereign power in Egypt.

hs-083.src: Standard histories of the Ottoman Empire (e.g. Inalcik, The Ottoman Empire: The Classical Age)
hs-083.q: Which leader is regarded as the founder of the Ottoman dynasty, around the end of the 7th century AH (c. 1299 CE)?
hs-083.e: The dynasty takes its name from Osman, a frontier leader in north-western Anatolia whose state grew from a small principality. His son Orhan took Bursa and expanded further.

hs-084.src: Standard histories of the Ottoman Empire (e.g. Imber, The Ottoman Empire 1300–1650)
hs-084.q: Which victory of Sulaymān the Magnificent in 1526 CE (932 AH) brought most of Hungary under Ottoman control?
hs-084.e: At Mohács the Ottoman army destroyed the Hungarian army and killed King Louis II. Chaldiran (1514) was against the Safavids, Lepanto (1571) was an Ottoman defeat at sea and Ankara (1402) was Timur's victory.

hs-085.src: Standard histories of the Mughal empire (e.g. Richards, The Mughal Empire)
hs-085.q: Which ruler founded the Mughal empire in India by winning the First Battle of Pānīpat in 1526 CE?
hs-085.e: Zahīr al-Dīn Bābur, a Timurid prince from Central Asia, defeated the Sultan of Delhi, Ibrāhīm Lodī, at Pānīpat. His grandson Akbar consolidated and enlarged the empire.

hs-086.src: al-Saʿdī, Taʾrīkh al-Sūdān; Maḥmūd Kaʿti, Taʾrīkh al-Fattāsh
hs-086.q: Which ruler of the Songhai empire made the pilgrimage to Makka in 1496–97 CE and was given the title of caliph of the Sudan?
hs-086.e: Askia Muḥammad took power from the Sunni dynasty, made a famous pilgrimage and received a title from the Abbasid caliph in Cairo. Under him Timbuktu became a leading centre of Islamic scholarship.

hs-087.src: Standard histories of West Africa (e.g. Last, The Sokoto Caliphate)
hs-087.q: Which scholar led the reform movement that founded the Sokoto Caliphate in northern Nigeria in the early 19th century CE?
hs-087.e: Usman dan Fodio, a Fulani scholar of the Qādirī order and the Mālikī school, called for a return to the sharīʿa from 1804; his son Muḥammad Bello and brother ʿAbd Allāh consolidated the caliphate.

hs-088.src: al-Dhahabī, Dhayl Tārīkh al-Islām; Ibn ʿAbd al-Hādī, al-ʿUqūd al-Durriyya
hs-088.q: Where was Ibn Taymiyya born in 661 AH, and where did he die in 728 AH?
o: Born in Ḥarrān; died in the citadel of Damascus
Born in Baghdad; died in Cairo
Born in Cordoba; died in Fez
Born in Makka; died in Madīna
hs-088.e: Ibn Taymiyya's family moved from Ḥarrān to Damascus because of the Mongol threat. He was imprisoned several times, and died in 728 AH in the Damascus citadel.

hs-089.src: al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, biography of al-Nawawī
hs-089.q: Which Shāfiʿī scholar of Syria (631–676 AH, commonly given), from the village of Nawā, wrote Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn and al-Arbaʿūn?
hs-089.e: Al-Nawawī lived most of his life in Damascus and, though he died at about forty-five, wrote Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, al-Majmūʿ and Riyāḍ al-Ṣāliḥīn. Ibn Qudāma was a Ḥanbalī scholar of the preceding century.

hs-090.src: Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa, ʿUyūn al-Anbāʾ; al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, biography of Ibn Rushd
hs-090.q: Which Andalusian scholar of Cordoba (520–595 AH, commonly given) wrote Bidāyat al-Mujtahid on comparative fiqh and commentaries on Aristotle?
hs-090.e: Ibn Rushd, qāḍī of Seville and Córdoba, wrote the Bidāya on the disagreement of the jurists and philosophical commentaries. Ibn Ḥazm lived a century earlier and al-Shāṭibī in Granada in the 8th century AH.

hs-091.src: Ibn Ḥajar, al-Durar al-Kāmina; al-Sakhāwī, al-Ḍawʾ al-Lāmiʿ
hs-091.q: Which hadith scholar of Cairo (773–852 AH, commonly given) wrote Fatḥ al-Bārī, the most widely used commentary on Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī?
hs-091.e: Ibn Ḥajar served as chief judge in Cairo and spent around twenty-five years on Fatḥ al-Bārī. Al-Nawawī wrote on Muslim; al-Dhahabī and al-Suyūṭī wrote on many other fields.

hs-092.src: Standard histories of Libya (e.g. Ahmida, The Making of Modern Libya)
hs-092.q: Which Libyan teacher of the Qurʾān and resistance leader, executed by the Italians in 1931, is known as the ‘Lion of the Desert’?
hs-092.e: ʿUmar al-Mukhtār led the Sanūsī-linked resistance in Cyrenaica against Italian colonisation for about twenty years, and was captured and hanged in September 1931 at about seventy.

hs-093.src: al-Māwardī, al-Aḥkām al-Sulṭāniyya, ch. 1 on the contract of the imamate; al-Bāqillānī, al-Tamhīd
hs-093.q: According to the view of the majority of Sunni jurists and theologians (e.g. al-Bāqillānī, al-Māwardī), how was the caliphate of Abū Bakr established?
o: By the choice and pledge of the community (ikhtiyār and bayʿa), without an explicit designation by the Prophet
By an explicit written designation by the Prophet
By inheritance within the Prophet's family
By a decree of the Anṣār alone
hs-093.e: The majority held that the imamate is contracted by the choice of the people of authority (ahl al-ḥall wa-l-ʿaqd) and the pledge of the community, as happened for Abū Bakr. Some, such as al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and a group of hadith scholars, thought the Prophet had hinted at Abū Bakr (implicit designation), and other groups held that ʿAlī had been designated.

hs-094.src: al-Māwardī, al-Aḥkām al-Sulṭāniyya, ch. 1; al-Juwaynī, Ghiyāth al-Umam
hs-094.q: Which two ways of concluding the imamate does al-Māwardī accept in al-Aḥkām al-Sulṭāniyya?
o: Election by the people of authority, and designation by the previous imam
Lot and consultation of the Anṣār
Succession by seniority and military acclaim
hs-094.e: Al-Māwardī describes the imamate as concluded either by election of the ahl al-ḥall wa-l-ʿaqd (as with Abū Bakr) or by designation of a successor by the imam (as with ʿUmar). Later jurists discussed the validity of the rule by conquest as a matter of necessity.

hs-095.src: al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-Buldān, on the dīwān and coinage; al-Maqrīzī, Shudhūr al-ʿUqūd
hs-095.q: Which reform is attributed to the caliph ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān in the years commonly dated 77–81 AH?
o: Introducing coins with Arabic-Islamic inscriptions and making Arabic the language of the state registers
hs-095.e: ʿAbd al-Malik replaced Byzantine and Persian coin designs with a purely Arabic-Islamic coinage and had the dīwāns of Syria and Iraq kept in Arabic rather than Greek and Persian. Baghdad was founded by the Abbasids.

hs-096.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, events of 64–73 AH
hs-096.q: Who claimed the caliphate from Makka after the death of Yazīd I, ruling the Hijāz until he was killed by al-Ḥajjāj's forces in 73 AH?
hs-096.e: Ibn al-Zubayr, son of the Companion al-Zubayr and grandson of Abū Bakr through Asmāʾ, was acknowledged in the Hijāz and elsewhere. The Umayyads under ʿAbd al-Malik beat him; the Kaʿba was damaged in the siege and later rebuilt.

hs-097.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk, events of 64 AH
hs-097.q: After which battle in 64 AH did Marwān ibn al-Ḥakam consolidate Umayyad rule in Syria, shifting the caliphate to the Marwānid line?
hs-097.e: At Marj Rāhiṭ near Damascus, Marwān defeated the supporters of Ibn al-Zubayr, mainly the Qaysī tribes, with the support of the Yamanī tribes. After him the caliphate stayed in his descendants. Al-Ḥarra (63 AH) was the Umayyad victory over Madīna.

hs-098.src: al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-Buldān, on Transoxiana and Sind
hs-098.q: Under al-Walīd I (86–96 AH), which commanders led the conquests of Transoxiana and of Sind respectively?
o: Qutayba ibn Muslim and Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim
Ṭāriq ibn Ziyād and Mūsā ibn Nuṣayr
Khālid ibn al-Walīd and ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ
ʿUqba ibn Nāfiʿ and Ḥassān ibn al-Nuʿmān
hs-098.e: Qutayba ibn Muslim, governor of Khurāsān, extended Muslim rule across the Oxus to Bukhārā, Samarkand and beyond, while the young Muḥammad ibn al-Qāsim al-Thaqafī conquered Sind around 93 AH. Ṭāriq and Mūsā conquered al-Andalus under the same caliph.

hs-099.src: Ibn Abī Zarʿ, Rawḍ al-Qirṭās, on the Idrīsids
hs-099.q: Who founded the first independent Muslim dynasty in Morocco, the Idrīsids, around 172 AH?
o: Idrīs ibn ʿAbd Allāh, a descendant of al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī
hs-099.e: Idrīs I fled the Abbasid suppression of a revolt in the Hijāz, reached Walīlī in the Maghrib and was recognised by Berber tribes. His son Idrīs II founded Fez as the capital.

hs-100.src: al-Balādhurī, Futūḥ al-Buldān; Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil, events of 212 AH
hs-100.q: Which North African dynasty began the conquest of Sicily in 212 AH (827 CE) under the judge Asad ibn al-Furāt?
hs-100.e: The Aghlabids, nominally under the Abbasids, ruled from Qayrawān and launched the long conquest of Sicily, completed in the following decades. The Fatimids later took over their territory.

hs-101.src: Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, events of 334 AH
hs-101.q: Which dynasty took control of Baghdad in 334 AH (945 CE), reducing the Abbasid caliph to a nominal head?
hs-101.e: Aḥmad ibn Buwayh (Muʿizz al-Dawla) entered Baghdad and the caliph became subordinate to the Buyid amirs, who held real power until the Seljuk entry in 447 AH.

hs-102.src: Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, events of 317 and 339 AH
hs-102.q: What did the Qarmaṭians, a breakaway Ismāʿīlī group of eastern Arabia, do at Makka in 317 AH (930 CE)?
o: They attacked the pilgrims and removed the Black Stone, which was returned about twenty years later
They destroyed the Prophet's Mosque in Madīna
They founded the city of Baghdad
hs-102.e: The Qarmaṭians under Abū Ṭāhir al-Jannābī raided Makka during the Ḥajj and carried off the Black Stone to al-Aḥsāʾ. It was restored in 339 AH (951 CE).

hs-103.src: Ibn Shaddād, al-Nawādir al-Sulṭāniyya wa-l-Maḥāsin al-Yūsufiyya
hs-103.q: Which treaty of 588 AH (1192 CE) between Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn and Richard I ended the Third Crusade?
hs-103.e: After Acre fell to the Crusaders in 587 AH, a truce was concluded at Ramla: Jerusalem remained in Muslim hands, with Christian pilgrims allowed to visit, while the Crusaders kept a coastal strip. Ibn Shaddād, Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn's secretary, narrates it.

hs-104.src: al-Maqrīzī, al-Sulūk li-Maʿrifat Duwal al-Mulūk, events of 659 AH
hs-104.q: Why did Sultan Baybars install an Abbasid prince as caliph in Cairo in 659 AH (1261 CE)?
o: To give the Mamluk sultanate religious legitimacy after the destruction of the caliphate in Baghdad
Because the Abbasids had conquered Egypt
To start a campaign against Spain
hs-104.e: After the Mongol fall of Baghdad, Baybars welcomed a surviving Abbasid, al-Mustanṣir, and had him recognised as caliph. The line stayed in Cairo as a ceremonial caliphate until the Ottoman conquest of 1517.

hs-105.src: Ibn Abī Zarʿ, Rawḍ al-Qirṭās; Ibn ʿIdhārī, al-Bayān al-Mughrib
hs-105.q: Which defeat of the Almohad caliph al-Nāṣir in 609 AH (1212 CE) marked the turning point of the Reconquista?
hs-105.e: At al-ʿIqāb in the Sierra Morena the combined Christian kings defeated the Almohad army. Alarcos (591 AH) was a Muslim victory, al-Zallāqa (479 AH) as well. Cordoba fell in 1236 and Seville in 1248, and Granada stayed as the last Muslim kingdom.

hs-106.src: Rashīd al-Dīn, Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya
hs-106.q: What significant event occurred around 694 AH (1295 CE) in the Mongol Ilkhanate of Iran?
o: The Ilkhan Ghāzān converted to Islam, making Islam the religion of the ruling house
The Ilkhanate was conquered by the Mamluks
hs-106.e: Ghāzān accepted Islam and proclaimed it the religion of the state, which transformed the relation between Mongol rulers and Muslim subjects. His vizier Rashīd al-Dīn compiled the great history Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh. Baghdad had been destroyed earlier, in 656 AH.

hs-107.src: Minhāj al-Sirāj al-Jūzjānī, Ṭabaqāt-i Nāṣirī; standard histories of the Delhi Sultanate
hs-107.q: Which commander of the Ghurids became the first sultan of Delhi and founded the dynasty known as the Mamluk (slave) dynasty, around 602 AH (1206 CE)?
hs-107.e: After the death of Muʿizz al-Dīn Muḥammad of Ghūr, his slave general Quṭb al-Dīn Aybak ruled from Lahore and Delhi, founding the Delhi Sultanate. Iltutmish was his son-in-law and later successor, Maḥmūd of Ghazna belonged to the previous century, and Bābur founded the Mughals.

hs-108.src: Standard histories of the Ottoman Empire (e.g. Imber, The Ottoman Empire 1300–1650)
hs-108.q: Which battle of 1514 CE (920 AH) between Selim I and Shāh Ismāʿīl, the first Safavid ruler, confirmed Ottoman control of eastern Anatolia?
hs-108.e: At Chaldiran in north-western Iran the Ottoman army with firearms defeated the Safavid cavalry, and Shāh Ismāʿīl's advance westward was halted. Marj Dābiq (1516) was against the Mamluks.

hs-109.src: Standard histories of the Ottoman Empire (e.g. Finkel, Osman's Dream)
hs-109.q: Which treaty of 1699 CE (1110 AH), after the failed siege of Vienna in 1683, is regarded as the first major Ottoman territorial loss in Europe?
hs-109.e: At Karlowitz the Ottomans ceded Hungary and Transylvania to the Habsburgs. Küçük Kaynarca (1774) followed as a defeat by Russia. Sèvres (1920) and Lausanne (1923) belong to the end of the empire.

hs-110.src: Standard histories of the Ottoman Empire (e.g. Lewis, The Emergence of Modern Turkey)
hs-110.q: What was the Tanzimat, begun with the Edict of Gülhane in 1839?
o: A period of Ottoman administrative, legal and military reform
hs-110.e: The Tanzimat (‘reorganisation’) introduced legal guarantees of life and property, reorganised the army and administration, and later produced new codes of law and the first Ottoman constitution in 1876.

hs-111.src: Ibn Khaldūn, al-Muqaddima, ch. 2 on the bedouin civilisation and ʿaṣabiyya
hs-111.q: In Ibn Khaldūn's Muqaddima, what is ʿaṣabiyya?
o: Group solidarity that drives the rise of dynasties and weakens as luxury grows
A legal term for inheritance shares
A method of verifying chains of narrators
hs-111.e: Ibn Khaldūn explains the rise and fall of states by ʿaṣabiyya, the bond of kinship or shared loyalty that helps a group win power; as the ruling group settles in luxury, solidarity fades and a new group with stronger ʿaṣabiyya replaces it, in a cycle of about three generations.

hs-112.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tārīkh al-Rusul wa-l-Mulūk; Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, introduction
hs-112.q: Al-Ṭabarī's Tārīkh ends in the year 302 AH. Which historian wrote a work that built on it and continued the chronicle far beyond, down to 628 AH?
o: Ibn al-Athīr, in al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh
hs-112.e: Ibn al-Athīr (555–630 AH) took al-Ṭabarī as his main source and abridged his chains of transmission, then continued the annals to the year 628. Later historians such as Ibn Kathīr in turn drew on Ibn al-Athīr.

hs-113.src: al-Masʿūdī, Murūj al-Dhahab wa-Maʿādin al-Jawhar, introduction
hs-113.q: Which historian and geographer of the 4th century AH wrote Murūj al-Dhahab wa-Maʿādin al-Jawhar, mixing history by topics and peoples with geography and anecdotes?
hs-113.e: Al-Masʿūdī (d. c. 345 AH) travelled widely and composed Murūj al-Dhahab, which treats the histories of nations and dynasties thematically rather than strictly year by year. Al-Balādhurī wrote on conquests, Ibn Saʿd on biographical classes.

hs-114.src: al-Sakhāwī, al-Iʿlān bi-l-Tawbīkh li-man Dhamma ahl al-Tārīkh; Franz Rosenthal, A History of Muslim Historiography
hs-114.q: Which historical genre arranges events year by year?
hs-114.e: Annals (ḥawliyyāt) present events under each year, as in al-Ṭabarī and Ibn al-Athīr. Ṭabaqāt group persons by generation, as in Ibn Saʿd, while tarājim collect lives alphabetically or by city.

hs-115.q: What type of work is Ibn Saʿd's al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā?
o: A large collection of biographies of the Prophet, the Companions and the Successors arranged in classes
A chronicle of the Abbasid caliphs year by year
hs-115.e: Ibn Saʿd (d. 230 AH) was the secretary of al-Wāqidī and compiled al-Ṭabaqāt, the earliest large biographical work, with the Prophet first, then the Companions and later generations grouped by their time and place.

hs-116.src: Ibn Khallikān, Wafayāt al-Aʿyān wa-Anbāʾ Abnāʾ al-Zamān, introduction; al-Maqrīzī, al-Mawāʿiẓ wa-l-Iʿtibār
hs-116.q: Which pair of authors and works matches correctly?
o: Ibn Khallikān: Wafayāt al-Aʿyān; al-Maqrīzī: al-Khiṭaṭ
Ibn Khallikān: al-Khiṭaṭ; al-Maqrīzī: Wafayāt al-Aʿyān
Ibn Khallikān: Murūj al-Dhahab; al-Maqrīzī: al-Kāmil
Ibn Khallikān: Futūḥ al-Buldān; al-Maqrīzī: al-Bidāya
hs-116.e: Ibn Khallikān (608–681 AH, commonly given) compiled the biographical dictionary Wafayāt al-Aʿyān, and the Cairo historian al-Maqrīzī (766–845 AH, commonly given) wrote al-Mawāʿiẓ wa-l-Iʿtibār (al-Khiṭaṭ) on the topography and history of Egypt.

hs-117.src: Ibn al-Athīr, al-Kāmil fī al-Tārīkh, events of 616 AH; al-Nasawī, Sīrat al-Sulṭān Jalāl al-Dīn
hs-117.q: What event is commonly cited as the immediate cause of the Mongol invasion of the Khwārazmian empire in 616 AH (1219 CE)?
o: The killing of Mongol merchants and envoys at Otrar by the Khwārazmian governor
A Mongol request to convert to Islam
A dispute over the pilgrimage route
hs-117.e: Chinggis Khan sent a trade caravan and envoys; at Otrar the governor had the merchants killed, and the Khwārazmshāh Muḥammad refused to give satisfaction. The Mongol campaign destroyed Bukhārā, Samarkand and Merv, and the empire fell. His son Jalāl al-Dīn resisted until 628 AH.

hs-118.src: Ibn ʿAbd al-Ẓāhir, al-Rawḍ al-Zāhir fī Sīrat al-Malik al-Ẓāhir; al-Maqrīzī, al-Sulūk
hs-118.q: Which Crusader principality did Sultan Baybars capture in 666 AH (1268 CE)?
hs-118.e: Baybars took Antioch, an important Crusader principality in northern Syria, after Edessa had fallen to Zangī in 1144 and Jerusalem to Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn in 1187. Tripoli was taken by Qalāwūn in 1289.

hs-119.src: al-Maqqarī, Nafḥ al-Ṭīb; standard histories of the Naṣrid kingdom of Granada
hs-119.q: Which dynasty ruled Granada from 629 AH (1232 CE) until its fall, and built the Alhambra?
hs-119.e: Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf ibn Naṣr (Ibn al-Aḥmar) founded the Naṣrid dynasty, which survived by paying tribute to Castile and trading across the Mediterranean. Its last ruler, Muḥammad XII (Abū ʿAbd Allāh, ‘Boabdil’), surrendered in 1492.

nhi-001.src: Ibn Hishām, Qaṭr al-Nadā wa-Ball al-Ṣadā, chapter on the genitive (al-majrūrāt)
nhi-001.q: What is the case and grammatical function of the highlighted word in the verse shown?
o: Genitive (majrūr), as the second term of an annexation (muḍāf ilayhi), marked by kasra
Nominative (marfūʿ), as subject of a nominal sentence, marked by ḍamma
Accusative (manṣūb), as direct object, marked by fatḥa
Genitive (majrūr), as a sound masculine plural, marked by yāʾ
nhi-001.e: The word is the second term of an annexation (iḍāfa) to ism, and the second term is always majrūr. As a singular noun it shows this with kasra. The yāʾ sign belongs only to sound masculine plurals and the dual.

nhi-002.src: Ibn Hishām, Qaṭr al-Nadā, chapter on the mubtadaʾ and the khabar
nhi-002.q: In the verse shown, what is the grammatical role of the highlighted word (in the reading of Ḥafṣ)?
nhi-002.e: The nominal sentence begins with this definite noun as mubtadaʾ; the khabar is the following prepositional phrase. In the reading of Ḥafṣ it is marfūʿ with ḍamma. There is no verb before it, so it cannot be a fāʿil.

nhi-003.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on the prepositional phrase as khabar
nhi-003.q: The highlighted word is the object of a preposition. What does the whole prepositional phrase (preposition plus this word) do in the sentence?
o: It serves as the khabar of the mubtadaʾ, attached to an understood word such as ‘established’
It serves as the fāʿil of the sentence
It serves as a ḥāl describing the mubtadaʾ
It serves as the object (mafʿūl bihi) of an understood verb
nhi-003.e: A prepositional phrase can be the khabar of a mubtadaʾ; grammarians say it is attached to an omitted active participle or verb such as ‘kāʾin’ or ‘istaqarra’. Nothing here is a fāʿil or object, and the mubtadaʾ is definite so a ḥāl is not possible.

nhi-004.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the signs of i‘rāb
nhi-004.q: What is the case of the highlighted word and what is its sign?
o: Genitive (majrūr), as muḍāf ilayhi; the sign is yāʾ because it is a sound masculine plural
Genitive (majrūr), as muḍāf ilayhi; the sign is kasra because it is a singular noun
Accusative (manṣūb), as object; the sign is yāʾ because it is a dual
Nominative (marfūʿ), as khabar; the sign is wāw because it is a sound masculine plural
nhi-004.e: The word is the muḍāf ilayhi of the preceding word and so is majrūr. It is a sound masculine plural, which takes yāʾ in both the genitive and the accusative; in the nominative it would take wāw.

nhi-005.src: Ibn Hishām, Qaṭr al-Nadā, chapter on the naʿt (al-tawābiʿ)
nhi-005.q: What is the highlighted word grammatically, and what case does it therefore take?
o: A naʿt (adjective) that follows the case of the word it describes, so it is genitive
A khabar that is always nominative
A mafʿūl bihi that is always accusative
A ḥāl that is always accusative
nhi-005.e: A naʿt is a follower (tābiʿ): it agrees with the word it describes in case, definiteness, gender and number. Here it describes the divine name and so is majrūr like it.

nhi-006.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the genitive nouns
nhi-006.q: Why is the highlighted word in the genitive in the verse shown?
o: Because it is the second term of an annexation (muḍāf ilayhi) to the word before it
Because a preposition stands directly before it
Because it is the khabar of a nominal sentence
Because it follows a verb in the passive voice
nhi-006.e: No preposition occurs here. A noun is genitive when it is the second term of an annexation, and the word before it is its muḍāf. The same word is in turn the muḍāf of the next one.

nhi-007.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyyat Ibn Mālik, chapter on the detached pronoun and on fronting the object
nhi-007.q: The highlighted word is a detached pronoun (ḍamīr munfaṣil). What is its role?
o: Mafʿūl bihi of the following verb, brought forward to express restriction and emphasis, in the position of an accusative
Fāʿil of the following verb, in the position of a nominative
Mubtadaʾ of a nominal sentence, in the position of a nominative
Muḍāf ilayhi, in the position of a genitive
nhi-007.e: Normally the object follows the verb, but here it is put first so that the worship is restricted to God alone. A detached pronoun is used because an attached one cannot come before the verb. It is mabnī, with the position (maḥall) of an accusative.

nhi-008.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the imperfect verb (al-fiʿl al-muḍāriʿ)
nhi-008.q: What is the state of the highlighted verb and what is its subject (fāʿil)?
o: Imperfect, nominative (marfūʿ) with ḍamma; the fāʿil is an implied pronoun meaning ‘we’
Imperfect, jussive (majzūm) with sukūn; the fāʿil is an implied pronoun meaning ‘we’
Imperfect, nominative with ḍamma; the fāʿil is the following pronoun
Perfect, built on fatḥa; the fāʿil is an implied ‘he’
nhi-008.e: The imperfect is marfūʿ when no particle puts it into the subjunctive or jussive; its sign for this form is ḍamma. Its fāʿil is a hidden pronoun (ḍamīr mustatir) meaning ‘we’, which cannot be shown on the surface here.

nhi-009.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on verbs taking two objects (aʿṭā wa-bābuhā)
nhi-009.q: The verb before the highlighted word takes two objects. What is the highlighted word?
o: The second object (mafʿūl bihi thānin), accusative; the first object is the attached pronoun ‘us’
The first object, accusative; the second is the attached pronoun
nhi-009.e: The imperative of ‘guide’ takes the pronoun ‘us’ as its first object and the word shown as its second, directly here (the second object can also come with a preposition). It is manṣūb with fatḥa.

nhi-010.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the naʿt
nhi-010.q: The highlighted word is an adjective of the word before it. What case does it take?
o: Accusative (manṣūb), because the word it describes is accusative
Nominative (marfūʿ), because adjectives are always nominative
Genitive (majrūr), because it is the last word of the sentence
Jussive (majzūm), because it follows an imperative
nhi-010.e: A naʿt copies the case of the word it describes. The described word is the second object of the verb and so is accusative. Jussive applies only to verbs.

nhi-011.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on pronouns
nhi-011.q: The highlighted word is an imperative with the attached pronoun ‘nā’ (us). What is the position of ‘nā’?
o: Accusative (maḥall naṣb), the first object of the verb
Nominative (maḥall rafʿ), the subject of the verb
Genitive (maḥall jarr), annexed to the verb
No position, it is only a plural marker
nhi-011.e: The subject of an imperative is an implied ‘you’. The attached ‘nā’ is the thing the guidance is asked for, so it is the object, in the position of an accusative; the pronoun is mabnī so no sign appears.

nhi-012.src: Ibn Hishām, Qaṭr al-Nadā, chapter on the conjunction (al-ʿaṭf)
nhi-012.q: What is the highlighted word grammatically?
o: Genitive, joined by ʿaṭf to the preceding genitive word; its sign is yāʾ
Accusative, a ḥāl; its sign is fatḥa
Nominative, a khabar; its sign is wāw
Genitive, a muḍāf; its sign is kasra
nhi-012.e: The conjunction wa- joins this word to the genitive word before it, so it is genitive too. It is a sound masculine plural, hence the yāʾ sign. The negative particle before it does not change this.

nhi-013.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on demonstratives (ismā al-ishāra)
nhi-013.q: The verse starts with a demonstrative pronoun. What is its position?
o: Mabnī (indeclinable) in the position of a nominative, as mubtadaʾ
Mabnī in the position of an accusative, as object
Muʿrab nominative with ḍamma, as fāʿil
Mabnī in the position of a genitive, as muḍāf ilayhi
nhi-013.e: Demonstratives are mabnī, so they show no case sign; they only have a position (maḥall). At the head of the nominal sentence the demonstrative is the mubtadaʾ, so its position is rafʿ.

nhi-014.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the signs of i‘rāb; Ibn Hishām, Qaṭr al-Nadā, on the maqṣūr
nhi-014.q: The highlighted word ends in alif maqṣūra. How is its case sign shown?
o: As an implied sign (muqaddar) on the final alif, since the alif cannot carry a vowel
As a visible ḍamma, fatḥa or kasra on the last letter
As a yāʾ in the genitive and accusative
It has no case at all because it is an indeclinable word
nhi-014.e: Nouns ending in alif maqṣūra (the maqṣūr) are declinable, but their final alif cannot take a vowel, so the nominative, accusative and genitive signs are only implied. The tanwīn shown in writing does not change this.

nhi-015.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the five verbs (al-afʿāl al-khamsa)
nhi-015.q: What is the sign of the nominative state of the highlighted verb?
o: The presence of the final nūn, since it is one of the five verbs
A ḍamma on the last letter
The omission of the final nūn
A sukūn on the last letter
nhi-015.e: Verbs of the pattern yafʿalūna/yafʿalāni/tafʿalīna are the ‘five verbs’; they are raised by keeping the nūn and put into the jussive or subjunctive by dropping it. The wāw is the subject pronoun.

nhi-016.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the accusative nouns
nhi-016.q: What is the highlighted word in the clause ‘and they establish …’?
o: The direct object (mafʿūl bihi), accusative with fatḥa
The muḍāf ilayhi, genitive with kasra
nhi-016.e: The verb already has its subject (the wāw). The word that receives the action is the direct object, which is always manṣūb; the sign is fatḥa.

nhi-017.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on inna and its sisters
nhi-017.q: The verse opens with the particle inna. What is the highlighted word, which follows it?
o: Its ism, in the position of an accusative
Its khabar, in the position of a nominative
The subject of a verb, nominative
nhi-017.e: Inna and its sisters enter a nominal sentence, put the mubtadaʾ into the accusative (as their ism) and keep the khabar in the nominative. The word shown is a relative pronoun, which is mabnī, so it only has the position of an accusative.

nhi-018.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the building of the imperative
nhi-018.q: The highlighted word is an imperative addressed to a group. On what is it built (mabnī)?
o: On the omission of the nūn, since its imperfect is one of the five verbs
On the omission of the weak letter
nhi-018.e: The imperative is built on whatever marks the jussive of its imperfect. For the five verbs this is the dropping of the nūn, so the plural imperative ends in -ū without nūn.

nhi-019.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the substitute for the agent (nāʾib al-fāʿil)
nhi-019.q: The verb before the highlighted word is passive. What is the highlighted word?
o: Nāʾib al-fāʿil (the deputy of the subject), nominative with ḍamma
Khabar of a nominal sentence, nominative
nhi-019.e: When a verb is passive, the agent is dropped and the object takes its place in the nominative: it is called nāʾib al-fāʿil (or the fāʿil of the passive). It therefore has ḍamma.

nhi-020.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the genitive nouns
nhi-020.q: The highlighted word follows the adverb ‘with’ (maʿa). What is its case and sign?
o: Genitive, as muḍāf ilayhi of maʿa; the sign is yāʾ
Accusative, as an adverb; the sign is fatḥa
Nominative, as khabar; the sign is wāw
Genitive, as object of a preposition; the sign is kasra
nhi-020.e: Maʿa is a noun of place (ẓarf) and is itself annexed to the following word, which is therefore the muḍāf ilayhi and majrūr. As a sound masculine plural it shows this with yāʾ.

nhi-021.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the fāʿil
nhi-021.q: Who does the action of the verb ‘it takes hold of him’ in the verse shown? What is the highlighted word?
o: The mubtadaʾ of a new sentence
nhi-021.e: The attached pronoun is the object; the agent of the verb is the word that follows it. A fāʿil is always marfūʿ, here with ḍammatān (tanwīn) because it is indefinite.

nhi-022.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the mubtadaʾ and khabar
nhi-022.q: The verse opens with ‘kull’ followed by ‘nafs’. What is the highlighted word ‘kull’?
o: Mubtadaʾ, nominative with ḍamma, and ‘nafs’ is its muḍāf ilayhi
Fāʿil, nominative, and ‘nafs’ is its object
Khabar, nominative, and ‘nafs’ is its subject
Mafʿūl muṭlaq, accusative, and ‘nafs’ is its adjective
nhi-022.e: The sentence is nominal: ‘kull’ starts it as mubtadaʾ and is annexed to ‘nafs’. The khabar is the next noun, which is itself annexed to ‘death’.

nhi-023.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the naʿt
nhi-023.q: The highlighted word describes the word before it (‘men’). What is its case?
o: Accusative (manṣūb), as naʿt of an accusative word
nhi-023.e: The preceding noun is the object of ‘He spread’ and is accusative. Its adjective follows it in case, so it is accusative as well, with tanwīn because it is indefinite.

nhi-024.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the ḥāl
nhi-024.q: The highlighted word describes the state of ‘the human being’ at the time of creation. What is it?
o: A ḥāl (circumstantial accusative), manṣūb with tanwīn fatḥa
A khabar of a mubtadaʾ, marfūʿ
nhi-024.e: A ḥāl is an indefinite accusative that tells in what state the doer or object is while the action happens. The verb is passive, ‘was created’, and the word shown gives the state of its deputy subject.

nhi-025.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapters on the fāʿil and the ʿaṭf
nhi-025.q: After the verb ‘came’, what is the highlighted word?
o: The fāʿil, nominative with ḍamma, annexed to the next word
nhi-025.e: The verb ‘came’ needs a doer. The highlighted word is that doer, marfūʿ with ḍamma, and it is annexed to the following name; the conjoined word after it shares the nominative case.

nhi-026.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the jussive (al-jazm)
nhi-026.q: The highlighted verb follows the particle ‘lam’. What is its state and sign?
o: Jussive (majzūm), with sukūn on the last letter
Built (mabnī) on fatḥa as a perfect verb
nhi-026.e: The particle ‘lam’ puts an imperfect verb into the jussive and gives it the past meaning. The sign for a sound verb is sukūn, which here is shown (and lightly vocalised with kasra when reading on).

nhi-027.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on inna and its sisters
nhi-027.q: In the verse shown, what is the highlighted word?
o: The ism of inna, accusative with fatḥa
The fāʿil of a verb, nominative
nhi-027.e: Inna puts the noun that follows it into the accusative as its ism, and its khabar comes later (here a prepositional phrase).

nhi-028.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the signs of i‘rāb
nhi-028.q: The highlighted word is the object of ‘they did’. What is its sign of case?
o: Kasra, standing in for fatḥa, because it is a sound feminine plural
Yāʾ, because it is a plural
Sukūn, because it is a verb
nhi-028.e: The sound feminine plural (jamʿ muʾannath sālim) takes kasra in place of fatḥa in the accusative. It is manṣūb as object of ‘they did’.

nhi-029.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on kāna and its sisters
nhi-029.q: The verse opens with kāna plus a pronoun. What is the highlighted word that follows?
nhi-029.e: Kāna puts the subject in the nominative (here the attached pronoun) and the predicate in the accusative: it is the khabar of kāna, which is annexed to the next noun.

nhi-030.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the perfect verb
nhi-030.q: The highlighted perfect verb ends with the attached ‘nā’ of the subject. On what is it built?
o: On sukūn, because a movable pronoun of the subject is attached
On fatḥa, as every perfect verb
On ḍamma, because a plural wāw is attached
On the omission of the nūn
nhi-030.e: A perfect verb is normally built on fatḥa, but when a movable subject pronoun (tāʾ, nā, nūn of the feminine) attaches, it is built on sukūn. With a plural wāw it is built on ḍamma instead.

nhi-031.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the ʿaṭf
nhi-031.q: The highlighted word follows the conjunction wa- after ‘eleven stars’. What is its case and why?
o: Accusative, because it is joined by ʿaṭf to the accusative object ‘stars’
Nominative, because it starts a new sentence
Genitive, because it follows the number
nhi-031.e: The verb ‘I saw’ governs the whole series. The conjunction wa- links this noun to the preceding accusative object, so it takes the same case.

nhi-032.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on kāna and its sisters
nhi-032.q: The highlighted word follows ‘you were’ (kuntum). What is it, and what is its sign?
o: Khabar of kāna, accusative; the sign is yāʾ because it is a sound masculine plural
Ism of kāna, nominative; the sign is wāw
Khabar of kāna, accusative; the sign is fatḥa
Muḍāf ilayhi, genitive; the sign is yāʾ
nhi-032.e: In ‘kuntum ṣādiqīna’ the attached tum is the ism of kāna. The predicate is accusative, and being a sound masculine plural it shows the accusative with yāʾ.

nhi-033.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the ʿaṭf
nhi-033.q: The verse says ‘God bears witness … and the angels …’. What is the highlighted word?
o: Joined by ʿaṭf to the nominative fāʿil, so it is nominative
nhi-033.e: The verb ‘bears witness’ has God as its subject. The conjunction wa- links the angels to that subject, so the word takes the nominative with ḍamma. The angels are also witnesses, the subject here being multiple.

nhi-034.src: Ibn Hishām, Qaṭr al-Nadā, chapter on the vocative (al-munādā)
nhi-034.q: The highlighted word is the vocative ‘our Lord’ (the particle of calling is omitted). What is it?
o: Munādā, an annexed noun, accusative with fatḥa
nhi-034.e: A vocative that is annexed to another word (muḍāf) is always accusative. The particle of calling is dropped here, as often in supplications.

nhi-035.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the five verbs
nhi-035.q: The highlighted verb is a dual form. What is its state and sign?
o: Nominative (marfūʿ), with the nūn kept; the alif is the subject pronoun
Nominative, with ḍamma on the last letter
nhi-035.e: The dual imperfect (yafʿalāni/tafʿalāni) is one of the five verbs; the alif is the subject, and the nūn is kept as sign of the nominative because nothing puts it into the subjunctive or jussive.

nhi-036.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on verbs taking two objects
nhi-036.q: The verb ‘We have given you’ takes two objects. What is the highlighted word?
o: The second object, accusative with fatḥa; the first is the attached ‘you’
nhi-036.e: The attached pronoun ‘ka’ is the recipient and the first object; the thing given is the second object, manṣūb. The ‘we’ is the subject (nā), attached to the verb.

nhi-037.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the mubtadaʾ and khabar
nhi-037.q: In the short nominal sentence of the verse shown, what is the highlighted word?
nhi-037.e: The first word is the mubtadaʾ (the divine name). The highlighted word completes the meaning as its khabar. Both are marfūʿ, and no verb is present.

nhi-038.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the accusative nouns
nhi-038.q: What is the highlighted word in the clause ‘and sheds …’?
o: The direct object, accusative with fatḥa
nhi-038.e: The verb ‘sheds’ has a hidden subject; the thing that is shed is its direct object, manṣūb. The sign is fatḥa.

nhi-039.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the prepositions (ḥurūf al-jarr)
nhi-039.q: The highlighted word begins with the preposition bi-. What is the status of the whole phrase?
o: A prepositional phrase (jār wa-majrūr) attached to the verb ‘I seek refuge’
nhi-039.e: The preposition makes the following noun majrūr, and the phrase is attached to the verb ‘I seek refuge’: it tells in whom the refuge is sought. It is not an independent part of the sentence in the way a fāʿil is.

nhi-040.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the imperative
nhi-040.q: The highlighted word is a singular imperative of a sound verb. On what is it built, and who is its hidden subject?
o: On sukūn; the hidden subject means ‘you’
On fatḥa; the hidden subject means ‘he’
On ḍamma; the hidden subject means ‘we’
On the omission of the nūn; the hidden subject means ‘they’
nhi-040.e: The imperative of a sound verb for one person is built on sukūn (its jussive form). Its fāʿil is always a hidden ‘anta’ (you).

nhi-041.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the genitive nouns
nhi-041.q: What is the highlighted word, the last word of the verse shown?
o: A muḍāf ilayhi, genitive with kasra
A mafʿūl bihi, accusative with fatḥa
nhi-041.e: It completes an annexation: the preceding noun is the muḍāf and this one the muḍāf ilayhi, which is always majrūr. Its sign is kasra.

nhi-042.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the genitive nouns
nhi-042.q: What is the highlighted word after ‘Lord’ in the verse shown?
nhi-042.e: ‘Lord of’ is a muḍāf; the word that completes it is the muḍāf ilayhi and is majrūr, whatever else follows.

nhi-043.src: Ibn Hishām, Qaṭr al-Nadā, chapter on the tawābiʿ
nhi-043.q: The highlighted word is a divine attribute that follows ‘the Ever-Living’. What is its case?
o: Nominative (marfūʿ) with ḍamma, as it agrees with the word before it
nhi-043.e: Both attributes are in the nominative, either as naʿt or as further khabars of the mubtadaʾ. In every analysis the word is marfūʿ with ḍamma, never accusative or genitive.

nhi-044.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the ʿaṭf
nhi-044.q: The highlighted word follows ‘and’ after the heavens. What is it?
o: Joined by ʿaṭf to the accusative ‘heavens’, so accusative with fatḥa
Joined to a genitive, so genitive
Khabar of a new sentence, nominative
nhi-044.e: The verb ‘encompasses’ has a subject and takes ‘the heavens’ as object. The conjunction wa- adds a second object. ‘Heavens’ is a sound feminine plural with kasra for accusative; this word, a singular, shows fatḥa.

nhi-045.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on mabnī and muʿrab
nhi-045.q: The highlighted verb ends with the subject pronoun ‘ta’ (you). What is the verb and what is the position of the ‘ta’?
o: A perfect verb built on sukūn; the ‘ta’ is the fāʿil, in the position of a nominative
A perfect verb built on fatḥa; the ‘ta’ is the mafʿūl, in the position of an accusative
An imperfect verb in the nominative; the ‘ta’ is a letter of prefix
A perfect verb built on ḍamma; the ‘ta’ is the muḍāf ilayhi
nhi-045.e: When a movable subject pronoun is attached to a perfect, the verb is built on sukūn. The ‘ta’ of the second person is the subject, mabnī, in the position of a nominative. The object is the following attached pronoun ‘them’ introduced by ʿalā.

nhi-046.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the fāʿil
nhi-046.q: The verb at the start of the verse is a perfect verb. What is the highlighted word that follows it?
o: The khabar of a nominal sentence
nhi-046.e: A verb is followed by its doer, always marfūʿ. The word is the one who believed, a definite noun with ḍamma.

nhi-047.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the accusative nouns
nhi-047.q: The verb ‘burdens’ has God as its subject. What is the highlighted word?
o: The first direct object, accusative with tanwīn fatḥa
nhi-047.e: ‘Burdens’ takes two objects in this construction: the person burdened and the thing laid on them. The highlighted word is the first, manṣūb and indefinite.

nhi-048.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the perfect verb
nhi-048.q: On what is the highlighted perfect verb built, with no pronoun attached to it?
nhi-048.e: A perfect verb with nothing attached (or with the dual alif or the feminine tāʾ) is built on fatḥa. Sukūn comes with movable subject pronouns, ḍamma with wāw.

nhi-049.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the genitive nouns
nhi-049.q: The preceding word, ‘one that tastes’, is a khabar annexed to the highlighted word. What is the highlighted word?
nhi-049.e: The active participle ‘tasting’ is annexed to what is tasted, an annexation of a participle to its object. The second term of any annexation is genitive.

nhi-050.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the signs of i‘rāb
nhi-050.q: The highlighted word is the object of the verb ‘created’ and is a sound feminine plural. What is its sign?
nhi-050.e: In the accusative the sound feminine plural takes kasra instead of fatḥa. Yāʾ is for the sound masculine plural and the dual; alif is for the nominative dual.

nhi-051.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on lā that negates the genus (lā al-nāfiya lil-jins)
nhi-051.q: What kind of particle is the highlighted lā, which stands before an indefinite singular noun in the accusative position?
o: Lā al-nāfiya lil-jins, negating the whole class and acting like inna
Lā al-nāhiya, a prohibition that jussives the verb
Lā al-zāʾida, a particle with no function
Lā that negates the present like laysa, with a nominative ism
nhi-051.e: The particle before an indefinite singular noun built on fatḥa, with no tanwīn, is lā of absolute negation of the genus. It works like inna: it gives its ism the accusative position and leaves the khabar nominative.

nhi-052.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on lā that negates the genus
nhi-052.q: What is the highlighted noun, which comes directly after the negating particle?
o: The ism of lā, built on fatḥa in the position of an accusative
A mafʿūl bihi, accusative with a visible fatḥa
nhi-052.e: After lā of genus negation, a singular noun (neither annexed nor resembling an annexation) is built on fatḥa without tanwīn. The fatḥa is a sign of building, not of case, and the position is accusative. The khabar is the following prepositional phrase.

nhi-053.src: Ibn Hishām, Qaṭr al-Nadā, chapter on the vocative (al-munādā)
nhi-053.q: In the vocative ‘yā ayyuhā’, what is ‘ayyu’ and what is ‘hā’?
o: ‘Ayyu’ is the munādā, built on ḍamma in the position of an accusative; ‘hā’ is a particle of attention (tanbīh)
‘Ayyu’ is a mubtadaʾ; ‘hā’ is its khabar
‘Ayyu’ is a fāʿil; ‘hā’ is a pronoun in the genitive
‘Ayyu’ is a particle; ‘hā’ is the munādā
nhi-053.e: A definite noun cannot be called directly with yā, so ‘ayyu’ serves as a bridge: it is the real munādā (a single word, built on ḍamma) and ‘hā’ is the particle of attention. The word that follows is its description.

nhi-054.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the active participle (ismu al-fāʿil)
nhi-054.q: The highlighted word is an active participle with tanwīn after inna. What is its role and what does it govern?
o: Khabar of inna, nominative; it governs the following noun as its object
Ism of inna, accusative; it has no object
Fāʿil, nominative; it governs a ḥāl
Muḍāf ilayhi, genitive; it governs a verb
nhi-054.e: The participle is the khabar of inna and keeps its verbal power because it indicates the present or future and has tanwīn: it can take an object (‘one who will place …’). Its object here is the accusative noun at the end of the clause.

nhi-055.src: Ibn Hishām, Awḍaḥ al-Masālik, chapter on the exception (al-istithnāʾ)
nhi-055.q: Why must the highlighted noun after illā be accusative in the verse shown?
o: Because the sentence before illā is complete and affirmative, so the excepted noun is obligatorily accusative
Because it is the object of the verb ‘prostrated’
Because illā is always followed by an accusative, in every sentence
nhi-055.e: In a complete affirmative sentence (the excepted-from group is mentioned and no negation precedes), the noun after illā takes the accusative as mustathnā. After a negative sentence a nominative substitute is allowed. This noun also has no tanwīn, being a non-Arabic name.

nhi-056.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the signs of i‘rāb (the diptote)
nhi-056.q: The highlighted name follows the preposition lām and is a non-Arabic proper name, a diptote. What is its sign?
o: Fatḥa in place of kasra, with no tanwīn
Yāʾ, as in a sound masculine plural
nhi-056.e: A diptote (mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf) takes fatḥa instead of kasra in the genitive and has no tanwīn, unless it is annexed or has al-. Non-Arabic proper names are among the causes of this restriction.

nhi-057.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the verb ending in a weak letter
nhi-057.q: The highlighted perfect verb ends in alif maqṣūra. How is its building shown?
o: Built on an implied fatḥa on the final alif
Built on the omission of the final letter
nhi-057.e: A perfect verb is built on fatḥa, but the alif cannot take a vowel, so the fatḥa is only implied (muqaddar) there, hindered by the impossibility of pronouncing it.

nhi-058.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the jussive (jawāzim al-muḍāriʿ)
nhi-058.q: The highlighted verb follows lā in a prohibition. What is its state and sign?
o: Jussive (majzūm) by lā al-nāhiya, with the omission of the final nūn
Subjunctive by an implied an, with fatḥa
Built on sukūn like an imperative
nhi-058.e: Lā of prohibition puts the imperfect in the jussive. This verb is one of the five verbs, whose sign of jussive is the loss of the nūn; the wāw is the subject.

nhi-059.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the ḥāl (the confirming ḥāl)
nhi-059.q: The highlighted word describes a state of those addressed whose meaning is already implied by the verb before it. What is it called?
nhi-059.e: The verb already means ‘to spread corruption’, so the participle that follows it adds nothing new but reinforces: a ḥāl muʾakkida for its verb. It is accusative with yāʾ as a sound masculine plural.

nhi-060.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on lā that negates the genus
nhi-060.q: In the reading of Ḥafṣ the highlighted word has a plain fatḥa and no tanwīn. What is the best explanation?
o: It is the ism of lā al-nāfiya lil-jins, built on fatḥa
It is a manṣūb object of the verb before it
It is a mubtadaʾ in the accusative
It is a diptote in the genitive
nhi-060.e: The fatḥa and the absence of tanwīn show the ism of lā of genus negation, built on fatḥa. In some other readings the first nouns of the series are marfūʿ with tanwīn, which changes the analysis.

nhi-061.src: Ibn Hishām, Awḍaḥ al-Masālik, chapter on the conditional particles (jawāzim)
nhi-061.q: The highlighted verb follows the particle that begins a conditional clause (‘whatever you do …’). What is its state?
o: Jussive (majzūm) as the verb of the condition, with the nūn dropped
Built on fatḥa as a perfect
nhi-061.e: ‘Mā’ here is a conditional noun and jussives two verbs, the condition and its answer. This verb is the condition; as one of the five verbs it is jussive by loss of the nūn, and the answer is the next verb.

nhi-062.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the subjunctive (nawāṣib)
nhi-062.q: The verb after lan is one of the five verbs. How is it put into the subjunctive?
o: By dropping the final nūn; the wāw is the subject
By a fatḥa on the last letter
By a sukūn on the last letter
nhi-062.e: Lan puts an imperfect into the subjunctive. For the five verbs the sign of the subjunctive is the loss of the nūn, the same as for the jussive.

nhi-063.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the conditional particles
nhi-063.q: In the clause ‘Whoever does evil …’, what is the highlighted verb?
o: The verb of the condition, jussive with sukūn, after the conditional noun man
nhi-063.e: Man here is conditional and jussives two verbs. This is the condition (jussive with sukūn) and the next verb is the answer, also jussive. If man were a relative pronoun the verb would be nominative.

nhi-064.src: Ibn Hishām, Awḍaḥ al-Masālik, chapter on the absolute object (al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq)
nhi-064.q: The highlighted verbal noun repeats the meaning of the verb before it to emphasise it. What is it?
nhi-064.e: A masdar of the same root as the verb, put after it to give emphasis, is a mafʿūl muṭlaq. It is manṣūb. The emphasis here denies any metaphorical reading of the speaking.

nhi-065.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the vocative annexed to the speaker's yāʾ
nhi-065.q: The highlighted word is a vocative meaning ‘my father’ and ends in tāʾ. What does this tāʾ stand for?
o: It replaces the speaker's yāʾ (‘my’); the word is an annexed munādā, accusative
It marks the feminine; the word is a feminine noun
It is the pronoun ‘you’ in the genitive
It is a dual ending; the word is a mubtadaʾ
nhi-065.e: When a child calls a parent, the yāʾ of the speaker (‘my’) can be replaced by tāʾ, which is why the word keeps a masculine sense although it ends in tāʾ. The noun is a muḍāf munādā and therefore manṣūb.

nhi-066.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the number and the tamyīz
nhi-066.q: The highlighted word explains the number ‘eleven’. What is it?
nhi-066.e: After the numbers 11 to 99 the counted noun is a singular indefinite accusative, called tamyīz, which removes the vagueness of the number.

nhi-067.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, chapter on the tawkīd
nhi-067.q: The highlighted word, ‘all of them’, repeats the meaning of ‘the angels’ for emphasis. What is it?
o: Tawkīd (emphasis), nominative, following the word it emphasises
nhi-067.e: ‘Kull’ annexed to a pronoun that refers back to the emphasised word is a tawkīd maʿnawī, a follower of the fāʿil in the nominative. The next word is a further tawkīd.

nhi-068.src: Ibn Hishām, Awḍaḥ al-Masālik, chapter on the adverb (al-mafʿūl fīhi)
nhi-068.q: The highlighted word says when the journey took place. What is it?
o: Ẓarf zamān (adverb of time), accusative, attached to the verb
nhi-068.e: A noun that answers ‘when?’ and implies the preposition ‘in’ is a mafʿūl fīhi (ẓarf), always manṣūb. The word is indefinite, which also hints at the shortness of the journey.

nhi-069.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the tamyīz (al-tamyīz al-muḥawwal)
nhi-069.q: The highlighted word explains in what respect the head burned. How is it classified?
o: Tamyīz muḥawwal ʿan al-fāʿil (the specifier converted from the subject)
nhi-069.e: The meaning is ‘the grey of the head blazed’: the original subject (grey hair) has been turned into a tamyīz, accusative, and the original subject word has become the fāʿil. This is called a converted tamyīz.

nhi-070.src: Ibn Hishām, Awḍaḥ al-Masālik, chapter on the object of purpose (al-mafʿūl lahu)
nhi-070.q: The highlighted word gives the reason for putting their fingers in their ears. What is it?
nhi-070.e: A verbal noun that states why an action is done, shares its time and doer with the verb, and is not a verb, is a mafʿūl lahu (li-ajlihi), manṣūb. The word is annexed to ‘death’.

nhi-071.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the annexation (al-iḍāfa)
nhi-071.q: The highlighted word is the interrogative noun ‘which’ preceded by the preposition bi-. What is its case?
o: Genitive, by the preposition; it is also annexed to the next word
Accusative, because it is a question word
Nominative, because it starts the clause
Built on sukūn in the position of an accusative
nhi-071.e: ‘Ayy’ is declinable. It is majrūr here by the preposition and is the muḍāf of the following noun. Most interrogative words are mabnī, but ‘ayy’ is an exception because of its annexation.

nhi-072.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on innamā; Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on inna and mā
nhi-072.q: The word after innamā is nominative. Why is it not accusative as the ism of inna?
o: Because mā is kāffa (restraining): it stops inna from governing, so the word is a mubtadaʾ
Because it is the khabar of kāna
nhi-072.e: When mā is attached to inna it normally cancels its government, so the clause becomes an ordinary nominal sentence. The word is the mubtadaʾ in the nominative, and its khabar follows.

nhi-073.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the lām of the khabar (lām al-ibtidāʾ)
nhi-073.q: The highlighted word begins with a lām before the khabar of inna. What is this lām called and what does it do?
o: Lām al-ibtidāʾ (the displaced lām, muzaḥlaqa), giving emphasis, moved from the mubtadaʾ to the khabar
Lām al-jarr, a preposition of ownership
Lām al-taʿlīl, a lām of purpose
nhi-073.e: Because inna and lām both give emphasis, the two cannot stand together. The lām of the mubtadaʾ is moved to the khabar and called muzaḥlaqa (the slid one). Here the khabar is a prepositional phrase.

nhi-074.src: Ibn Hishām, Awḍaḥ al-Masālik, chapter on the exception
nhi-074.q: The group introduced by illā is excepted from the human being, which is generic. How is the relative pronoun analysed?
o: As the excepted noun, in the position of an accusative
As the subject of a verb, nominative
nhi-074.e: The relative pronoun is mabnī and stands in the position of the accusative as mustathnā. The human being is taken in the sense of a class, so the exception removes the believers who do righteous deeds from the loss.

nhi-075.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the jussive of the defective verb
nhi-075.q: The highlighted verb ‘see’ follows lam. How is the jussive shown?
o: By dropping the final weak letter (ḥadhf ḥarf al-ʿilla)
By a sukūn on the last letter
nhi-075.e: A verb ending in a weak letter is jussive by dropping the weak letter, here the final alif (the previous vowel remains as a clue). Sukūn is for sound verbs and loss of the nūn for the five verbs.

nhi-076.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on ammā; Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on fronting the object
nhi-076.q: The highlighted word is placed before a verb that governs it. What is its role?
o: Mafʿūl bihi of the verb that follows, brought forward, accusative
Fāʿil of the verb that follows
nhi-076.e: In ammā constructions an element must follow ammā, so the object of the verb is moved forward in front of it. It is manṣūb by the verb that comes after the fāʾ.

nhi-077.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on the pronoun of separation
nhi-077.q: The pronoun between the mubtadaʾ and its definite khabar is called what, and what does it do?
o: Ḍamīr al-faṣl: it separates khabar from adjective and adds emphasis
Ḍamīr al-shaʾn: it replaces a subject
Ḍamīr mustatir: it is a hidden subject
Ḍamīr muttaṣil: it completes the verb
nhi-077.e: A pronoun of the third person placed between a mubtadaʾ and a definite khabar is called faṣl: it makes clear that what follows is a khabar and not a description, and adds restriction. Basran grammarians say it has no i‘rāb position.

nhi-078.src: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 12:82; Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on ḥadhf al-muḍāf
nhi-078.q: Literally the accusative object is a town, but the meaning is its inhabitants. How is this analysed?
o: As mafʿūl bihi with an understood muḍāf (‘the people of’) that has been dropped
As ẓarf makān, the place of questioning
nhi-078.e: Grammarians explain that a muḍāf is omitted (ḥadhf al-muḍāf) and the muḍāf ilayhi takes its place in the accusative: ‘ask the people of the town’. This is figurative speech, not asking the stones.

nhi-079.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the diptote (mā lā yanṣarif)
nhi-079.q: The highlighted word is a non-Arabic proper name that is the object of the verb. What are its case and sign?
o: Accusative with fatḥa and no tanwīn, as a diptote
nhi-079.e: As an accusative object it is manṣūb; the fatḥa without tanwīn shows that the name does not take tanwīn (diptote: foreign proper name). It is placed before the subject because of the pronoun in the subject.

nhi-080.src: Ibn Hishām, Qaṭr al-Nadā, chapter on the vocative (the word Allāhumma)
nhi-080.q: What is the mīm at the end of the highlighted word and what is the word as a whole?
o: The doubled mīm stands in for the particle yā; the word is a munādā built on an implied ḍamma
The mīm is a dual marker; the word is a mubtadaʾ
The mīm is a pronoun in the genitive; the word is a muḍāf
The mīm is a letter of prefix; the word is a verb
nhi-080.e: According to the Basrans, the doubled mīm replaces the particle of calling yā, so the two never stand together; the word is a munādā mufrad, built on an implied ḍamma, in the position of an accusative.

nhi-081.src: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on the beginning of al-Baqara; Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb
nhi-081.q: Which statement gives a recognised analysis of the highlighted word?
o: A ḥāl from ‘the Book’ (or from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase), with the case sign implied on the final alif
A tamyīz specifying the preceding negated noun
A mafʿūl muṭlaq of an omitted verb
A muḍāf ilayhi of the prepositional phrase before it
nhi-081.e: Commentators and grammarians analyse the word as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of the Book, while others take it as a second khabar or as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ. In all cases it ends in alif maqṣūra, so the sign is only implied. It is not a tamyīz, since nothing before it needs specifying.

nhi-082.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the fāʿil (the cases of obligatory fronting of the object)
nhi-082.q: Why must the object stand before the subject in the clause shown?
o: Because the subject carries a pronoun that refers back to the object, and the pronoun may not precede its referent
Because the object is a proper name
nhi-082.e: When the fāʿil contains an attached pronoun that returns to the object, the object must be put first; otherwise the pronoun would refer to something not yet mentioned. Being a diptote or a name does not require fronting.

nhi-083.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the noun annexed to the speaker's yāʾ
nhi-083.q: The highlighted word is nominative and is annexed to the speaker's yāʾ. How is its ḍamma shown?
o: As an implied ḍamma on the last letter, blocked by the kasra required before the yāʾ
As a yāʾ in place of ḍamma
It has no case because the yāʾ makes it mabnī
nhi-083.e: A noun annexed to the speaker's yāʾ is declinable, but the letter before the yāʾ must carry kasra, so the case sign (here ḍamma) is only implied, prevented by the vowel that suits the yāʾ (ishtighāl al-maḥall bi-ḥarakat al-munāsaba).

nhi-084.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on lā; Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on lā
nhi-084.q: In the reading of Ḥafṣ this noun has ḍamma with tanwīn after lā. How is it analysed?
o: As a mubtadaʾ in the nominative (with lā not the genus-negating one), whose khabar is the prepositional phrase
As the ism of lā al-nāfiya lil-jins, built on fatḥa
As a fāʿil of an omitted verb
nhi-084.e: The genus-negating lā requires an ism built on fatḥa without tanwīn. Ḍamma with tanwīn shows that the noun is a mubtadaʾ after a negative lā (which some grammarians let work like laysa and others treat as non-working), with the prepositional phrase as khabar. Readers who build it on fatḥa have the other analysis.

nhi-085.src: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 2:177; Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on laysa
nhi-085.q: In the reading of Ḥafṣ this noun is accusative after laysa. What is its role, and what is the subject of laysa?
o: Khabar of laysa, put first; the ism is the following clause ‘an’ plus the subjunctive, a verbal noun in the nominative
Ism of laysa; the khabar is the following clause
Mafʿūl bihi of the following verb; laysa has no ism
Ḥāl; the ism of laysa is a hidden pronoun
nhi-085.e: In this reading (Ḥamza and Ḥafṣ) the accusative noun is the khabar fronted, and the ism of laysa is the verbal noun made by ‘an tuwallū’. Other readers make the noun nominative as the ism and the clause the khabar; both are grammatical.

nhi-086.src: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 2:197; Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on ḥadhf al-muḍāf
nhi-086.q: ‘Ḥajj’ is an action, but the highlighted word names a period of time. How do the grammarians reconcile the sentence?
o: By an omitted muḍāf, such as ‘the time of Ḥajj is the months …’ or ‘Ḥajj takes place in the months …’
By taking the word as an accusative adverb
By taking the word as a vocative
By saying that the khabar is the verb that follows
nhi-086.e: A nominal sentence needs the khabar to match the mubtadaʾ. Since an action cannot be identical to a time, a word like ‘time’ is understood before the subject or before the khabar. This is the standard ḥadhf al-muḍāf explanation.

nhi-087.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on illā and on the formula of tawḥīd
nhi-087.q: The statement is negative and the pronoun comes after illā. Which analysis of the highlighted pronoun is correct?
o: A badal from the position of lā and its ism (a nominative), the sentence being negative so a substitute is preferred
A mustathnā that must be accusative, as the sentence is complete
The khabar of lā, built on fatḥa
A tawkīd of the ism of lā
nhi-087.e: After a complete negative sentence the excepted word is preferably a badal rather than an obligatory accusative. As the subject of lā + ism is in the position of a mubtadaʾ, the pronoun, which is mabnī, stands in the position of a nominative. Some grammarians prefer a badal from the pronoun in the omitted khabar.

nhi-088.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the types of tanwīn (tanwīn al-ʿiwaḍ)
nhi-088.q: The highlighted word is a mubtadaʾ with tanwīn although it is followed by a verb. What kind of tanwīn is this?
o: Tanwīn al-ʿiwaḍ, standing in for an omitted muḍāf ilayhi
Tanwīn al-tamkīn (the ordinary sign of a fully declinable noun)
Tanwīn al-tankīr (marking indefiniteness of an indeclinable word)
Tanwīn al-muqābala (the sign of the sound feminine plural)
nhi-088.e: The word means ‘each of them’; the omitted muḍāf ilayhi (‘them’) is replaced by tanwīn. A word like ‘kull’ is normally annexed, so this tanwīn is a compensation. The khabar is the following verb.

nhi-089.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the particles of the subjunctive
nhi-089.q: What puts the highlighted verb, which follows ḥattā, into the subjunctive?
o: An understood an after ḥattā, with the nūn dropped
The earlier lan in the verse, as the same clause
The jussive that follows the conditional mā
nhi-089.e: Ḥattā is a preposition and cannot govern a verb; the subjunctive comes from an implied an (obligatory after ḥattā), forming a verbal noun that the preposition governs. The earlier lan governs the earlier verb only. The word is one of the five verbs, so the sign is the loss of the nūn.

nhi-090.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the jussive of defective verbs
nhi-090.q: The highlighted verb is the answer to the condition. What is its form?
o: Jussive passive, the final weak letter dropped as the sign of the jussive
Nominative with an implied ḍamma on the final alif
Built on sukūn like a perfect
nhi-090.e: The answer of a jussive-causing condition is itself jussive. Its root ends in a weak letter, so the jussive is shown by dropping that letter and leaving the vowel before it. The verb is passive: ‘he will be requited with it’.

nhi-091.src: Sībawayh, al-Kitāb, chapter on what is put in the accusative for glorification and praise; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, on difficult cases
nhi-091.q: This noun is accusative in the middle of a series of nominatives. Which explanation is attributed to Sībawayh?
o: Accusative of praise (madḥ) after an understood verb such as ‘I single out’, the series being cut off
ʿAtf on the khabar of the series, with a normal accusative
A ḥāl of the believers in the series
A mafʿūl muṭlaq of the verb ‘they believe’
nhi-091.e: Sībawayh cites this verse as an example of qaṭʿ for praise: the speaker breaks the series by an accusative with an omitted verb, to stress the point. Other grammarians proposed coordination with an earlier word, but his explanation is the qaṭʿ one.

nhi-092.src: Sībawayh, al-Kitāb, chapter on the noun after in; Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on the verb after the conditional particle
nhi-092.q: According to the Basran view, how is the nominative noun after the conditional ‘in’ analysed?
o: As the fāʿil of an omitted verb, explained by the verb that follows it
As a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is the verb that follows
As the ism of in, accusative
As a ḥāl of the verb that follows
nhi-092.e: The Basrans (following Sībawayh) hold that the conditional particles ‘in’ and ‘idhā’ are followed by a verb, so a noun after them is a fāʿil of an omitted verb that the later verb interprets. Al-Akhfash and some others allowed a mubtadaʾ here.

nhi-093.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on mā, lā, lāta and in that work like laysa
nhi-093.q: The highlighted noun is accusative after the demonstrative. Which usage explains this?
o: The Ḥijāzī usage in which mā works like laysa: the demonstrative is its ism and this noun its khabar, accusative
The Tamīmī usage in which mā does not work and the noun would be nominative
nhi-093.e: In the dialect of the Ḥijāz, the negative mā works like laysa and puts the khabar in the accusative; the Banū Tamīm treat it as non-working and use the nominative. The verse shown follows the Ḥijāzī usage.

nhi-094.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the absolute object (omitted verbs)
nhi-094.q: The verse opens with an accusative word. How is it analysed?
o: Mafʿūl muṭlaq of an obligatorily omitted verb (‘I declare … glorified’), annexed to the relative pronoun
nhi-094.e: The word is a verbal noun that has taken the place of its verb; the verb is omitted by obligation (ḥadhf wājib), so the noun is accusative as mafʿūl muṭlaq and is annexed to ‘He who’.

nhi-095.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the noun-verb (ismu al-fiʿl)
nhi-095.q: The highlighted word is an expression of disgust. What is its grammatical class?
o: An ism fiʿl muḍāriʿ (a noun standing for a verb meaning ‘I am annoyed’), built on kasra
A muḍāf ilayhi in the genitive
A mafʿūl muṭlaq in the accusative
nhi-095.e: Interjection-like words that stand for a verb are called asmāʾ al-afʿāl. This one stands for the present tense (‘I feel disgust’), is mabnī, and ends in kasra with tanwīn in this reading (tanwīn of indefiniteness).

nhi-096.src: Ibn Hishām, Awḍaḥ al-Masālik, chapter on the subjunctive after lām al-taʿlīl
nhi-096.q: The highlighted verb begins with a lām. Which analysis is correct?
o: Lām al-taʿlīl; the verb is subjunctive by an understood an, with a visible fatḥa on the yāʾ
Lām al-amr; the verb is jussive with the yāʾ dropped
Lām al-ibtidāʾ; the verb is nominative with an implied ḍamma
Lām al-jarr; the verb is a genitive noun
nhi-096.e: A lām followed by a verb to give a reason is lām al-taʿlīl, after which an is implied and puts the verb in the subjunctive; the yāʾ shows the fatḥa. Lām al-amr would give a jussive with the final yāʾ dropped, but the sense here is purpose, not command.

nhi-097.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the nūn of emphasis
nhi-097.q: The highlighted verb answers a condition but is not jussive. Why?
o: Because it is built on fatḥa through direct contact with the heavy nūn of emphasis, and it answers an oath
Because it is a perfect verb
Because it is the khabar of kāna
Because a nominative cannot follow in
nhi-097.e: A verb that directly meets the nūn of emphasis (nūn al-tawkīd) is mabnī on fatḥa and not declinable. The clause with lām is the answer of an implied oath, which takes the place of the answer of the condition.

nhi-098.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on the tamyīz (al-tamyīz al-muḥawwal ʿan al-mafʿūl)
nhi-098.q: The highlighted word is the specifier in ‘We made the earth burst forth …’. How is it classified?
o: Tamyīz converted from the object (‘We made the springs of the earth burst forth’)
nhi-098.e: The original meaning is ‘We caused the springs of the earth to burst forth’: the object (springs) became a tamyīz and its muḍāf ilayhi (the earth) became the object. That is a tamyīz muḥawwal ʿan al-mafʿūl.

nhi-099.src: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 36:82; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, on Yā Sīn
nhi-099.q: In the reading of Ḥafṣ this verb is nominative. How is the nominative explained?
o: The fāʾ is resumptive: it starts a new clause with an understood subject, ‘so it comes to be’
The verb is the answer to an imperative, which requires the nominative
The verb is jussive, written as nominative
The verb is the khabar of an omitted inna
nhi-099.e: After a command, a verb with fāʾ can be accusative as a reply to the imperative, as some of the ten readers read it. Ḥafṣ reads it nominative: the clause is separate and means ‘and it then is’. The nominative presents the coming-to-be as a fresh statement.

nhi-100.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on compound numbers (al-ʿadad al-murakkab)
nhi-100.q: The highlighted word is the first part of the number twelve. How is the number ‘twelve’ treated?
o: The first part is declined like a dual (alif here, nominative), the second part is built on fatḥa
Both parts are built on fatḥa
Both parts are declined with their own endings
The first part is built, the second declined
nhi-100.e: Compound numbers from 11 to 19 are built on fatḥa in both parts, with the exception of twelve: its first part (two) is declined like the dual and the second is built on fatḥa. Here it is the subject and takes the nominative alif.

nhi-101.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, chapter on kāna (the order of its ism and khabar)
nhi-101.q: The clause begins with a negated kāna, then a prepositional phrase and a noun with ‘equal’. What is the highlighted final word?
o: The ism of kāna, nominative, placed last
A badal from the pronoun in the prepositional phrase
A fāʿil of the prepositional phrase
nhi-101.e: The jussive kāna governs an ism and a khabar. The ism here is placed last because the khabar and the prepositional phrase come first (for emphasis on the negation of anything comparable). Hence the last word is nominative.

nhi-102.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on ḍamīr al-shaʾn
nhi-102.q: Which statement gives a recognised analysis of the highlighted pronoun?
o: Ḍamīr al-shaʾn (pronoun of the matter), a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is the entire clause after it
A tawkīd of the imperative before it
A mafʿūl bihi of the imperative, accusative
nhi-102.e: A third-person pronoun that comes at the head of a sentence without antecedent, and is explained by the sentence that follows, is ḍamīr al-shaʾn (or al-qiṣṣa). The pronoun is the mubtadaʾ, and the clause after it is its khabar. Other analyses take it as an ordinary mubtadaʾ with the divine name as khabar.

nhi-103.src: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 2:285; Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on omitted verbs
nhi-103.q: The highlighted verbal noun is accusative, yet there is no verb governing it in the clause. How is it explained?
o: By an omitted verb such as ‘We ask for’, which the supplication implies
By the verb ‘they said’ earlier in the clause, which takes it as a direct object
By annexation to the next word
nhi-103.e: Supplications often leave out the verb; a verbal noun such as ‘forgiveness’ is then accusative as a mafʿūl muṭlaq or object of an implied verb (we ask your forgiveness). The next word ‘our Lord’ is a separate vocative.

nht-001.q: Into which three parts do the grammarians divide the word (al-kalima)?
nht-001.e: Every Arabic word is either a noun (ism), a verb (fiʿl) or a particle (ḥarf) that brings a meaning. Adjectives and pronouns are kinds of nouns, and subject or predicate are functions, not parts of speech.

nht-002.q: Which of these is a sign that a word is a noun (ism)?
o: It can take the definite article al-
It can be preceded by the particle qad
It can be preceded by the particle sawfa
It can take a silent feminine tāʾ
nht-002.e: Nouns are recognised by jarr, tanwīn, the article al- and the prepositions. Qad, sīn, sawfa and the silent feminine tāʾ (as in qāmat) are signs of the verb.

nht-003.q: Which phrase begins with a particle that marks the following word as a verb?
nht-003.e: Qad enters only on verbs, so it is one of the signs of the verb. Fī, ilā and min are prepositions, which enter only on nouns.

nht-004.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb ʿalāmāt al-iʿrāb
nht-004.q: What is the original sign of rafʿ (the nominative case)?
nht-004.e: The original signs are ḍamma for rafʿ, fatḥa for naṣb, kasra for jarr and sukūn for jazm. Other signs (letters, deletion) are substitutes.

nht-005.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb ʿalāmāt al-iʿrāb
nht-005.q: What is the original sign of jazm (the jussive mood)?
nht-005.e: Jazm is found only in the present-tense verb, and its original sign is sukūn, as in lam yaktub. Its substitute sign is deletion of a letter.

nht-006.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb makhfūḍāt al-asmāʾ
nht-006.q: In the sentence ذَهَبَ الوَلَدُ إِلَى المَسْجِدِ, what is the case of المَسْجِدِ?
nht-006.e: The noun comes after the preposition ilā, and a noun after a preposition is majrūr, here with a kasra. Jazm never occurs in nouns.

nht-007.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb al-mubtadaʾ wa-l-khabar
nht-007.q: In the sentence الطَّالِبُ مُجْتَهِدٌ, what is الطَّالِبُ?
nht-007.e: A nominal sentence opens with a noun, the mubtadaʾ, which is marfūʿ and free of any governing word; مُجْتَهِدٌ is its khabar. There is no verb, so there can be no fāʿil.

nht-008.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb al-mubtadaʾ wa-l-khabar
nht-008.q: In the sentence الجَوُّ جَمِيلٌ, what function does جَمِيلٌ have?
nht-008.e: جَمِيلٌ completes the meaning of the mubtadaʾ and is marfūʿ, so it is the khabar. It cannot be a naʿt here: an attribute of a definite noun would itself be definite (al-jamīl).

nht-009.q: In the sentence كَتَبَ الطَّالِبُ الدَّرْسَ, what is the iʿrāb of الطَّالِبُ?
nht-009.e: The student is the one who performed the action of the verb kataba, so he is the fāʿil, which is always marfūʿ. الدَّرْسَ is the object.

nht-010.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb al-mafʿūl bihi
nht-010.q: In the sentence كَتَبَ الطَّالِبُ الدَّرْسَ, what is the iʿrāb of الدَّرْسَ?
nht-010.e: The lesson is what the action fell upon, so it is the direct object (mafʿūl bihi), manṣūb with a fatḥa.

nht-011.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on the divisions of the sentence
nht-011.q: Which of these is a verbal sentence (jumla fiʿliyya)?
nht-011.e: A verbal sentence is one that begins with a verb, here yaqraʾu. The other three contain no verb at all and are nominal sentences (the last with a fronted khabar).

nht-012.src: Ibn Hishām, Sharḥ Qaṭr al-Nadā, on the built and the declined
nht-012.q: Which kind of verb is always mabnī (fixed in its ending)?
nht-012.e: The past-tense verb is always mabnī. The present-tense verb is muʿrab: it changes for rafʿ, naṣb and jazm (lan yaktuba, lam yaktub), unless a nūn of emphasis or of the feminine plural is attached.

nht-013.q: Who wrote the short primer of grammar known as al-Ājurrūmiyya?
nht-013.e: Al-Ājurrūmiyya is named after its author, Abū ʿAbd Allāh Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad ibn Ājurrūm al-Ṣanhājī of Fez. It is traditionally the first grammar text memorised by beginners.

nht-014.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb ʿalāmāt al-iʿrāb
nht-014.q: In the sentence جَاءَ الطَّالِبَانِ, which sign shows that الطَّالِبَانِ is marfūʿ?
