nht-014.e: The dual is marfūʿ with an alif in place of the ḍamma, and manṣūb or majrūr with a yāʾ. The nūn is not a case sign: it compensates for the tanwīn of the singular.

nht-015.src: al-Ḥamlāwī, Shadhā al-ʿArf fī Fann al-Ṣarf, on the root and the mīzān
nht-015.q: What is the root of the word مَكْتَبَة (library)?
nht-015.e: The mīm and the final tāʾ marbūṭa are added letters; the three root letters kāf, tāʾ, bāʾ carry the core meaning of writing, as in kataba, kitāb and kātib.

nht-016.src: al-Ḥamlāwī, Shadhā al-ʿArf fī Fann al-Ṣarf, on the active participle
nht-016.q: What is the active participle (ism al-fāʿil) of ذَهَبَ?
nht-016.e: From a form I verb the active participle is built on the pattern fāʿil, so dhahaba gives dhāhib. Dhahāb is the maṣdar and madhhab a noun of place.

nht-017.src: al-Ḥamlāwī, Shadhā al-ʿArf fī Fann al-Ṣarf, on the passive participle
nht-017.q: What is the passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl) of كَتَبَ?
nht-017.e: From a form I verb the passive participle follows the pattern mafʿūl, so kataba gives maktūb, "written". Kātib is the active participle.

nht-018.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb makhfūḍāt al-asmāʾ
nht-018.q: Which of these words is a preposition (ḥarf jarr)?
nht-018.e: ʿAlā puts the following noun in jarr. Lam makes the present verb majzūm, lan makes it manṣūb, and inna governs a nominal sentence.

nht-019.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb al-ʿawāmil al-dākhila ʿalā al-mubtadaʾ wa-l-khabar
nht-019.q: In the sentence كَانَ الجَوُّ بَارِدًا, what is بَارِدًا?
nht-019.e: Kāna enters a nominal sentence, leaves the mubtadaʾ marfūʿ as its ism and makes the khabar manṣūb. So al-jaww is the ism of kāna and bāridan its khabar.

nht-020.src: Ibn al-Anbārī, Nuzhat al-Alibbāʾ fī Ṭabaqāt al-Udabāʾ, biography of Abū al-Aswad
nht-020.q: Who is commonly credited with laying the first foundations of Arabic grammar?
nht-020.e: Most reports name Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī, many of them saying he did so at the prompting of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib. Sībawayh came later and wrote the first comprehensive book on grammar.

nht-021.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb ʿalāmāt al-iʿrāb
nht-021.q: In the sentence جَاءَ أَبُوكَ, what is the sign of rafʿ in أَبُوكَ?
nht-021.e: Abū is one of the five nouns (ab, akh, ḥam, fū, dhū). When they are muḍāf to something other than the yāʾ of the speaker, they take wāw for rafʿ, alif for naṣb and yāʾ for jarr.

nht-022.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb ʿalāmāt al-iʿrāb
nht-022.q: In the sentence مَرَرْتُ بِأَخِيكَ, what is the sign of jarr in أَخِيكَ?
nht-022.e: Akh is one of the five nouns, which are majrūr with a yāʾ in place of the kasra. Here it follows the preposition bi-.

nht-023.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb ʿalāmāt al-iʿrāb
nht-023.q: In the sentence رَأَيْتُ المُعَلِّمِينَ, what is the sign of naṣb in المُعَلِّمِينَ?
nht-023.e: The sound masculine plural is marfūʿ with wāw and manṣūb or majrūr with yāʾ. Its nūn is fatḥa-voweled, unlike the kasra-voweled nūn of the dual.

nht-024.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb ʿalāmāt al-iʿrāb
nht-024.q: In the sentence رَأَيْتُ الطَّالِبَاتِ, what is the sign of naṣb in الطَّالِبَاتِ?
o: A kasra in place of the fatḥa
A yāʾ in place of the fatḥa
An alif in place of the fatḥa
nht-024.e: The sound feminine plural is manṣūb with a kasra in place of the fatḥa, so its naṣb and jarr look the same.

nht-025.src: Ibn Hishām, Sharḥ Qaṭr al-Nadā, bāb mā lā yanṣarif
nht-025.q: In the sentence مَرَرْتُ بِأَحْمَدَ, why does أَحْمَدَ end in a fatḥa although it is majrūr?
o: It is a diptote: a proper name on a verb pattern
It is the object of the verb marartu
It is a ḥāl describing the speaker
The preposition bi- requires a fatḥa
nht-025.e: Aḥmad combines being a proper name (ʿalamiyya) with a verb pattern (wazn al-fiʿl), so it is mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf: no tanwīn, and fatḥa in place of kasra in jarr. With al- or as muḍāf it takes a kasra again.

nht-026.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb ʿalāmāt al-iʿrāb
nht-026.q: In the sentence الطُّلَّابُ يَكْتُبُونَ, what is the sign of rafʿ in يَكْتُبُونَ?
o: A ḍamma assumed on the nūn
nht-026.e: Yaktubūna is one of the five verbs (present verbs ending in alif of the dual, wāw of the plural or yāʾ of the feminine addressee plus nūn). They are marfūʿ by keeping the nūn; the wāw itself is the fāʿil pronoun.

nht-027.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb ʿalāmāt al-iʿrāb
nht-027.q: In the sentence لَمْ يَكْتُبُوا, what is the sign of jazm in يَكْتُبُوا?
nht-027.e: The five verbs are manṣūb and majzūm by dropping the nūn. The alif written after the wāw is the so-called separating alif and has no case function.

nht-028.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb ʿalāmāt al-iʿrāb
nht-028.q: In the sentence لَمْ يَدْعُ, what is the sign of jazm in يَدْعُ?
o: Deletion of the final weak letter
nht-028.e: Yadʿū ends in a weak letter (wāw). A present verb with a weak final letter is majzūm by deleting that letter; the ḍamma that remains is just a sign of the deleted wāw.

nht-029.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb iʿrāb al-afʿāl
nht-029.q: Which particle puts the following present-tense verb into jazm?
nht-029.e: Lam negates the past meaning and makes the present verb majzūm (lam yadhhab). Lan, an and kay all make it manṣūb.

nht-030.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb iʿrāb al-afʿāl
nht-030.q: In the sentence لَنْ يَتَأَخَّرَ الطَّالِبُ, why is يَتَأَخَّرَ manṣūb?
o: It comes after the particle lan
It is the object of the sentence
nht-030.e: Lan negates the future and makes the present verb manṣūb with a fatḥa. Verbs are never objects or governed by prepositions.

nht-031.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb al-ʿawāmil al-dākhila ʿalā al-mubtadaʾ wa-l-khabar
nht-031.q: Which of these verbs is one of the sisters of kāna?
nht-031.e: Aṣbaḥa works like kāna: rafʿ for the ism, naṣb for the khabar. Ẓanna belongs to the verbs that take two objects, while laʿalla and kaʾanna are sisters of inna.

nht-032.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb al-ʿawāmil al-dākhila ʿalā al-mubtadaʾ wa-l-khabar
nht-032.q: Which of these words is one of the sisters of inna?
nht-032.e: Lākinna, like inna, makes the ism manṣūb and the khabar marfūʿ. Laysa, ṣāra and mā zāla are sisters of kāna, which work the other way round.

nht-033.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb al-ʿawāmil al-dākhila ʿalā al-mubtadaʾ wa-l-khabar
nht-033.q: In the sentence إِنَّ العِلْمَ نُورٌ, what is the iʿrāb of العِلْمَ?
nht-033.e: Inna makes the former mubtadaʾ manṣūb as its ism and leaves the khabar marfūʿ, so al-ʿilma is its ism and nūrun its khabar. Inna is a particle, so it has no object.

nht-034.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb al-mafʿūl alladhī lam yusamma fāʿiluh
nht-034.q: In the sentence كُتِبَ الدَّرْسُ, what is the iʿrāb of الدَّرْسُ?
nht-034.e: Kutiba is passive: the doer is not named and the former object takes its place in rafʿ. The book of al-Ājurrūmiyya calls this "the object whose agent is not named".

nht-035.q: In the sentence جَاءَ الطَّالِبُ مُسْرِعًا, what is مُسْرِعًا?
nht-035.e: Musriʿan is an indefinite manṣūb word that describes the state of the student at the time he came, which is the definition of the ḥāl.

nht-036.q: In the sentence اشْتَرَيْتُ عِشْرِينَ كِتَابًا, what is كِتَابًا?
nht-036.e: "Twenty" is vague until kitāban specifies what is counted, so kitāban is tamyīz of a number, singular and manṣūb. The object of ishtaraytu is ʿishrīna itself.

nht-037.q: In the sentence جَلَسْتُ جُلُوسًا هَادِئًا, what is جُلُوسًا?
nht-037.e: Julūsan is the maṣdar of the same verb jalasa, used manṣūb to describe the kind of sitting; such a maṣdar is the mafʿūl muṭlaq. Jalasa is intransitive, so it has no mafʿūl bihi.

nht-038.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb ẓarf al-zamān wa-ẓarf al-makān
nht-038.q: In the sentence صُمْتُ يَوْمَ الخَمِيسِ, what is يَوْمَ?
nht-038.e: Yawma names the time in which the fasting took place and carries the meaning of fī, so it is a ẓarf of time (mafʿūl fīhi), manṣūb and muḍāf to al-khamīsi.

nht-039.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb al-mafʿūl min ajlih
nht-039.q: In the sentence وَقَفَ الطُّلَّابُ احْتِرَامًا لِلْمُعَلِّمِ, what is احْتِرَامًا?
nht-039.e: Iḥtirāman is a manṣūb maṣdar that states the reason for standing (out of respect), which defines the mafʿūl li-ajlihi. It is not mafʿūl muṭlaq because it is not from the root of waqafa.

nht-040.q: In the sentence رَأَيْتُ رَجُلًا كَرِيمًا, what is كَرِيمًا?
nht-040.e: Karīman follows the indefinite rajulan in case and indefiniteness and describes it permanently, so it is a naʿt. A ḥāl normally needs a definite owner, which rajulan is not.

nht-041.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb makhfūḍāt al-asmāʾ
nht-041.q: In the phrase هَذَا كِتَابُ الطَّالِبِ, what is الطَّالِبِ?
nht-041.e: Kitābu is the muḍāf and al-ṭālibi the muḍāf ilayh, which is always majrūr. There is no preposition in the phrase; the jarr comes from the iḍāfa.

nht-042.src: al-Ḥamlāwī, Shadhā al-ʿArf fī Fann al-Ṣarf, on the augmented triliteral
nht-042.q: To which verb form does عَلَّمَ (to teach) belong?
nht-042.e: ʿAllama doubles the middle radical of ʿalima, the mark of form II, which often makes a verb transitive or causative: "to make someone know".

nht-043.src: al-Ḥamlāwī, Shadhā al-ʿArf fī Fann al-Ṣarf, on the meanings of istafʿala
nht-043.q: Which meaning does the pattern istafʿala most often carry, as in اسْتَغْفَرَ?
nht-043.e: The commonest meaning of form X is ṭalab, seeking: istaghfara is to seek forgiveness. Mutual action belongs to tafāʿala and colours to ifʿalla.

nht-044.q: In the call يَا طَالِبَ العِلْمِ, what is the iʿrāb of طَالِبَ?
nht-044.e: A vocative noun that is muḍāf is manṣūb, here ṭāliba before al-ʿilmi. Only the single proper name and the intended indefinite are mabnī on ḍamma.

nht-045.q: In the sentence حَضَرَ الطُّلَّابُ إِلَّا خَالِدًا, why is خَالِدًا manṣūb?
o: It is excepted from a complete affirmative sentence
It is the direct object of the verb ḥaḍara
It is a ḥāl coming after illā
The noun after illā is always manṣūb
nht-045.e: When the sentence is complete (the excepted-from, al-ṭullāb, is mentioned) and affirmative, the mustathnā after illā must be manṣūb. The last option is a common mistake: in negative or incomplete sentences other cases occur.

nht-046.q: In the sentence مَا حَضَرَ إِلَّا خَالِدٌ, what is the iʿrāb of خَالِدٌ?
nht-046.e: The excepted-from is not mentioned (istithnāʾ mufarragh), so illā has no effect and the noun takes the case its position demands. The verb ḥaḍara needs a fāʿil, so khālidun is the fāʿil.

nht-047.q: In the sentence مَا حَضَرَ الطُّلَّابُ إِلَّا خَالِد, which ending(s) may خَالِد take?
o: Naṣb, or rafʿ as a badal of al-ṭullāb
Naṣb only, as after any illā
Rafʿ only, as the fāʿil of ḥaḍara
Jarr only, as a muḍāf ilayh
nht-047.e: In a complete negative sentence the mustathnā may be manṣūb or follow the excepted-from as a badal; the badal (khālidun) is the preferred option when the exception is of the same kind.

nht-048.q: In the sentence حَضَرَ الطُّلَّابُ غَيْرَ خَالِدٍ, why is خَالِدٍ majrūr?
o: It is the muḍāf ilayh of ghayr
Ghayr is a particle of jarr
It is a badal of al-ṭullāb
nht-048.e: Ghayr is a noun that carries the case of the exception itself (here manṣūb), and the excepted noun after it is always majrūr as its muḍāf ilayh. The same applies to siwā.

nht-049.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb al-mafʿūl maʿah
nht-049.q: In the classic grammar example سِرْتُ وَالنِّيلَ, what is النِّيلَ?
nht-049.e: The wāw here means "along with" (wāw al-maʿiyya): I travelled alongside the Nile. Coordination is impossible because the river does not travel, so the noun is manṣūb as mafʿūl maʿahu.

nht-050.q: In the sentence أَكَلْتُ الرَّغِيفَ ثُلُثَهُ, what kind of badal is ثُلُثَهُ?
o: Badal of a part from the whole
Badal of the whole from the whole
nht-050.e: A third is part of the loaf, so it is badal baʿḍ min kull. Such a badal normally carries a pronoun referring back to the whole, here the -hu.

nht-051.q: In the sentence جَاءَ المُدِيرُ نَفْسُهُ, what is نَفْسُهُ?
nht-051.e: Nafs, ʿayn, kull, ajmaʿ and their like are words of semantic emphasis: they remove the possibility that only a messenger of the director came. Lafẓī emphasis would repeat the same word.

nht-052.src: Ibn Hishām, Sharḥ Qaṭr al-Nadā, on the particles that put two verbs in jazm
nht-052.q: In the sentence إِنْ تَجْتَهِدْ تَنْجَحْ, what is تَنْجَحْ?
o: A ḥāl in the place of naṣb
nht-052.e: In is a conditional particle that puts two verbs in jazm: the first (tajtahid) is the condition, the second (tanjaḥ) its answer and consequence.

nht-053.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on the letter fāʾ
nht-053.q: Why must the answer in إِنْ جَاءَكَ ضَيْفٌ فَأَكْرِمْهُ be introduced by fāʾ?
o: The answer is an imperative, a request
The condition is a past-tense verb
The answer is a past-tense verb
In is always followed by fāʾ
nht-053.e: The fāʾ is required when the answer cannot itself stand as a condition, for example a nominal sentence, a request (amr, nahy), or a verb with lan, qad or sīn. A past verb as condition needs no fāʾ.

nht-054.src: al-Ḥamlāwī, Shadhā al-ʿArf fī Fann al-Ṣarf, on the sound and weak verb
nht-054.q: How is the verb وَجَدَ classified in ṣarf?
nht-054.e: A verb whose first radical is a weak letter (wāw or yāʾ) is called mithāl. Ajwaf has a weak middle radical, nāqiṣ a weak final one, and mahmūz contains a hamza.

nht-055.q: In the call يَا خَالِدُ, what is the iʿrāb of خَالِدُ?
o: Mabnī on ḍamma, in the position of naṣb
nht-055.e: A single proper name in the vocative is built on what it would have in rafʿ, here a ḍamma without tanwīn, but its position is naṣb because it is the object of an implied "I call".

nht-056.src: al-Ḥamlāwī, Shadhā al-ʿArf fī Fann al-Ṣarf, on the sound and weak verb
nht-056.q: Which of these verbs is nāqiṣ (weak in its final radical)?
nht-056.e: Ramā goes back to the root r-m-y, with a weak final radical. Waʿada is mithāl, qāla is ajwaf (root q-w-l), and kataba is sound.

nht-057.src: al-Ḥamlāwī, Shadhā al-ʿArf fī Fann al-Ṣarf, on the mīzān ṣarfī
nht-057.q: What is the morphological pattern (mīzān) of the verb قَالَ?
nht-057.e: The mīzān follows the original letters: qāla comes from qawala, whose voweled wāw after a fatḥa turned into alif. So it is weighed faʿala, with the ʿayn standing for the changed wāw.

nht-058.src: Ibn Hishām, Sharḥ Qaṭr al-Nadā, on estimated case signs
nht-058.q: In the sentence جَاءَ الفَتَى, how is الفَتَى marked as marfūʿ?
o: By an estimated ḍamma, since it cannot be pronounced
By an apparent ḍamma on the alif
By the alif as a substitute sign
It is mabnī and has no rafʿ
nht-058.e: Al-fatā is ism maqṣūr, ending in a fixed alif. All three case vowels are estimated on it because pronouncing them on the alif is impossible (taʿadhdhur).

nht-059.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyyat Ibn Mālik, bāb jamʿ al-taksīr
nht-059.q: Which of these is one of the patterns of the plural of paucity (jamʿ al-qilla)?
nht-059.e: The plurals of paucity, used in principle for three to ten, have four patterns: afʿul, afʿāl, afʿila and fiʿla. Fuʿūl, fiʿāl and mafāʿīl are plurals of multitude.

nht-060.src: Ibn Hishām, Sharḥ Qaṭr al-Nadā, bāb mā lā yanṣarif
nht-060.q: In the sentence صَلَّيْتُ فِي مَسَاجِدَ كَثِيرَةٍ, why is مَسَاجِدَ majrūr with a fatḥa?
o: It has the pattern of muntahā al-jumūʿ
It is a sound feminine plural
It is muḍāf to the following noun
It is a foreign proper name
nht-060.e: Masājid is on the pattern mafāʿil, a "furthest plural" form, which alone is enough to make a noun mamnūʿ min al-ṣarf. Without al- or iḍāfa it takes a fatḥa in jarr and no tanwīn.

nht-061.q: In the sentence لَا رَجُلَ فِي الدَّارِ, what is the iʿrāb of رَجُلَ?
o: Ism of lā, mabnī on fatḥa
Ism of lā, manṣūb with tanwīn
nht-061.e: Lā that negates the whole genus governs like inna. When its ism is a single indefinite noun directly after it, the ism is mabnī on fatḥa, without tanwīn, in the position of naṣb.

nht-062.src: Ibn Ājurrūm, al-Ājurrūmiyya, bāb ẓanantu wa-akhawātuhā
nht-062.q: In the sentence ظَنَنْتُ الجَوَّ بَارِدًا, what is بَارِدًا?
nht-062.e: Ẓanna and its sisters enter a nominal sentence and make both parts manṣūb as two objects: al-jaww is the first, bāridan the second. It cannot be a naʿt, since it is indefinite after a definite noun.

nht-063.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyyat Ibn Mālik, bāb al-ʿadad
nht-063.q: Which of these phrases is grammatically correct?
nht-063.e: The numbers three to ten take the opposite gender of the counted noun and their tamyīz is a majrūr plural. Qalam is masculine, so the number is khamsatu, followed by aqlāmin.

nht-064.src: al-Ḥamlāwī, Shadhā al-ʿArf fī Fann al-Ṣarf, on the mithāl verb
nht-064.q: What is the present tense of the form I verb وَصَلَ (to arrive)?
nht-064.e: In a mithāl wāwī verb of the pattern faʿala–yafʿilu, the wāw drops in the present: waṣala gives yaṣilu, as waʿada gives yaʿidu. Yūṣilu is the present of form IV awṣala.

nht-065.src: al-Sīrāfī, Akhbār al-Naḥwiyyīn al-Baṣriyyīn, on Sībawayh
nht-065.q: Which teacher of Sībawayh is quoted more than any other in al-Kitāb?
nht-065.e: Sībawayh's chief teacher was al-Khalīl, founder of the science of prosody, whose views fill al-Kitāb. Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ were Kūfan contemporaries and rivals, and al-Mubarrad belongs to a later Baṣran generation.

nht-066.q: Which pair are both leading grammarians of the Kūfan school?
nht-066.e: Al-Kisāʾī, also one of the seven Quran readers, and his student al-Farrāʾ are the pillars of Kūfan grammar. All the other names are Baṣrans.

nht-067.src: Abū al-Barakāt al-Anbārī, al-Inṣāf fī Masāʾil al-Khilāf, on the origin of derivation
nht-067.q: Which statement correctly describes the dispute over the origin of derivation (aṣl al-ishtiqāq)?
o: Baṣrans: the maṣdar is the origin; Kūfans: the verb
Baṣrans: the verb is the origin; Kūfans: the maṣdar
Both schools hold the verb is the origin
Both schools hold the participle is the origin
nht-067.e: The Baṣrans argued that the maṣdar, which names the event without time, is the source from which verb and participles derive. The Kūfans held that the maṣdar comes from the verb, citing among other things that it follows the verb in soundness and weakness.

nht-068.src: Abū al-Barakāt al-Anbārī, al-Inṣāf fī Masāʾil al-Khilāf bayna al-Naḥwiyyīn al-Baṣriyyīn wa-l-Kūfiyyīn
nht-068.q: Who wrote al-Inṣāf, the classic work on the points of disagreement between the Baṣran and Kūfan grammarians?
nht-068.e: Abū al-Barakāt al-Anbārī set out over a hundred disputed questions in al-Inṣāf, giving the arguments of both schools and usually siding with the Baṣrans. Ibn Jinnī is known for al-Khaṣāʾiṣ.

nht-069.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on ḍamīr al-faṣl
nht-069.q: The pronoun that Kūfans call ʿimād (support), as in زَيْدٌ هُوَ القَائِمُ, is called by the Baṣrans:
nht-069.e: The Baṣrans call it faṣl because it separates khabar from naʿt, making clear that al-qāʾim is the predicate; the Kūfans call it ʿimād because the speaker leans on it. The pronoun of the matter is a different construction, which Kūfans call al-ḍamīr al-majhūl.

nht-070.src: Ibn Hishām, Qaṭr al-Nadā wa-Ball al-Ṣadā
nht-070.q: Who wrote Qaṭr al-Nadā wa-Ball al-Ṣadā together with his own commentary on it?
nht-070.e: Qaṭr al-Nadā is one of Ibn Hishām's teaching texts, which he explained himself in Sharḥ Qaṭr al-Nadā. He also wrote Shudhūr al-Dhahab and Mughnī al-Labīb. Ibn ʿAqīl is known for his commentary on the Alfiyya.

nht-071.q: In which poetic metre is the Alfiyya of Ibn Mālik composed?
nht-071.e: Like most didactic poems (manẓūmāt), the Alfiyya is in rajaz, whose flexible metre and rhyming couplets make it easy to memorise. Its roughly one thousand lines give it its name.

nht-072.src: Ibn Mālik, al-Khulāṣa (Alfiyyat Ibn Mālik), introduction
nht-072.q: Which earlier grammar poem does Ibn Mālik name in the introduction to his Alfiyya, claiming to surpass it while acknowledging its precedence?
nht-072.e: Ibn Mālik says his poem surpasses the Alfiyya of Ibn Muʿṭī, then concedes that Ibn Muʿṭī has the merit of precedence and prays for him. The Ājurrūmiyya was written after Ibn Mālik, and the Kāfiya is prose.

nht-073.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyyat Ibn Mālik, bāb lā allatī li-nafy al-jins
nht-073.q: In the sentence لَا طَالِبَ عِلْمٍ خَاسِرٌ, what is the iʿrāb of طَالِبَ?
o: Ism of lā, muʿrab and manṣūb
Ism of lā, mabnī on fatḥa
nht-073.e: The ism of lā al-nāfiya li-l-jins is mabnī only when it is a single word (mufrad). When it is muḍāf, as here, or resembles a muḍāf, it is declinable and manṣūb with an apparent fatḥa; khāsirun is the khabar.

nht-074.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyyat Ibn Mālik, bāb kāna wa-akhawātuhā
nht-074.q: In the often-cited grammar example إِذَا كَانَ الشِّتَاءُ فَأَدْفِئُونِي, how is kāna analysed?
o: Kāna tāmma; al-shitāʾ is its fāʿil
Kāna nāqiṣa with an omitted khabar
Kāna zāʾida with no effect at all
Kāna nāqiṣa; al-shitāʾ is its khabar
nht-074.e: Here kāna means "to come, to occur" and is complete in itself: it needs only a marfūʿ fāʿil and no khabar. Ibn Mālik says the tāmm kāna is content with its rafʿ.

nht-075.src: Ibn Hishām, Sharḥ Qaṭr al-Nadā, on mā, lā, lāta and in that work like laysa
nht-075.q: Which statement correctly describes the two Arab usages in مَا خَالِدٌ مُسَافِر?
o: Ḥijāz makes mā work like laysa (musāfiran); Tamīm leave it marfūʿ
Tamīm make mā work like laysa; Ḥijāz leave the khabar marfūʿ
Both make the khabar manṣūb when it comes after the ism
Both leave the khabar marfūʿ, since mā is a particle
nht-075.e: In the dialect of the Ḥijāz, mā governs like laysa under conditions (e.g. the khabar not placed first, no illā), giving mā khālidun musāfiran. Banū Tamīm do not let it govern and say mā khālidun musāfirun.

nht-076.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyyat Ibn Mālik, bāb al-ibtidāʾ
nht-076.q: In the question أَقَادِمٌ أَخَوَاكَ؟, what is the iʿrāb of أَخَوَاكَ?
o: Fāʿil of qādim, standing in for the khabar
Mubtadaʾ placed after its khabar qādim
nht-076.e: Qādim is an active participle relying on the interrogative, so it is mubtadaʾ and works like its verb; akhawāka is its fāʿil, which fills the place of the khabar. It cannot be a delayed mubtadaʾ, since a khabar for a dual would have to be dual (qādimāni).

nht-077.src: al-Ḥamlāwī, Shadhā al-ʿArf fī Fann al-Ṣarf, on the lafīf verb
nht-077.q: How is the verb وَقَى (to protect), root w-q-y, classified?
nht-077.e: Its first and last radicals are weak, separated by a sound letter, which is lafīf mafrūq. Lafīf maqrūn has two adjacent weak radicals, as in ṭawā (ṭ-w-y).

nht-078.src: al-Ḥamlāwī, Shadhā al-ʿArf fī Fann al-Ṣarf, on ibdāl in iftaʿala
nht-078.q: What is the form VIII (iftaʿala) verb from the root ṣ-b-r?
nht-078.e: When the first radical of iftaʿala is ṣād, ḍād, ṭāʾ or ẓāʾ, the infixed tāʾ becomes ṭāʾ for ease of pronunciation: iṣṭabara. After dāl, dhāl or zāy it becomes dāl, as in izdaḥama.

nht-079.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyyat Ibn Mālik, bāb al-fāʿil
nht-079.q: Which sentence follows the usage of most Arabs when a dual fāʿil comes after its verb?
nht-079.e: When an explicit dual or plural fāʿil follows the verb, the verb stays singular. Adding a dual marker (ḥaḍarā al-ṭālibāni) is a known dialect of some tribes, nicknamed lughat akalūnī al-barāghīth, not the general usage.

nht-080.src: Ibn Hishām, Sharḥ Qaṭr al-Nadā, on the conditional nouns
nht-080.q: In the sentence مَنْ يَجْتَهِدْ يَنْجَحْ, what is the iʿrāb of مَنْ?
o: Conditional noun, mabnī, in the position of rafʿ as mubtadaʾ
Relative noun, mabnī, in the position of rafʿ as fāʿil
Conditional particle with no position in iʿrāb
Interrogative noun, mabnī, in the position of naṣb
nht-080.e: Man is a conditional noun that puts both verbs in jazm, so it is not a relative (which would leave them marfūʿ) nor a particle. As a noun it needs a position, and since the verb yajtahid is intransitive, man is in the position of a mubtadaʾ.

pr-001.q: How many prophets are mentioned by name in the Quran according to the common count?
pr-001.e: The commonly taught count is 25 prophets named in the Quran, from Ādam to Muḥammad ﷺ. Many more prophets were sent whose names are not given.

pr-002.src: Ibn Kathīr, Qaṣaṣ al-Anbiyāʾ, story of Ādam
pr-002.q: In the verse shown, what did Allah teach Ādam?
pr-002.e: Allah taught Ādam the names, then presented them to the angels, who could not name them. This showed Ādam's honour through knowledge.

pr-003.q: Who refused to prostrate to Ādam when Allah commanded it?
pr-003.e: All the angels prostrated except Iblīs, who refused out of arrogance, claiming he was better because he was created from fire.

pr-004.src: Ibn Kathīr, Qaṣaṣ al-Anbiyāʾ, story of Nūḥ
pr-004.q: Which prophet built the Ark by Allah's command?
pr-004.e: Nūḥ was commanded to build the Ark; the believers and pairs of animals were saved in it when the flood came.

pr-005.q: The verse shown mentions a sign given to Ṣāliḥ. What was it?
pr-005.e: Ṣāliḥ was sent to Thamūd and given the she-camel of Allah as a sign; they were warned not to harm her, but they hamstrung her.

pr-006.q: According to the verse shown, what did Allah command the fire into which Ibrāhīm was thrown?
o: To be cool and safe for him
To rise up to the sky
pr-006.e: Allah commanded the fire to be coolness and safety for Ibrāhīm, so it did not harm him.

pr-007.q: The verse shown describes two prophets raising the foundations of the House. Who were they?
pr-007.e: Ibrāhīm and his son Ismāʿīl raised the foundations of the Kaʿba in Mecca while praying that Allah accept it from them.

pr-008.q: In the verse shown, Yūsuf tells his father of a dream. What did he see prostrating to him?
o: Eleven stars, the sun and the moon
Seven fat and seven lean cows
pr-008.e: Yūsuf saw eleven stars, the sun and the moon prostrating to him; it was fulfilled when his parents and eleven brothers came to him in Egypt.

pr-009.q: Which prophet was swallowed by a large fish?
pr-009.e: Yūnus left his people, was cast from a ship and swallowed by a large fish, where he glorified Allah until he was rescued.

pr-010.src: Ibn Kathīr, Qaṣaṣ al-Anbiyāʾ, story of Mūsā
pr-010.q: To which ruler was Mūsā sent together with Hārūn?
pr-010.e: Mūsā and Hārūn were sent to Firʿawn, who claimed lordship and oppressed the Children of Israel in Egypt.

pr-011.q: Who was the mother of the prophet ʿĪsā?
pr-011.e: ʿĪsā was born to Maryam without a father by the command of Allah; the Quran calls him ʿĪsā ibn Maryam.

pr-012.q: The highlighted word describes Muḥammad ﷺ as what in relation to the prophets?
o: Their seal, the last of them
Their judge on the Last Day
pr-012.e: The verse calls him the seal of the prophets: no prophet comes after him. This is agreed upon by the Muslims.

pr-013.src: al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda al-Ṭaḥāwiyya, on the revealed books
pr-013.q: Which scripture was revealed to Mūsā?
pr-013.e: The Tawrāt was revealed to Mūsā; the Zabūr was given to Dāwūd and the Injīl to ʿĪsā.

pr-014.q: The verse shown names a scripture given to Dāwūd. Which one?
pr-014.e: The verse states that Allah gave Dāwūd the Zabūr. The Tawrāt went to Mūsā, the Injīl to ʿĪsā.

pr-015.q: To which people was Hūd sent, as stated in the verse shown?
pr-015.e: Hūd was sent to his brother-people ʿĀd; Ṣāliḥ went to Thamūd and Shuʿayb to Madyan.

pr-016.q: Which sin of his people did Shuʿayb especially condemn, as in the verse shown?
pr-016.e: Shuʿayb called Madyan to worship Allah alone and to give full measure and weight, not cheating people of their goods.

pr-017.q: Which prophet is the Quran's great example of patience in illness and loss?
pr-017.e: Ayyūb was afflicted in his body, family and wealth and remained patient; Allah said of him that He found him patient, an excellent servant.

pr-018.q: Which prophet was taught the speech of birds and heard an ant warn its colony?
pr-018.e: Sulaymān was taught the speech of birds, heard the ant in the valley of ants and sent the hoopoe to the Queen of Sabaʾ (Sūrat al-Naml).

pr-019.q: Which prophet prayed in old age for a son and was given Yaḥyā?
pr-019.e: Zakariyyā called on his Lord secretly despite his old age and his wife's barrenness, and was given the glad tidings of Yaḥyā.

pr-020.q: Which prophet's people were destroyed after their town was overturned and stones rained on them?
pr-020.e: The people of Lūṭ persisted in their indecency; their town was turned upside down and stones of baked clay rained upon them.

pr-021.q: Which two signs were given to Mūsā at the first revelation?
o: The staff and the shining hand
pr-021.e: At the valley of Ṭuwā Mūsā was shown his staff turning into a moving snake and his hand coming out white without blemish.

pr-022.q: For which prophet did Allah make iron soft so he could make coats of mail?
pr-022.e: Allah softened iron for Dāwūd and taught him to make full coats of mail; the mountains and birds also glorified Allah with him.

pr-023.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on names of the surahs
pr-023.q: Which of these surahs is named after a prophet?
pr-023.e: Hūd is a prophet; Maryam is the mother of ʿĪsā, Luqmān a wise man (most scholars hold he was not a prophet), and al-Kahf means the cave.

pr-024.src: Ibn Kathīr, Qaṣaṣ al-Anbiyāʾ, story of Yūsuf
pr-024.q: Who was the father of the prophet Yūsuf?
pr-024.e: Yūsuf was the son of Yaʿqūb, son of Isḥāq, son of Ibrāhīm.

pr-025.q: When people accused Maryam, how did the infant ʿĪsā respond?
pr-025.e: Maryam pointed to the child and ʿĪsā spoke in the cradle, declaring that he was a servant of Allah given the Book and made a prophet.

pr-026.q: After Ibrāhīm broke his people's idols, which one did he leave untouched?
pr-026.e: He left the biggest idol so they would turn to it; when they asked him, he told them to ask the idols, exposing that they could not speak.

pr-027.q: In the verse shown, ʿĪsā gives glad tidings of a messenger. What name is highlighted?
pr-027.e: ʿĪsā announced a messenger coming after him whose name is Aḥmad, one of the names of the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ.

pr-028.q: Which surah tells the story of one prophet from beginning to end in a single continuous narrative?
pr-028.e: Sūrat Yūsuf narrates Yūsuf's story as one unbroken account; in other surahs the stories of prophets are spread over several passages.

pr-029.q: The highlighted word opens the phrase ulū al-ʿazm, describing a group of messengers. According to the best-known view, who are they?
o: Nūḥ, Ibrāhīm, Mūsā, ʿĪsā and Muḥammad
Ādam, Nūḥ, Ibrāhīm, Mūsā and ʿĪsā
Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq, Yaʿqūb, Yūsuf and Mūsā
Dāwūd, Sulaymān, Mūsā, ʿĪsā and Muḥammad
pr-029.e: The best-known view names five messengers of firm resolve: Nūḥ, Ibrāhīm, Mūsā, ʿĪsā and Muḥammad ﷺ. The same five are singled out together in 33:7 and 42:13.

pr-030.q: How does the verse shown describe the prophet whose name is highlighted?
o: A man of truth, a prophet
A messenger to the Children of Israel
pr-030.e: Idrīs is described as ṣiddīq and nabī, and the next verse says Allah raised him to a high station. Little more is said about him in the Quran.

pr-031.q: The verse shown praises three prophets as patient. Which three?
pr-031.e: The verse names Ismāʿīl, Idrīs and Dhū al-Kifl, all among the patient. Dhū al-Kifl is named only here and in 38:48.

pr-032.q: In the verse shown Ibrāhīm addresses his father. What name is highlighted?
pr-032.e: The Quran names Ibrāhīm's father Āzar in this verse, where Ibrāhīm rebukes him for taking idols as gods.

pr-033.q: According to the verse shown, how long did Nūḥ remain among his people?
pr-033.e: The verse states he stayed among them a thousand years less fifty, i.e. 950 years, before the flood seized them.

pr-034.q: The highlighted word names the place where the Ark came to rest. What is it?
pr-034.e: After the waters subsided the Ark settled on al-Jūdī. Ṭūr Sīnāʾ is linked with Mūsā, al-Aḥqāf with ʿĀd and al-Ḥijr with Thamūd.

pr-035.q: What happened to the son of Nūḥ who refused to board the Ark?
o: He reached a mountain and survived
He boarded at the last moment
He was carried away by a wind
pr-035.e: He thought a mountain would protect him, but a wave came between them and he was among the drowned. Allah told Nūḥ that he was not of his family in faith.

pr-036.q: How were the people of ʿĀd destroyed?
o: By the sea closing over them
pr-036.e: ʿĀd were destroyed by a screaming, violent wind over seven nights and eight days. The flood was for Nūḥ's people, the stones for Lūṭ's and the sea for Pharaoh.

pr-037.q: For what skill were Thamūd known in the Quran?
pr-037.e: Thamūd carved homes into the mountains and built palaces on the plains; they were reminded of Allah's favours but rejected Ṣāliḥ.

pr-038.q: In the verse shown, how did Ibrāhīm learn that he was to sacrifice his son?
o: He saw it in a dream
An angel told him in the market
It was written on a stone
pr-038.e: Ibrāhīm saw in a dream that he was sacrificing his son; the dreams of prophets are revelation, and the son answered that he would be patient.

pr-039.q: Which title does the Quran give Ibrāhīm in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ?
o: Kalīm Allāh, the one spoken to
Rūḥ Allāh, a spirit from Him
pr-039.e: Allah took Ibrāhīm as a khalīl (4:125). Kalīm is associated with Mūsā and rūḥ minhu with ʿĪsā.

pr-040.q: The highlighted word stresses how Allah spoke to Mūsā. What does it emphasise?
o: That Allah truly spoke to him directly
That he received a written tablet
That an angel carried the speech
That he heard it in a dream
pr-040.e: The verbal noun taklīman confirms the verb: Allah really spoke to Mūsā, which is why he is called Kalīm Allāh.

pr-041.q: What did Mūsā ask Allah regarding his brother Hārūn?
o: To make him a helper sharing his task
To make him king over Egypt
To let him stay behind in Madyan
To give him the Tawrāt instead
pr-041.e: Mūsā asked that Hārūn be made a minister (wazīr) from his family to strengthen him and share in his mission, and the request was granted.

pr-042.q: Who led the Children of Israel to worship the calf while Mūsā was away?
pr-042.e: al-Sāmirī fashioned the calf that produced a lowing sound. Qārūn is known for his wealth and Hāmān as Pharaoh's minister.

pr-043.q: The Children of Israel are named after which prophet, who was also called Isrāʾīl?
pr-043.e: Isrāʾīl is another name of Yaʿqūb; his twelve sons and their descendants are the Banū Isrāʾīl.

pr-044.q: How did Yūsuf interpret the king's dream of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones?
o: Seven fertile years followed by seven of drought
Seven kings followed by seven tyrants
Seven victories followed by seven defeats
Seven floods followed by seven fires
pr-044.e: He explained it as seven years of good harvest followed by seven hard years, and advised storing the grain in its ears.

pr-045.q: When his sons brought Yūsuf's shirt stained with false blood, what did Yaʿqūb say?
o: He cursed his sons and left them
He went out to search the desert
He asked the king of Egypt for help
pr-045.e: Yaʿqūb sensed the lie and resolved on beautiful patience, seeking Allah's help, and repeated the same words when Binyāmīn was kept in Egypt.

pr-046.q: With the highlighted word the verse calls a prophet the one of al-Nūn. What does al-Nūn mean here, and who is meant?
pr-046.e: Dhū al-Nūn means the man of the fish, a title of Yūnus; in 68:48 he is likewise called ṣāḥib al-ḥūt, the companion of the fish.

pr-047.q: What is special about the people of Yūnus according to the verse shown?
o: They believed and the punishment was lifted
They were the last people destroyed by flood
They followed Yūnus before he was sent
They migrated with him to another land
pr-047.e: The verse states that no town benefited from belief at the sight of punishment except the people of Yūnus: when they believed, the disgrace was removed from them.

pr-048.q: What was Ayyūb told to do when his relief came?
o: Strike the ground with his foot
Climb to the top of a mountain
pr-048.e: He was told to strike with his foot, and a spring came forth: cool water to wash with and to drink, and he was healed.

pr-049.q: According to the verse shown, how did the jinn learn that Sulaymān had died?
o: A creature ate his staff and he fell
A bird announced it from the palace roof
The wind stopped blowing at his command
His ring was found in a fish
pr-049.e: Only a creature of the earth gnawing his staff revealed his death; when he fell, the jinn realised they did not know the unseen.

pr-050.q: Which of these is among the signs of ʿĪsā listed in the verse shown?
o: Healing the blind and the leper
Splitting the sea with a staff
pr-050.e: The verse lists his signs by Allah's permission: shaping a bird from clay that becomes a bird, healing the born-blind and the leper, reviving the dead and telling what people store in their homes.

pr-051.q: What does the verse shown state about ʿĪsā?
o: He was neither killed nor crucified
He died on the cross and rose again
He was killed but not crucified
He fled to India and died there
pr-051.e: The verse denies both killing and crucifixion: it was made to appear so to them; the next verse states that Allah raised him to Himself.

pr-052.q: The verse shown mentions scrolls (ṣuḥuf) of two prophets. Which two?
pr-052.e: The surah ends by saying its teaching is in the earlier scrolls, the scrolls of Ibrāhīm and Mūsā; 53:36-37 mentions them as well.

pr-053.q: How does the Quran describe what Ādam did after eating from the forbidden tree?
o: He repented and Allah accepted his repentance
He blamed Iblīs and was cast out forever
He denied it until the Day of Judgement
He was punished by losing his prophethood
pr-053.e: Ādam and Ḥawwāʾ admitted their wrong and asked forgiveness; Ādam received words from his Lord and Allah turned to him in mercy, unlike Iblīs who persisted.

pr-054.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on names in the Quran
pr-054.q: How many times does the name Muḥammad occur in the Quran?
pr-054.e: The name Muḥammad occurs four times (3:144, 33:40, 47:2, 48:29); the name Aḥmad occurs once (61:6).

pr-055.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on names in the Quran
pr-055.q: Which prophet is mentioned by name most often in the Quran?
pr-055.e: Mūsā is named far more often than any other prophet, well over a hundred times; his dealings with Pharaoh and the Children of Israel recur throughout the Quran.

pr-056.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on Sūrat Maryam
pr-056.q: Which woman is the only one mentioned by her own name in the Quran?
pr-056.e: Maryam is the only woman named in the Quran, and a whole surah carries her name; other women are referred to by description, e.g. the wife of Pharaoh.

pr-057.q: In Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ, by what name are the people of Shuʿayb also called?
o: Aṣḥāb al-Ayka, people of the thicket
Aṣḥāb al-Ḥijr, people of the rocky tract
Aṣḥāb al-Rass, people of the well
Aṣḥāb al-Kahf, people of the cave
pr-057.e: In 26:176 those who rejected Shuʿayb are called aṣḥāb al-Ayka; they were seized by the punishment of the day of the canopy (26:189). al-Ḥijr refers to Thamūd.

pr-058.q: In Sūrat al-Taḥrīm, whose wives are given as an example for those who disbelieve?
o: The wives of Nūḥ and Lūṭ
The wives of Ibrāhīm and Lūṭ
The wives of Pharaoh and Nūḥ
The wives of Ayyūb and Yūnus
pr-058.e: 66:10 sets the wives of Nūḥ and Lūṭ as an example for disbelievers: being married to prophets did not save them. 66:11 sets Pharaoh's wife as an example for believers.

pr-059.q: What sign was Zakariyyā given that his prayer for a son would be fulfilled?
o: He would not speak to people for three days
His wife would see an angel in a dream
A star would appear over the sanctuary
pr-059.e: His sign was that he could not speak to people for three days (three nights in Sūrat Maryam) except by gestures, while remaining healthy and glorifying Allah.

pr-060.q: What does the verse shown say about the name Yaḥyā?
o: No one had been given that name before
It was the name of his grandfather
It means the one who is patient
It was chosen by Zakariyyā himself
pr-060.e: Allah announced the boy's name and stated that no one before him had been called by it, a sign of special honour.

pr-061.q: In Sūrat al-Ṣāffāt, which idol did Ilyās forbid his people to worship?
pr-061.e: Ilyās asked his people whether they would call upon Baʿl and abandon the best of creators (37:125). Wadd is among the idols of Nūḥ's people; al-Lāt and Hubal were Arabian idols.

pr-062.q: The verse shown belongs to a passage of Sūrat al-Anʿām (6:83-86) that names many prophets together. How many prophets are named in that passage?
pr-062.e: The passage names Ibrāhīm and then seventeen more, eighteen in all. The remaining seven of the twenty-five (Ādam, Idrīs, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Shuʿayb, Dhū al-Kifl, Muḥammad) are named elsewhere.

pr-063.q: Which of these prophets is NOT named in the passage 6:83-86 of Sūrat al-Anʿām?
pr-063.e: Ilyās and Zakariyyā appear in 6:85, al-Yasaʿ and Lūṭ in 6:86. Ṣāliḥ belongs to the seven named elsewhere, together with Ādam, Idrīs, Hūd, Shuʿayb, Dhū al-Kifl and Muḥammad.

pr-064.q: Scholars often cite the verse shown as evidence for which point about prophets?
o: That rasūl and nabī are not identical terms
That every prophet was given a scripture
That prophets were sent only to Arabs
That a prophet may come after Muḥammad
pr-064.e: The verse mentions a messenger and a prophet side by side, and conjunction implies difference; hence most scholars hold that every rasūl is a nabī but not every nabī is a rasūl.

pr-065.q: Which quality is Ismāʿīl specifically praised for in the verse shown, besides being a messenger and prophet?
o: Being the first to write with a pen
Being raised to a high place
pr-065.e: Ismāʿīl is praised as ṣādiq al-waʿd, true to his promise, and as rasūl nabī. Being raised to a high place is said of Idrīs (19:57).

pr-066.q: What does the verse shown teach about the stories of the messengers?
o: Some were related to the Prophet, others were not
All of them are told in full in the Quran
Only the stories of Arab prophets are told
Their stories were left to the earlier scriptures
pr-066.e: Allah states that He related the stories of some messengers and not of others. Hence Muslims believe in all prophets in general and in the named ones specifically.

pr-067.q: The verse shown says some messengers were preferred over others, while 2:285 says believers make no distinction between them. How are the two reconciled?
o: No distinction in believing in them; the ranking is Allah's
The first verse was abrogated by the second
The preference applies only to their nations
The second verse concerns only the five ulū al-ʿazm
pr-067.e: Believers accept all messengers equally, rejecting none, as the Jews and Christians rejected some; yet Allah Himself raised some in rank, e.g. by speaking to Mūsā.

pr-068.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī, Kitāb al-Tafsīr, hadith of intercession
pr-068.q: In the long hadith of intercession in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, how is Nūḥ described?
o: The first messenger to the people of the earth
The first to receive a written scripture
The first prophet raised to heaven
pr-068.e: In the intercession hadith people say to Nūḥ that he was the first messenger Allah sent to the people of the earth. Ādam, the first human, is regarded as a prophet but not described there as a messenger.

pr-069.q: In the case of the sheep that grazed in a field at night, what does the verse shown say?
o: Sulaymān understood the case; both had wisdom and knowledge
Dāwūd's judgement was right and Sulaymān's was wrong
Both judgements were rejected by Allah as unjust
Sulaymān judged alone because Dāwūd had already died
pr-069.e: Allah gave Sulaymān the better understanding of the case, yet praised both with judgement and knowledge; scholars use this for ijtihād, where one may be more correct without the other being blamed.

pr-070.q: In the debate shown, which argument of Ibrāhīm left the king speechless?
o: Allah brings the sun from the east; bring it from the west
Allah created the heavens; now create a single fly
Allah sends down the rain; now hold back the rain
Allah gives kingship; now keep your kingdom forever
pr-070.e: When the king claimed to give life and death, Ibrāhīm moved to a sign he could not twist: the sun rising in the east. The disbeliever was confounded.

pr-071.q: In the verse shown, where did Ibrāhīm settle some of his offspring?
o: In a barren valley by the Sacred House
In the blessed and fertile land of al-Shām
On the green banks of the river Nile
In the ancient city of Ur in Iraq
pr-071.e: Ibrāhīm prayed for the family he left in the barren valley of Mecca: that they establish prayer, that hearts incline to them and that they be provided with fruits.

pr-072.q: When the angels visited Ibrāhīm, what good news did his wife receive, as in the verse shown?
o: Lūṭ, and after him his daughters
pr-072.e: Ibrāhīm's wife was given the glad tidings of Isḥāq and, after Isḥāq, of Yaʿqūb, a grandson; she marvelled because she was old and her husband elderly.

pr-073.q: What does the verse shown report about Lūṭ?
o: He refused to emigrate with Ibrāhīm
pr-073.e: Lūṭ believed in Ibrāhīm, and Ibrāhīm declared that he would emigrate for the sake of his Lord. Lūṭ was then sent as a prophet to his own people.

pr-074.q: According to the verse shown, why could Yūsuf not simply keep his brother under the king's law?
o: The king's law did not allow it; Allah planned it
His brothers had already paid a ransom for him
His father had forbidden it in a sealed letter
The drinking cup belonged to Yūsuf personally
pr-074.e: Under the king's law a thief would not be detained in this way, so Allah planned it through the brothers' own judgement (the thief is held). The verse adds that above every knower is one more knowing.

pr-075.q: In the verse shown Yūsuf's parents and brothers prostrate to him. How do mainstream exegetes explain this?
o: A greeting allowed in their law, not permitted in Islam
An act of worship directed to Yūsuf as a prophet
A metaphor only; no one actually bowed
A mistake that Yūsuf then rebuked
pr-075.e: Exegetes such as Ibn Kathīr explain it as a prostration of greeting and honour that was permitted in earlier laws; in the law of Muḥammad ﷺ prostration is for Allah alone.

pr-076.q: What was the mother of Mūsā inspired to do, and what was she promised, according to the verse shown?
o: Cast him in the river; he would return and be a messenger
Hide him in a cave; he would one day become king
Send him to Madyan; he would grow up and marry there
Give him to Pharaoh's wife; she would adopt him forever
pr-076.e: She was inspired to nurse him and, when she feared, to place him in the river, with two promises: he would be returned to her and made one of the messengers.

pr-077.q: Does the Quran name the old man of Madyan whose daughter Mūsā married?
o: No; exegetes discuss whether he was Shuʿayb
Yes, it names him Shuʿayb explicitly there
Yes, it names him Yathrūn in al-Qaṣaṣ
No, but it states he was not a prophet
pr-077.e: Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ calls him only an old man (shaykh kabīr). Many identified him with Shuʿayb, while others, e.g. as discussed by Ibn Kathīr, doubted this on chronological grounds.

pr-078.q: In the verse shown Mūsā asks to see his Lord. What happened?
o: The mountain crumbled and Mūsā fell unconscious
Mūsā saw Allah clearly and then descended
The angels carried Mūsā up to the heavens
Mūsā was rebuked and his request was erased
pr-078.e: Allah said he would not see Him in this world, then manifested to the mountain, which was levelled, and Mūsā fell unconscious; on waking he repented and affirmed he was first of the believers.

pr-079.q: What was the consequence of the Children of Israel refusing to enter the holy land, according to the verse shown?
o: Forty years of wandering in the land
Seven years of famine in Egypt
pr-079.e: Because they refused to enter, the land was forbidden to them for forty years in which they wandered; Mūsā was told not to grieve over the disobedient.

pr-080.q: Which three acts of al-Khiḍr did Mūsā object to on their journey?
o: Holing a boat, killing a boy, repairing a wall
Burning a farm, freeing a slave, breaking idols
Sinking a ship, blinding a king, digging a well
Taking a ring, opening a gate, killing a lion
pr-080.e: al-Khiḍr holed the boat to save it from a seizing king, killed the boy who would have burdened his believing parents, and repaired the wall to protect two orphans' treasure.

pr-081.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī, Kitāb al-ʿIlm, hadith of Mūsā and al-Khiḍr
pr-081.q: The verse shown introduces the man Mūsā met as a servant of Allah. Where does the name al-Khiḍr come from?
o: From the hadith in al-Bukhārī and Muslim
From a later verse of Sūrat al-Kahf
From the Tawrāt as quoted in the Quran
pr-081.e: The Quran calls him only a servant from among Our servants given mercy and knowledge; his name al-Khiḍr is given in the authentic hadith of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb in al-Bukhārī and Muslim.

pr-082.q: Who brought the throne of the Queen of Sabaʾ to Sulaymān in the blink of an eye, according to the verse shown?
o: One who had knowledge from the Book
A powerful ʿifrīt of the jinn
pr-082.e: An ʿifrīt offered to bring it before Sulaymān rose from his seat, but the one with knowledge from the Book brought it before his glance returned; Sulaymān saw it as a test of gratitude.

pr-083.q: In the story of Ṭālūt's army, what does the verse shown say about Dāwūd?
o: He killed Jālūt and was given kingship
He led the army as its appointed king
He refused to drink from the river at all
He built the sanctuary in Jerusalem
pr-083.e: Dāwūd, then a soldier in Ṭālūt's army, killed Jālūt; Allah gave him kingship and wisdom (understood as prophethood) and taught him what He willed.

pr-084.q: What argument does the verse shown make about ʿĪsā?
o: His creation is like Ādam's, by Allah's word Be
He is Allah's son because he had no father
He is an angel in human form
pr-084.e: If birth without a father made ʿĪsā divine, Ādam, created without father or mother, would have a greater claim; both were created by Allah's command Be.

pr-085.q: What distinguishes the mission of Muḥammad ﷺ from earlier prophets, as the verse shown indicates?
o: He was sent to all of mankind
He was sent only to the Arabs
He was sent only to the People of the Book
He was sent to his own tribe first and last
pr-085.e: The verse says he was sent to all people as a bearer of good news and a warner; the hadith of the five distinctions in al-Bukhārī adds that earlier prophets were sent to their own people specifically.

pr-086.q: What does the verse shown state was revealed to every messenger?
o: That there is no god but Allah, so worship Him
That the law of every nation is the same
That every messenger must perform miracles
That the Last Day will come in their lifetime
pr-086.e: All messengers shared the same core message of tawḥīd, even if their laws differed; this is why each prophet in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf opens with the call to worship Allah alone.

pr-087.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ 26:105-191
pr-087.q: The statement in the verse shown is repeated by Nūḥ, Hūd, Ṣāliḥ, Lūṭ and Shuʿayb in Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ. What lesson does it teach?
o: The caller seeks no worldly reward, only Allah's
A prophet must be paid by the state
Only the rich may become callers to faith
Charity must always precede the call to faith
pr-087.e: Each of these prophets tells his people that he asks no payment, his reward being only with the Lord of the worlds; sincerity and freedom from worldly gain mark the true caller.

pr-088.q: In the verse shown the Prophet ﷺ is told not to be like the companion of the fish. What is the lesson?
o: Be patient and await Allah's decree
Do not travel by sea during your mission
Do not pray alone in the darkness
Do not draw lots to settle disputes
pr-088.e: Yūnus left his people in anger before Allah's permission; the Prophet ﷺ is told to remain patient for his Lord's judgement. Yūnus was then forgiven and chosen again (68:50).

pr-089.q: Which distinction between nabī and rasūl is associated with Ibn Taymiyya in Kitāb al-Nubuwwāt?
o: A rasūl goes to deniers; a nabī guides believers by an earlier law
A rasūl gets revelation awake; a nabī only ever in dreams
A rasūl is sent to men; a nabī is sent only to the women
A rasūl has a miracle; a nabī never has any miracle at all
pr-089.e: Ibn Taymiyya held that the rasūl is sent to people who oppose and deny him, whereas the nabī receives revelation and teaches believers according to a previous messenger's law, as the prophets of the Children of Israel did with the Tawrāt.

pr-090.src: Ibn Taymiyya, Kitāb al-Nubuwwāt; al-Safārīnī, Lawāmiʿ al-Anwār al-Bahiyya
pr-090.q: A widespread definition says a nabī receives revelation but is not commanded to convey it. Which objection, drawing on the verse shown, is raised against it?
o: The verse says Allah sent both, and a sent one must convey
The verse names only messengers, never prophets
The verse proves that nabī and rasūl are synonyms
The verse limits revelation to those with scriptures
pr-090.e: Critics note that the verse uses arsalnā (We sent) for both rasūl and nabī; one who is sent is by definition charged with conveying, so a nabī with nothing to convey does not fit the verse.

pr-091.src: al-Laqānī, Jawharat al-Tawḥīd, with al-Bayjūrī, Tuḥfat al-Murīd
pr-091.q: In the Ashʿarī creed manual Jawharat al-Tawḥīd, what is said about the prophets named in the Quran?
o: The legally responsible must know the 25 of them in detail
Only the five ulū al-ʿazm must be known by name
Knowing their names is merely recommended for scholars
Belief in them is required only in general
pr-091.e: al-Laqānī states that knowing the prophets named in the Quran in detail is obligatory on the mukallaf, while the rest are believed in generally; al-Bayjūrī's commentary lists the twenty-five.

pr-092.src: al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, al-Shifā bi-Taʿrīf Ḥuqūq al-Muṣṭafā, section on ʿiṣma
pr-092.q: Which statement correctly describes the Sunni position on the ʿiṣma (protection) of prophets?
o: Agreed in conveying; views differ on minor slips
Agreed that they never made any slip at all
Agreed only after prophethood, never before it
Agreed that they may err in conveying revelation
pr-092.e: Sunni scholars agree that prophets are protected from lying or error in conveying the message and from major sins. Whether minor, non-degrading slips can occur, without being persisted in, is discussed, with different positions among Ashʿarīs, Māturīdīs and others.

pr-093.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 37:100-113; Ibn al-Qayyim, Zād al-Maʿād
pr-093.q: Scholars differed over which son was to be sacrificed. How do Ibn Kathīr and Ibn al-Qayyim use the verse shown to argue for Ismāʿīl?
o: Isḥāq's good news comes after the sacrifice story
The verse names Ismāʿīl as the one ransomed
Isḥāq is described there as too young to walk
The verse places the sacrifice in Jerusalem itself
pr-093.e: The sacrifice narrative concerns the first son given after Ibrāhīm's prayer; only afterwards does the verse shown bring the glad tidings of Isḥāq, so the son earlier was Ismāʿīl. Some early authorities held it was Isḥāq, but this argument made the Ismāʿīl view prevail with these scholars.

pr-094.src: Ibn Kathīr, Qaṣaṣ al-Anbiyāʾ, story of al-Khiḍr; al-Qurṭubī, al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān, on 18:65
pr-094.q: Scholars differ on whether al-Khiḍr was a prophet. Which argument from the verse shown is used by those who say he was?
o: He says he did not act of his own accord
He is called a messenger in the verse
He performs a miracle in front of a king
He receives a scripture at the end of the verse
pr-094.e: al-Khiḍr says he did not do it of his own accord; killing a boy and similar acts could only be done by revelation, which supports prophethood. Others held he was a righteous walī given special knowledge.

pr-095.q: What is the majority view about the status of Luqmān, after whom Sūrat Luqmān is named?
o: A wise righteous man, not a prophet
A messenger sent to the Arabs
A prophet of the Children of Israel
pr-095.e: Ibn Kathīr reports that most of the early scholars held Luqmān was a wise, righteous servant given ḥikma, not a prophet; a minority considered him a prophet.

pr-096.q: Why do Ibn Kathīr and others incline to the view that Dhū al-Kifl was a prophet, although some said he was only a righteous man?
o: He is listed and praised among the prophets
The verse calls him a messenger to a named people
A whole surah is named after him
The Quran narrates a miracle he performed
pr-096.e: In 21:85 and the verse shown he is listed together with prophets and praised with them; Ibn Kathīr says this context suggests prophethood, while noting the view that he was a righteous man.

pr-097.src: Ibn Ḥazm, al-Fiṣal fī al-Milal; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 12:109
pr-097.q: Ibn Ḥazm held that women such as Maryam received prophethood. Which point from the verse shown does the majority cite against prophethood of women?
o: Those sent before were only men
Revelation came only to city dwellers
Messengers were all from Ibrāhīm's line
pr-097.e: The verse says Allah sent before the Prophet only men to whom He revealed. The majority take this to restrict prophethood and messengership to men, regarding Maryam as a ṣiddīqa; Ibn Ḥazm and some others affirmed prophethood (not messengership) for certain women.

pr-098.src: Muslim, al-Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Ādāb; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 19:28
pr-098.q: In the verse shown Maryam is addressed as sister of Hārūn. How did the Prophet ﷺ explain this, according to the hadith of al-Mughīra ibn Shuʿba in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim?
o: People were named after earlier prophets and the righteous
Maryam was literally the sister of Mūsā's own brother
Hārūn was another name used for her father ʿImrān
It was an insult meaning a sinful and low woman
pr-098.e: When Christians of Najrān raised this, the Prophet ﷺ explained that they used to be named after the prophets and righteous people before them; it does not mean she was the sister of Mūsā's brother.

pr-099.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, Sūrat al-Aḥzāb
pr-099.q: How do the ten readers differ on the highlighted word?
o: ʿĀṣim reads it with fatḥa, the rest with kasra
Nāfiʿ reads it with fatḥa, the rest with kasra
All read it with kasra except Ḥamza alone
There is no difference among the ten
pr-099.e: ʿĀṣim alone reads khātam (seal, the last that closes), the others khātim (the one who seals). Both readings affirm that he ﷺ is the last of the prophets.

pr-100.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 21:87; al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 21:87
pr-100.q: How do Ibn Kathīr and most exegetes explain the highlighted word in the story of Yūnus?
o: That Allah would not constrain or restrict him
That Allah had no power over him
That Allah would not decree anything for him
That Allah would not judge him at all
pr-100.e: The root q-d-r here is taken in the sense of constriction (as in yaqdiru al-rizq, to restrict provision): he thought he would not be put in straits. Reading it as having no power over him is rejected, since a prophet would not think that of Allah.

pr-101.q: How does Ibn Kathīr treat the widely circulated reports that a devil took Sulaymān's ring and sat on his throne, offered to explain the verse shown?
o: As isrāʾīliyyāt, some of them objectionable
As the agreed explanation of the Companions
As the only meaning the verse can bear
pr-101.e: Ibn Kathīr notes that these reports go back to People of the Book material and that parts are objectionable, especially regarding the prophet's household; the verse itself only says Sulaymān was tried and then turned back to Allah.

pr-102.src: Ibn Taymiyya, Muqaddima fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, introduction
pr-102.q: According to Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Kathīr, how should a report from the People of the Book about a prophet be handled if our sources neither confirm nor contradict it?
o: Neither affirmed nor denied; it may be narrated
Accepted as binding detail of the story
Accepted only if it names a place
pr-102.e: They divide such reports into three: what our revelation confirms (accepted), what it contradicts (rejected), and what it is silent about, which is neither believed nor denied and may be related, though it rarely brings religious benefit.

pr-103.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī, Kitāb Aḥādīth al-Anbiyāʾ, on the three statements of Ibrāhīm
pr-103.q: The hadith in al-Bukhārī and Muslim mentions three statements of Ibrāhīm, such as saying the biggest idol had done it. How do scholars like Ibn Ḥajar classify them?
o: As indirect expressions (maʿārīḍ), true in meaning
As real sins for which he was later punished
As statements made before his prophethood only
As fabrications inserted into the hadith
pr-103.e: They are called lies only in outward form; in reality they were taʿrīḍ, expressions with a true hidden meaning used for Allah's sake. Ibrāhīm's mentioning them on the Day of Judgement reflects his humility.

pr-104.src: al-Nawawī, Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, Kitāb al-Faḍāʾil, on the virtues of Mūsā
pr-104.q: The Prophet ﷺ said not to prefer him over Mūsā, yet he is the best of creation. Which reconciliation do al-Nawawī and others mention?
o: Forbidden is preference that belittles another prophet
Preferring any prophet is forbidden in every case
The hadith was abrogated by the verse on ulū al-ʿazm
The prohibition concerns only the Children of Israel
pr-104.e: Among the answers given: he said it out of humility, or before being told he was the best, or the forbidden kind is preference that degrades another prophet or arises from partisanship; preference as Allah established it (2:253) is not forbidden.

pr-105.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī, Kitāb al-Riqāq, hadith of intercession
pr-105.q: In the hadith of the great intercession, to which prophet do people go immediately before coming to Muḥammad ﷺ?
pr-105.e: People go in turn to Ādam, Nūḥ, Ibrāhīm, Mūsā and ʿĪsā; each excuses himself, and ʿĪsā directs them to Muḥammad ﷺ, who intercedes. The sequence after Ādam matches the five ulū al-ʿazm.

pr-106.q: Whom does the verse shown name as chosen by Allah above the worlds?
o: Ādam, Nūḥ, the house of Ibrāhīm and of ʿImrān
Ādam, Idrīs, Nūḥ and the family of Yaʿqūb
Nūḥ, Ibrāhīm, Mūsā and the family of Dāwūd
Ibrāhīm, Ismāʿīl, Isḥāq and the family of Mūsā
pr-106.e: The verse names Ādam, Nūḥ, the family of Ibrāhīm and the family of ʿImrān; the surah then turns to the family of ʿImrān: Maryam's mother, Maryam, Zakariyyā, Yaḥyā and ʿĪsā.

pr-107.q: In Sūrat al-Naml, what does the verse shown say about the opposition to Ṣāliḥ in the city of Thamūd?
o: Nine men spread corruption and plotted against him
Seven elders were sent to kill the she-camel
Twelve chiefs fled with Ṣāliḥ to Madyan
Forty youths dug a trap in the mountains
pr-107.e: Nine men (tisʿat rahṭ) caused corruption; in the following verses they swore to attack Ṣāliḥ and his family at night, but Allah foiled their plot and destroyed them.

pr-108.q: The verse shown is part of what Sūrat al-Najm attributes to the scrolls of Mūsā and Ibrāhīm. Which principle does it state?
o: No soul bears the burden of another
Every nation has its own prayer direction
Fasting is prescribed for every people
Prophethood passes from father to son
pr-108.e: 53:36-41 summarise teachings of those scrolls: no bearer of burdens bears another's burden, a person has only what he strives for, and his striving will be seen and fully repaid.

pr-109.q: The verse shown mentions Iram of the lofty pillars. With which people is it connected in the context?
pr-109.e: Sūrat al-Fajr mentions ʿĀd, then Iram of the pillars, then Thamūd and Pharaoh; most exegetes identify Iram with ʿĀd, whose land 46:21 places at al-Aḥqāf.

pr-110.src: al-Qurṭubī, al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān, on 38:44; Ibn al-ʿArabī, Aḥkām al-Qurʾān
pr-110.q: In the verse shown Ayyūb is told to strike with a bundle so as not to break his oath. Which statement correctly describes how jurists used it?
o: They differed whether it is general or specific to Ayyūb
They agreed it permits any trick to evade an obligation
They agreed it was abrogated and has no legal use
They agreed it concerns only oaths sworn by wives
pr-110.e: Some jurists drew from it that an oath to strike a number of blows can be fulfilled by one strike with a bundle of that many stalks; others held it was a special concession for Ayyūb. No one took it as licence to evade obligations in general.

qr-001.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Munjid al-Muqriʾīn wa-Murshid al-Ṭālibīn, definition of qirāʾāt
qr-001.q: What does the science of qirāʾāt study?
o: How the words of the Quran are recited and how the transmitted readings differ
The occasions on which individual verses were revealed
The rules for writing the Quran in calligraphy
The meanings of rare words in the Quran
qr-001.e: ʿIlm al-qirāʾāt studies the manner of pronouncing the Quran's words and the differences between the transmitted readings, each attributed to its transmitter. Occasions of revelation and rare words belong to other Quranic sciences.

qr-002.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb unzila al-Qurʾān ʿalā sabʿat aḥruf
qr-002.q: According to the well-known hadith in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, the Quran was revealed in how many aḥruf?
qr-002.e: The hadith reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim states that the Quran was revealed in seven aḥruf. Ten is the number of canonical readers, which is a different matter.

qr-003.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb unzila al-Qurʾān ʿalā sabʿat aḥruf
qr-003.q: In the hadith of the seven aḥruf, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb heard Hishām ibn Ḥakīm recite a sūra differently from how he had learned it. Which sūra was it?
qr-003.e: In the account in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, ʿUmar heard Hishām ibn Ḥakīm recite Sūrat al-Furqān; the Prophet approved both recitations and said the Quran was revealed in seven aḥruf.

qr-004.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction
qr-004.q: How many canonical readers (qurrāʾ) are recognised in the mainstream tradition of qirāʾāt today?
qr-004.e: Ibn al-Jazarī established the ten readings (the seven of Ibn Mujāhid plus Abū Jaʿfar, Yaʿqūb and Khalaf) as the accepted canon. The four beyond them are classed as shādhdh.

qr-005.src: Ibn Mujāhid, Kitāb al-Sabʿa fī al-Qirāʾāt, introduction
qr-005.q: Which scholar selected the seven readers in his book Kitāb al-Sabʿa?
qr-005.e: Abū Bakr Ibn Mujāhid (d. 324 AH) chose seven readers in Kitāb al-Sabʿa. Al-Dānī, al-Shāṭibī and Ibn al-Jazarī came later and built on this selection.

qr-006.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, chapter on ʿĀṣim and his transmitters
qr-006.q: Which riwāya is the most widely recited in the Muslim world today?
qr-006.e: Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim is read across most of the Arab East, Turkey, South Asia and beyond, and is the riwāya of most printed muṣḥafs. Warsh, Qālūn and al-Dūrī are regionally widespread.

qr-007.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya fī Ṭabaqāt al-Qurrāʾ, entry Warsh
qr-007.q: In which region is the riwāya of Warsh ʿan Nāfiʿ predominantly recited today?
o: North and West Africa, e.g. Morocco, Algeria and Mauritania
South Asia, e.g. Pakistan and India
qr-007.e: Warsh ʿan Nāfiʿ spread with the Mālikī tradition of the Maghrib and is the dominant riwāya in Morocco, Algeria, Mauritania and much of West Africa. South Asia, Turkey and the Gulf mainly read Ḥafṣ.

qr-008.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb asmāʾ al-qurrāʾ wa-ruwātihim
qr-008.q: Ḥafṣ is the transmitter (rāwī) of which reader (imām)?
qr-008.e: Ḥafṣ ibn Sulaymān transmitted the reading of ʿĀṣim of Kufa; his riwāya is called Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim.

qr-009.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb asmāʾ al-qurrāʾ wa-ruwātihim
qr-009.q: Warsh is the transmitter (rāwī) of which reader?
qr-009.e: Warsh (ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd al-Miṣrī) travelled to Medina and learned the reading of Nāfiʿ, which he brought back to Egypt.

qr-010.src: Ibn Mujāhid, Kitāb al-Sabʿa fī al-Qirāʾāt, introduction
qr-010.q: Which city was Nāfiʿ, one of the seven readers, the leading reader of?
qr-010.e: Nāfiʿ ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān was the imam of recitation in Medina; his two rāwīs are Qālūn and Warsh.

qr-011.src: Ibn Mujāhid, Kitāb al-Sabʿa fī al-Qirāʾāt, introduction
qr-011.q: Ibn Kathīr, one of the seven readers, was the reader of which city?
qr-011.e: ʿAbd Allāh Ibn Kathīr was the imam of recitation in Mecca. He should not be confused with the later exegete Ibn Kathīr, author of the famous tafsīr.

qr-012.src: Ibn Mujāhid, Kitāb al-Sabʿa fī al-Qirāʾāt, introduction
qr-012.q: Ibn ʿĀmir, one of the seven readers, represents the reading of which region?
qr-012.e: ʿAbd Allāh Ibn ʿĀmir was the imam of recitation in Damascus; his two rāwīs, Hishām and Ibn Dhakwān, were also Damascenes.

qr-013.src: Ibn Mujāhid, Kitāb al-Sabʿa fī al-Qirāʾāt, introduction
qr-013.q: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ, one of the seven readers, was the reader of which city?
qr-013.e: Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ was the reader and a leading linguist of Basra. Kufa was represented by ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī.

qr-014.src: Ibn Mujāhid, Kitāb al-Sabʿa fī al-Qirāʾāt, introduction
qr-014.q: ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd, whose reading Ḥafṣ transmitted, was the reader of which city?
qr-014.e: ʿĀṣim was the leading reader of Kufa; both his rāwīs, Shuʿba and Ḥafṣ, were Kufans.

qr-015.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction on qirāʾa, riwāya and ṭarīq
qr-015.q: In the terminology of the qurrāʾ, a difference attributed to one of the transmitters of an imam (e.g. Ḥafṣ) is called a …
qr-015.e: A difference attributed to the imam himself is a qirāʾa, one attributed to his transmitter is a riwāya, and one attributed to someone who took from the transmitter is a ṭarīq. A wajh is an option left to the reciter's choice.

qr-016.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb asmāʾ al-qurrāʾ wa-ruwātihim
qr-016.q: In the standard presentation (al-Shāṭibiyya, al-Durra, al-Nashr), how many principal rāwīs are listed for each of the ten readers?
qr-016.e: Each imam is presented through two principal rāwīs, e.g. Qālūn and Warsh for Nāfiʿ, or Shuʿba and Ḥafṣ for ʿĀṣim, giving twenty riwāyāt in total.

qr-017.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb asmāʾ al-qurrāʾ wa-ruwātihim
qr-017.q: Who are the two rāwīs of ʿĀṣim?
qr-017.e: ʿĀṣim's reading is transmitted by Shuʿba (Abū Bakr ibn ʿAyyāsh) and Ḥafṣ ibn Sulaymān. Qālūn and Warsh transmit Nāfiʿ, Khalaf and Khallād transmit Ḥamza, al-Bazzī and Qunbul transmit Ibn Kathīr.

qr-018.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Fātiḥa
qr-018.q: How does Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim read the highlighted word?
o: With a long ā after the mīm (mālik)
With a short a after the mīm, without alif (malik)
With a doubled lām after the mīm
With a sukūn on the mīm
qr-018.e: ʿĀṣim (and so Ḥafṣ), al-Kisāʾī, Yaʿqūb and Khalaf read mālik with the long ā; the other readers read malik without it. Both fit the rasm, which is written without an alif.

qr-019.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction on the seven aḥruf
qr-019.q: Are the seven aḥruf of the hadith the same as the seven readings of the seven readers?
o: No; scholars state that equating them is a mistake
Yes; each reader preserves exactly one ḥarf
Yes; Ibn Mujāhid chose them to match the hadith
No; the seven readings are later than the ten
qr-019.e: Scholars such as Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Abū Shāma and Ibn al-Jazarī stressed that the seven readings are not the seven aḥruf. The readers lived generations after the hadith, and their number was a later choice of Ibn Mujāhid.

qr-020.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī wa-Wajh al-Tahānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), introduction
o: A didactic poem on the seven readings
A prose commentary on the ten readings
A poem on the rules of tajwīd for beginners
A biographical dictionary of the readers
qr-020.e: Al-Shāṭibiyya (Ḥirz al-Amānī wa-Wajh al-Tahānī) by al-Qāsim ibn Fīrruh al-Shāṭibī is a rhymed poem teaching the seven readings through their rāwīs. A short tajwīd poem for beginners would be e.g. Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl.

qr-021.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb asmāʾ al-qurrāʾ wa-ruwātihim
qr-021.q: Qālūn is the rāwī of which reader?
qr-021.e: Qālūn (ʿĪsā ibn Mīnā) of Medina transmitted the reading of Nāfiʿ alongside Warsh.

qr-022.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction on the pillars of a sound reading
qr-022.q: What is meant by a mutawātir reading?
o: One transmitted by so many in every generation that agreement on error is impossible
One transmitted by a single reliable reader from a Companion
One that matches the rasm but has no known chain
One that is used only to explain the meaning of a verse
qr-022.e: Tawātur means transmission by a large number from a large number in every generation, so that collusion or error is ruled out. The ten readings are regarded as mutawātir.

qr-023.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction on the pillars of a sound reading
o: A reading lacking one of the conditions of acceptance, so it is not recited as Quran
A reading of one of the ten that is rarely heard today
A reading transmitted only by the second rāwī of an imam
A reading that differs from Ḥafṣ in pronunciation only
qr-023.e: A reading is shādhdh when it fails one of the conditions (sound chain, agreement with the ʿUthmānī rasm, agreement with Arabic). It is not recited as Quran, though scholars may cite it in tafsīr or grammar.

qr-024.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ṭayyibat al-Nashr, opening verses; al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction
qr-024.q: Which of the following is one of Ibn al-Jazarī's three conditions for an accepted reading?
o: Agreement with the rasm of one of the ʿUthmānī muṣḥafs
Being read by at least seven of the readers
Agreement with the reading of the people of Medina
Being recorded in one of the six hadith collections
qr-024.e: Ibn al-Jazarī names three pillars: agreement with Arabic grammar (even in one way), agreement with one of the ʿUthmānī muṣḥafs (even implicitly), and a sound chain of transmission. A fixed number of readers or a particular city is not a condition.

qr-025.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb asmāʾ al-qurrāʾ wa-ruwātihim
qr-025.q: Who are the two rāwīs of Ibn Kathīr al-Makkī?
qr-025.e: Ibn Kathīr's reading reaches us through al-Bazzī and Qunbul, both Meccans. Hishām and Ibn Dhakwān transmit Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Dūrī and al-Sūsī transmit Abū ʿAmr.

qr-026.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb asmāʾ al-qurrāʾ wa-ruwātihim
qr-026.q: Who are the two rāwīs of Abū ʿAmr al-Baṣrī?
qr-026.e: Abū ʿAmr's reading is transmitted by al-Dūrī and al-Sūsī. Abū al-Ḥārith and al-Dūrī are the rāwīs of al-Kisāʾī (the same al-Dūrī transmits from both), and Ruways and Rawḥ transmit Yaʿqūb.

qr-027.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb asmāʾ al-qurrāʾ wa-ruwātihim
qr-027.q: Who are the two rāwīs of Ibn ʿĀmir al-Shāmī?
qr-027.e: Ibn ʿĀmir's reading is transmitted by Hishām and Ibn Dhakwān, both of Damascus. Ibn Wardān and Ibn Jammāz transmit Abū Jaʿfar.

qr-028.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb asmāʾ al-qurrāʾ wa-ruwātihim
qr-028.q: Who are the two rāwīs of Ḥamza al-Zayyāt?
qr-028.e: Ḥamza's reading is transmitted by Khalaf and Khallād. Isḥāq and Idrīs are the rāwīs of Khalaf al-ʿĀshir in his own reading.

qr-029.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb asmāʾ al-qurrāʾ wa-ruwātihim
qr-029.q: Who are the two rāwīs of al-Kisāʾī?
qr-029.e: Al-Kisāʾī's reading is transmitted by Abū al-Ḥārith (al-Layth ibn Khālid) and Ḥafṣ al-Dūrī. Al-Sūsī transmits Abū ʿAmr, not al-Kisāʾī.

qr-030.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Durra al-Muḍiyya fī al-Qirāʾāt al-Thalāth al-Mutammima li-l-ʿAshr, introduction
qr-030.q: Which three readers complete the seven to make the ten?
o: Abū Jaʿfar, Yaʿqūb and Khalaf al-ʿĀshir
al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Ibn Muḥayṣin and Yaʿqūb
qr-030.e: The three that complete the ten are Abū Jaʿfar of Medina, Yaʿqūb of Basra and Khalaf al-ʿĀshir. Ibn Muḥayṣin, al-Yazīdī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and al-Aʿmash are the four beyond the ten, whose readings are classed as shādhdh.

qr-031.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Durra al-Muḍiyya fī al-Qirāʾāt al-Thalāth al-Mutammima li-l-ʿAshr
qr-031.q: What does Ibn al-Jazarī's poem al-Durra al-Muḍiyya cover?
o: The three readings that complete the ten
The seven readings with all their ṭuruq
The rules of the ʿUthmānī rasm
The biographies of the twenty rāwīs
qr-031.e: Al-Durra versifies the readings of Abū Jaʿfar, Yaʿqūb and Khalaf, in the same metre and rhyme as al-Shāṭibiyya, so that the two poems together give the ten readings.

qr-032.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya fī Ṭabaqāt al-Qurrāʾ, entry al-Qāsim ibn Fīrruh al-Shāṭibī
qr-032.q: The author of al-Shāṭibiyya, al-Qāsim ibn Fīrruh, takes his name al-Shāṭibī from Shāṭiba. Where was Shāṭiba?
qr-032.e: Al-Shāṭibī was born in Shāṭiba (Xàtiva) in eastern al-Andalus; he later settled in Cairo, where he taught his poem.

qr-033.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ṭayyibat al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction
o: Ibn al-Jazarī's poem on the ten readings via the ṭuruq of al-Nashr
Al-Shāṭibī's poem on the seven readings
A prose work by al-Dānī on the seven readings
Ibn Mujāhid's book on the seven readers
qr-033.e: Ṭayyibat al-Nashr is Ibn al-Jazarī's poem of about a thousand lines that versifies his al-Nashr, covering the ten readings through many more ṭuruq than al-Shāṭibiyya and al-Durra.

qr-034.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), division into uṣūl and farsh al-ḥurūf
qr-034.q: In qirāʾāt books, what is meant by uṣūl?
o: General rules that recur throughout the Quran, such as madd, hamz and imāla
Word-specific differences treated sūra by sūra
The chains of transmission of each reader
The conditions for accepting a reading
qr-034.e: Uṣūl are recurring rules that apply wherever their conditions occur (e.g. lengthening, hamza, imāla, idghām). Word-specific differences treated in the order of the sūras are farsh al-ḥurūf.

qr-035.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), division into uṣūl and farsh al-ḥurūf
qr-035.q: What does farsh al-ḥurūf refer to?
o: Differences in particular words, treated in the order of the sūras
Rules of lengthening that apply in every sūra
The order in which the readers are listed
The pauses that every reader observes
qr-035.e: Farsh al-ḥurūf (lit. 'spreading out of the words') are differences limited to specific words, set out where they occur, sūra by sūra. Rules that apply generally are uṣūl.

qr-036.src: Ibn Mujāhid, Kitāb al-Sabʿa fī al-Qirāʾāt, introduction
qr-036.q: Which city is represented by three of the seven readers?
qr-036.e: ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī were all Kufans; Medina, Mecca, Basra and Damascus are each represented by one of the seven.

qr-037.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya fī Ṭabaqāt al-Qurrāʾ, entry Qālūn
qr-037.q: In which country is the riwāya of Qālūn ʿan Nāfiʿ the predominant public recitation today?
qr-037.e: Qālūn ʿan Nāfiʿ is the dominant riwāya of Libya and is also read in parts of Tunisia. Morocco mainly reads Warsh, Sudan widely al-Dūrī ʿan Abī ʿAmr, Pakistan Ḥafṣ.

qr-038.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, chapter on Abū ʿAmr and his transmitters
qr-038.q: The riwāya of al-Dūrī ʿan Abī ʿAmr is still widely recited today in which country?
qr-038.e: Al-Dūrī ʿan Abī ʿAmr is widely read in Sudan and neighbouring regions of Africa; muṣḥafs in this riwāya are printed for that readership. Libya reads mainly Qālūn, Turkey and Indonesia Ḥafṣ.

qr-039.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya fī Ṭabaqāt al-Qurrāʾ, entry Abū Jaʿfar Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ
qr-039.q: Abū Jaʿfar Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ, one of the three completing the ten, was the reader of which city and the teacher of which of the seven?
o: Medina; he was a teacher of Nāfiʿ
Basra; he was a teacher of Abū ʿAmr
Mecca; he was a teacher of Ibn Kathīr
Kufa; he was a teacher of Ḥamza
