qr-039.e: Abū Jaʿfar was a Medinan Successor and the leading reader of Medina before Nāfiʿ, who read with him. His rāwīs are Ibn Wardān and Ibn Jammāz.

qr-040.q: Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī, one of the ten, is the reader of which city, and who are his two rāwīs?
o: Medina; Ibn Wardān and Ibn Jammāz
qr-040.e: Yaʿqūb was the leading reader of Basra after Abū ʿAmr; his reading reaches us through Ruways and Rawḥ.

qr-041.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Baqara
qr-041.q: The highlighted word is read in two ways: with a light dhāl (yakdhibūn, 'they used to lie') and with a doubled dhāl (yukadhdhibūn, 'they used to deny'). Who reads the light form?
o: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr
Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Jaʿfar alone
qr-041.e: The Kufans (ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf) read the light form, which is why Ḥafṣ reads it so; the others read yukadhdhibūn. Both meanings describe the hypocrites: they lied and they denied.

qr-042.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Fātiḥa
qr-042.q: Which rāwī of Ibn Kathīr reads the highlighted word with sīn instead of ṣād?
qr-042.e: Qunbul reads the word with sīn throughout the Quran, while al-Bazzī reads it with ṣād like most readers. Among the rāwīs of Ḥamza, Khalaf reads it with ishmām (ṣād mixed with zāy).

qr-043.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya fī Ṭabaqāt al-Qurrāʾ, entry ʿAlī ibn Ḥamza al-Kisāʾī
qr-043.q: Besides being one of the seven readers, al-Kisāʾī is famous as …
o: the leading grammarian of the Kufan school
the first compiler of a qirāʾāt poem
the scribe who wrote the ʿUthmānī muṣḥaf
the founder of the Basran school of grammar
qr-043.e: ʿAlī ibn Ḥamza al-Kisāʾī headed the Kufan school of grammar and taught at the ʿAbbāsid court in Baghdad. The Basran school traces back to scholars such as Abū ʿAmr's circle and Sībawayh.

qr-044.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb asmāʾ al-qurrāʾ wa-ruwātihim
qr-044.q: One rāwī appears in the lists of two different imams of the seven. Who is he?
o: Ḥafṣ al-Dūrī, rāwī of Abū ʿAmr and of al-Kisāʾī
Khalaf, rāwī of Ḥamza and of ʿĀṣim
Hishām, rāwī of Ibn ʿĀmir and of Nāfiʿ
Warsh, rāwī of Nāfiʿ and of Ibn Kathīr
qr-044.e: Abū ʿUmar Ḥafṣ ibn ʿUmar al-Dūrī transmitted the reading of Abū ʿAmr (via al-Yazīdī) and also read directly with al-Kisāʾī, so he is listed for both.

qr-045.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya fī Ṭabaqāt al-Qurrāʾ, entry Khalaf ibn Hishām al-Bazzār
qr-045.q: How is Khalaf al-ʿĀshir related to the reading of Ḥamza?
o: He is the same Khalaf who is one of Ḥamza's two rāwīs
He is Ḥamza's teacher in Kufa
He is a grandson of Ḥamza who opposed his reading
He has no link to Ḥamza's reading at all
qr-045.e: Khalaf ibn Hishām al-Bazzār transmitted Ḥamza's reading (via Sulaym) and also has his own reading (ikhtiyār), counted as the tenth; hence the name Khalaf al-ʿĀshir.

qr-046.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb al-fatḥ wa-l-imāla
qr-046.q: Under which part of a qirāʾāt book is imāla (inclining the ā toward ē) mainly treated?
o: Uṣūl, because it is a recurring rule
Farsh, because it differs word by word
The introduction on the conditions of acceptance
The chapter on the biographies of the readers
qr-046.e: Imāla has its own chapter among the uṣūl, since it follows general rules for whole classes of words (Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī are best known for it). Isolated single-word cases may still be mentioned in the farsh.

qr-047.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya fī Ṭabaqāt al-Qurrāʾ, entry Ḥafṣ ibn Sulaymān
qr-047.q: What was the personal relationship between Ḥafṣ ibn Sulaymān and ʿĀṣim?
qr-047.e: The biographers describe Ḥafṣ as ʿĀṣim's stepson (rabīb), who grew up in his household and learned the reading from him closely.

qr-048.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction on the ʿUthmānī maṣāḥif
qr-048.q: Why do the canonical readers come from cities such as Medina, Mecca, Basra, Kufa and Damascus?
o: ʿUthmān sent copies of the muṣḥaf to these centres, each with a teacher
These were the only cities where Arabic was spoken
The Prophet appointed one reader for each of these cities
Ibn Mujāhid lived in each of these cities in turn
qr-048.e: ʿUthmān sent copies of the muṣḥaf to the main centres, and recitation there was taught in line with that copy. The great readers of each centre therefore represent the reading of their region.

qr-049.src: Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Ṣalāt al-Musāfirīn, bāb bayān anna al-Qurʾān ʿalā sabʿat aḥruf
qr-049.q: According to the hadith reports on the seven aḥruf, what was the purpose of revealing the Quran in several aḥruf?
o: Ease for the community, since people differed in dialect and ability
To give each Arab tribe its own separate Quran
To allow anyone to replace words with synonyms freely
To make memorisation harder and so more rewarding
qr-049.e: In the reports in Muslim, the Prophet asked repeatedly for ease for his community until seven aḥruf were granted. The aḥruf were revealed and taught, not left to free substitution by individuals.

qr-050.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Munjid al-Muqriʾīn, on the attribution of readings to the imams
qr-050.q: Why is a reading attributed to an imam such as Nāfiʿ or ʿĀṣim?
o: He selected it from what he received, adhered to it and taught it
He composed the variant wordings himself
He was the first to write the muṣḥaf of his city
He received it in a dream from the Prophet
qr-050.e: A reading is named after an imam because of his ikhtiyār: he chose among the transmitted readings he received, kept to them and became known for teaching them. The readings themselves go back to the Prophet through chains of transmission.

qr-051.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction (agreement with the rasm 'even implicitly')
qr-051.q: The highlighted word is written in the ʿUthmānī rasm without an alif, yet some readers read it with a long ā. How does this fit Ibn al-Jazarī's rasm condition?
o: The condition is met 'even implicitly': the rasm can carry the reading with ā
It does not fit; the long ā reading is accepted only because of its chain
Readers with ā use a separate muṣḥaf that writes the alif
The rasm condition applies only to consonants added at word ends
qr-051.e: Ibn al-Jazarī requires agreement with the rasm 'even if only implicitly' (wa-law iḥtimālan). The muṣḥafs omit this alif, so the written form fits malik explicitly and mālik implicitly; both readings therefore meet the condition.

qr-052.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction (agreement with Arabic 'even in one way')
qr-052.q: Ibn al-Jazarī requires that a reading agree with Arabic 'even in one way' (wa-law bi-wajh). What does this qualification mean?
o: It suffices that the reading is valid in some recognised usage of Arabic, even if not the most common
The reading must follow the majority view of the Basran grammarians
The reading must be the most eloquent possible form
It must be accepted by both Basran and Kufan grammarians
qr-052.e: A soundly transmitted reading that matches the rasm is not rejected because some grammarians preferred another form; it is enough that it has a valid aspect in Arabic. Ibn al-Jazarī stresses that the readings are a proof for grammar, not the reverse.

qr-053.src: al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Rasm Maṣāḥif al-Amṣār, chapter on differences between the regional maṣāḥif
qr-053.q: Before the highlighted word, Ibn Kathīr reads an additional preposition 'min' ('from beneath'). Why is this reading compatible with the rasm?
o: The Meccan muṣḥaf contains the additional word
The rasm leaves room for any added preposition
Ibn Kathīr took it from a non-ʿUthmānī codex
It is a pausal form that does not affect the rasm
qr-053.e: The regional ʿUthmānī maṣāḥif differ in a few letters and words; the Meccan copy has the extra 'min' here, and Ibn Kathīr, the Meccan reader, follows it. This shows the rasm condition is met by agreement with any one of the ʿUthmānī maṣāḥif.

qr-054.src: al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Rasm Maṣāḥif al-Amṣār, chapter on differences between the regional maṣāḥif
qr-054.q: Which readers omit the highlighted word, in agreement with the muṣḥafs of Medina and al-Shām?
o: Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Jaʿfar
Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb
qr-054.e: Nāfiʿ and Abū Jaʿfar (Medina) and Ibn ʿĀmir (Damascus) read without the pronoun, matching their regional muṣḥafs; the others read it, as written in the remaining copies.

qr-055.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Baqara
qr-055.q: Which readers read the highlighted word in the same form as the first word of the verse (with alif after the khāʾ)?
o: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr
Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Jaʿfar and Yaʿqūb
qr-055.e: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr repeat the form of the first verb here; the others, including ʿĀṣim (and so Ḥafṣ), read the shorter form without alif.

qr-056.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Baqara
qr-056.q: The highlighted word is read with zāy ('how We raise up and assemble') or with rāʾ ('how We bring to life'). Who reads it with zāy?
o: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr only
qr-056.e: ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Khalaf and Ibn ʿĀmir read with zāy, describing the bones being raised and fitted together; Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Abū Jaʿfar and Yaʿqūb read with rāʾ, from bringing back to life. Both letters fit the undotted rasm.

qr-057.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Nisāʾ (where the word first occurs)
qr-057.q: The highlighted word is read by some as 'verify carefully' (fa-tabayyanū) and by others as 'make sure, be firm' (fa-tathabbatū). Who reads fa-tathabbatū?
o: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr
qr-057.e: Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read fa-tathabbatū, the others fa-tabayyanū; the undotted rasm carries both. The meanings complement each other: do not act on a report until it is clear and established.

qr-058.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Nisāʾ; al-Qurṭubī, al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān, on 4:43
qr-058.q: Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read the highlighted word without the alif after the lām. How do commentators usually describe the effect of the two readings?
o: One form suggests mutual contact, the other touching by one party; both are cited in the fiqh debate on touching
The two readings give opposite rulings, so one must be rejected
The reading without alif refers to prayer, the other to fasting
There is no difference in meaning at all between them
qr-058.e: The form with alif (lāmastum) is a mutual form, the one without (lamastum) a simple verb of touching; commentators cite both when discussing whether touching nullifies wuḍūʾ or refers to intercourse. Readings that differ in nuance are treated like two verses, not as contradictions.

qr-059.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Baqara
qr-059.q: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read the highlighted word with thāʾ ('much') instead of bāʾ ('great'). What makes both readings fit the rasm?
o: The letters bāʾ and thāʾ share one undotted shape
The word was left unwritten in the Kufan muṣḥaf
Thāʾ and bāʾ are pronounced alike in Kufan Arabic
The Kufan muṣḥaf wrote both letters one above the other
qr-059.e: The ʿUthmānī maṣāḥif were written without dots, so one skeleton serves bāʾ and thāʾ alike; the readings then follow transmission, not the reader's choice of dots.

qr-060.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat Ṭā Hā
qr-060.q: Which reader reads the highlighted word with yāʾ (hādhayni) instead of alif, after a stressed 'inna'?
qr-060.e: Abū ʿAmr reads 'inna hādhayni', the regular accusative after inna. Ḥafṣ reads 'in' lightened with hādhāni, Ibn Kathīr likewise with a doubled nūn, and the rest 'inna hādhāni'. This is among the best-known places discussed in tawjīh al-qirāʾāt.

qr-061.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat Hūd
qr-061.q: What is special about Ḥafṣ's reading of the highlighted word?
o: It is the only place where Ḥafṣ reads with full imāla
It is the only place where Ḥafṣ reads with tashīl
It is one of Ḥafṣ's four places of sakt
It is the only place where Ḥafṣ reads with ishmām
qr-061.e: Via al-Shāṭibiyya, Ḥafṣ reads the rāʾ of this word with major imāla (ā inclined toward ē), the only such case in his riwāya. His single tashīl is in 41:44 and his sakt places include 18:1.

qr-062.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Kahf
qr-062.q: Ḥafṣ (via al-Shāṭibiyya) makes a brief sakt after the highlighted word when continuing. Which statement about Ḥafṣ's sakt is correct?
o: He has four such places, the others being in Yā Sīn, al-Qiyāma and al-Muṭaffifīn
He makes sakt after every verse that ends in tanwīn
This is his only sakt in the whole Quran
He makes it only when stopping, never when continuing
qr-062.e: Via al-Shāṭibiyya Ḥafṣ has four obligatory places of sakt: here (18:1), in 36:52, 75:27 and 83:14. Sakt is a short pause without breath while continuing, which is why it concerns continuous reading.

qr-063.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb al-hamzatayn min kalima; farsh Sūrat Fuṣṣilat
qr-063.q: How does Ḥafṣ read the two hamzas at the start of the highlighted word?
o: The first fully, the second with tashīl (between hamza and alif)
Both hamzas fully pronounced with no change
An alif inserted between the two full hamzas
qr-063.e: This is the only place where Ḥafṣ applies tashīl: the second hamza is pronounced between hamza and alif. Inserting an alif between hamzas (idkhāl) is known from other rāwīs such as Qālūn and Hishām.

qr-064.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Kahf
qr-064.q: Among the ten, who reads the highlighted name and the one after it with a hamza (yaʾjūj wa-maʾjūj)?
qr-064.e: Only ʿĀṣim reads both names with hamza, which is why the Ḥafṣ muṣḥaf shows it; the other readers read them with a long ā without hamza.

qr-065.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Baqara (where the root first occurs)
qr-065.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word with a ḍamma on the fāʾ and wāw instead of hamza. Which reader reads it with a sukūn on the fāʾ followed by hamza?
qr-065.e: Ḥamza (and Khalaf al-ʿĀshir) read with sukūn of the fāʾ and hamza; Ḥafṣ has ḍamma with wāw, and the rest read ḍamma with hamza. The same pattern applies to the related word in al-Baqara where the qirāʾāt books first treat it.

qr-066.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb mīm al-jamʿ
qr-066.q: Ibn Kathīr is known for an uṣūl feature concerning the plural mīm (mīm al-jamʿ) before a consonant. What is it?
o: He connects it with a wāw (ṣila), e.g. ʿalayhimū
He always reads it with kasra
He assimilates it into the following letter
He drops it in pause and in continuous reading
qr-066.e: Ibn Kathīr reads mīm al-jamʿ with ṣila (a ḍamma lengthened to wāw) before a consonant; Qālūn has this as an option, and Warsh does it before a hamza. Ḥafṣ reads the mīm with sukūn.

qr-067.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb naql ḥarakat al-hamza ilā al-sākin qablahā
qr-067.q: What is naql, a well-known feature of Warsh's reading?
o: Moving the vowel of a hamza to the preceding sākin letter and dropping the hamza
Lengthening every madd to six counts
Pronouncing lām with a heavy sound after ṣād
Reading the plural mīm with a connecting wāw
qr-067.e: In naql, Warsh transfers the vowel of a hamza to the sākin consonant before it (e.g. the lām of the article) and drops the hamza. Six-count madd and heavy lām are separate features of Warsh's uṣūl.

qr-068.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb al-madd wa-l-qaṣr
qr-068.q: According to al-Shāṭibiyya, which two readers lengthen both the connected and the separated madd (muttaṣil and munfaṣil) to the full length (ishbāʿ, six counts)?
qr-068.e: In al-Shāṭibiyya, Warsh and Ḥamza have the longest madd in both types. Ibn Kathīr and al-Sūsī shorten the munfaṣil (qaṣr), Qālūn and al-Dūrī have shortening or medium length, and Ḥafṣ reads medium length.

qr-069.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb al-idghām al-kabīr
qr-069.q: Al-idghām al-kabīr (assimilating a voweled letter into a following similar or close letter) is chiefly associated with which riwāya in al-Shāṭibiyya?
qr-069.e: Al-Shāṭibiyya teaches al-idghām al-kabīr in its own chapter as a feature of Abū ʿAmr, read through al-Sūsī. It is called 'major' because the first letter is voweled, unlike ordinary idghām of a sākin letter.

qr-070.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction on the meaning of the seven aḥruf
qr-070.q: Ibn Qutayba, Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī and Ibn al-Jazarī are associated with which view of the seven aḥruf?
o: Seven kinds of variation, e.g. in nouns, verb forms, iʿrāb, order and substitution
Seven Arab tribes, each with its own complete dialect version
Seven themes such as command, prohibition and parables
Seven readers whose readings the hadith foretold
qr-070.e: These scholars understood the aḥruf as seven types of difference (wujūh al-ikhtilāf), listed differently by each but all describing kinds of variation. Other views identify them with tribal dialects or synonyms; the topical view (command, prohibition, etc.) was widely criticised.

qr-071.src: al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, introduction on the seven aḥruf
qr-071.q: What view of the seven aḥruf is associated with al-Ṭabarī?
o: They were different words with the same meaning, and ʿUthmān's muṣḥaf retained one ḥarf
They are the seven readings later chosen by Ibn Mujāhid
They are seven kinds of grammatical variation all kept in the muṣḥaf
They refer to seven topics, such as lawful and unlawful
qr-071.e: Al-Ṭabarī held that the aḥruf were variations in wording with agreeing meaning, and that the community, through ʿUthmān, settled on one ḥarf. Others, such as Ibn al-Jazarī, held that the muṣḥafs retain whatever of the aḥruf their rasm can carry.

qr-072.q: Al-Shāṭibiyya is a versification of which prose work?
qr-072.e: Al-Shāṭibī says in his introduction that he put al-Taysīr of Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī into verse, adding some points. Al-Nashr is later (Ibn al-Jazarī), and is the basis of Ṭayyibat al-Nashr.

qr-073.src: al-Bannāʾ al-Dimyāṭī, Itḥāf Fuḍalāʾ al-Bashar fī al-Qirāʾāt al-Arbaʿat ʿAshar, introduction
qr-073.q: Which four readers are commonly listed beyond the ten, giving the 'fourteen' whose additional readings are classed as shādhdh?
o: Ibn Muḥayṣin, al-Yazīdī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and al-Aʿmash
Abū Jaʿfar, Yaʿqūb, Khalaf and Ibn Muḥayṣin
Ubayy, Ibn Masʿūd, Zayd and ʿAlī
qr-073.e: Al-Bannāʾ's Itḥāf covers the fourteen: the ten plus Ibn Muḥayṣin, al-Yazīdī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and al-Aʿmash. Abū Jaʿfar, Yaʿqūb and Khalaf belong to the ten; Ubayy and the others are Companions, not the later imams of reading.

qr-074.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction; al-Nawawī, al-Majmūʿ, Kitāb al-Ṣalāt (reciting in prayer)
qr-074.q: What is the majority position on reciting a shādhdh reading in the prayer?
o: It is not permitted as Quran recitation in prayer, though it may be used in tafsīr and language
It is recommended because it adds a further meaning
It is permitted if the reader is a recognised scholar
It is obligatory once in every prayer to preserve it
qr-074.e: The majority hold that only readings meeting the conditions of the Quran may be recited as Quran, so a shādhdh reading is not recited in prayer; scholars still cite such readings for meaning and grammar. Some later discussions record differing details, but this is the prevailing view.

qr-075.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction; al-Bannāʾ, Itḥāf Fuḍalāʾ al-Bashar, introduction
qr-075.q: A reciter of Ḥafṣ may stop on a word with either sukūn or rawm, as he chooses. In qirāʾāt terminology such a free option is called a …
qr-075.e: A wajh (pl. awjuh) is an option left to the reciter; leaving one out is not a fault in transmission. A ṭarīq, riwāya or qirāʾa, by contrast, is a transmitted line that must be followed exactly once chosen.

qr-076.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Māʾida; Makkī, al-Kashf ʿan Wujūh al-Qirāʾāt, on 5:6
qr-076.q: The highlighted word is read with fatḥa (accusative) or kasra (genitive) on the lām. Which two rāwīs of the same imam differ here?
o: al-Bazzī (fatḥa) and Qunbul (kasra) from Ibn Kathīr
al-Dūrī (fatḥa) and al-Sūsī (kasra) from Abū ʿAmr
qr-076.e: Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥafṣ, al-Kisāʾī and Yaʿqūb read the accusative, linking the feet to the washed limbs; Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Shuʿba, Ḥamza, Abū Jaʿfar and Khalaf read the genitive. Commentators explain the genitive by proximity (jarr al-jiwār) or as referring to wiping over khuffs, so both readings are reconciled with washing the feet.

qr-077.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Baqara; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 2:222
qr-077.q: Some readers read the highlighted word with doubled ṭāʾ and hāʾ (yaṭṭahharna, 'until they purify themselves') instead of the light form (yaṭhurna, 'until they become pure'). Who are they?
o: Ḥafṣ, Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr
Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū Jaʿfar and Yaʿqūb
qr-077.e: Shuʿba, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read the doubled form; the others, including Ḥafṣ, read the light form. Jurists cite the two readings when discussing whether the end of bleeding suffices or a ritual bath is also required.

qr-078.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Baqara
qr-078.q: Ibn Kathīr reads the highlighted name in the accusative and the word 'words' (kalimāt) in the nominative. How is his reading explained?
o: The words reached Ādam, so 'words' is the subject and Ādam the object
Ādam is a vocative, so the case ending changes
It is an error of a rāwī that the readers tolerated
The Meccan muṣḥaf placed the two words in reverse order
qr-078.e: In Ibn Kathīr's reading the words 'met' Ādam (subject: the words; object: Ādam), while the others make Ādam the one who received them. Both express the same event, since what one meets also meets one.

qr-079.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Baqara
qr-079.q: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read the highlighted verb with fatḥa on the khāʾ. What is the effect?
o: It becomes a past-tense report that people took the station as a place of prayer
It becomes a command addressed to Ibrāhīm alone
It becomes a passive verb with no stated agent
It becomes a dual addressed to Ibrāhīm and Ismāʿīl
qr-079.e: With kasra (the others, including Ḥafṣ) the verb is an imperative; with fatḥa (Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir) it is a past-tense verb continuing the narrative. The rasm fits both.

qr-080.src: al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Rasm Maṣāḥif al-Amṣār, chapter on differences between the regional maṣāḥif
qr-080.q: Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Jaʿfar read the highlighted verb with a hamza and a single ṣād (awṣā) instead of a doubled ṣād. What supports their reading?
o: The muṣḥafs of Medina and al-Shām write an alif here
The Kufan muṣḥaf writes the word without any wāw
It is a dialectal pronunciation that leaves the rasm unaffected
It is supported by a Companion codex outside the ʿUthmānī ones
qr-080.e: Al-Dānī records that the Medinan and Shāmī maṣāḥif write this word with an alif between the two wāws, while the others do not; each group of readers follows the muṣḥaf of its region. Both verb forms mean 'enjoined'.

qr-081.src: al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Rasm Maṣāḥif al-Amṣār, chapter on differences between the regional maṣāḥif
qr-081.q: Which reader reads the highlighted word without its initial wāw, following the muṣḥaf of his region?
qr-081.e: Ibn ʿĀmir reads without the wāw, in agreement with the Shāmī muṣḥaf, which omits it here; the others read with the wāw as in their copies. Without the wāw the sentence begins a new statement rather than being joined to the previous one.

qr-082.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Baqara
qr-082.q: Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read the highlighted word with fatḥa on the nūn and a hamza (nansaʾhā). What meaning does their reading carry?
o: 'Or We cause it to be forgotten', from nisyān
'Or We copy it out', from naskh
'Or We abrogate its ruling only', from rafʿ
qr-082.e: Their reading derives from nasʾ, deferring; the reading of the others (nunsihā) derives from causing to be forgotten. Tafsīr works discuss both meanings in the context of abrogation.

qr-083.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat Yūsuf; al-Durra al-Muḍiyya, farsh Sūrat Yūsuf
qr-083.q: Among the ten, who reads the highlighted word with a light dhāl (kudhibū) rather than a doubled one (kudhdhibū)?
o: The Kufans (ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Khalaf) and Abū Jaʿfar
Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir
qr-083.e: The Kufans and Abū Jaʿfar read the light form, the remaining readers the doubled form ('they were disbelieved'). Commentators devote long discussions to whom the pronoun in the light reading refers, which makes this a classic case of tawjīh.

qr-084.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh Sūrat al-Rūm
qr-084.q: How does Ḥafṣ read the ḍād of the highlighted word (and its two repetitions in the verse) via al-Shāṭibiyya?
o: With both ḍamma and fatḥa as valid options
Only with fatḥa, like Shuʿba and Ḥamza
Only with ḍamma, like the majority
With kasra, as in the Kufan dialect
qr-084.e: Shuʿba and Ḥamza read the ḍād with fatḥa, the others with ḍamma; Ḥafṣ has both. Al-Shāṭibī reports both ways for Ḥafṣ, so either may be recited in his riwāya.

qr-085.src: al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Rasm Maṣāḥif al-Amṣār, chapter on differences between the regional maṣāḥif
qr-085.q: Which readers read the highlighted word without its initial wāw?
o: Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir and Abū Jaʿfar
Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb
Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀmir only
qr-085.e: The Medinan and Shāmī maṣāḥif omit the wāw here, so Nāfiʿ, Abū Jaʿfar (Medina) and Ibn ʿĀmir (al-Shām) read without it; the others read it with the wāw. The pattern of these three agreeing matches 57:24.

qr-086.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya fī Ṭabaqāt al-Qurrāʾ, entry Ibn Shanabūdh; al-Dhahabī, Maʿrifat al-Qurrāʾ al-Kibār
qr-086.q: Ibn Shanabūdh, a Baghdadi reader contemporary with Ibn Mujāhid, was tried and made to recant. What was the charge?
o: Reciting in prayer readings with sound reports that contradict the ʿUthmānī rasm
Allowing any reading that fits the rasm and Arabic even without transmission
Restricting the readings to exactly seven readers
Teaching the readings for payment in the mosque
qr-086.e: Ibn Shanabūdh recited readings reported from Companions (e.g. Ibn Masʿūd, Ubayy) that went against the ʿUthmānī rasm. The opposite error, accepting what fits rasm and Arabic without transmission, is associated with Ibn Miqsam.

qr-087.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction (on Ibn Miqsam); al-Dhahabī, Maʿrifat al-Qurrāʾ al-Kibār
qr-087.q: Abū Bakr Ibn Miqsam was censured and recanted. Which of Ibn al-Jazarī's three conditions did his method disregard?
o: Agreement with the reading of Medina
qr-087.e: Ibn Miqsam held that any reading fitting the rasm and valid in Arabic could be recited, even without transmission. The scholars rejected this because the Quran is received by transmission, not derived by analogy; the sound chain is indispensable.

qr-088.src: Ibn Qudāma, al-Mughnī, Kitāb al-Aymān (fasting in expiation); al-Nawawī, al-Majmūʿ, Kitāb al-Aymān
qr-088.q: The verse shown prescribes three days of fasting in expiation of an oath; Ibn Masʿūd is reported to have read 'three consecutive days'. Which statement correctly describes how the schools treat this?
o: Ḥanafīs and Ḥanbalīs require consecutive days, citing this reading among their evidence; Mālikīs and the relied-upon Shāfiʿī view do not
All four schools require consecutive days because the reading is mutawātir
Only the Mālikīs require consecutive days, citing a reading of Ubayy
Ḥanafīs reject consecutive days because a shādhdh reading carries no weight
qr-088.e: Since the reading is shādhdh it is not recited as Quran, but the Ḥanafīs and Ḥanbalīs treat it as a report that can serve as evidence and require consecutive fasting. The Mālikīs and the Shāfiʿīs (in their relied-upon view) do not make consecutiveness a condition.

qr-089.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya fī Ṭabaqāt al-Qurrāʾ, entries ʿĀṣim and Ḥafṣ; al-Nashr, chapter on the chains of ʿĀṣim
qr-089.q: According to a well-known report from ʿĀṣim, through which teachers did he give Ḥafṣ and Shuʿba their respective readings?
o: Ḥafṣ via Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī from ʿAlī; Shuʿba via Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh from Ibn Masʿūd
Ḥafṣ via Zirr from Ibn Masʿūd; Shuʿba via al-Sulamī from ʿAlī
Both via Abū al-ʿĀliya from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb
Ḥafṣ via Mujāhid from Ibn ʿAbbās; Shuʿba via Nāfiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar
qr-089.e: ʿĀṣim is reported to have told Ḥafṣ that what he taught him came through al-Sulamī from ʿAlī, and what he taught Shuʿba through Zirr from Ibn Masʿūd. This helps explain why the two riwāyāt of ʿĀṣim differ in many words.

qr-090.src: Abū Shāma, al-Murshid al-Wajīz ilā ʿUlūm Tataʿallaq bi-l-Kitāb al-ʿAzīz; Makkī, al-Ibāna ʿan Maʿānī al-Qirāʾāt
qr-090.q: Some later scholars wished that Ibn Mujāhid had chosen a number other than seven for his readers. What was their main concern?
o: The number led less informed people to equate the seven readings with the seven aḥruf
Seven was too few to cover the five regional muṣḥafs
Seven readers excluded Mecca and Medina
The number seven contradicted the hadith of the aḥruf
qr-090.e: Writers such as Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib and Abū Shāma noted that choosing exactly seven caused many to think these readings were the seven aḥruf of the hadith. The choice itself covered all five regional centres.

qr-091.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction (on the first compilers)
qr-091.q: Whom does Ibn al-Jazarī name as the first recognised imam to collect the readings in a book?
qr-091.e: In al-Nashr, Ibn al-Jazarī names Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām as the first noted imam to compile the readings in a book, covering more readers than the later seven. Ibn Mujāhid came after him and restricted the selection to seven.

qr-092.src: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, al-Ḥujja li-l-Qurrāʾ al-Sabʿa, introduction
qr-092.q: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī's al-Ḥujja li-l-Qurrāʾ al-Sabʿa belongs to which genre?
o: Tawjīh (iḥtijāj): explaining the linguistic grounds of each reading
Rasm: describing the spelling of the regional muṣḥafs
Ṭabaqāt: biographies of readers by generation
Waqf wa-ibtidāʾ: rules of stopping and starting
qr-092.e: Al-Ḥujja explains the grammatical and linguistic justification of the readings of the seven collected by Ibn Mujāhid. Makkī's al-Kashf and Ibn Khālawayh's al-Ḥujja belong to the same genre of tawjīh.

qr-093.src: al-Shāṭibī, ʿAqīlat Atrāb al-Qaṣāʾid fī Asnā al-Maqāṣid (al-Rāʾiyya), introduction
qr-093.q: Besides Ḥirz al-Amānī, al-Shāṭibī composed ʿAqīlat Atrāb al-Qaṣāʾid. What is its subject and its main source?
o: The rasm of the muṣḥaf, based on al-Dānī's al-Muqniʿ
The ten readings, based on Ibn Mujāhid's al-Sabʿa
Tajwīd for beginners, based on Makkī's al-Riʿāya
Verse counting, based on al-Dānī's al-Bayān
qr-093.e: ʿAqīlat Atrāb al-Qaṣāʾid, known as al-Rāʾiyya from its rhyme in rāʾ, versifies the rules of the ʿUthmānī spelling from al-Dānī's al-Muqniʿ. Al-Shāṭibī also has a poem on verse counting, but that is a different work.

qr-094.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, chapter on the chains of the readers
qr-094.q: Which pair of rāwīs did NOT learn directly from their imam but through intermediaries?
o: al-Bazzī and Qunbul from Ibn Kathīr
Abū al-Ḥārith and al-Dūrī from al-Kisāʾī
qr-094.e: Ibn Kathīr died long before al-Bazzī and Qunbul, who received his reading through chains of Meccan teachers. Qālūn and Warsh read with Nāfiʿ, Shuʿba and Ḥafṣ with ʿĀṣim, and al-Kisāʾī's two rāwīs with al-Kisāʾī himself.

qr-095.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, chapter on the ṭuruq of Warsh; al-Shāṭibiyya, introduction
qr-095.q: Warsh's riwāya as taught in al-Shāṭibiyya comes through one ṭarīq. Which one, and which ṭarīq does Ṭayyibat al-Nashr add?
qr-095.e: Al-Shāṭibiyya (following al-Taysīr) gives Warsh via al-Azraq, the basis of Warsh as read in the Maghrib. Al-Nashr and al-Ṭayyiba also bring Warsh via al-Aṣbahānī, which differs in several uṣūl. Al-Ḥulwānī is known as a transmitter of Qālūn and Hishām.

qr-096.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction (on requiring tawātur)
qr-096.q: Some later scholars made tawātur a separate condition for every reading. Which statement describes Ibn al-Jazarī's response in al-Nashr?
o: If tawātur were established, the other two pillars would add nothing; a sound, widely accepted chain suffices with them
He agreed and dropped the condition of agreement with Arabic
He held that tawātur applies only to the seven, not to the three
He replaced the chain condition with consensus of the five cities
qr-096.e: Ibn al-Jazarī argues that tawātur would make the conditions of rasm and Arabic superfluous, and that requiring it for every detail would exclude much that is firmly transmitted; a sound chain that is widely known and accepted, together with rasm and Arabic, is the criterion. Elsewhere he still affirms that the ten readings are mutawātir.

xaq-001.src: al-Shahrastānī, al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal; al-Subkī, Ṭabaqāt al-Shāfiʿiyya; Ibn Taymiyya, Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā; al-Ashʿarī, Maqālāt al-Islāmiyyīn
xaq-001.q: Which statement correctly describes the three main Sunni creedal traditions?
o: The Ashʿarīs follow Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī (d. 324 AH), the Māturīdīs follow Abū Manṣūr al-Māturīdī (d. 333 AH) and the Atharīs (Ḥanbalī tradition) stress adherence to the transmitted texts and the way of the early generations
All three follow the same founder
The Ashʿarīs follow al-Māturīdī and the Māturīdīs follow Ibn Taymiyya
They are the three Shīʿī schools
xaq-001.e: The three traditions are distinguished by method. The Ashʿarīs, originally with al-Ashʿarī’s turn from Muʿtazilism, use rational proofs alongside the texts; the Māturīdīs, based in Samarqand and followed by many Ḥanafīs, give more weight to reason on some questions; the Atharīs, associated with Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and later Ibn Taymiyya, stress the apparent text. All three are regarded as Ahl al-Sunna by their followers, with disputes over the boundaries.

xaq-002.src: al-Sanūsī, Umm al-Barāhīn; al-Bayjūrī, Tuḥfat al-Murīd; al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda al-Ṭaḥāwiyya
xaq-002.q: How do Ashʿarī and Māturīdī manuals differ in counting the attributes of God proved by reason?
o: The Ashʿarī manuals count seven essential attributes (life, knowledge, power, will, hearing, sight, speech), while the Māturīdīs add takwīn (creating) as a separate attribute
xaq-002.e: Ashʿarī works such as al-Sanūsī’s Umm al-Barāhīn list seven attributes of meaning (ṣifāt al-maʿānī): ḥayāt, ʿilm, qudra, irāda, samʿ, baṣar and kalām. The Māturīdīs affirm the same and add takwīn (bringing into being), which the Ashʿarīs include under power. The Atharīs affirm what the texts affirm without limiting to a fixed number.

xaq-003.src: al-Ashʿarī, al-Ibāna ʿan Uṣūl al-Diyāna; al-Bayhaqī, al-Asmāʾ wa-l-Ṣifāt; Ibn Taymiyya, Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā; al-Juwaynī, al-Irshād
xaq-003.q: How did the traditions explain that the Quran is not created while it is recited, written and heard?
o: The Ashʿarīs and Māturīdīs distinguish the inner speech of God (al-kalām al-nafsī), which is eternal, from the recited words, which are created as sounds; the Atharīs held the Quran to be God’s speech, uncreated, in letter and sound, and disliked saying that the recitation is created
All traditions say the Quran is created
All traditions say the ink is eternal
xaq-003.e: The controversy about the Quran’s createdness (the miḥna under al-Maʾmūn, with Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal’s resistance) led to doctrinal formulas. The Ashʿarīs say the Quran as God’s speech is eternal, while the readings and writing are created in the sense of the reciter’s acts; the Māturīdīs say similarly. Ahl al-Athar, with Aḥmad, held that the Quran is God’s speech, uncreated, and rejected statements on the recitation (lafẓ) either way.

xaq-004.src: al-Juwaynī, al-ʿAqīda al-Niẓāmiyya; Ibn Qudāma, Lumʿat al-Iʿtiqād; Ibn Taymiyya, al-Tadmuriyya; al-Bayhaqī, al-Asmāʾ wa-l-Ṣifāt
xaq-004.q: How do the traditions differ in dealing with the apparent attributes of God such as ‘hand’ and ‘face’ (ṣifāt khabariyya)?
o: The Atharīs affirm them as they came without asking how (bi-lā kayf) and without likeness; many early Ashʿarīs favoured delegating the meaning (tafwīḍ), while later Ashʿarīs and Māturīdīs often allowed figurative interpretation (taʾwīl)
All traditions interpret them as bodily limbs
All traditions reject any mention of them
xaq-004.e: The texts of Quran and Sunna mention God’s face, hand, eye and ascension above the throne. The Atharīs, with Ibn Qudāma and Ibn Taymiyya, affirm them as befits God without likening or asking how. Al-Juwaynī in al-ʿAqīda al-Niẓāmiyya reports the way of the early generations as delegation (tafwīḍ), and later Ashʿarīs, such as al-Rāzī and Ibn Fūrak, gave figurative readings, for instance interpreting ‘hand’ as power. The traditions disagree about which approach is that of the early Muslims.

xaq-005.src: Ibn Taymiyya, Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā; Ibn Abī al-ʿIzz, Sharḥ al-ʿAqīda al-Ṭaḥāwiyya; al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Manda (early uses)
xaq-005.q: What are the three categories of tawḥīd as taught in the Atharī tradition, and how do other traditions regard the division?
o: Tawḥīd al-rubūbiyya, al-ulūhiyya and al-asmāʾ wa-l-ṣifāt, a classification later associated with Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Abī al-ʿIzz; other scholars accept the content but not always the division as a method
Tawḥīd of men, women and children
Tawḥīd of the heart, the tongue and the limbs only, rejected by all
Tawḥīd of the East, the West and the South
xaq-005.e: The threefold division of tawḥīd (lordship, divinity and names and attributes) is used in the Atharī/Salafī tradition, citing early scholars such as Ibn Manda and developed by Ibn Taymiyya. Ashʿarīs and Māturīdīs describe tawḥīd by the oneness of essence, attributes and acts, and some scholars object that the three-part scheme was not used by the early generations, while its defenders say it reflects the texts.

xaq-006.src: Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Fiqh al-Akbar; al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda al-Ṭaḥāwiyya; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-īmān; Ibn Abī al-ʿIzz, Sharḥ al-Ṭaḥāwiyya
xaq-006.q: How did the traditions define īmān, and does it increase and decrease?
o: The Atharīs define īmān as speech, action and belief, increasing and decreasing; the Ḥanafī/Māturīdī tradition (Abū Ḥanīfa) defined it as affirmation with the tongue and assent of the heart, with works outside it, and denied increase and decrease in its core; many Ashʿarīs allowed increase in some reports
All traditions define faith as only an utterance
All traditions say faith is only works
xaq-006.e: Atharī scholars, with al-Bukhārī, included works in faith, and said it rises with obedience and falls with sin. Abū Ḥanīfa held that works are not part of faith itself, so that the faith of people is equal in its essence, which the Atharīs called irjāʾ; his school responded that the dispute is largely verbal as both agree that sins damage a believer and works are required. Ashʿarīs differ: some allow increase and decrease through its effects.

xaq-007.src: al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda al-Ṭaḥāwiyya; Ibn Abī al-ʿIzz, Sharḥ al-Ṭaḥāwiyya; al-Bayhaqī, Shuʿab al-Īmān
xaq-007.q: What is the debate on saying 'I am a believer, if God wills' (al-istithnāʾ fī al-īmān)?
o: Many Atharīs and Shāfiʿīs allowed it out of humility or doubt about the final outcome, while the Ḥanafīs generally disliked it as implying doubt in present faith
All traditions forbade any mention of God’s will
xaq-007.e: The question divided early scholars. Those who allowed it, such as many Atharīs and Shāfiʿīs, meant uncertainty about one’s final state or humility, not doubt about present assent. The Ḥanafīs, and Abū Ḥanīfa in a report, rejected it, saying it expresses doubt, and preferred ‘I am a believer in truth’. Some, like al-Ṭaḥāwī, discussed the permissible meanings.

xaq-008.src: al-Ghazālī, Fayṣal al-Tafriqa bayna al-Islām wa-l-Zandaqa; Ibn Taymiyya, Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā; al-Shawkānī, al-Sayl al-Jarrār; al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda
xaq-008.q: What general principle about takfīr (declaring a Muslim an unbeliever) is stated in the classical creeds?
o: That Ahl al-Qibla are not declared unbelievers for sins, and takfīr of a person requires conditions (knowledge, absence of coercion, removal of doubt) and an authorised judgment, as stressed by al-Ghazālī and Ibn Taymiyya
That any Muslim may declare another an unbeliever freely
That takfīr is the first duty of faith
That takfīr applies to anyone who has a different school
xaq-008.e: Al-Ṭaḥāwī and others write that we do not declare any of Ahl al-Qibla unbelievers for a sin so long as he does not deem it lawful. Al-Ghazālī in Fayṣal al-Tafriqa warned against hastiness in takfīr and limited it to denial of what is known to be of the religion by necessity. Ibn Taymiyya distinguished the ruling on a statement from the ruling on the speaker, who must have knowledge and no excuse.

xaq-009.src: al-Ashʿarī, al-Lumaʿ; al-Māturīdī, Kitāb al-Tawḥīd; al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda; Ibn Taymiyya, Minhāj al-Sunna
xaq-009.q: How did the traditions explain human acts and God’s creation of them (kasb and ikhtiyār)?
o: Al-Ashʿarī taught that God creates the act and the servant acquires (kasb) it; the Māturīdīs gave the servant a real choice (ikhtiyār) in directing the created power; the Atharīs affirmed God’s creation of acts and the servant’s will and ability without elaborate theory
All traditions say humans create their acts independently
All traditions say humans have no will whatsoever
xaq-009.e: The Muʿtazila held that humans create their acts. The Sunni traditions affirmed God’s creation of all things, including acts, while preserving responsibility. The Ashʿarī theory of kasb says that the act is created by God and acquired by the servant; the Māturīdīs say that the servant’s choice is real and is the ground for accountability; the Atharīs state that humans have will and ability and God is Creator of both, without a formal theory.

xaq-010.src: Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-īmān (ḥadīth ʿUmar on Jibrīl); al-Dhahabī, Mīzān al-Iʿtidāl; al-Shahrastānī, al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal
xaq-010.q: Who is named as the first to speak of denying qadar in Islam, according to the account of Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar in Muslim?
o: Maʿbad al-Juhanī in Baṣra, as Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar and Ḥumayd al-Ḥimyarī reported to ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar
xaq-010.e: Muslim opens Kitāb al-īmān with the account of Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar, who told Ibn ʿUmar that people in Baṣra denied qadar and claimed that matters are unforeseen; Ibn ʿUmar disowned them and related the ḥadīth of ʿUmar on Jibrīl. Maʿbad al-Juhanī is named as the first to speak so in Baṣra, later executed in the time of ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān according to the sources.

xaq-011.src: Ibn Taymiyya, Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā; Ibn al-Qayyim, Shifāʾ al-ʿAlīl; al-Māturīdī, Kitāb al-Tawḥīd; al-Ashʿarī, al-Lumaʿ
xaq-011.q: How do the traditions relate God’s will (irāda) to His command (amr)?
o: Ashʿarīs hold that God’s will includes everything that occurs, even disobedience, and that command is separate from will; Māturīdīs similarly distinguish God’s will from His pleasure and love; Atharīs such as Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim distinguish the creative will (kawniyya) from the legislative will (sharʿiyya)
All traditions say will and command are always identical
All traditions say God has no will
All traditions say will applies only to obedience
xaq-011.e: The Muʿtazila held that God does not will evil, only commands good. The Sunni traditions affirm that nothing occurs but by God’s will, yet He does not love or command evil. Ashʿarīs and Māturīdīs distinguish will from pleasure and love; Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim distinguish two kinds of will, the creative (what occurs) and the legislative (what God loves and commands), to explain how disobedience occurs by His will yet against His command.

xaq-012.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-shurūṭ and al-tawḥīd (ninety-nine names); al-Tirmidhī, Jāmiʿ (list of names); Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī; Ibn Taymiyya, Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā
xaq-012.q: What do scholars say about the hadith of the ninety-nine names and the list in al-Tirmidhī?
o: The statement that God has ninety-nine names is in the Ṣaḥīḥayn, while the detailed list in al-Tirmidhī is judged a later insertion by several scholars such as Ibn Ḥajar and Ibn Taymiyya, and God’s names are not limited to ninety-nine
The hadith is fabricated and does not exist
The list is part of the Quran
The Ṣaḥīḥayn contain the full list
xaq-012.e: The Ṣaḥīḥayn report that God has ninety-nine names, and whoever enumerates (aḥṣāhā) them enters Paradise. The long list with names comes in al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah through al-Walīd ibn Muslim, with differences between the lists. Scholars like Ibn Ḥajar and Ibn Taymiyya considered the enumeration an insertion by a narrator or later hand, and argued that the names are not limited to that count.

xaq-013.src: al-Bayhaqī, al-Asmāʾ wa-l-Ṣifāt; al-Ghazālī, al-Maqṣad al-Asná; al-Rāzī, Lawāmiʿ al-Bayyināt; Ibn Qudāma, Lumʿat al-Iʿtiqād
xaq-013.q: Are the names of God fixed by revelation (tawqīfiyya), according to the traditions?
o: The Atharīs and most Ashʿarīs held that God’s names are known only from the Quran and Sunna; some Māturīdīs and al-Bāqillānī allowed names that are correct in meaning even without a text
All traditions allow inventing names freely
All traditions allow only the names in the Torah
All traditions say the names are meaningless
xaq-013.e: The prevailing view, held by the Atharīs, al-Bayhaqī and most Ashʿarīs, is that God’s names are tawqīfiyya: they are taken only from texts and not by analogy. Others, including al-Bāqillānī in one report and some Muʿtazila, allowed a name if its meaning is sound and not forbidden. The question affects whether one may call God by names not found in revelation, such as ‘the cause’ or ‘the necessary being’.

xaq-014.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-tawḥīd and Kitāb mawāqīt al-ṣalāh (ḥadīth Jarīr); al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda; al-Ashʿarī, al-Ibāna
xaq-014.q: What is the Sunni position on seeing God in the hereafter, and who denied it?
o: Ahl al-Sunna affirm that the believers will see their Lord in the hereafter, based on the Quran and the ḥadīth of Jarīr (seeing the full moon); the Muʿtazila and Jahmiyya denied it and interpreted the texts figuratively
All groups affirmed that God can be seen in this world
xaq-014.e: The Sunni creeds affirm the vision (ruʾya) of God by believers in the hereafter without limit or likeness. The ḥadīth of Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh in al-Bukhārī compares the vision to seeing the full moon. The Muʿtazila denied it on rational grounds and interpreted the verses as meaning waiting for God’s reward. Ahl al-Sunna also differ on whether the Prophet ﷺ saw his Lord with his eyes on the Night of the Ascent, with ʿĀʾisha denying it and Ibn ʿAbbās affirming a vision by the heart or eye.

xaq-015.src: al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda; al-Bāqillānī, al-Bayān; al-Subkī, Ṭabaqāt; Ibn Taymiyya, al-Nubuwwāt
xaq-015.q: What distinguishes a miracle of a prophet (muʿjiza) from the wonder given to a righteous person (karāma) in the classical creeds?
o: The muʿjiza is joined to a claim of prophecy with a challenge and cannot be matched; the karāma is a wonder shown at the hands of a righteous follower, without a claim of prophecy, and is affirmed by Ahl al-Sunna against the Muʿtazila
The karāma is greater than the muʿjiza
Both are only done by Satan
There is no difference and neither is affirmed
xaq-015.e: Ahl al-Sunna affirm karāmāt for the saints (awliyāʾ) such as the story of Maryam’s food or the Companions’ reported wonders. The Muʿtazila mostly denied them, fearing confusion with prophecy. The muʿjiza is distinguished by claim of prophecy, challenge (taḥaddī) and inability of others to match it. The Ashʿarī al-Bāqillānī and others set out the conditions.

xaq-016.src: al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, al-Shifā, Part 2; Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī; al-Taftāzānī, Sharḥ al-ʿAqāʾid al-Nasafiyya; al-Rāzī, ʿIṣmat al-Anbiyāʾ
xaq-016.q: What do Sunni scholars hold about the infallibility (ʿiṣma) of prophets?
o: Prophets are protected from major sins and from error in conveying the message; whether minor slips occurred before or after prophecy is debated, with al-Rāzī and al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ giving detailed positions
Prophets sin like any other person without any protection
Only the final Prophet ﷺ has any protection
xaq-016.e: Sunni scholars agree on protection in conveying the message and from disbelief. For sins, most hold that prophets are protected from major sins and from those that show baseness, while some permit minor slips that God corrects, as in some verses about Adam and Yūnus. Al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ in al-Shifā and al-Rāzī in ʿIṣmat al-Anbiyāʾ give extended discussions and read such verses as leaving the better course (khilāf al-awlā).

xaq-017.src: al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda; Ibn Abī al-ʿIzz, Sharḥ al-Ṭaḥāwiyya; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ (Ibn ʿUmar: ranking in the Prophet’s time); Ibn Taymiyya, Minhāj al-Sunna
xaq-017.q: How do Sunni creeds rank the four Rightly Guided Caliphs, and what disagreement existed between ʿUthmān and ʿAlī?
o: In order Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī in caliphate; early scholars in Kūfa debated whether ʿAlī was better than ʿUthmān, and Ahl al-Sunna settled on ʿUthmān before ʿAlī
ʿAlī before Abū Bakr by consensus
ʿUmar before Abū Bakr by consensus
All four are exactly equal in rank
xaq-017.e: Al-Ṭaḥāwī and the Sunni creeds affirm the order in excellence matching the order of caliphate. In early times some of the people of Kūfa preferred ʿAlī to ʿUthmān, and the Sunni consensus later settled on ʿUthmān first, as Ibn Taymiyya states. Abū Ḥanīfa is reported to have first held ʿAlī better and later returned to the majority. The Shīʿa hold ʿAlī was the rightful successor.

xaq-018.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī; Ibn Taymiyya, Minhāj al-Sunna; al-Dhahabī, Siyar; al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda; Ibn al-ʿArabī, al-ʿAwāṣim min al-Qawāṣim
xaq-018.q: What is the Sunni principle about the conflicts between the Companions (Jamal and Ṣiffīn)?
o: To refrain from speaking ill of the Companions, to consider them mujtahids who may have erred or been right, and to hold that ʿAlī was closer to the truth in these conflicts, as most Sunni scholars state
To curse the Companions who fought
To say all participants were unbelievers
To avoid mentioning that these battles occurred
xaq-018.e: Al-Ṭaḥāwī and other creeds say we love the Companions and mention only good of them. For the conflicts, most scholars hold that ʿAlī was right in the Battle of the Camel and Ṣiffīn, while Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, ʿĀʾisha and Muʿāwiya acted from ijtihād, and are excused and may be rewarded once. Some early Basran scholars were more reserved, and Ibn al-ʿArabī in al-ʿAwāṣim defended the Companions strongly.

xaq-019.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-janāʾiz (ʿadhāb al-qabr); Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ; al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda; Ibn Abī al-ʿIzz, Sharḥ al-Ṭaḥāwiyya
xaq-019.q: What is the Sunni position on the punishment and bliss of the grave, and who denied it?
o: Ahl al-Sunna affirm it on the basis of Quran and numerous reports, while some Muʿtazila and others denied it or reinterpreted it
All schools denied the grave’s punishment
It is held to apply to the body only, never to the soul
xaq-019.e: The reports in the Ṣaḥīḥayn on the questioning in the grave and the punishment or bliss of the grave are numerous, and the Sunni creeds affirm them. Some Muʿtazila (like Ḍirār ibn ʿAmr) and the Khawārij denied it, as it was thought to be against reason. Ahl al-Sunna do not specify the manner beyond the texts, with differing views on whether it is on the soul alone or on both soul and body.

xaq-020.src: al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-riqāq and Kitāb al-tawḥīd; Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-īmān; al-Nasafī, al-ʿAqāʾid
xaq-020.q: Which items of the afterlife do the Sunni creeds affirm, and what did the Muʿtazila say regarding intercession?
o: The Scale, the Bridge (al-ṣirāṭ), the Pond (al-ḥawḍ) and intercession for people of major sin; the Muʿtazila denied intercession for those who committed major sins and died without repentance
Only the Scale; all others are rejected
Only the Pond; the Bridge is rejected by all
The creeds do not mention any of them
xaq-020.e: The Sunni creeds (such as al-Ṭaḥāwī’s) affirm the questioning, the Scale (al-mīzān), the Bridge (al-ṣirāṭ), the Pond (al-ḥawḍ) and the intercession (shafāʿa) of the Prophet ﷺ for those of his community who committed major sins, based on mutawātir-level reports. The Muʿtazila limited intercession to raising the rank of the righteous, since in their view the unrepentant major sinner is eternally in the Fire. Sunnis hold that such a person is under God’s will.

xaq-021.src: al-Ashʿarī, Maqālāt al-Islāmiyyīn; al-Shahrastānī, al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal; al-Baghdādī, al-Farq bayna al-Firaq
xaq-021.q: Which statement correctly summarises the early disputes about the status of the grave sinner (murtakib al-kabīra)?
o: The Khawārij called him an unbeliever, the Murjiʾa postponed judgment and stressed faith, the Muʿtazila placed him in an intermediate position, and Ahl al-Sunna held him a believer with sin under God’s will
All groups said he is a perfect believer
All groups said he is an unbeliever
xaq-021.e: The dispute began after the first civil strife. The Khawārij held that a major sinner leaves the community of believers. The Murjiʾa postponed his final judgment to God and gave faith priority. Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ and the Muʿtazila held he is neither believer nor unbeliever but in an intermediate state, and will remain in the Fire if he dies unrepentant. Ahl al-Sunna say he remains a believer with deficient faith, under God’s will.

xaq-022.src: al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār, Sharḥ al-Uṣūl al-Khamsa; al-Ashʿarī, Maqālāt al-Islāmiyyīn; al-Shahrastānī, al-Milal wa-l-Niḥal
xaq-022.q: Which are the five principles (al-uṣūl al-khamsa) of the Muʿtazila?
o: Divine unity (tawḥīd), justice (ʿadl), the promise and threat (al-waʿd wa-l-waʿīd), the intermediate position (al-manzila bayna al-manzilatayn) and commanding right and forbidding wrong
Prayer, fasting, zakāt, ḥajj and testimony
Sharia, tarīqa, ḥaqīqa, maʿrifa and tawba
The Quran, the Sunna, consensus, analogy and custom
xaq-022.e: The Muʿtazila, as set out by al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār, built their doctrine on five principles. Tawḥīd for them includes denial of eternal attributes distinct from the essence; ʿadl includes the claim that God does not create evil acts; the waʿd wa-l-waʿīd says reward and punishment must be carried out; the intermediate position concerns the grave sinner. These led to disputes with the Ashʿarīs and Atharīs.

xaq-023.src: al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya; Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, al-Radd ʿalā al-Zanādiqa wa-l-Jahmiyya; al-Ṭabarī, Taʾrīkh
xaq-023.q: What was the miḥna in the caliphates of al-Maʾmūn, al-Muʿtaṣim and al-Wāthiq, and what role did Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal play?
o: A state inquisition requiring scholars to say the Quran is created; Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal refused and was flogged and imprisoned, and the policy was ended under al-Mutawakkil
A ban on teaching hadith in Baghdad only
xaq-023.e: From about 218 AH, al-Maʾmūn imposed the doctrine of the Quran’s createdness, supported by the Muʿtazilī judge Aḥmad ibn Abī Duʾād, and tested judges and scholars. Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal refused, was imprisoned and flogged under al-Muʿtaṣim, and became a symbol of steadfastness to Ahl al-Sunna. Al-Mutawakkil ended the inquisition around 234 AH and supported the Sunni scholars.

xaq-024.src: Ibn ʿAsākir, Tabyīn Kadhib al-Muftarī; al-Subkī, Ṭabaqāt al-Shāfiʿiyya al-Kubrā; al-Ashʿarī, al-Ibāna and al-Lumaʿ; Ibn Taymiyya, Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā
xaq-024.q: What are the stages usually attributed to al-Ashʿarī’s intellectual life, and what is debated?
o: Muʿtazilī, then a Kullābī phase, then a return to the way of Aḥmad as stated in al-Ibāna; the Ashʿarīs hold that the later view is the Ashʿarī system in al-Lumaʿ, while others see al-Ibāna as his final book
He was born in Madīna and never changed opinions
He was a Christian convert and wrote nothing
xaq-024.e: Al-Ashʿarī (d. 324 AH) studied under the Muʿtazilī al-Jubbāʾī, then left Muʿtazilism. Later authors, such as Ibn Taymiyya, describe a Kullābī stage, then a final stage in which he affirmed the creed of Aḥmad in al-Ibāna. The Ashʿarīs, including Ibn ʿAsākir and al-Subkī, hold that al-Ibāna and al-Lumaʿ agree in essence, and the dispute over which expresses his final view continues.

xaq-025.src: al-Māturīdī, Kitāb al-Tawḥīd and Taʾwīlāt Ahl al-Sunna; Abū al-Muʿīn al-Nasafī, Tabṣirat al-Adilla; al-Bazdawī, Uṣūl al-Dīn; al-Nasafī, al-ʿAqāʾid
xaq-025.q: What are the principal Māturīdī works and what is the relation to Abū Ḥanīfa?
o: Kitāb al-Tawḥīd and Taʾwīlāt Ahl al-Sunna of al-Māturīdī, with later systematic works by al-Nasafī and al-Bazdawī; the school sees itself as the creedal expression of the Ḥanafī tradition
al-Muwaṭṭaʾ of Mālik; the school follows Mālik
al-Risāla of al-Shāfiʿī; the school follows al-Shāfiʿī
Nahj al-Balāgha; the school is Shīʿī
xaq-025.e: Abū Manṣūr al-Māturīdī (d. 333 AH) of Samarqand wrote Kitāb al-Tawḥīd on creed and Taʾwīlāt Ahl al-Sunna on Quranic exegesis. Later Māturīdī works include al-Bazdawī’s Uṣūl al-Dīn, Abū al-Muʿīn al-Nasafī’s Tabṣirat al-Adilla and Najm al-Dīn al-Nasafī’s al-ʿAqāʾid, widely taught with al-Taftāzānī’s commentary. The school sees its method as continuing Abū Ḥanīfa’s positions.

xaq-026.src: al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda al-Ṭaḥāwiyya; al-Nasafī, al-ʿAqāʾid; al-Sanūsī, Umm al-Barāhīn; Ibn Qudāma, Lumʿat al-Iʿtiqād; al-Ghazālī, al-Iqtiṣād fī al-Iʿtiqād
xaq-026.q: Which statement correctly matches creedal texts with traditions or authors?
o: al-ʿAqīda al-Ṭaḥāwiyya (al-Ṭaḥāwī, a Ḥanafī, accepted across Sunni traditions), al-ʿAqāʾid al-Nasafiyya (Māturīdī), Umm al-Barāhīn (al-Sanūsī, Ashʿarī) and Lumʿat al-Iʿtiqād (Ibn Qudāma, Ḥanbalī/Atharī)
al-Ṭaḥāwiyya is a Muʿtazilī text; Umm al-Barāhīn is Ḥanbalī
Lumʿat al-Iʿtiqād is Māturīdī; al-Nasafiyya is Atharī
xaq-026.e: Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭaḥāwī (d. 321 AH) wrote his short creed to state the beliefs of Abū Ḥanīfa and his students, and it is accepted widely. The Nasafiyya is the standard Māturīdī text; al-Sanūsī (d. 895 AH) wrote Umm al-Barāhīn in the Ashʿarī tradition; Ibn Qudāma’s Lumʿat al-Iʿtiqād is a Ḥanbalī/Atharī creed. Al-Ghazālī’s al-Iqtiṣād is a major Ashʿarī work.

xaq-027.src: al-Subkī, Ṭabaqāt al-Shāfiʿiyya; al-Juwaynī, al-Irshād; al-Ghazālī, Tahāfut al-Falāsifa and al-Munqidh min al-Ḍalāl; al-Rāzī, Muḥaṣṣal Afkār al-Mutaqaddimīn
xaq-027.q: Which sequence of authors marks the development of Ashʿarī kalām?
o: al-Bāqillānī, al-Juwaynī, al-Ghazālī and Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
Ibn Ḥazm, Ibn Rushd, Ibn Khaldūn and Ibn Khallikān
Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfa, al-Shāfiʿī and Aḥmad
Sībawayh, al-Mubarrad, Ibn Jinnī and Ibn Mālik
xaq-027.e: Al-Bāqillānī (d. 403 AH) set Ashʿarī kalām on atomist and rational foundations. Al-Juwaynī (d. 478 AH) wrote al-Irshād and al-ʿAqīda al-Niẓāmiyya, his student al-Ghazālī (d. 505 AH) wrote al-Iqtiṣād and Tahāfut al-Falāsifa against the philosophers, and al-Rāzī (d. 606 AH) brought philosophy and kalām together. Later scholars wrote commentaries on their works, and Ibn Rushd’s Tahāfut al-Tahāfut answered al-Ghazālī.

xaq-028.src: al-Ghazālī, Tahāfut al-Falāsifa; Ibn Rushd, Tahāfut al-Tahāfut and Faṣl al-Maqāl; al-Munqidh min al-Ḍalāl
xaq-028.q: On which three questions did al-Ghazālī declare the philosophers disbelievers in Tahāfut al-Falāsifa?
o: The eternity of the world, God’s knowledge of only universals, and the denial of bodily resurrection
The existence of angels, jinn and Satan
The number of prayers, the amount of zakāt and the months of the year
The authority of the Quran, the Sunna and consensus
xaq-028.e: Al-Ghazālī in Tahāfut al-Falāsifa discussed twenty questions, and said the philosophers should be declared unbelievers for three: the claim that the world is eternal, that God knows only universals (not particulars), and the denial of bodily resurrection. In the rest, he called them innovators. Ibn Rushd replied in Tahāfut al-Tahāfut and Faṣl al-Maqāl, disputing the representation of philosophical positions and the call of takfīr.

xaq-029.src: al-Qushayrī, al-Risāla; al-Ghazālī, Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn; Ibn Taymiyya, Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā; al-Junayd, Rasāʾil
xaq-029.q: What is the classical Sunni attitude of Sufi manuals like al-Qushayrī’s Risāla towards creed?
o: They present Sufism as grounded in the creed of Ahl al-Sunna and the Sharia, citing al-Junayd’s saying that the path is bound by the Quran and Sunna, while critics such as Ibn Taymiyya distinguished sound Sufis from excesses
They teach that the Sharia is unnecessary
They have no connection to creed
xaq-029.e: Al-Qushayrī (d. 465 AH) opens the Risāla with a creedal statement in the Ashʿarī tradition. Al-Junayd of Baghdad is quoted as saying that his knowledge is bound by the Quran and Sunna. Al-Ghazālī built Iḥyāʾ on the same grounds. Ibn Taymiyya praised the early Sufis who held to the Sharia but criticised ideas such as waḥdat al-wujūd and claims to exemption from the law.

xaq-030.src: al-Māwardī, al-Aḥkām al-Sulṭāniyya; al-Ījī, al-Mawāqif; al-Nasafī, al-ʿAqāʾid; Ibn Taymiyya, Minhāj al-Sunna
xaq-030.q: How do Sunni creeds and Shīʿī thought differ about the imamate?
o: Sunnis treat the imamate as a matter of public interest, established by choice or consultation with conditions such as Qurashī descent in the common view; the Twelver Shīʿa hold that it is a matter of faith, designated by text and ʿiṣma
Sunnis hold the imam is infallible; the Shīʿa deny it
Both deny any role for a leader
xaq-030.e: Sunni creeds (al-Nasafī, al-Ījī) treat the imamate as a branch matter and hold that it is established by pledge, consultation or designation, with al-Māwardī listing conditions (justice, knowledge, competence, Qurashī lineage in the majority view). The Twelver Shīʿa hold that the imamate is a pillar of faith, that imams are designated and protected from error, starting with ʿAlī. This divide goes back to the Saqīfa.

xaq-031.src: Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām, Qawāʿid al-Aḥkām; al-Shāfiʿī as quoted in Ḥilyat al-Awliyāʾ; al-Shāṭibī, al-Iʿtiṣām; Ibn Rajab, Jāmiʿ al-ʿUlūm wa-l-Ḥikam
xaq-031.q: How do scholars divide innovation (bidʿa), and who objected to the division?
o: Al-Shāfiʿī and al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salām distinguished good and bad innovation (and five rulings), while al-Shāṭibī and Ibn Rajab held that every innovation in religion is misguidance and the ‘good’ cases are linguistic or fall under sunna
All agree that innovation concerns only food
xaq-031.e: Al-Shāfiʿī is quoted as dividing innovation into the praiseworthy (agreeing with Sunna) and blameworthy. Al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salām in Qawāʿid al-Aḥkām applied five rulings to innovations. Al-Shāṭibī in al-Iʿtiṣām and Ibn Rajab argued that the hadith ‘every innovation is misguidance’ is general, and the examples of ‘good innovation’ either fall under the Sunna or are innovations only in a linguistic sense.

xaq-032.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-istisqāʾ (ʿUmar and al-ʿAbbās); Ibn Taymiyya, Qāʿida Jalīla fī al-Tawassul wa-l-Wasīla; al-Subkī, Shifāʾ al-Siqām
xaq-032.q: How did the scholars treat tawassul (seeking means through the righteous in supplication)?
o: All accept tawassul through the Prophet’s supplication and one’s own good deeds; they differ on tawassul by the person or status of a righteous being, which many Shāfiʿīs and Ḥanafīs allowed and Ibn Taymiyya and many Ḥanbalīs restricted
All scholars allowed worship of saints
xaq-032.e: The report in al-Bukhārī of ʿUmar asking al-ʿAbbās to pray for rain is cited as tawassul by a living righteous person’s supplication, accepted by all. Tawassul by the status of a person or by their name after death is allowed by many scholars (al-Subkī, many Shāfiʿīs and Ḥanafīs) and held impermissible or unproven by Ibn Taymiyya and others, who regarded asking the dead as a serious matter. Treatises exist on both sides.

xaq-033.src: al-Ṭabarī, Tafsīr, on sūrat al-Baqara; al-Jaṣṣāṣ, Aḥkām al-Qurʾān; al-Rāzī, al-Tafsīr al-Kabīr; Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī
xaq-033.q: What disagreement is there on the reality of magic (siḥr) among the schools?
o: Most Sunni scholars held that magic has a real effect by God’s permission, while some Muʿtazilīs and certain Ḥanafīs such as al-Jaṣṣāṣ held it to be mainly illusion and trickery
All held that magic is impossible
All held that magic changes the nature of things in all cases
xaq-033.e: Sunni scholars, citing the account of the Prophet being affected by magic in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, held that magic is real and affects bodies and hearts by God’s permission. Some of the Muʿtazila and scholars such as al-Jaṣṣāṣ thought it mostly consists of deception (takhyīl), and disagreed over details such as its ability to cause illness. The jurists also differ on the penalty for the magician.

xaq-034.src: Ibn Taymiyya, Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā (Idāḥ al-Dalāla fī ʿUmūm al-Risāla); al-Ṭabarī, Tafsīr; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on sūrat al-Jinn; al-Nasafī, al-ʿAqāʾid
xaq-034.q: What do the Sunni creeds say about the nature of angels and jinn, and which difference is noted between Iblīs and the angels?
o: Angels are created from light and do not disobey, while jinn are created from fire and are accountable; the debate on whether Iblīs was an angel or a jinn is settled by most Sunni scholars as a jinn, according to the verse naming him from the jinn
Angels are created from fire and jinn from light
Jinn and angels are the same
xaq-034.e: The creeds affirm belief in angels, created of light and in worship, and jinn, created from smokeless fire, who are accountable and include believers and unbelievers. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and many others held that Iblīs was never an angel. Some commentators in the early period held he was an angel, drawing on the context of the command to prostrate, but most classical Sunni exegetes favoured the first view.

xaq-035.src: Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-janāʾiz; al-Suyūṭī, Masālik al-Ḥunafāʾ; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr; al-Ṭabarī, Tafsīr
xaq-035.q: What do scholars say about the fate of those who died in the interval between messengers (ahl al-fatra)?
o: Scholars differed: some held they are not punished until a message reaches them, others that they will be tested in the hereafter, and others that they are judged by what they could know by reason; reports exist for each view
All scholars agree they are certainly in Paradise
All scholars agree they are certainly in the Fire
xaq-035.e: The question of those who never received a message is treated through the verse that God does not punish until He sends a messenger, with the reports of testing in the hereafter in Aḥmad and others. Ashʿarīs generally hold no punishment without a message; the Māturīdīs hold that some knowledge of God is obligatory by reason; the Atharīs prefer the report of testing. A report in Muslim concerning the Prophet’s father is also discussed, with al-Suyūṭī writing treatises on the topic.

xaq-036.src: Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-fitan wa-ashrāṭ al-sāʿa (ḥadīth Ḥudhayfa); Abū Dāwūd, Sunan, Kitāb al-mahdī; Ibn Khaldūn, Muqaddima; Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī
xaq-036.q: Which are the major signs of the Hour in the report of Ḥudhayfa ibn Asīd in Muslim, and what is the scholarly discussion about the Mahdī?
o: Smoke, the Dajjāl, the beast, the rising of the sun from the west, the descent of ʿĪsā, Gog and Magog, three landslides and a fire from Yemen; the Mahdī is not in the Ṣaḥīḥayn, and scholars such as Ibn Khaldūn weakened the reports while others like Ibn Ḥajar and al-Suyūṭī considered them well-supported
Only an earthquake and a flood
xaq-036.e: Muslim records Ḥudhayfa ibn Asīd’s report of ten signs: the smoke, the Dajjāl, the beast, the sun rising from its place of setting, the descent of ʿĪsā, Yājūj and Mājūj, three landslides (east, west and Arabian Peninsula) and a fire from Yemen. The Mahdī reports are in Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and others, and Ibn Khaldūn criticised them in the Muqaddima, while many scholars held the reports to be collectively supported.

xaq-037.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar; Ibn Qudāma, Rawḍat al-Nāẓir; al-Āmidī, al-Iḥkām; Ibn al-Qayyim, Mukhtaṣar al-Ṣawāʿiq al-Mursala
xaq-037.q: Is a single-narrator report (khabar al-āḥād) accepted in matters of creed, according to the traditions?
o: The Atharīs, with Aḥmad and the muḥaddithūn, accepted authentic āḥād reports in creed; many Ashʿarīs and Māturīdīs required certainty for fundamental matters and accepted āḥād for details, while the Muʿtazila rejected them
All traditions accepted any report without condition
None of the traditions discussed it
xaq-037.e: The question divides: the Atharīs hold that sound āḥād reports establish creed (as seen in Ibn al-Qayyim’s defence), and the Ashʿarīs and Māturīdīs divide matters of creed into those requiring a decisive proof (such as God’s existence and prophecy) and those that can rest on probable reports, though many accept them as binding on practice and belief in details. The Muʿtazila rejected āḥād for creed, requiring certainty.

xaq-038.src: Mālik as quoted in al-Bayhaqī, al-Asmāʾ wa-l-Ṣifāt; al-Dhahabī, al-ʿUluww li-l-ʿAliyy al-Ghaffār; Ibn al-Jawzī, Daf‘ Shubah al-Tashbīh; al-Ṭaḥāwī, al-ʿAqīda
xaq-038.q: What is the report attributed to Mālik ibn Anas about God’s ‘istiwāʾ’ above the Throne, and how did traditions use it?
o: That istiwāʾ is known, how is unknown, belief in it is obligatory and asking about it is an innovation; all the traditions cite it, with the Atharīs taking it as affirmation and the Ashʿarīs often as denial of the how and delegation of the meaning
That God is in every place
xaq-038.e: A saying attributed to Mālik (and in some versions to Umm Salama and Rabīʿa) in answer to a question about the verse on istiwāʾ states that the istiwāʾ is not unknown, the how is not understood, faith in it is obligatory and the question is an innovation. The Atharīs read this as affirming the attribute without asking how; many Ashʿarīs read it as supporting delegation of the meaning; al-Bayhaqī and al-Dhahabī transmitted it in their works.

xaq-039.src: al-Māturīdī, Kitāb al-Tawḥīd; al-Ashʿarī, al-Lumaʿ; Ibn Taymiyya, Dar’ Taʿāruḍ al-ʿAql wa-l-Naql; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-janāʾiz (ḥadīth al-fiṭra)
xaq-039.q: Is knowing God obligatory by reason alone before revelation reaches, according to the traditions?
o: The Muʿtazila held that reason alone obliges knowledge of God; the Ashʿarīs held that obligation arises only through revelation; the Māturīdīs held that reason obliges knowing God though punishment depends on revelation; the Atharīs stressed the innate disposition (fiṭra) and the Prophetic report on it
All traditions held that nothing is obligatory
All traditions held that reason alone settles all law
xaq-039.e: The question of rational obligation (al-taḥsīn wa-l-taqbīḥ al-ʿaqliyyayn) divides: the Muʿtazila said reason knows good and evil and obliges knowing God; the Ashʿarīs said good and evil are known by revelation, so no obligation before it; the Māturīdīs gave reason a role in knowing God, although punishment awaits the message; the Atharīs spoke of fiṭra, citing the ḥadīth that every child is born upon the fiṭra.

xaq-040.src: al-Tirmidhī, Jāmiʿ, Kitāb al-īmān (ḥadīth iftirāq al-umma); al-Baghdādī, al-Farq bayna al-Firaq; al-Shāṭibī, al-Iʿtiṣām; Ibn Taymiyya, Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā
xaq-040.q: What is the discussion about the hadith of the community’s division into seventy-three groups?
o: The hadith is in al-Tirmidhī, Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah and is graded ḥasan or ṣaḥīḥ by many, with differing wording on the saved group; scholars disagree on who is meant, with Atharīs, Ashʿarīs, Māturīdīs and others each identifying the saved group with themselves, while some stress it refers to the main body of the Muslims
It is in the Quran only
It was graded fabricated by every scholar
It is reported only by al-Bukhārī
xaq-040.e: The hadith of division (Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah) says the community will divide into seventy-three groups, all in the Fire except one (in some versions the one that follows what the Prophet and his Companions were upon, or the main body, al-jamāʿa). Some scholars (e.g. Ibn Ḥazm) weakened the addition about the Fire. Authors such as al-Baghdādī and al-Shāṭibī used the hadith, with each tradition applying it to itself, while others read it as a warning about method.

xhd-001.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima fī ʿUlūm al-Ḥadīth (ʿUlūm al-Ḥadīth), naw‘ 1 (al-ṣaḥīḥ)
xhd-001.q: What are the five conditions that Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ gives for a ṣaḥīḥ hadith (li-dhātihi)?
o: A continuous chain, upright narrators, precise narrators, absence of irregularity (shudhūdh) and absence of a hidden defect (ʿilla)
Narration by at least four Companions, a famous narrator, a short chain, a known author and agreement with the Quran
A chain of Madinan narrators, a legal ruling, a famous collection, a date and a witness
Narration in a Ṣaḥīḥ collection, by two narrators, with the Prophet’s companions named, and a text in classical Arabic
xhd-001.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ (d. 643 AH) defines the ṣaḥīḥ as a hadith with a connected chain (ittiṣāl al-sanad) of upright (ʿadl) and precise (ḍābiṭ) narrators from beginning to end, free from shudhūdh and ʿilla. If the precision of a narrator is lighter, the hadith is ḥasan li-dhātihi. This definition has been the basis of the later textbooks.

xhd-002.src: Ibn Ḥajar, al-Nukat ʿalā Kitāb Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima; al-Tirmidhī, Jāmiʿ and al-ʿIlal al-Ṣaghīr
xhd-002.q: What does al-Tirmidhī mean by ‘ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ’ for a single hadith, according to Ibn Ḥajar’s widely accepted explanation?
o: That it has two chains, one ḥasan and the other ṣaḥīḥ, or that the critic hesitated between the two grades
That the hadith is higher than ṣaḥīḥ
That it is a single-chain hadith with a Companion who is unknown
xhd-002.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ asked how a hadith can be both and answered that al-Tirmidhī’s phrase applies to a hadith with two chains, so that it is ṣaḥīḥ by one and ḥasan by the other. Ibn Ḥajar added another possibility, that the critic could not decide between the two grades. If the hadith has only one chain, the phrase expresses that hesitation. The explanation is accepted because the grades differ in precision.

xhd-003.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar and Nuzhat al-Naẓar; al-Suyūṭī, Qaṭf al-Azhār al-Mutanāthira fī al-Akhbār al-Mutawātira
xhd-003.q: Which statement about the mutawātir hadith is correct?
o: It is narrated by so many in every generation that agreement on falsehood is impossible; it is either verbal (lafẓī) or in meaning (maʿnawī), and al-Suyūṭī collected examples
It is any hadith with two chains
It is any hadith narrated by one Companion
It is any hadith accepted by one scholar
xhd-003.e: The mutawātir yields certain knowledge. Scholars differ on the minimum number of narrators, but all insist on the impossibility of conspiracy. The verbal kind is rare, and the commonly cited example is the warning against lying about the Prophet. Examples of the maʿnawī kind include the raising of the hands in supplication and wiping over the khuffs. Al-Suyūṭī wrote Qaṭf al-Azhār on them.

xhd-004.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar and Nuzhat al-Naẓar
xhd-004.q: How does Ibn Ḥajar’s Nukhba define the mashhūr, the ʿazīz and the gharīb hadith?
o: Mashhūr has three or more narrators at each level; ʿazīz not fewer than two at any level; gharīb a single narrator at some level
Mashhūr has one narrator; ʿazīz two; gharīb ten
Mashhūr is a hadith from Makka; ʿazīz from Madīna; gharīb from Baṣra
xhd-004.e: In the Nukhba, the mashhūr is what has three or more chains but has not reached the level of mutawātir; the ʿazīz is the hadith that does not have fewer than two narrators at any stage; the gharīb is one narrated by a single narrator at some stage. Al-Suyūṭī and others use ‘mustafīḍ’ for what many call mashhūr; the three terms describe the number of narrators, not the grade of the hadith.

xhd-005.src: Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, introduction (muqaddima); Ibn Ḥajar, Hady al-Sārī, introduction; al-Nawawī, Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, introduction
xhd-005.q: What is the classical contrast between the conditions of al-Bukhārī and Muslim regarding the link between a narrator and his teacher?
o: Al-Bukhārī required proof of an actual meeting (liqāʾ); Muslim was satisfied with the possibility of meeting (muʿāṣara) when the narrator is not a mudallis
Muslim required proof of an actual meeting, and al-Bukhārī was satisfied with contemporaneity
Neither considered the link, only the text
xhd-005.e: In the introduction to his Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim argues against those who demanded proof of meeting and says contemporaneity with the possibility of meeting is enough for a non-mudallis who uses ‘from’. Al-Bukhārī, with ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī, required proof of at least one meeting for the muʿanʿan chains. Scholars say this makes the Bukhārī conditions stricter, though Muslim’s tarjīḥ also has its supporters.

xhd-006.src: al-Shāfiʿī, al-Risāla, bāb khabar al-wāḥid; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 5; al-ʿAlāʾī, Jāmiʿ al-Taḥṣīl
xhd-006.q: What are the views of the schools and of al-Shāfiʿī on using the mursal hadith (when a Successor cites the Prophet directly) as evidence?
o: Abū Ḥanīfa and Mālik accept it; most hadith critics reject it as weak; al-Shāfiʿī accepts the mursal of a senior Successor only if conditions are met, such as being supported by another chain
All schools accept every mursal without condition
All schools reject every mursal without exception
xhd-006.e: The mursal omits the Companion and so a link is missing. Abū Ḥanīfa and Mālik (and Aḥmad in one report) accept it from trustworthy narrators; most muḥaddithūn consider it weak for the missing link. Al-Shāfiʿī in the Risāla accepts the mursal of senior Successors such as Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab if it is also confirmed by a musnad chain, by another mursal from a different source, by a Companion’s statement or by most scholars’ ruling.

xhd-007.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Ṭabaqāt al-Mudallisīn (Taʿrīf Ahl al-Taqdīs); Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 12
xhd-007.q: Which statement correctly describes the types of tadlīs?
o: Tadlīs al-isnād (concealing the narrator from whom one actually took), tadlīs al-shuyūkh (naming one’s teacher by an unfamiliar name) and tadlīs al-taswiya (omitting a weak narrator between two reliable ones)
Tadlīs al-matn, tadlīs al-ḥurūf and tadlīs al-ṣawt
Tadlīs al-ṣaḥāba, tadlīs al-tābiʿīn and tadlīs al-fuqahāʾ
Tadlīs al-qiblā, tadlīs al-ṣalā and tadlīs al-zakā
xhd-007.e: In tadlīs al-isnād the narrator reports from a contemporary with a word that suggests hearing, though he did not hear from him. In tadlīs al-shuyūkh the narrator gives his teacher a name or title that obscures him. In tadlīs al-taswiya, associated with Baqiyya ibn al-Walīd and al-Walīd ibn Muslim, the narrator drops the weak narrator between two reliable ones, making the chain look strong. Taswiya is the worst, since even the statement of hearing between the surviving pair is correct.

xhd-008.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Ṭabaqāt al-Mudallisīn (Taʿrīf Ahl al-Taqdīs bi-Marātib al-Mawṣūfīn bi-l-Tadlīs)
xhd-008.q: How does Ibn Ḥajar’s Ṭabaqāt al-Mudallisīn organise the narrators known for tadlīs?
o: In five ranks, from those who rarely did it or only from reliable sources (whose ʿanʿana is accepted) to those whose ʿanʿana is rejected unless they state hearing
In two ranks, Makkan and Madinan
In three ranks, Companions, Successors and their followers
In ten ranks by the number of their students
