xhd-008.e: Ibn Ḥajar sorted the mudallisīn into five ranks: those who did tadlīs rarely or who are not known for it; those whose tadlīs is accepted because they only did it from reliable teachers; those who did it often, accepted only with a statement of hearing; those who were disqualified for their tadlīs from the weak; and those whose ʿanʿana is rejected even for other reasons. The ranking tells a critic how to handle a ‘from’ in a chain.

xhd-009.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar and Nuzhat al-Naẓar; al-Shāfiʿī as cited in Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 7–8
xhd-009.q: How does Ibn Ḥajar’s Nukhba distinguish shādhdh from munkar?
o: Shādhdh is a hadith of an acceptable narrator that contradicts a more reliable one; munkar is a hadith of a weak narrator that contradicts a reliable one
Shādhdh is a hadith with a long chain; munkar is a hadith with a short chain
Shādhdh is any rare hadith; munkar is any hadith of a Madinan
xhd-009.e: Ibn Ḥajar adopts the criterion of opposition: if a maqbūl narrator conflicts with someone more reliable, his report is shādhdh and the report of the more reliable is maḥfūẓ. If the opposed narrator is weak, his report is munkar, and the other is maʿrūf. Al-Shāfiʿī’s older definition of shādhdh is a narrator’s opposition to what the people have transmitted, and others (like al-Ḥākim) defined it as a lone report by a trustworthy narrator.

xhd-010.src: Ibn Rajab, Sharḥ ʿIlal al-Tirmidhī; al-Dāraquṭnī, al-ʿIlal; Ibn Abī Ḥātim, ʿIlal al-Ḥadīth; ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī, ʿIlal al-Ḥadīth
xhd-010.q: What is an ʿilla in the science of hadith, and who was an early master of it?
o: A hidden, subtle defect in a hadith that appears sound on the surface; ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī, Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn and Aḥmad were early masters
A visible weakness such as an unknown narrator; al-Bukhārī was the first writer on it
A decoration of the chain; Ibn Ḥajar was the first
A name for a fabricated hadith; al-Suyūṭī was the first
xhd-010.e: An ʿilla (also mulalla) is a defect that is not obvious and is found only by experts through collecting chains, such as a hidden break or an error in attributing the hadith to a Companion. ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī, Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn, Aḥmad, al-Bukhārī, Abū Ḥātim al-Rāzī and later al-Dāraquṭnī are masters, and works on ʿilal include those of Ibn Abī Ḥātim and al-Dāraquṭnī.

xhd-011.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Taqrīb al-Tahdhīb, introduction; Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Jarḥ wa-l-Taʿdīl, introduction
xhd-011.q: How does Ibn Ḥajar arrange the narrators in his Taqrīb al-Tahdhīb?
o: In twelve ranks from the Companions through the Successors and their followers down to the weakest, with a single phrase of judgement for each
In two ranks, trustworthy and untrustworthy
In four ranks by the Companion they narrated from
In seven ranks by the Quran reader they followed
xhd-011.e: The Taqrīb begins with the Companions and then orders narrators in twelve ṭabaqāt of generation and then by status, giving each a concise judgement (such as thiqa, ṣadūq, layyin, matrūk). Ibn Abī Ḥātim’s earlier al-Jarḥ wa-l-Taʿdīl set four ranks of taʿdīl and four ranks of jarḥ; the Taqrīb is a refined summary of Tahdhīb al-Kamāl of al-Mizzī.

xhd-012.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 23; al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī, al-Kifāya fī ʿIlm al-Riwāya
xhd-012.q: What do most hadith scholars hold when an explained criticism (jarḥ mufassar) conflicts with a general praise (taʿdīl) of a narrator?
o: The explained criticism takes priority, since the critic knows something the praiser did not
The two cancel out and the narrator is accepted
The opinion of the later critic always prevails
xhd-012.e: The majority say that jarḥ mufassar outweighs taʿdīl because it adds knowledge. Some scholars add the condition that the reason of the criticism must be one that really damages, since critics may differ about what counts as a flaw. If the criticism is not explained, praise by a recognised critic is preferred. Al-Khaṭīb and Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ state the rule.

xhd-013.src: al-Dhahabī, Dhikr Man Yuʿtamad Qawluhu fī al-Jarḥ wa-l-Taʿdīl; al-Dhahabī, al-Mūqiẓa; Ibn Ḥajar, Lisān al-Mīzān, introduction
xhd-013.q: How do hadith scholars classify the critics of narrators by their strictness?
o: As strict (mutashaddid) such as Ibn Maʿīn and Ibn al-Qaṭṭān, lenient (mutasāhil) such as al-Tirmidhī and al-Ḥākim, and moderate (muʿtadil) such as Aḥmad and al-Bukhārī
As Makkan, Madinan and Baṣran critics
As early and late critics only
xhd-013.e: Al-Dhahabī classified the critics into those who are severe in criticism, those who are lenient and the moderate. A strict critic’s weakening of a narrator must be examined; a lenient critic’s authentication is received with caution. The classification guides how to weigh conflicting judgements. Ibn Ḥibbān is also known for leniency in authenticating unknown narrators.

xhd-014.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 39 (maʿrifat al-ṣaḥāba); Ibn Ḥajar, al-Iṣāba fī Tamyīz al-Ṣaḥāba, introduction; al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī, al-Kifāya
xhd-014.q: What is the position of the Sunni scholars of hadith on the uprightness (ʿadāla) of the Companions?
o: All Companions are considered upright for narration; one does not need to investigate their uprightness, though their individual reports are still examined for accuracy of transmission
All Companions must be investigated like later narrators
Only the first four caliphs are upright
Only those who fought in Badr are upright
xhd-014.e: Ahl al-Sunna hold that the Companions are all ʿudūl, as God praised them in the Quran and the Prophet bore witness to them, so their uprightness is not subject to assessment. This does not mean they were infallible or that every attribution to a Companion is correct: the chain up to the Companion is still examined. Al-Khaṭīb and Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ discuss the rule.

xhd-015.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 25; al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī, al-Kifāya; al-Suyūṭī, Tadrīb al-Rāwī
xhd-015.q: What is the majority view on narrating a hadith by meaning (riwāya bi-l-maʿnā) rather than by exact wording?
o: It is permitted for a narrator who knows Arabic and the meanings, and understands what changes the sense, while verbatim narration is preferred; some early scholars, such as Ibn Sīrīn in one report, insisted on exact wording
It is allowed without any condition
It is required in all cases
xhd-015.e: The majority, including the four imams, allowed narrating by meaning under conditions: the narrator must understand the meaning and the nuances of the language so as not to alter the sense, and it is not for religious formulas such as those of dhikr and adhān. Some scholars, such as Ibn Sīrīn, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar in a report, and some of the Ahl al-Ḥadīth, required exact wording. Verbatim narration is preferable.

xhd-016.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 24–29; al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī, al-Kifāya; al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, al-Ilmāʿ
xhd-016.q: Which list names the eight classical modes of receiving hadith (taḥammul), from the highest to the lowest?
o: Samāʿ (hearing from the teacher), qirāʾa (reading to the teacher), ijāza, munāwala, mukātaba, iʿlām, waṣiyya and wijāda
Samāʿ, ruʾya, ḥifẓ, kitāba, fahm, ʿamal, ijmāʿ and ikhtiyār
Samāʿ, qiyās, istiḥsān, ijmāʿ, ʿurf, sadd, masāliḥ and istiṣḥāb
Ḥifẓ, ruʾya, qirāʾa, tarjama, tafsīr, taʾwīl, istikhrāj and iʿjāz
xhd-016.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ lists eight: samāʿ min lafẓ al-shaykh (the highest for most), qirāʾa ʿalā al-shaykh (ʿarḍ), ijāza (permission), munāwala (handing over), mukātaba (writing), iʿlām (informing), waṣiyya (bequest of a book) and wijāda (finding a writing). The first two are accepted by all; the others differ in force and some are disputed. The order shows the strength of the connection to the teacher.

xhd-017.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar; al-Kattānī, al-Risāla al-Mustaṭrafa; Abū ʿAwāna, al-Mustakhraj ʿalā Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim; al-Ḥākim, al-Mustadrak
xhd-017.q: Which pair correctly distinguishes a mustakhraj from a mustadrak among the types of hadith books?
o: A mustakhraj re-narrates the hadith of an earlier book with the author’s own chains reaching the same teacher or higher; a mustadrak adds hadith that, in the author’s view, meet the conditions of an earlier book but were omitted
A mustakhraj collects only fabricated hadith; a mustadrak collects only Quranic verses
A mustakhraj is an alphabetical index; a mustadrak is a dictionary of narrators
They are two names for the same type
xhd-017.e: Examples of the mustakhraj are Abū ʿAwāna’s Mustakhraj on Muslim and the Mustakhrajāt of al-Ismāʿīlī on al-Bukhārī. The mustadrak is exemplified by al-Ḥākim’s al-Mustadrak ʿalā al-Ṣaḥīḥayn, which is known for lenient grading, so al-Dhahabī wrote his Talkhīṣ to correct it. The two types are distinguished by whether the author re-narrates or adds.

xhd-018.src: Ibn Ṭāhir al-Maqdisī, Shurūṭ al-Aʾimma al-Sitta; Ibn Ḥajar, Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb, on Ibn Mājah; Ibn al-Athīr, Jāmiʿ al-Uṣūl
xhd-018.q: Which scholar is credited with adding Sunan Ibn Mājah as the sixth of the canonical books, and what other works were proposed for that place?
o: Abū al-Faḍl ibn Ṭāhir al-Maqdisī (d. 507 AH); al-Muwaṭṭaʾ of Mālik (Razīn) and Sunan al-Dārimī (Ibn Ḥajar) were proposed instead
Ibn Ḥajar; the Ṣaḥīḥ of Ibn Khuzayma
xhd-018.e: The ‘five books’ (Ṣaḥīḥayn, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, al-Nasāʾī) were widely accepted. Ibn Ṭāhir al-Maqdisī included Ibn Mājah as the sixth. Others, such as Razīn ibn Muʿāwiya, preferred al-Muwaṭṭaʾ, and Ibn al-Athīr put it in place of Ibn Mājah in his Jāmiʿ al-Uṣūl, while later Ibn Ḥajar suggested al-Dārimī. Ibn Mājah contains more weak hadith than the other five.

xhd-019.src: al-Ḥākim, Maʿrifat ʿUlūm al-Ḥadīth; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 1; al-Nawawī, al-Taqrīb
xhd-019.q: Which chain did al-Bukhārī call the ‘golden chain’ (silsilat al-dhahab), and what is its sense?
o: Mālik from Nāfiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar from the Prophet; it is thought the most reliable chain
Abū Hurayra from the Prophet directly
Al-Zuhrī from Sālim from his father
xhd-019.e: Al-Bukhārī (as cited by al-Ḥākim and others) called the chain of Mālik from Nāfiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar the most authentic of chains. The term ‘golden chain’ was also applied by others to other lines, such as al-Shāfiʿī from Mālik from Nāfiʿ from Ibn ʿUmar, but the best-known sense is that attributed to al-Bukhārī.

xhd-020.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar; al-Suyūṭī, Tadrīb al-Rāwī; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 20–21
xhd-020.q: How do the books of terminology define the muḍṭarib and the mudraj hadith?
o: Muḍṭarib: a hadith narrated in contradictory ways of equal strength, so that none can be preferred; mudraj: a hadith in which some words of the narrator or another source have been inserted into the text or chain
Muḍṭarib: a hadith narrated in anger; mudraj: a hadith about drawing graves
Muḍṭarib: a hadith with a short chain; mudraj: a hadith with a long chain
Both are names for forged hadith
xhd-020.e: A hadith is muḍṭarib when its chain or text is narrated differently, with equal force and without possibility of preference or harmonisation; it is weak because it shows poor precision. A mudraj hadith contains an insertion (idrāj), such as a Companion’s or Successor’s explanatory comment mixed into the Prophet’s words, which can be discovered by comparing chains.

xhd-021.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 22 and 23
xhd-021.q: How are maqlūb and muṣaḥḥaf defined?
o: Maqlūb: a hadith in which a word or narrator is swapped or reversed; muṣaḥḥaf: a hadith changed because the dots or letters of a word are misread
Maqlūb: a hadith read backwards; muṣaḥḥaf: a hadith written in a book
Maqlūb: a hadith with a famous author; muṣaḥḥaf: a hadith from the muṣḥaf
Maqlūb and muṣaḥḥaf are the same
xhd-021.e: A maqlūb hadith has a part reversed, in the text (a word changed with another) or in the chain (the narrator’s name and his father’s name swapped), either by mistake or to test the narrator, as in the famous test of al-Bukhārī in Baghdad. The muṣaḥḥaf (taṣḥīf) is a mistake of reading letters whose shapes are alike, for example by confusing two words differing only in dots.

xhd-022.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 33 (al-mazīd fī muttaṣil al-asānīd); al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī, Tamyīz al-Mazīd fī Muttaṣil al-Asānīd
xhd-022.q: What is the ‘addition in a connected chain’ (al-mazīd fī muttaṣil al-asānīd)?
o: The mention of an extra narrator in one version of a chain that is elsewhere connected without him, often judged a mistake in the longer version
An added Companion in the text
An extra verse in the Quran
An addition of a commentary by a later scholar
xhd-022.e: In this kind of defect, a narrator inserts a name between two narrators who elsewhere heard from each other directly, as when the chain has a person that others omit, though the contacts are established. Scholars judge, by comparing chains, whether the addition is an error of a narrator (in which case it is rejected) or genuine, as al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī showed in Tamyīz al-Mazīd.

xhd-023.src: al-Shāfiʿī, Ikhtilāf al-Ḥadīth; Ibn Qutayba, Taʾwīl Mukhtalif al-Ḥadīth; al-Ṭaḥāwī, Sharḥ Mushkil al-Āthār
xhd-023.q: Which works are classical sources on reconciling apparently conflicting hadith (mukhtalif al-ḥadīth)?
o: al-Shāfiʿī’s Ikhtilāf al-Ḥadīth, Ibn Qutayba’s Taʾwīl Mukhtalif al-Ḥadīth and al-Ṭaḥāwī’s Sharḥ Mushkil al-Āthār
xhd-023.e: Mukhtalif al-ḥadīth deals with hadith that seem to conflict, solved by harmonisation (jamʿ), abrogation, preference or suspension, in that order for most scholars. The three works are well-known writings on the topic; the other works named concern etiquette, narrators’ names and tafsīr.

xhd-024.src: Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Mawḍūʿāt; al-Suyūṭī, al-Laʾāli’ al-Maṣnūʿa fī al-Aḥādīth al-Mawḍūʿa; Ibn Ḥajar, al-Qawl al-Musaddad
xhd-024.q: What criticism is commonly made of Ibn al-Jawzī’s al-Mawḍūʿāt, and which works responded to it?
o: That it includes hadith that are weak or even sound, not only fabricated; al-Suyūṭī’s al-Laʾāliʾ al-Maṣnūʿa and Ibn Ḥajar’s al-Qawl al-Musaddad examined and corrected it
That it includes only hadith from Makka
That it was written before hadith criticism existed
xhd-024.e: Ibn al-Jawzī (d. 597 AH) was severe in judging hadith as fabricated and sometimes classed weak or even reliable hadith as such, and so the scholars checked the book. Al-Suyūṭī’s al-Laʾāliʾ and its additions, and Ibn Ḥajar’s defence of Aḥmad’s Musnad in al-Qawl al-Musaddad, answered many of his judgements. His book remains useful in gathering the material.

xhd-025.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 21 (al-mawḍūʿ); Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Majrūḥīn; al-Suyūṭī, Tadrīb al-Rāwī
xhd-025.q: Why did some pious people fabricate hadith in the virtues of Quranic sūras, and how did the scholars respond?
o: They believed they were encouraging people to read the Quran, but the scholars declared the practice forbidden and fabrications false, identifying narrators such as Abū ʿIṣma Nūḥ ibn Abī Maryam who admitted it
They fabricated them under orders of caliphs, and the scholars accepted them
They were fabricated by orientalists only
The scholars accepted all of them as reliable
xhd-025.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ and others mention that some ascetics fabricated hadith to encourage devotion; Nūḥ ibn Abī Maryam is reported to have acknowledged that he made up hadith in the virtues of the Quran’s sūras, attributing them to Ibn ʿAbbās, to turn people to the Quran. The scholars denounced this on the basis of the Prophet’s warning against lying about him, and said that no good purpose justifies it.

xhd-026.src: Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, introduction (muqaddima); Ibn Ḥibbān, al-Majrūḥīn; al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī, Sharaf Aṣḥāb al-Ḥadīth
xhd-026.q: According to Muslim’s introduction, when did the practice of demanding the chain become common, and who is quoted?
o: After the strife (fitna), when it became important to ask for the names of the narrators; Ibn Sīrīn is quoted as saying they had not asked about the chain before that
In the time of the Prophet, who demanded chains
In the time of al-Bukhārī, who invented it
xhd-026.e: In the introduction to the Ṣaḥīḥ, Muslim reports from Ibn Sīrīn that the people had not asked about the chain, but when the fitna occurred they said ‘name us your men’, so that the sunna of the Ahl al-Sunna is accepted and that of the Ahl al-Bidʿa rejected. Ibn al-Mubārak is also quoted that the chain is part of the religion and without it anyone could say what he wished.

xhd-027.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar; Ibn Ḥajar, Nukhbat al-Fikar; al-ʿIrāqī, al-Alfiyya fī ʿUlūm al-Ḥadīth
xhd-027.q: Which statement correctly matches works of hadith terminology with their authors?
o: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ: Muqaddima; al-ʿIrāqī: Alfiyya; Ibn Ḥajar: Nukhbat al-Fikar
Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ: Nukhba; al-ʿIrāqī: Muqaddima; Ibn Ḥajar: Alfiyya
Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ: Alfiyya; al-ʿIrāqī: Nukhba; Ibn Ḥajar: Muqaddima
All three are titles by al-Bukhārī
xhd-027.e: The Muqaddima of Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ (the first systematic textbook) was versified by al-ʿIrāqī in his Alfiyya and abridged in other works. Ibn Ḥajar’s Nukhbat al-Fikar is a concise work with its own commentary Nuzhat al-Naẓar. These three form the core of the study of muṣṭalaḥ al-ḥadīth.

xhd-028.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Taghlīq al-Taʿlīq ʿalā Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī; Ibn Ḥajar, Hady al-Sārī, introduction
xhd-028.q: What are the muʿallaqāt in al-Bukhārī’s Ṣaḥīḥ, and who traced their chains?
o: Hadith cited with the chain cut at the beginning, which Ibn Ḥajar traced in Taghlīq al-Taʿlīq
Hadith with a gap at the end of the chain
xhd-028.e: In places al-Bukhārī gives a hadith or a report from the beginning of the chain missing (taʿlīq). Some are in the firm form (‘he said’), which are generally authentic, and some in the doubtful form (‘it was said’). Ibn Ḥajar compiled their chains from other books in Taghlīq al-Taʿlīq. The muʿallaqāt do not count as hadith of the strict conditions of the Ṣaḥīḥ in themselves.

xhd-029.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar; al-Nawawī, al-Taqrīb; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 2
xhd-029.q: What is ḥasan li-ghayrihi, and how does it arise?
o: A weak hadith whose weakness is light, raised to ḥasan by corroborating chains or witnesses
A sound hadith whose chain is long
A fabricated hadith that is repeated by many
A hadith of a Companion about the Prophet’s dress
xhd-029.e: A hadith that is slightly weak, for example through a narrator with poor memory, can be strengthened by other chains of similar or better strength, so it rises to ḥasan li-ghayrihi. This does not apply to hadith with severe weakness, such as fabrication or the narrator’s known lying. The scholars therefore speak of ‘weak with an excusable weakness’ and ‘weak with an inexcusable weakness’.

xhd-030.src: Ibn Ḥajar, al-Qawl al-Badīʿ; al-Nawawī, al-Adhkār, introduction; al-Suyūṭī, Tadrīb al-Rāwī
xhd-030.q: What are the conditions that Ibn Ḥajar attributes to scholars who allow acting on weak hadith in virtuous deeds (faḍāʾil al-aʿmāl)?
o: That the weakness is not severe, that the deed falls under an established general principle, and that one does not believe the hadith itself is established
That the hadith be fabricated but useful
That the hadith be about the law of inheritance
xhd-030.e: Ibn Ḥajar, reporting from al-ʿAlāʾī and others, gives three conditions for those who allow weak hadith in faḍāʾil: the weakness must not be severe, the content must be under a recognised principle, and one should not believe it is established from the Prophet. Some scholars, like Ibn al-ʿArabī and others, rejected acting on weak hadith altogether, so the topic is disputed.

xhd-031.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Taqrīb al-Tahdhīb, introduction; Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 39–40
xhd-031.q: What is a mukhaḍram narrator in hadith terminology?
o: One who lived in both the pre-Islamic period and the time of the Prophet and accepted Islam, but did not see him, so he is counted among the Successors
A narrator who lived only among the Companions
A narrator who was a woman
A narrator who narrated from a jinn
xhd-031.e: A mukhaḍram (plural mukhaḍramūn) is someone who reached the time of Jāhiliyya and the time of the Prophet ﷺ, and became Muslim in his lifetime but never met him. The scholars count such people among the senior Successors. They are distinguished from Companions by the lack of meeting, as the Companion is defined as one who met the Prophet ﷺ as a believer and died as one.

xhd-032.src: Ibn Ḥajar, al-Iṣāba, introduction; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 39; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb faḍāʾil aṣḥāb al-nabī (opening)
xhd-032.q: How do the scholars differ in defining a Companion (ṣaḥābī)?
o: Most hadith scholars, with al-Bukhārī and Aḥmad, count anyone who met the Prophet ﷺ as a believer and died Muslim; some, such as Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab in one report, required a year or a battle with him
All scholars required ten years of companionship
All scholars required only to have lived in his time
All scholars required narrating at least ten hadith
xhd-032.e: The majority definition, from al-Bukhārī and Ibn Ḥajar, is broad: whoever saw or met the Prophet ﷺ as a believer and died in Islam. The narrower view, attributed to Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab and followed by some Uṣūlīs, asks for lengthy companionship, for example a year or participation in a campaign. The wider view prevailed in hadith because of the honour of seeing him ﷺ.

xhd-033.src: Ibn al-Jawzī, Talqīḥ Fuhūm Ahl al-Athar; al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ; Ibn Ḥazm, Asmāʾ al-Ṣaḥāba al-Ruwāt
xhd-033.q: Who are the Companions known as ‘al-muksirūn’ (those who narrated over 1,000 hadith) in the classical lists?
o: Abū Hurayra, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, Anas ibn Mālik, ʿĀʾisha, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās and Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, with Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī usually added
Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān and ʿAlī only
Khālid ibn al-Walīd, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ and Bilāl
Only the women among the Companions
xhd-033.e: Lists of the muksirūn (those who narrated many hadith) include Abū Hurayra, who is first by far, then Ibn ʿUmar, Anas, ʿĀʾisha, Ibn ʿAbbās and Jābir; Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī is also usually included though his numbers are a little lower. The exact counts differ between lists depending on how repeated chains are counted, so scholars speak in approximate numbers.

xhd-034.src: al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ; Ibn Ḥajar, al-Iṣāba; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-ʿilm (Ibn ʿAbbās)
xhd-034.q: Why is ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās called ‘ḥabr al-umma’ and ‘tarjumān al-Qurʾān’?
o: Because of his deep knowledge of the Quran’s interpretation, following the Prophet’s prayer for him to be given understanding of the religion
Because he was the first caliph
Because he led the first conquests
Because he compiled the first Muṣḥaf
xhd-034.e: Ibn ʿAbbās (d. c. 68 AH) was a young cousin of the Prophet ﷺ, and reports record the Prophet’s supplication that he be given understanding in the religion and knowledge of interpretation. Companions like ʿUmar consulted him despite his youth. He is the main source of the Makkan school of tafsīr through students such as Mujāhid, ʿIkrima and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr.

xhd-035.src: Ibn Ḥajar, al-Qawl al-Musaddad fī al-Dhabb ʿan Musnad al-Imām Aḥmad; al-Dhahabī, Siyar; Ibn al-Jawzī, Khaṣāʾiṣ Musnad Aḥmad
xhd-035.q: How do hadith scholars generally regard the status of Musnad Aḥmad with respect to authenticity?
o: It contains sound, good and some weak hadith, and a few that scholars described as fabricated, though Ibn Ḥajar defended it against the claim that it includes many fabrications
It contains only sound hadith, like the Ṣaḥīḥayn
It contains only hadith of the Ahl al-Bayt
xhd-035.e: Musnad Aḥmad is arranged by Companion and is very large. Aḥmad did not claim that all were sound; the scholars assess it as containing the whole range. Ibn al-Jawzī listed some hadith in it as fabricated, and Ibn Ḥajar in al-Qawl al-Musaddad defended the Musnad, accepting a small number as fabricated. The Musnad is nonetheless a major source.

xhd-036.src: al-Nawawī, Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, introduction; Ibn Ḥajar, Hady al-Sārī; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 2
xhd-036.q: What is the majority view of hadith scholars on the relative rank of the Ṣaḥīḥs of al-Bukhārī and Muslim?
o: Al-Bukhārī’s is generally considered more authentic, though some Maghribi scholars preferred Muslim’s for its arrangement and lack of repetition
Muslim’s is more authentic by consensus
They are equal in every respect by consensus
xhd-036.e: The majority holds al-Bukhārī’s Ṣaḥīḥ above Muslim’s because of its stricter conditions (proof of meeting) and the greater precision of its narrators. Some Maghribi scholars and Abū ʿAlī al-Naysābūrī in one report preferred Muslim’s, and Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ says Muslim’s book has a better arrangement. Both are received with acceptance by the Umma.

xhd-037.src: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima, naw‘ 2; al-Nawawī, al-Taqrīb; Ibn Ḥajar, Nuzhat al-Naẓar
xhd-037.q: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ held that the hadith in the Ṣaḥīḥayn yield certain knowledge. What did al-Nawawī say, and what other views exist?
o: Al-Nawawī said they yield probable knowledge (ẓann), as for all single-narrator reports, while Ibn Ḥajar supported the view that the Umma’s acceptance gives certainty for what is not criticised
Al-Nawawī said they give no knowledge
Al-Nawawī said they are all mutawātir
xhd-037.e: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ said that what both al-Bukhārī and Muslim agree on yields certain knowledge because the Umma accepted it. Al-Nawawī in al-Taqrīb disagreed, holding that a single-narrator report yields only probable knowledge, though the two books are of the highest grade. Ibn Ḥajar supported the former view for what the critics did not criticise, so the topic remains debated.

xhd-038.src: al-Dāraquṭnī, al-Istidrākāt wa-l-Tatabbuʿ; Ibn Ḥajar, Hady al-Sārī, muqaddima (chapter on the criticised hadith)
xhd-038.q: What is al-Dāraquṭnī’s al-Tatabbuʿ, and how did Ibn Ḥajar respond?
o: A book listing about 200 hadith in the Ṣaḥīḥayn he criticised for chain or text; Ibn Ḥajar answered most of the criticisms in the introduction to Fatḥ al-Bārī (Hady al-Sārī)
A book listing hadith missing from the Ṣaḥīḥayn, which Ibn Ḥajar adopted
A compilation of the sermons of the caliphs
xhd-038.e: Al-Dāraquṭnī (d. 385 AH) wrote al-Istidrākāt wa-l-Tatabbuʿ, criticising a number of hadith in the Ṣaḥīḥayn, said to be about 200, for weaknesses such as disagreements in the chain or breaks. Ibn Ḥajar in Hady al-Sārī reviewed them, answering most and conceding that a few criticisms had weight. Most of these hadith have supporting chains.

xhd-039.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī; al-ʿAynī, ʿUmdat al-Qārī; al-Qasṭallānī, Irshād al-Sārī; al-Nawawī, al-Minhāj
xhd-039.q: Which commentary matches which book: Fatḥ al-Bārī, ʿUmdat al-Qārī and al-Minhāj?
o: Fatḥ al-Bārī (Ibn Ḥajar) and ʿUmdat al-Qārī (al-ʿAynī) on al-Bukhārī; al-Minhāj (al-Nawawī) on Muslim
Fatḥ al-Bārī on Muslim; ʿUmdat al-Qārī on al-Tirmidhī; al-Minhāj on al-Bukhārī
xhd-039.e: Ibn Ḥajar’s Fatḥ al-Bārī is the best-known commentary on al-Bukhārī, and al-ʿAynī’s ʿUmdat al-Qārī is an extensive rival work, written partly in response to Ibn Ḥajar. Al-Nawawī’s al-Minhāj fī Sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj is the standard commentary on Muslim. Al-Qasṭallānī’s Irshād al-Sārī is another commentary on al-Bukhārī.

xhd-040.src: al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī, al-Jāmiʿ li-Akhlāq al-Rāwī wa-Ādāb al-Sāmiʿ; Ibn Rajab, Sharḥ ʿIlal al-Tirmidhī
xhd-040.q: What does the method of ‘collecting the chains’ (jamʿ al-ṭuruq) mean in the work of the early critics?
o: Gathering all the versions of a hadith and comparing them to find errors, additions and breaks, as ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī and Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn did
Collecting the poetry of a narrator
Gathering the Prophet’s sayings in one book without chains
Collecting the fees paid to narrators
xhd-040.e: A famous saying attributed to ʿAlī ibn al-Madīnī and Yaḥyā ibn Maʿīn is that if you do not collect the routes of a hadith you will not understand its error. By bringing together all routes and comparing wordings and narrators, the critic detects who made a mistake and whether a hadith is firmly supported. This method is the foundation of ʿilal-criticism, as Ibn Rajab explains.

xnh-001.src: Sībawayh, al-Kitāb, bāb al-ʿaṭf ʿalā ism inna; Ibn al-Anbārī, al-Inṣāf fī Masāʾil al-Khilāf, masʾala on the coordination to inna’s ism
xnh-001.q: The highlighted noun is nominative although it is joined to nouns that follow inna. Which analysis is attributed to Sībawayh and the Basrans?
o: It is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is understood after it, the khabar of inna having been given earlier (niyyat al-taʾkhīr)
It is joined to the khabar of inna with ʿaṭf
It is a mistake of the scribes
It is the khabar of a second inna that was omitted
xnh-001.e: Sībawayh explained the nominative by taqdīm and taʾkhīr in meaning: the khabar of inna is given for the first group, and the noun is a mubtadaʾ whose own khabar is omitted, as in ‘and so are the Ṣābiʾūn’. The Kufans (al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ) allowed ʿaṭf on the position of the ism of inna before the khabar, at least when the ism is indeclinable, as alladhīna is here. The claim of a scribal slip is a late and rejected view.

xnh-002.src: Sībawayh, al-Kitāb, bāb mā yanṣub ʿalā al-taʿẓīm wa-l-madḥ; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 2:177
xnh-002.q: Why is the highlighted noun accusative while the other nouns in this long list are nominative?
o: It is accusative as an object of praise (madḥ) governed by an omitted verb such as ‘I praise’, the series of descriptions being cut off (qaṭʿ)
It is accusative because it is the object of the verb ‘gave’ in the same verse
It is accusative because it follows a number
It is accusative as a ḥāl
xnh-002.e: When a series of descriptions of the same subject is long, Arabic allows a break: the speaker puts one of them into the accusative or the nominative with an omitted verb or subject, to draw attention to it. Sībawayh and al-Zamakhsharī cite this verse. The accusative is therefore a naʿt maqṭūʿ for praise of the steadfast.

xnh-003.src: Sībawayh, al-Kitāb, bāb al-ibtidāʾ and on the khabar with fāʾ; al-Mubarrad, al-Muqtaḍab; Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb
xnh-003.q: The highlighted nominative noun is followed by an imperative with fāʾ. Which analysis of the syntax is attributed to Sībawayh?
o: A mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted, e.g. ‘among what is recited to you is …’, the imperative being the explanation of the rule
A mubtadaʾ whose khabar is the imperative with the fāʾ, because the noun is like a conditional
A fāʿil of an omitted verb
A khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ with no further meaning
xnh-003.e: Sībawayh took the noun as a mubtadaʾ with an omitted khabar of the type ‘in what We have laid down for you’ and the imperative as the statement of the ruling. Other grammarians, including al-Mubarrad, allowed the imperative clause to be the khabar, with the fāʾ added because the mubtadaʾ is a relative-like noun with the sense of a condition. Others preferred the accusative by ishtighāl, but the nominative is the reading preserved.

xnh-004.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on inna; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 20:63; al-Farrāʾ, Maʿānī al-Qurʾān
xnh-004.q: The highlighted dual is nominative with alif although it follows the particle inna. Which of these is a recorded explanation?
o: It follows the dialect of some Arab tribes, such as Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb, who keep the alif of the dual in all cases
It is an accusative with an implied tanwīn
It is a mistake that copyists should correct
xnh-004.e: Grammarians gave several explanations: the dialect of Balḥārith ibn Kaʿb and others that keep the alif of the dual in every case; a pronoun of the situation understood after inna; or that the particle is the light in with the lām separating it from the negation, as in the reading of Ibn Kathīr and Ḥafṣ. The suggestion of a scribal error was rejected by the scholars of qirāʾāt.

xnh-005.src: Sībawayh, al-Kitāb, bāb al-jawāb bi-l-wāw; Ibn Hishām, Awḍaḥ al-Masālik, bāb al-nawāṣib; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xnh-005.q: In the reading of Ḥafṣ the highlighted verb is accusative after wāw in the wish clause. How do the Basrans explain the accusative?
o: By an understood an after the wāw of accompaniment (wāw al-maʿiyya) in the answer to a wish (tamannī)
By the particle laytanā governing it directly
By the particle lā, which always governs the accusative
By a jussive that was changed to accusative for rhyme
xnh-005.e: In an answer to a wish, a verb after the fāʾ or the wāw of accompaniment is put in the subjunctive by an understood an. The wāw means ‘and in conjunction with’: they wish to be returned while not denying and being believers. Others read the verb nominative (a new statement), and the grammarians discuss the meaning of both.

xnh-006.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, bāb kāna wa-akhawātuhā (kāna al-tāmma); al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf
xnh-006.q: How is the highlighted verb ‘be’ analysed here, followed by a nominative noun and no accusative khabar?
o: As a kāna tāmma (complete), meaning ‘there is’ or ‘occurs’, with the nominative noun as its fāʿil
As a kāna nāqiṣa with an omitted khabar
As an auxiliary of the past with no function
As a particle of condition only
xnh-006.e: Kāna has two uses: the incomplete (nāqiṣa), needing a khabar, and the complete (tāmma), meaning to exist or to occur, with a fāʿil. Here the noun after it is nominative and nothing is missing, so it is tāmma: ‘if there is someone in difficulty’. In the reading with the accusative, the verb would be incomplete.

xnh-007.src: Sībawayh, al-Kitāb; Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, entry hal; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 76:1
xnh-007.q: What is the meaning of the interrogative particle at the start of this verse, according to many commentators and grammarians?
o: It has the meaning of qad, so the sentence affirms, ‘there has indeed come upon man a long time’
It asks a real question whose answer is unknown
xnh-007.e: Many commentators, such as Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Farrāʾ, take hal here as equivalent to qad (affirmation). Others, such as al-Zamakhsharī, keep the question sense as a question of affirmation (istifhām taqrīrī): ‘Has there not come …?’ and the answer is yes. In either case there is no real doubt.

xnh-008.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on lām al-ibtidāʾ and the oath; Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya
xnh-008.q: The highlighted word begins with a lām of emphasis and is annexed to a pronoun. How is it analysed?
o: As a mubtadaʾ whose khabar must be omitted, the meaning being ‘by your life is my oath’
As a fāʿil of an omitted verb
xnh-008.e: In the oath formula the noun is a mubtadaʾ, and its khabar (‘my oath’) is omitted by necessity because the oath is understood. The lām is the lām of ibtidāʾ that emphasises the oath. The noun is a verbal noun of the root meaning ‘to live’ and the formula is used for swearing by someone’s life.

xnh-009.src: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 37:96; Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, al-Tafsīr al-Kabīr; Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, entry mā
xnh-009.q: The highlighted mā has two main analyses with a theological side. Which statement correctly describes them?
o: It can be a relative pronoun (‘what you make’, the idols), favoured by Muʿtazilī commentators, or a verbal-noun particle (‘your making’), used by many Ashʿarīs to prove that God creates human actions
It is only a negation, so the verse denies that God made the actions
It is only an interrogative, so the verse is a question
It is only a conditional, so the verse is a threat
xnh-009.e: The context concerns Ibrāhīm’s people and the idols they carved. A relative mā means ‘what you carve’; a maṣdarī mā means ‘and your deeds’, which many Ashʿarīs used as a proof text for khalq al-afʿāl. Many Sunni commentators accepted the relative sense and still held the doctrine from other proofs. The grammar allows both.

xnh-010.src: Ibn al-Anbārī, al-Inṣāf fī Masāʾil al-Khilāf, masʾala on the competing verbs (al-tanāzuʿ); Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, bāb al-tanāzuʿ
xnh-010.q: The highlighted noun can be the object of either of two verbs. How do the Basrans and the Kufans differ?
o: The Basrans give the work to the nearer verb (the second), the Kufans to the first, and the other verb takes a pronoun or has its object omitted
Both schools give it to the first verb
Both give it to the second verb and forbid any alternative
The Basrans say it is an object of neither
xnh-010.e: This is the issue of tanāzuʿ (two verbs sharing one noun). The Basrans prefer the nearer verb because of proximity, the Kufans the first, because of precedence. The verse at hand is a standard illustration: the first verb has a pronoun, so the Basran analysis makes the noun the object of the second verb. Both ways are recorded.

xnh-011.src: Sībawayh, al-Kitāb; Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, entry al-bāʾ
xnh-011.q: The highlighted word begins with the preposition bi- after the verb ‘suffices’. What is its function?
o: The bāʾ is extra (zāʾida), and the noun is genitive in form but is the fāʿil of ‘suffices’ in meaning (nominative in position)
The bāʾ is a bāʾ of accompaniment and the noun is a ḥāl
The bāʾ is a bāʾ of means and the noun is a maf ʿūl bihi
The bāʾ is for oath and the noun is a muḍāf ilayhi
xnh-011.e: After kafā the subject is often introduced by an added bāʾ, which adds emphasis. The noun is majrūr in form (ʿalā al-lafẓ) and marfūʿ as fāʿil in position (ʿalā al-maḥall). The noun that follows in the accusative is a tamyīz or ḥāl, as grammarians discuss.

xnh-012.src: al-Qazwīnī, al-Īḍāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Balāgha, bāb al-tashbīh; ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī, Asrār al-Balāgha
xnh-012.q: Which type of simile is this, in which spouses are said to be garments for each other?
o: Tashbīh baligh: the particle and the point of resemblance are both omitted and the two terms are put in apposition
Tashbīh mursal mujmal: the particle is stated and the point omitted
Tashbīh tamthīlī: a composite picture is compared
Istiʿāra makniyya: an object is compared to a living being
xnh-012.e: A simile with the particle and the point of comparison both dropped is called baligh (the strongest), because the two sides are presented as identical. In this case ‘they are your garment’, the closeness, covering and mutual protection are the implied points. The Qazwīnī school ranks this kind highest in force.

xnh-013.src: al-Qazwīnī, al-Īḍāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Balāgha, bāb al-majāz al-mursal; al-Sakkākī, Miftāḥ al-ʿUlūm
xnh-013.q: Which figure explains the use of the highlighted word, since people put only the tips of their fingers into their ears?
o: Majāz mursal: the whole is named for the part (the fingers for the fingertips)
xnh-013.e: In majāz mursal the relationship between literal and intended meaning is something other than resemblance. Here it is the relation of whole and part (kulliyya or juziʾiyya): ‘fingers’ stand for the tips that are really put in the ears. There is no simile, so the other options do not apply.

xnh-014.src: al-Qazwīnī, al-Īḍāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Balāgha, bāb al-majāz al-ʿaqlī; ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī, Asrār al-Balāgha
xnh-014.q: The verse says that ‘their trade made no profit’. Which figure is this?
o: Majāz ʿaqlī: the profit is attributed to the trade, though it is the traders who profit
xnh-014.e: In a majāz ʿaqlī the verb is attributed to something other than its true doer because of a relationship, here that the trade is the place or cause of profit. The words themselves are used literally; the figure lies in the ascription (isnād), as al-Jurjānī and al-Qazwīnī explain.

xnh-015.src: al-Qazwīnī, al-Īḍāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Balāgha, bāb al-istiʿāra; ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī, Asrār al-Balāgha
xnh-015.q: The highlighted word and ‘the light’ stand for disbelief and faith. Which figure is this?
o: Istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya aṣliyya: the borrowed terms are stated and the originals (the things compared) are omitted
xnh-015.e: In an explicit metaphor (taṣrīḥiyya) the thing compared to (the borrowed term) is stated, while the thing compared (here, disbelief and faith) is dropped. It is aṣliyya because the borrowed words are nouns, not verbs. The context makes the intended resemblance clear: darkness hides the path, light shows it.

xnh-016.src: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on Sūrat al-Fātiḥa; Ibn al-Athīr, al-Mathal al-Sāʾir; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān
xnh-016.q: Which rhetorical device is shown by the change in the highlighted word, after four verses speaking of God in the third person?
o: Iltifāt: a shift from the third person (absent) to the second person (direct address)
Ḥadhf: omission of a part of the sentence
xnh-016.e: After praising God as ‘He’ in the first verses, the speech turns to direct address. This iltifāt, as al-Zamakhsharī notes, keeps the listener alert and expresses the movement from praise about God to a plea made to Him. The device is common in the Quran.

xnh-017.src: al-Qazwīnī, al-Īḍāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Balāgha, bāb al-qaṣr; ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī, Dalāʾil al-Iʿjāz
xnh-017.q: What does the fronting of the object before the verb achieve in the highlighted word?
o: Restriction (qaṣr / ikhtiṣāṣ): worship is limited to God alone
xnh-017.e: Putting the object before its verb is normally for specification. In this verse it limits worship and seeking help to God, as al-Jurjānī describes the effect of taqdīm. If the order were normal, the sentence would only state that the speaker worships God without the exclusive sense.

xnh-018.src: al-Qazwīnī, al-Īḍāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Balāgha, bāb al-kināya; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 17:29
xnh-018.q: The command not to make the hand ‘bound to the neck’ is not literal. Which figure is it, and what does it mean?
o: Kināya ʿan ṣifa: a metaphoric expression for stinginess, while its literal sense is also possible
xnh-018.e: Kināya is an expression whose literal meaning is possible but whose intended meaning is something else; here the image of the bound hand signifies miserliness, as the next phrase about opening it fully signifies extravagance. The verse thus teaches the middle way in spending.

xnh-019.src: al-Qazwīnī, al-Īḍāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Balāgha, bāb al-badīʿ (al-maḥassināt al-maʿnawiyya); Ibn al-Muʿtazz, Kitāb al-Badīʿ
xnh-019.q: The highlighted word and the word that follows the next ‘and they’ are opposites. What is the figure?
o: Ṭibāq (muṭābaqa): the pairing of two opposites, ‘awake’ and ‘asleep’
xnh-019.e: Ṭibāq is the combination of a word and its opposite in one sentence. Here ‘awake’ and ‘asleep’ describe the youths of the cave, whom one would think awake though they are sleeping. It belongs to the branch of badīʿ and adds both beauty and meaning.

xnh-020.src: al-Qazwīnī, al-Īḍāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Balāgha, bāb al-jinās; Ibn al-Muʿtazz, Kitāb al-Badīʿ
xnh-020.q: The highlighted word is repeated in the same form later in the verse with a different meaning. Which figure is this?
o: Jinās tāmm: identical words with different meanings (the Hour of judgement and an hour of time)
xnh-020.e: In jinās tāmm the two words agree in letters, vowels, number and order but differ in meaning. Here the first means the Last Hour and the second a short period of time. Al-Qazwīnī counts it among the strongest kinds of jinās.

xnh-021.src: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī, Asrār al-Balāgha, on al-tamthīl; al-Qazwīnī, al-Īḍāḥ
xnh-021.q: What type of simile is the comparison of those who take protectors besides God with the spider that built a house?
o: Tashbīh tamthīlī: the point of resemblance is a picture drawn from several elements, not from a single feature
xnh-021.e: In al-Jurjānī’s analysis tamthīl is a simile in which the point of resemblance is derived from several things together: here the spider’s fragile house, its effort, and what it offers no protection against. The simile is explicitly stated with kāf, so it is not an istiʿāra. The verse concludes that the weakest of houses is the spider’s.

xnh-022.src: al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 5:6; Ibn Rushd, Bidāyat al-Mujtahid, Kitāb al-Ṭahāra (touching and wuḍūʾ); Ibn Qudāma, al-Mughnī
xnh-022.q: The highlighted verb is understood differently by the schools: literal touch or kināya for intercourse. Which statement describes the main positions?
o: The Ḥanafīs read it as kināya for intercourse; the Shāfiʿīs as literal touch that breaks wuḍūʾ; the Mālikīs and Ḥanbalīs hold that touch with desire breaks it
All schools read it only as touch with no further condition
All schools read it only as intercourse
The Ḥanafīs read it as literal touch and the others as intercourse
xnh-022.e: The verb lāmasa can mean touching or be a polite expression (kināya) for sexual intercourse. The Ḥanafīs, with a report from Ibn ʿAbbās, take the latter; the Shāfiʿīs take touch literally, as reported from Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn Masʿūd; the Mālikīs and Ḥanbalīs combine them by requiring desire. The case is a classical example of how a rhetorical decision (haqīqa or kināya) shapes a legal ruling.

xnh-023.src: al-Qazwīnī, al-Īḍāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Balāgha, bāb al-majāz al-ʿaqlī
xnh-023.q: The slaughter of the sons is attributed to Pharaoh, though soldiers carried it out. Which figure is this?
o: Majāz ʿaqlī by attributing the act to its cause (the one who gave the order)
Majāz mursal by naming the whole for the part
xnh-023.e: In a majāz ʿaqlī the act is ascribed to someone other than its doer because that person is its cause. Pharaoh gave the order, so the slaying is ascribed to him. The words are used in their literal senses, which distinguishes this figure from majāz lughawī.

xnh-024.src: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 10:22; Ibn al-Athīr, al-Mathal al-Sāʾir
xnh-024.q: The address ‘you were in the ships’ changes to a third-person verb in the highlighted word. What is the figure and its purpose?
o: Iltifāt from second to third person, to describe the event to others and to show that those sailing are of little account
Taqdīm of the object for restriction
xnh-024.e: Al-Zamakhsharī explains the change from ‘you’ to ‘they’ as turning to others to marvel at the sailors’ behaviour, so that the listeners may wonder at their ingratitude in distress and gratitude in safety. The shift also gives variety to the style, an aim of iltifāt.

xnh-025.src: al-Qazwīnī, al-Īḍāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Balāgha, bāb al-muqābala; Ibn Abī al-Iṣbaʿ, Taḥrīr al-Taḥbīr
xnh-025.q: The verse sets ‘little’ with ‘laughing’ against ‘much’ with ‘weeping’. What is this figure called, as distinct from a simple ṭibāq?
o: Muqābala: a series of two or more meanings is set against the same number of opposites in order
Jinās: a play on identical sounds
xnh-025.e: While ṭibāq pairs one word with its opposite, muqābala sets groups against groups in the same order. Here ‘laugh little’ is set against ‘weep much’: the first pair of meanings against their opposites in the reverse sense. The device is cited as a standard example in the books of badīʿ.

xnh-026.src: Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya, bāb al-iḍāfa (al-iḍāfa al-lafẓiyya); Ibn Hishām, Awḍaḥ al-Masālik
xnh-026.q: The highlighted active participle is annexed to its object. How is this annexation classified, and what follows?
o: Iḍāfa lafẓiyya (ghayr maḥḍa): it brings only lightness in speech and does not make the first term definite
Iḍāfa maʿnawiyya (maḥḍa): it makes the first term definite
Iḍāfa of a mubtadaʾ to its khabar
Iḍāfa that requires the genitive of a pronoun
xnh-026.e: An annexation of an active participle to its object, with the sense of present or future, is only verbal: it removes the tanwīn for lightness but does not specify the first noun, so it may still describe an indefinite noun. A true annexation (maʿnawiyya) gives definiteness or specification. The distinction matters for agreement and for the adjective rules.

xnh-027.src: al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 3:7; Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb; al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān
xnh-027.q: The highlighted nominative noun is analysed in two ways, which affects where one may stop in the verse. What are they?
o: Coordinated with ‘God’ (so the firmly rooted in knowledge also know the interpretation), or a new mubtadaʾ with ‘they say’ as its khabar (so only God knows it)
A fāʿil of the previous verb and an object of the next verb
A diptote and a muḍāf ilayhi
xnh-027.e: If the word is coordinated with the name of God, the interpretation is known to both God and the firmly rooted scholars, as Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid are reported to have said; if it begins a new sentence, the interpretation is known to God alone, and the scholars say ‘we believe in it’, as reported from Ubayy, Ibn Masʿūd and ʿĀʾisha. Both views have defenders, and the stop in the verse is chosen accordingly.

xnh-028.src: Ibn al-Anbārī, al-Inṣāf fī Masāʾil al-Khilāf bayn al-Naḥwiyyīn al-Baṣriyyīn wa-l-Kūfiyyīn
xnh-028.q: Which scholar wrote al-Inṣāf fī Masāʾil al-Khilāf, setting out the disagreements of the Basran and Kufan grammarians with judgments between them?
xnh-028.e: Ibn al-Anbārī (d. 577 AH) wrote the Inṣāf, in which he presents each issue with the arguments of both schools and usually sides with the Basrans. Sībawayh (al-Kitāb) and al-Mubarrad (al-Muqtaḍab) were earlier and Ibn Jinnī (al-Khaṣāʾiṣ) wrote on the principles of grammar.

xnh-029.src: Ibn al-Nadīm, al-Fihrist; Ibn Khallikān, Wafayāt al-Aʿyān
xnh-029.q: Which scholar wrote al-Muqtaḍab, a major Basran work of grammar and morphology, and had a famous rivalry with Thaʿlab of Kūfa?
xnh-029.e: Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Mubarrad (d. 285 AH) wrote al-Muqtaḍab and al-Kāmil, and is considered the head of the Basrans of his time, while Thaʿlab (d. 291 AH) led the Kūfan school in Baghdad. Al-Zajjāj was his student, and Ibn Jinnī lived later.

xnh-030.src: Ibn al-Nadīm, al-Fihrist; al-Zubaydī, Ṭabaqāt al-Naḥwiyyīn wa-l-Lughawiyyīn; Ibn al-Anbārī, Nuzhat al-Alibbāʾ
xnh-030.q: Who is traditionally credited with beginning the science of Arabic grammar and with placing dots to mark the vowels of the Quran?
xnh-030.e: According to the common account, Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī (d. 69 AH), at the instruction of ʿAlī or Ziyād, laid down the first rules of grammar and marked vowels with coloured dots. Al-Khalīl later replaced the dots with the vowel signs in use. The attribution is traditional and the details vary in the sources.

xnh-031.src: Ibn al-Nadīm, al-Fihrist; al-Zubaydī, Ṭabaqāt al-Naḥwiyyīn wa-l-Lughawiyyīn; Ibn Khallikān, Wafayāt al-Aʿyān
xnh-031.q: Which scholar of Baṣra, teacher of Sībawayh, devised the vowel signs now in use and began the first Arabic dictionary, Kitāb al-ʿAyn?
xnh-031.e: Al-Khalīl (d. c. 170 AH) introduced the small letter-shaped signs for fatḥa, ḍamma, kasra and others, set out the science of prosody and began the dictionary arranged by points of articulation, called al-ʿAyn after its first letter. The Kitāb of Sībawayh preserves much of his teaching.

xnh-032.src: Ibn al-Nadīm, al-Fihrist; al-Zubaydī, Ṭabaqāt al-Naḥwiyyīn wa-l-Lughawiyyīn
xnh-032.q: How have later grammarians referred to Sībawayh’s al-Kitāb, because of its authority in the science?
o: As ‘the Quran of grammar’ (Qurʾān al-naḥw), or simply al-Kitāb (‘the Book’)
xnh-032.e: Sībawayh (Amr ibn ʿUthmān, d. about 180 AH), a Persian-born student of al-Khalīl, wrote a work so complete that it was simply called al-Kitāb. Later grammarians came to call it the Quran of grammar because every later work depends on it.

xnh-033.src: Ibn al-Anbārī, Luma‘ al-Adilla fī Uṣūl al-Naḥw; al-Suyūṭī, al-Iqtirāḥ fī ʿIlm Uṣūl al-Naḥw; Shawqī Ḍayf, al-Madāris al-Naḥwiyya
xnh-033.q: Which statement correctly describes the usual contrast between the Basran and the Kufan schools in method?
o: The Basrans were stricter, building rules on widespread usage and analogy, while the Kufans accepted rarer usages and individual lines of poetry as a basis for rules
The Kufans were stricter and the Basrans accepted any usage
Both schools accepted only the Quran as a source
xnh-033.e: Traditional accounts say the Basrans, strict in their choice of speakers and relying on qiyās, rejected rare or isolated forms, whereas the Kufans took wider material, including dialects and single verses. The contrast should not be overdrawn, since later grammarians of Baghdad combined both approaches.

xnh-034.src: Ibn Mālik, al-Alfiyya (Khulāṣat al-Alfiyya); Ibn ʿAqīl, Sharḥ Alfiyya Ibn Mālik
xnh-034.q: Which poem of grammar, in about a thousand verses, did Ibn Mālik compose, and whose commentary by Ibn ʿAqīl is among the most widely read?
xnh-034.e: Ibn Mālik (d. 672 AH) condensed grammar and morphology in the Alfiyya, which became a base of teaching in the madrasas; Ibn ʿAqīl’s commentary and al-Ushmūnī’s are among the best known. The Ājurrūmiyya is a short prose primer, the Jazariyya is on tajwīd and Mulḥat al-Iʿrāb is al-Ḥarīrī’s poem.

xnh-035.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb ʿan Kutub al-Aʿārīb; Ibn Khaldūn, al-Muqaddima (on the arabic sciences)
xnh-035.q: What is Ibn Hishām’s Mughnī al-Labīb known for, among the books of grammar?
o: A reference on the particles and the types of sentences, with their uses, mostly illustrated with Quranic verses
A short poem for beginners on case endings
xnh-035.e: Ibn Hishām (d. 761 AH) devoted the first chapter to the particles in alphabetical order, with discussion of their meanings, then to sentences and their positions, and to common errors of grammarians. Grammarians refer to it for difficult passages of the Quran. Ibn Khaldūn praised his work.

xnh-036.src: ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī, Dalāʾil al-Iʿjāz; ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī, Asrār al-Balāgha
xnh-036.q: What is ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī’s main thesis in Dalāʾil al-Iʿjāz?
o: That eloquence lies in the arrangement (naẓm) of words according to the meanings of grammar (maʿānī al-naḥw), not in single words alone
That the inimitability lies only in the single words
That the Quran is inimitable only because of its rhyme
That inimitability lies in the prophecy of the unseen alone
xnh-036.e: Al-Jurjānī (d. 471 AH) argued that excellence is in how words are arranged and related by grammatical meanings: fronting, omission, definiteness, restriction and so on, not in isolated words or sounds. This theory of naẓm became the foundation of the science of maʿānī and strongly influenced the doctrine of Quranic inimitability.

xnh-037.src: al-Sakkākī, Miftāḥ al-ʿUlūm; al-Qazwīnī, Talkhīṣ al-Miftāḥ and al-Īḍāḥ
xnh-037.q: Under which of the three branches of balāgha do the studies of simile, metaphor and kināya fall?
xnh-037.e: In the arrangement of al-Sakkākī and al-Qazwīnī, ʿilm al-maʿānī studies how the sentence fits the situation, ʿilm al-bayān the ways of expressing one meaning in various forms (tashbīh, majāz, kināya), and ʿilm al-badīʿ the embellishments. Prosody is a separate science.

xnh-038.src: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf ʿan Ḥaqāʾiq Ghawāmiḍ al-Tanzīl; Ibn al-Munayyir, al-Intiṣāf min al-Kashshāf; Abū Ḥayyān, al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ
xnh-038.q: How is al-Zamakhsharī’s al-Kashshāf regarded in the Sunni tradition?
o: Praised for its linguistic and rhetorical insight, but read with caution because it reflects the author’s Muʿtazilī doctrine, with glosses and rebuttals by later Sunni scholars
Rejected without exception and never used
Accepted without reservation as a Sunni commentary
xnh-038.e: Al-Zamakhsharī (d. 538 AH) was a master of language and balāgha, and his commentary is full of insights drawn from them; but he was a Muʿtazilī and his creed shapes some interpretations. Sunni scholars such as Ibn al-Munayyir (al-Intiṣāf) and Abū Ḥayyān wrote notes pointing out these places while using his linguistic work.

xnh-039.src: al-Rummānī, al-Nukat fī Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān; al-Khaṭṭābī, Bayān Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān; ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī, Dalāʾil al-Iʿjāz; al-Bāqillānī, Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān
xnh-039.q: Which scholar wrote Bayān Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān, one of the classic treatises on the inimitability of the Quran, alongside those of al-Rummānī and al-Jurjānī?
xnh-039.e: Al-Khaṭṭābī (d. 388 AH) wrote the Bayān, al-Rummānī (d. 384 AH) the Nukat and al-Jurjānī the Dalāʾil; the three are often published together as ‘Thalāth Rasāʾil fī Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān’. Al-Bāqillānī wrote his own Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān.

xnh-040.src: al-Qazwīnī, al-Īḍāḥ fī ʿUlūm al-Balāgha; Ibn Taymiyya, al-Īmān al-Kabīr; Ibn al-Qayyim, al-Ṣawāʿiq al-Mursala
xnh-040.q: Which statement correctly describes the scholarly disagreement over the existence of majāz (figurative usage) in language and the Quran?
o: The majority of rhetoricians and scholars accept it, while some, such as Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim, reject majāz as a category and treat such uses as part of usage in context
Everyone agrees that majāz does not exist in the Quran
Everyone agrees on the same definition and the same list of majāz
Only the Muʿtazila accepted it, and the rest rejected it
xnh-040.e: Most rhetoricians (al-Zamakhsharī, al-Qazwīnī) and many scholars of all schools accept majāz, including in the Quran. Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn al-Qayyim, among others, argued against the division into ḥaqīqa and majāz, holding that all language use depends on context, and that the division was introduced late. The practical examples are not in dispute, only the category.

xnh-041.src: Ibn Jinnī, al-Khaṣāʾiṣ, bāb al-ishtiqāq al-akbar; Ibn al-Nadīm, al-Fihrist
xnh-041.q: What is the ‘greater derivation’ (al-ishtiqāq al-akbar) that Ibn Jinnī discusses in al-Khaṣāʾiṣ?
o: The link between roots that share the same letters in different orders, which suggests a shared core meaning
The derivation of the verb from the verbal noun
The derivation of plurals from singulars
The derivation of the participle from the imperfect
xnh-041.e: Besides the ordinary derivation (ishtiqāq ṣaghīr) from one root and the middle one (kabīr) that links words with the same letters in varying order, Ibn Jinnī describes the greater derivation (akbar) linking roots that share two letters and a similar sound and meaning. He treats it as a source of insight rather than a firm rule.

xqr-001.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, sūrat al-Fātiḥa; Ibn Mujāhid, Kitāb al-Sabʿa fī al-Qirāʾāt
xqr-001.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word with an alif (mālik). Which two of the Seven read it with the alif, the others reading it without (malik)?
xqr-001.e: Among the Seven only ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī read it with the alif; Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥamza read it without. Yaʿqūb and Khalaf among the Ten follow the alif. Commentators note that both forms are attested names of God’s attributes: ‘owner’ (mālik) and ‘king’ (malik), and each is supported by other verses.

xqr-002.src: al-Dānī, al-Taysīr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-Sabʿ; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh sūrat al-Baqara
xqr-002.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word with a single ẓāʾ (taẓāharūna). Which three of the Seven read it this way, whereas the rest double the ẓāʾ (taẓẓāharūna)?
o: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr
xqr-002.e: The three Kūfan readers ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read it with takhfīf, a single ẓāʾ; the readers of Madīna, Makka, Baṣra and Shām (Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir) read with tashdīd. Both forms come from the verb meaning to support one another against someone, the doubled ẓāʾ being an assimilation of the tāʾ of the form VI.

xqr-003.src: al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Maʿrifat Marsūm Maṣāḥif Ahl al-Amṣār; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh sūrat al-Baqara
xqr-003.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word in the form with a doubled ṣād (waṣṣā). Which readers read the alternative wa-awṣā with a hamza, and which muṣḥafs are said to carry the alif in the rasm?
o: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir; the muṣḥafs of Madīna and Shām
Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr; the muṣḥafs of Makka and Baṣra
ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza; the muṣḥaf of Kūfa
Al-Kisāʾī and Ibn ʿĀmir; the muṣḥaf of Shām only
xqr-003.e: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir (and Abū Jaʿfar) read awṣā, and the Madinan and Syrian copies write an alif in the word. The others read waṣṣā, in agreement with the other copies where the alif is not written. The case is a standard example of how a variant in the rasm correlates with readings from the same region.

xqr-004.src: al-Dānī, al-Taysīr; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh sūrat al-Baqara
xqr-004.q: Ḥafṣ reads ‘food of a poor person’ (ṭaʿāmu miskīnin), with the second word singular. Which two of the Seven read it as plural, masākīna?
xqr-004.e: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir (with Abū Jaʿfar) read the second word as masākīna in the plural and the first word without tanwīn in an annexation, so the expiation is food of poor people for the days not fasted. The singular reading gives the sense of feeding one poor person for each day.

xqr-005.src: al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 2:222; Ibn Rushd, Bidāyat al-Mujtahid, Kitāb al-Ṭahāra (chapter on menstruation); al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī
xqr-005.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted verb as yaṭhurna (‘they become clean’). Shuʿba, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read yaṭṭahharna (‘they purify themselves’). Which statement correctly describes how the two readings figured in the legal discussion?
o: Most jurists required ghusl before intercourse, relying on the reading yaṭṭahharna and the following verb; the Ḥanafīs allowed it once bleeding ended at its maximum period, relying on yaṭhurna
All schools agree that the two readings give different rulings that cannot be harmonised
The Ḥanafīs required ghusl while the other schools did not
The readings were not used in the legal discussion at all
xqr-005.e: The reading yaṭhurna means bleeding has stopped, and the continuation tataṭahharna means they have washed. The majority (Mālikīs, Shāfiʿīs, Ḥanbalīs) took the verse to require ghusl before intercourse, supported by the stronger form. The Ḥanafīs held that intercourse becomes lawful when the bleeding stops at the maximum period of ten days, even without ghusl. This is a classical case in which a qirāʾa variant is part of the discussion of the schools.

xqr-006.src: al-Dānī, al-Taysīr; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh sūrat Āl ʿImrān
xqr-006.q: In 3:19 the highlighted particle is read inna (with kasra) by Ḥafṣ. Which of the Seven reads it as anna (with fatḥa)?
xqr-006.e: Al-Kisāʾī reads anna l-dīna with fatḥa, making the clause a substitute (badal) for the preceding ‘annahu lā ilāha illā huwa’ in the previous verse, so that the content of God’s testimony includes the statement about the religion. The others read inna as a new sentence. The two readings give different grammar but compatible meaning.

xqr-007.src: al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Maʿrifat Marsūm Maṣāḥif Ahl al-Amṣār
xqr-007.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word with a wāw at the beginning (wa-sāriʿū). Which two of the Seven read it without the wāw, in agreement with the rasm of which copies?
o: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir; the Madinan and Syrian copies
Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr; the Meccan and Basran copies
ʿĀṣim and al-Kisāʾī; the Kūfan copy
Ḥamza and Abū ʿAmr; the Basran copy
xqr-007.e: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read sāriʿū without a wāw, and the Madinan and Syrian copies lack the wāw in the rasm, while the other copies have it. The omission turns the clause into a direct command to hasten, instead of a command joined to the preceding sentence.

xqr-008.src: al-Dānī, al-Taysīr; Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Kashf ʿan Wujūh al-Qirāʾāt
xqr-008.q: Ḥafṣ reads qātala (‘fought’). Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read qutila (‘was killed’). How does the meaning change?
o: With qātala, many devoted men fought together with the prophet; with qutila, many devoted men were killed fighting with him, yet the rest did not lose heart
With qutila, the prophet alone is killed; with qātala, he fights alone
The two readings have exactly the same meaning
With qātala the rabbānīs fled; with qutila they stayed
xqr-008.e: The verse praises steadfastness of the followers of earlier prophets. With qātala it says that many rabbānīs fought together with the prophet and did not weaken. With qutila (passive), on one analysis, it says that many were killed with him, and those who remained still did not weaken. The commentators note that both readings serve the point of the verse, which was revealed after Uḥud.

xqr-009.src: Sībawayh, al-Kitāb, on the coordination to a pronoun in the genitive; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh sūrat al-Nisāʾ; Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb
xqr-009.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word in the accusative (wa-l-arḥāma). Which of the Seven reads it as genitive (wa-l-arḥāmi), and what was the grammatical objection of the Basrans?
o: Ḥamza; the objection was that a noun cannot be joined to an attached pronoun in the genitive without repeating the preposition
Nāfiʿ; the objection was that the word has no case ending
Ibn Kathīr; the objection was that it must be nominative
Abū ʿAmr; the objection was that it is a diptote
xqr-009.e: Ḥamza reads the genitive, joining the word to the pronoun in ‘by whom you ask one another’, and the Basrans held that coordination to an attached genitive pronoun requires repeating the preposition, so they called the reading weak. The Kufans permitted it, and defenders cite the authority of the reading and examples from poetry. Ḥafṣ’s accusative is joined to the name of God (‘fear God … and the wombs’), meaning to respect kinship ties.

xqr-010.src: al-Dānī, al-Taysīr; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh sūrat al-Māʾida
xqr-010.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word in the accusative (arjulakum). Which of the Seven read it in the genitive (arjulikum)?
o: Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza and Shuʿba ʿan ʿĀṣim
Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ
Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and Abū ʿAmr
xqr-010.e: The accusative (Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Kisāʾī and Ḥafṣ) joins ‘your feet’ to ‘your faces and hands’, which are washed. The genitive (Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza and Shuʿba) joins it to ‘your heads’, which are wiped. In the case of Ḥafṣ the washing is therefore explicit; the genitive reading is explained by the majority as the genitive of proximity, or as referring to the wiping over the khuffs.

xqr-011.src: al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 5:6; al-Qurṭubī, al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān; Ibn Rushd, Bidāyat al-Mujtahid
xqr-011.q: How did the majority of jurists deal with the genitive reading of the feet in the wuḍūʾ verse?
o: They held that the feet must be washed, explaining the genitive as one of proximity (jarr al-jiwār) or as referring to wiping over the khuffs, and they relied on the reports of washing
They concluded that the feet need only be wiped, in every case
They rejected the genitive reading as invalid
They held that the feet need not be washed or wiped at all
xqr-011.e: The reading arjulikum can be read as coordinated with the wiped heads, which some early authorities, such as Ibn ʿAbbās in one report, understood as wiping. The majority of jurists reconcile the readings by washing, for the Prophet is reported to have washed his feet and to have said ‘woe to the heels from the fire’. They said the genitive is by adjacency or indicates wiping on khuffs, which the Sunna permits.

xqr-012.src: al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Maʿrifat Marsūm Maṣāḥif Ahl al-Amṣār; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xqr-012.q: The word is written in the rasm without a final yāʾ and is read by Ḥafṣ as yaquṣṣu (‘narrates’). Which readers read it as yaqḍī (‘decides’), and what does this show?
o: Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī; the rasm without a final letter allows both forms
Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr; the rasm requires only yaquṣṣu
ʿĀṣim alone; the rasm has a yāʾ
None of the Seven; yaqḍī is a shādhdh reading
xqr-012.e: Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr and ʿĀṣim read yaquṣṣu, while Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read yaqḍī bi-l-ḥaqq. The reading of both forms is possible because the Uthmānic rasm omits the final letter (it is one form for both). It is a classical example of a rasm that supports two mutawātir readings.

xqr-013.src: al-Dānī, al-Taysīr; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh sūrat al-Anʿām
xqr-013.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word with shadda (munazzalun). Which of the Seven read it with the shadda too, whereas the others read munzalun?
o: Ibn ʿĀmir (and ʿĀṣim in the riwāya of Ḥafṣ)
xqr-013.e: Ibn ʿĀmir and Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim read the intensive form munazzalun, with the sense of being sent down in stages; the other readers, including Shuʿba, read munzalun. The difference does not change the reference, since the Quran came down gradually and as a whole to the lowest heaven.

xqr-014.src: al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Maʿrifat Marsūm Maṣāḥif Ahl al-Amṣār; Abū ʿUbayd, Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān
xqr-014.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word ‘beneath them’ without the preposition. Who reads it with the preposition (min taḥtihā), and which muṣḥaf has it written?
xqr-014.e: Ibn Kathīr reads min taḥtihā with the preposition min, and the Meccan copy is reported to be the only one that has it written here. In all other places in the Quran, the expression has no min. The case is a standard proof that a reading follows the rasm of its region.

xqr-015.src: al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Maʿrifat Marsūm Maṣāḥif Ahl al-Amṣār; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī
xqr-015.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word with a wāw at the start (wa-alladhīna). Who reads it without the wāw, and in agreement with which copies?
o: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir; the Madinan and Syrian copies
Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr; the Meccan and Basran copies
ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza; the Kūfan copy
Al-Kisāʾī and Ḥamza; the Kūfan and Basran copies
xqr-015.e: Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read alladhīna ittakhadhū without the wāw, as in the Madinan and Syrian muṣḥafs, making the relative clause a description or a new sentence directly after the previous verse. The other readers have the wāw, as in the other copies, and read the clause as coordinated.

xqr-016.src: Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Kashf ʿan Wujūh al-Qirāʾāt; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xqr-016.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word as la-sāḥirun (‘a magician’). Which of the Seven read la-siḥrun (‘magic’)?
o: Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir
xqr-016.e: The unbelievers speak of the Prophet in the first reading (la-sāḥirun, referring to the man) and of what he brings in the second (la-siḥrun, referring to the message). Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir read siḥr, whereas Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read sāḥir. Both are the kind of attribution unbelievers made, the one to the man and the other to the revelation.

xqr-017.src: al-Dānī, al-Taysīr; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh sūrat al-Kahf
xqr-017.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted name with a hamza (yaʾjūj). Which of the Seven reads it with a hamza as he does?
o: ʿĀṣim alone; the others read yājūj without hamza
xqr-017.e: ʿĀṣim alone among the Seven reads yaʾjūj and maʾjūj with hamza (in 18:94 and 21:96); the others read yājūj and mājūj, with a soft alif. Those who read with hamza derive the name from ajja (to blaze or rush); the others treat it as a foreign name pronounced with a soft alif.

xqr-018.src: al-Dānī, al-Taysīr; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr
xqr-018.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted verb li-ahaba (‘that I may give’). Which reader of the Seven, and which transmitter of another of them, read li-yahaba (‘that He may give’)?
o: Abū ʿAmr, and Warsh from Nāfiʿ
Ibn Kathīr, and Qālūn from Nāfiʿ
Ibn ʿĀmir, and Hishām from him
xqr-018.e: In this verse the angel says ‘to give you a pure boy’. The reading li-ahaba has the angel as the giver by God’s command, and li-yahaba puts the giving directly on God. Abū ʿAmr and Warsh, with Yaʿqūb, read li-yahaba; Qālūn from Nāfiʿ reads li-ahaba. The case shows that two transmitters of the same reader may differ.

xqr-019.src: Ibn Khālawayh, al-Ḥujja fī al-Qirāʾāt al-Sabʿ; Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Kashf ʿan Wujūh al-Qirāʾāt; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī
xqr-019.q: In 20:63 the highlighted word and the one before it have three readings among the Seven. Which statement is correct?
o: Abū ʿAmr reads inna hādhayni, Ibn Kathīr and Ḥafṣ read in hādhāni with a light in, and the others read inna hādhāni
All the Seven read inna hādhāni
Abū ʿAmr reads in hādhāni and Ibn Kathīr inna hādhayni
Ḥafṣ reads inna hādhayni and the others in hādhāni
xqr-019.e: The text has a dual with alif where the particle inna would require the oblique ending. Abū ʿAmr reads the oblique form hādhayni to fit the grammar; Ibn Kathīr (who also doubles the nūn of the dual) and Ḥafṣ read the light in with the lām of the predicate separating it from the negation; the rest keep inna and explain the alif by the dialect that uses alif for all cases (Balḥārith ibn Kaʿb), or by a pronoun of the situation. It is a famous problem in the books of grammar.

xqr-020.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted name with tanwīn (sabaʾin). Which two of the Seven read it without tanwīn, as a name that does not take it (sabaʾa)?
xqr-020.e: Ibn Kathīr and Abū ʿAmr read sabaʾa with fatḥa and no tanwīn, taking it as the name of a city or a tribe that is a diptote; the others read it as a declinable name with tanwīn. The two forms agree on the reference to the people of Saba in Yemen, whom the hoopoe mentions.

xqr-021.src: al-Dānī, al-Taysīr; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh sūrat al-Wāqiʿa
xqr-021.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word as a plural (mawāqiʿ). Which of the Seven read it as a singular (mawqiʿ)?
xqr-021.e: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī (with Khalaf) read the singular mawqiʿ, a verbal noun that covers the places or the setting of the stars; the others read the plural mawāqiʿ, the places where the stars set or the portions in which the Quran came down. Commentators mention both meanings for this oath.

xqr-022.src: Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Kashf ʿan Wujūh al-Qirāʾāt; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xqr-022.q: Ḥafṣ reads the highlighted word with ḍād (biḍanīn, ‘miserly’). Some of the Seven read it with ẓāʾ (bi-ẓanīn). Who are they, and what does the reading mean?
o: Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī; ‘suspected’ (of withholding the unseen)
xqr-022.e: Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī read bi-ẓanīn with the meaning ‘suspected or accused’; the Prophet is not accused regarding the unseen. The others read biḍanīn, ‘stingy’, so he does not withhold what was revealed to him. The two readings are compatible and are both attested defences of the Prophet.

xqr-023.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction; Ibn al-Jazarī, Ṭayyibat al-Nashr
xqr-023.q: Which three conditions did Ibn al-Jazarī lay down for a reading to be accepted?
o: Agreement with Arabic grammar in some way, agreement with one of the Uthmānic copies, and a sound chain of transmission
Agreement with the dialect of Quraysh, with the first copy and with the majority of readers
A chain of ten transmitters, agreement with Arabic poetry, and acceptance by a ruler
Agreement with the rules of tajwīd, a famous reader, and written authorisation (ijāza)
xqr-023.e: In his poem he states that every reading that agrees with Arabic in any way, agrees with one of the copies, even by probability, and has a sound chain is a true reading. If one of the three is missing, the reading is shādhdh, weak or invalid. The conditions were set in contrast to those who demanded tawātur only.

xqr-024.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on the types of readings
xqr-024.q: Ibn al-Jazarī in al-Nashr discussed the view that tawātur is a condition for a reading. Which is his position?
o: He considered the sound chain, agreement with the muṣḥaf and with Arabic enough, and argued that requiring tawātur would exclude readings accepted by the whole community
He required a tawātur of at least ten transmitters at every level
He rejected all readings that are not tawātur, including some of the Ten
He held that chains do not matter if the reading is eloquent
xqr-024.e: He remarked that the community had accepted readings whose chains were sound without being of the kind of tawātur some demanded, and that insisting on it would drop well-known readings. At the same time, he treated the Ten as being mutawātir. The topic remains one of the major debates of the Quranic sciences.

xqr-025.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction; Ibn al-Jazarī, Munjid al-Muqriʾīn
xqr-025.q: In the terminology of the qurrāʾ, what is the difference between qirāʾa, riwāya, ṭarīq and wajh?
o: Qirāʾa is attributed to the imam, riwāya to his transmitter, ṭarīq to those who transmit from the transmitter, and wajh is an option within a way
Qirāʾa is a single word, riwāya a verse, ṭarīq a chapter and wajh a juz’
Qirāʾa is an oral reading, riwāya a written one, ṭarīq a reading aloud and wajh a silent one
xqr-025.e: Ibn al-Jazarī and later scholars say that what is attributed to an imam is his qirāʾa, what is attributed to a transmitter from the imam is a riwāya, what is attributed to a person after them is a ṭarīq, and the options of the reader inside a way are awjuh. For example, Ḥafṣ is a riwāya of ʿĀṣim’s qirāʾa.

xqr-026.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on the readers
xqr-026.q: Which four readers are usually listed as the ‘four after the ten’, whose readings are treated as shādhdh?
o: Ibn Muḥayṣin, al-Yazīdī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and al-Aʿmash
Ibn Mujāhid, Ibn Shannabūdh, al-Dānī and al-Shāṭibī
Abū Jaʿfar, Yaʿqūb, Khalaf and al-Kisāʾī
xqr-026.e: The four are Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Muḥayṣin, Yaḥyā ibn al-Mubārak al-Yazīdī, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Sulaymān al-Aʿmash. Their readings are not recited in prayers but are collected for linguistic and exegetical use. The others in the options are transmitters, scholars, or members of the Ten.

xqr-027.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya fī Ṭabaqāt al-Qurrāʾ; al-Dhahabī, Maʿrifat al-Qurrāʾ al-Kibār
xqr-027.q: Khalaf ibn Hishām al-Bazzār (d. 229 AH) is counted among the Ten. What is distinctive about his status?
o: He is both a transmitter of Ḥamza and an independent imam with his own choice, as the tenth reader
He is only the transmitter of Nāfiʿ
He is the teacher of Ibn Mujāhid
He is a transmitter of ʿĀṣim
xqr-027.e: Khalaf transmitted the reading of Ḥamza, and also made his own selection (ikhtiyār), which differs from Ḥamza in a limited number of places; this selection is called Khalaf al-ʿĀshir, the tenth. Care must be taken to distinguish the two Khalafs, since one (Khalaf ʿan Ḥamza) is a riwāya and the other a separate qirāʾa.

xqr-028.src: al-Dhahabī, Maʿrifat al-Qurrāʾ al-Kibār, on ʿĀṣim; Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya
xqr-028.q: Through whom did the two transmitters of ʿĀṣim receive his reading, according to the standard account of the chains?
o: Ḥafṣ is traced through Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī to ʿAlī, and Shuʿba through Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh to Ibn Masʿūd
Ḥafṣ through Zirr to Ibn Masʿūd and Shuʿba through al-Sulamī to ʿAlī
Both through Ibn ʿAbbās to the Prophet directly
xqr-028.e: ʿĀṣim ibn Abī al-Najūd studied with two teachers: Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī, who read to ʿAlī (and ʿUthmān), and Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh, who read to Ibn Masʿūd. Ḥafṣ is said to have reported mostly the line of al-Sulamī and ʿAlī, while Shuʿba reported the line of Zirr and Ibn Masʿūd. All lines go back to the Prophet.

xqr-029.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya fī Ṭabaqāt al-Qurrāʾ; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xqr-029.q: Which pair are the two classical transmitters of Nāfiʿ, whose riwāyas are used mostly in North and West Africa?
xqr-029.e: Qālūn (ʿĪsā ibn Mīnā) and Warsh (ʿUthmān ibn Saʿīd) transmitted Nāfiʿ’s reading of Madīna, and Warsh’s riwāya is widespread in the Maghrib, Sudan and West Africa. Al-Bazzī and Qunbul transmitted Ibn Kathīr, Hishām and Ibn Dhakwān Ibn ʿĀmir, and al-Dūrī and al-Sūsī Abū ʿAmr.

xqr-030.src: Ibn Mujāhid, Kitāb al-Sabʿa fī al-Qirāʾāt; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, introduction
xqr-030.q: Which statement correctly describes Ibn Mujāhid’s Kitāb al-Sabʿa and its reception?
o: He chose seven imams of the main cities, and the selection later led some people to confuse the seven readings with the seven aḥruf, which scholars such as Ibn al-Jazarī corrected
He wrote it to prove that the Quran has exactly seven aḥruf in the form of the seven readers
He chose ten readers and excluded the Basrans
He wrote it after the work of al-Shāṭibī
xqr-030.e: Ibn Mujāhid (d. 324 AH) selected seven well-known imams of the major cities in his Kitāb al-Sabʿa. Because the number was the same as that of the aḥruf in the hadith, some thought they were the same.
