Scholars point out that the aḥruf are not the readers: other competent readers existed, and later scholars added three more to the seven.

xqr-031.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī wa-Wajh al-Tahānī; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-Sabʿ
xqr-031.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between al-Shāṭibiyya and al-Taysīr?
o: The Shāṭibiyya (Ḥirz al-Amānī) is a poem that versifies al-Dānī’s al-Taysīr, with additions, on the Seven readings
The Shāṭibiyya is a prose commentary on the Muqniʿ of al-Dānī
The two works treat different readings, the Seven and the Ten
xqr-031.e: Al-Shāṭibī (d. 590 AH) condensed al-Dānī’s al-Taysīr into a poem of about 1,170 verses, using letter codes for the readers. It became the main text for studying the Seven, while the Ten are covered by Ibn al-Jazarī’s al-Nashr and the poems al-Durra and al-Ṭayyiba.

xqr-032.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Durra al-Muḍiyya; Ibn al-Jazarī, Ṭayyibat al-Nashr
xqr-032.q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship of Ibn al-Jazarī’s works to the Shāṭibiyya?
o: Al-Durra al-Muḍiyya completes the Seven of the Shāṭibiyya with the three readings of Abū Jaʿfar, Yaʿqūb and Khalaf, and Ṭayyibat al-Nashr versifies al-Nashr for all ten
Al-Durra replaces the Shāṭibiyya for the Seven, and al-Ṭayyiba contains only the Seven
Both works treat only shādhdh readings
Al-Nashr is a poem and al-Ṭayyiba a prose work
xqr-032.e: Ibn al-Jazarī (d. 833 AH) wrote al-Durra al-Muḍiyya fī al-Qirāʾāt al-Thalātha al-Marḍiyya as a supplement to the Shāṭibiyya, adding Abū Jaʿfar, Yaʿqūb and Khalaf. Ṭayyibat al-Nashr is a poem of about 1,014 verses that versifies al-Nashr for the ten readings, and al-Nashr itself is the large prose work.

xqr-033.src: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, al-Ḥujja li-l-Qurrāʾ al-Sabʿa; Ibn Khālawayh, al-Ḥujja fī al-Qirāʾāt al-Sabʿ
xqr-033.q: Which work by Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī is a major classical book of tawjīh, explaining the grammatical grounds of the Seven’s readings?
xqr-033.e: Al-Ḥujja li-l-Qurrāʾ al-Sabʿa by Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī (d. 377 AH) argues for the readings of the Seven by grammar and usage. Ibn Khālawayh wrote a work with a similar title; Makkī’s al-Kashf is another standard source. Al-Nashr is a collection of chains, al-Taysīr a transmission manual, and al-Muqniʿ a book on the rasm.

xqr-034.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on the seven aḥruf; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān; Abū Shāma, al-Murshid al-Wajīz
xqr-034.q: Which statement correctly states the relation between the seven aḥruf of the hadith and the Seven readings?
o: Scholars distinguish them: the seven aḥruf are the permitted aspects of difference in the revelation, whereas the Seven are a later selection by Ibn Mujāhid
They are identical and each reader corresponds to one ḥarf
The Seven are the seven aḥruf recited by seven Companions
There is no relation, because the aḥruf were abolished by the Prophet
xqr-034.e: Ibn al-Jazarī and many others, including Abū Shāma, warn against equating the two, because the number of the aḥruf in the hadith is older than the selection of Ibn Mujāhid and the Seven readings do not correspond to the aḥruf one by one. The ʿUthmānic copies kept what was established in the final recitation, which the readings reflect.

xqr-035.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. 22 on the types of readings
xqr-035.q: Which six categories of readings does al-Suyūṭī list in al-Itqān, in order from the strongest to the weakest?
o: Mutawātir, mashhūr, āḥād, shādhdh, mawḍūʿ and mudraj
Ṣaḥīḥ, ḥasan, ḍaʿīf, munkar, mawḍūʿ and mudraj
Mutawātir, ṣaḥīḥ, ḥasan, marfūʿ, mawqūf and maqṭūʿ
Mashhūr, ṣaḥīḥ, ḥasan, ḍaʿīf, mursal and mudallas
xqr-035.e: Al-Suyūṭī, following Ibn al-Jazarī’s and earlier analysis, divides the readings into six: mutawātir (the Ten), mashhūr, āḥād (sound chain but contrary to the rasm or Arabic), shādhdh, mawḍūʿ (fabricated) and mudraj (explanatory additions inserted). The terms are borrowed from hadith but adapted to readings.

xqr-036.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, on the riwāyas in use; Mannāʿ al-Qaṭṭān, Mabāḥith fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān
xqr-036.q: Which statement fairly explains why the riwāya of Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim is today the most widespread in the Muslim world?
o: Historical reasons, such as its adoption in the lands of the Ottoman state and in printed muṣḥafs, rather than any scholarly ranking of readings above others
It is the only reading that is mutawātir
The Prophet preferred it to all others
It was the only reading authorised by the Uthmānic copies
xqr-036.e: The wide use of Ḥafṣ is explained historically: it was the reading favoured in the Ottoman and later Eastern world and became standard in printing. Scholars do not rank it above the other mutawātir readings, all of which are valid. Today other riwāyas, such as Warsh and Qālūn, continue in North and West Africa.

xqr-037.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on the benefits of the differences in readings; al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān
xqr-037.q: How do the classical scholars of qirāʾāt, such as Ibn al-Jazarī, describe the nature of the differences between the accepted readings?
o: As a difference of variety and diversity (ikhtilāf tanawwuʿ), not of contradiction, where each reading adds a meaning or a facility
As a difference of contradiction in which only one reading can be true
As a difference only in pronunciation that never touches meaning
As a difference that the community resolved by abolishing all but one
xqr-037.e: Ibn al-Jazarī and others stress that the accepted differences are not contradictory: each reading either adds a meaning (as in the verse of the feet) or gives a facility to the nations’ dialects, and the readings together are like different verses. This is why jurists and commentators may use one reading to explain another.

xqr-038.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, bāb al-sakt ʿalā al-sākin qabl al-hamz; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xqr-038.q: Which reader of the Seven is known for making a sakta on the sākin letter before a hamza (for example on the lām of the article before a hamza)?
xqr-038.e: Ḥamza makes a sakta in continuation on a sākin letter before a hamza, a famous feature of his reading, as on the lām of the article before a hamza in the same word and in separate words, and on a few words such as ‘shayʾ’. Ḥafṣ makes a sakta only in four places. Warsh has a similar feature in a different form.

xqr-039.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, bāb al-fatḥ wa-l-imāla; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-imāla
xqr-039.q: Which of the Seven are best known for a wide use of imāla (inclining the fatḥa and alif toward kasra and yāʾ)?
xqr-039.e: Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī (and Khalaf) make imāla in many words, in a rule-based way, while Abū ʿAmr and others do so in selected words and Ibn Kathīr does not. Ḥafṣ makes only one imāla in the whole Quran (11:41).

xqr-040.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, Ghāyat al-Nihāya fī Ṭabaqāt al-Qurrāʾ; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Durra al-Muḍiyya
xqr-040.q: Which transmitters are associated with the two readers Abū Jaʿfar and Yaʿqūb, respectively?
o: Abū Jaʿfar: Ibn Wardān and Ibn Jammāz; Yaʿqūb: Ruways and Rawḥ
Abū Jaʿfar: Qālūn and Warsh; Yaʿqūb: Hishām and Ibn Dhakwān
Abū Jaʿfar: Shuʿba and Ḥafṣ; Yaʿqūb: al-Bazzī and Qunbul
Abū Jaʿfar: al-Dūrī and al-Sūsī; Yaʿqūb: Khalaf and Khallād
xqr-040.e: Abū Jaʿfar of Madīna is transmitted by ʿĪsā ibn Wardān and Sulaymān ibn Jammāz, and Yaʿqūb al-Ḥaḍramī of Baṣra by Ruways and Rawḥ. The other pairs belong to Nāfiʿ, Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and Ḥamza. These three readers complete the Seven to make the Ten in al-Durra.

xsr-001.src: Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra al-Nabawiyya; Ibn Isḥāq as cited by al-Ṭabarī, Taʾrīkh; al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ
xsr-001.q: How has Ibn Isḥāq’s Sīra reached us, and how did scholars regard him?
o: Through the recension of Ibn Hishām, who edited it from the transmission of Ziyād al-Bakkāʾī; scholars praised him in maghāzī but some, like Mālik, criticised him, and hadith critics were more cautious about his lone reports on legal matters
Through a manuscript he wrote himself in the Prophet’s lifetime
It has not survived at all in any form
xsr-001.e: Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq (d. c. 150 AH) wrote the earliest comprehensive biography. His book survives in the edited recension of Ibn Hishām (d. c. 218 AH), who omitted and added material, and in quotations, notably in al-Ṭabarī. Al-Zuhrī praised his knowledge of the maghāzī, and some hadith critics accepted him in that field but were cautious in rulings and criticised his tadlīs; Mālik is reported to have been harsh on him.

xsr-002.src: al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ; Ibn Ḥajar, Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb; al-Bayhaqī, Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa
xsr-002.q: Whose Maghāzī was considered by some early scholars to be the most reliable work on the campaigns, and who transmitted from him?
o: Mūsā ibn ʿUqba (d. 141 AH), a student of al-Zuhrī, whose work survives only in fragments and quotations
Ibn al-Jawzī, in the 6th century AH
Al-Wāqidī, whose work was praised by all hadith critics
Ibn Kathīr, in the 8th century AH
xsr-002.e: Mūsā ibn ʿUqba, a freedman of the family of al-Zubayr and a student of al-Zuhrī, wrote a Maghāzī that Mālik is reported to have recommended as the most reliable. Only fragments and quotations survive (for example in al-Bayhaqī’s Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa). It contrasts with al-Wāqidī’s large Maghāzī, which is rich in detail but criticised as a source by hadith critics.

xsr-003.src: Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā; al-Wāqidī, al-Maghāzī; al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ
xsr-003.q: What is the relation of al-Wāqidī to Ibn Saʿd, and how is each regarded?
o: Ibn Saʿd (d. 230 AH) was his scribe (kātib al-Wāqidī) and drew heavily on his material in al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā; Ibn Saʿd is regarded as trustworthy and al-Wāqidī as a weak narrator though valued for historical detail
Ibn Saʿd was his teacher and rejected his work
Ibn Saʿd lived in the Prophet’s time
xsr-003.e: Ibn Saʿd was called ‘scribe of al-Wāqidī’ because he took heavily from him, and from other sources, in his Ṭabaqāt, an early biographical work on the Prophet, Companions and Successors. Hadith scholars considered al-Wāqidī weak as a narrator of hadith (some called him matrūk), though historians continue to use his detail on campaigns with caution. Ibn Saʿd himself is generally considered trustworthy.

xsr-004.src: Ibn Isḥāq as in Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; al-Ṭabarī, Taʾrīkh; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya
xsr-004.q: How do the classical sources relate the Prophet’s birth to the Year of the Elephant, and what differences are noted?
o: Most placed his birth in the Year of the Elephant, in the month of Rabīʿ al-Awwal, with differing opinions on the day (the second, eighth, tenth or twelfth being cited); the twelfth is most widespread in popular practice
Most placed it ten years before the Year of the Elephant, in Ramadan
All agreed on one specific day with no differences
Most placed it after the Hijra
xsr-004.e: Most scholars followed Ibn Isḥāq in saying he ﷺ was born in the Year of the Elephant, in Rabīʿ al-Awwal. As for the day, the sources record the second, eighth, tenth and twelfth, and the twelfth is the best-known in practice. Some scholars (such as the astronomer Maḥmūd Pasha al-Falakī in modern times) computed a ninth date, but the classical sources do not agree.

xsr-005.src: Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra al-Nabawiyya; Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā; Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-īmān (shaqq al-ṣadr)
xsr-005.q: Who nursed the Prophet ﷺ in his infancy, and which event is reported from his time with her tribe?
o: Ḥalīma al-Saʿdiyya of Banū Saʿd; the splitting of his chest (shaqq al-ṣadr) is reported in a sound report in Muslim
Umm Ayman, in Madīna; the opening of Makka
Khadīja, in Makka; the first revelation
xsr-005.e: In Arab custom children were sent to the desert tribes. The Prophet ﷺ was nursed by Ḥalīma bint Abī Dhuʾayb of Banū Saʿd ibn Bakr, and stayed with her until about the age of four or five. A report in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim from Anas describes how Jibrīl opened his chest and washed his heart, an event placed in this period by the sources, although some authors differ over the time.

xsr-006.src: Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra al-Nabawiyya; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya; al-Suhaylī, al-Rawḍ al-Unuf
xsr-006.q: What was the Ḥilf al-Fuḍūl, and what is reported of the Prophet’s attitude to it after prophecy?
o: A pact of Makkan clans to support the wronged in Makka, which the Prophet ﷺ attended in his youth and later said he would respond to if called to it in Islam
A treaty with the Byzantines to protect trade
A pact among poets for contests at ʿUkāẓ
A treaty with Madīna signed after the Hijra
xsr-006.e: The Ḥilf al-Fuḍūl was a covenant among some Makkan clans in the house of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judʿān to give justice to the wronged, whoever they were. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said he witnessed it in the house of Ibn Judʿān and would not exchange it for red camels, and that if invited to it in Islam he would respond. The report is cited in Ibn Hishām and in other works, with discussion about its chain.

xsr-007.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Bad’ al-waḥy; Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-īmān; Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī
xsr-007.q: Which report is the main source on the beginning of revelation, and what is debated about the period after it (fatrat al-waḥy)?
o: The report of ʿĀʾisha in al-Bukhārī and Muslim (the true dreams, Ḥirāʾ, and Waraqa); the length of the pause is disputed, and its wording in the account of Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh is the basis for the descent of the verses of al-Muddaththir
The report of Abū Hurayra on the day of Badr
The report of Anas on the Night Journey
The report of Ibn ʿAbbās on the farewell sermon
xsr-007.e: ʿĀʾisha’s long report in the first chapter of al-Bukhārī gives the true dream, seclusion in Ḥirāʾ, the first descent of Jibrīl and the visit to Waraqa ibn Nawfal. The pause of revelation that followed is reported in the account of Jābir, who relates the descent of the verses of al-Muddaththir after it. The length of the pause is differently reported, the figures of two and a half years or three years in some reports being weak or disputed.

xsr-008.src: Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt; al-Ṭabarī, Taʾrīkh; al-Tirmidhī, Jāmiʿ (on first Muslims)
xsr-008.q: How do classical sources describe the first people to accept Islam, and what is debated?
o: Khadīja among women, Abū Bakr among free adult men, ʿAlī among children and Zayd ibn Ḥāritha among freedmen are commonly named; scholars reconciled the claims by dividing them into categories
Only ʿUmar and ʿUthmān are named
All sources agree that Abū Lahab was first
No source mentions the first Muslims
xsr-008.e: There are reports that ‘the first to believe’ was Khadīja, Abū Bakr, ʿAlī or Zayd. Scholars such as Ibn Isḥāq and al-Ṭabarī reconcile them: Khadīja was the first of all, Abū Bakr the first free man, ʿAlī the first child and Zayd the first freedman. Others included Bilāl and ʿAmmār. This approach is common in Ibn Kathīr’s treatment.

xsr-009.src: Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; Aḥmad, Musnad (account of Umm Salama); Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya
xsr-009.q: Which report preserves the account of the first Hijra to Abyssinia, including the speech of Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib to the Negus?
o: The report of Umm Salama in Musnad Aḥmad and in Ibn Isḥāq, in which Jaʿfar explains Islam and recites from the sūra of Maryam
The report of Abū Hurayra in Muslim on the Night Journey
The report of ʿUmar on the treaty of Ḥudaybiya
The report of Anas on the Battle of Uḥud
xsr-009.e: Umm Salama, who was among the emigrants, narrated how Quraysh sent ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Rabīʿa to the Negus to ask for the return of the Muslims, and how Jaʿfar answered by describing the Jāhiliyya and the message of the Prophet ﷺ and by reciting the beginning of sūrat Maryam. The account is in Aḥmad’s Musnad and in Ibn Isḥāq, with a chain regarded as good.

xsr-010.src: Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-manāqib (mention of al-Muḥaṣṣab)
xsr-010.q: What was the boycott of the Prophet’s clan in Shiʿb Abī Ṭālib, and how did the sources say it ended?
o: Quraysh wrote a document boycotting Banū Hāshim and Banū al-Muṭṭalib; the sources say it lasted about two to three years and ended when some Makkans, including Hishām ibn ʿAmr and Zuhayr ibn Abī Umayya, worked to cancel it
Quraysh banned the Muslims from fasting; it ended with the Hijra
The Romans blocked the road; it ended with Mu’ta
Madīna closed its markets; it ended at Badr
xsr-010.e: Quraysh wrote a pact against Banū Hāshim and Banū al-Muṭṭalib to prevent marriage and trade with them until they handed over the Prophet ﷺ, and hung it in the Kaʿba. The clans stayed in the glen of Abū Ṭālib. The sources give the duration as two or three years, and tell that some Makkans, such as Hishām ibn ʿAmr and Zuhayr, led an effort to annul it, and that the pact was found eaten by termites except the Name of God.

xsr-011.src: Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ (ʿĀʾisha on al-Ṭāʾif, Bad’ al-khalq); Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt
xsr-011.q: What do the sources say about the Prophet’s journey to al-Ṭāʾif?
o: He went after Abū Ṭālib’s and Khadīja’s deaths to seek support from Thaqīf, was rejected and mistreated; ʿĀʾisha’s report in al-Bukhārī mentions the angel of the mountains who offered to crush Makka’s two mountains and the Prophet’s refusal
He went to al-Ṭāʾif to marry and was welcomed
He went to buy horses and returned in a week
He went for ḥajj with the Companions after the conquest
xsr-011.e: After the deaths of Khadīja and Abū Ṭālib, the Prophet ﷺ went to al-Ṭāʾif to invite Thaqīf, but their leaders rejected him and urged their slaves and children to throw stones. Al-Bukhārī and Muslim record ʿĀʾisha’s question about the hardest day since Uḥud, with his reply about the trip and the offer of the angel of the mountains to crush the two mountains (al-Akhshabayn), which he declined, hoping for believers from their descendants.

xsr-012.src: Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī (Kitāb manāqib al-anṣār, bāb al-miʿrāj); Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on sūrat al-Isrāʾ; al-Bukhārī and Muslim (Anas, Mālik ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa)
xsr-012.q: What are the classical differences over the Isrāʾ and Miʿrāj regarding time and manner?
o: Reports differ on the date (before the Hijra by one year, or three or five years, in various months) and some scholars said it was one night while others split it into separate events; most Sunni scholars hold it was in body and soul, while a report from ʿĀʾisha and Muʿāwiya is cited for spirit only
All reports agree on the same date and manner
All reports say it happened in Madīna
All reports place it after Badr
xsr-012.e: Ibn Ḥajar discusses the date, citing views from before the Hijra by one year, by eighteen months, by three or five years and others, and different months. Most hold the Isrāʾ and Miʿrāj was in one night and in body and soul, while a report attributed to ʿĀʾisha and Muʿāwiya says it was spiritual; the first is the dominant Sunni view, as Ibn Kathīr states.

xsr-013.src: Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; Aḥmad, Musnad (Jābir on ʿAqaba); al-Ṭabarī, Taʾrīkh
xsr-013.q: How do the sources describe the two pledges of al-ʿAqaba?
o: The first in the year 12 of prophecy with twelve men and the second in the year 13 with about seventy-three men and two women, who pledged to protect him as they protected their families
Both took place in Madīna in the year 2 AH
The first with Quraysh and the second with Thaqīf
xsr-013.e: Ibn Isḥāq places the first pledge (with twelve men from Aws and Khazraj) in the twelfth year of prophecy and the second, in which seventy-three men and two women pledged to protect the Prophet ﷺ, in the thirteenth. Muṣʿab ibn ʿUmayr was sent to teach them. The details are in Ibn Hishām and in Aḥmad’s Musnad from Jābir, who was present.

xsr-014.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb manāqib al-anṣār (ʿĀʾisha on the Hijra); Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; Aḥmad, Musnad
xsr-014.q: According to ʿĀʾisha’s long report in al-Bukhārī, how did the Prophet ﷺ and Abū Bakr leave Makka?
o: They left at night from the back of Abū Bakr’s house, hid for three nights in the cave of Thawr, and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Urayqiṭ guided them by the coastal route
They left openly by day with an armed escort
They left by ship from Jidda
They left with the caravan of Quraysh to Syria
xsr-014.e: ʿĀʾisha narrated how the Prophet ﷺ came to Abū Bakr’s house at midday, they left through a back window by night, hid in Thawr, with ʿAbd Allāh ibn Abī Bakr bringing news, ʿĀmir ibn Fuhayra the food and ʿAbd Allāh ibn Urayqiṭ (a non-Muslim guide, then still a polytheist) leading them along the coast. Surāqa ibn Mālik pursued them in the account.

xsr-015.src: Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra (the Ṣaḥīfa); Abū ʿUbayd, al-Amwāl; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya; Ibn Isḥāq
xsr-015.q: What is the 'Ṣaḥīfa of Madīna' (often called its constitution), and how is it known?
o: A document of the early Madīnan period that regulated relations between the Emigrants, Anṣār and Jewish tribes, preserved in the Sīra of Ibn Isḥāq/Ibn Hishām and in Abū ʿUbayd’s al-Amwāl
A poem by Ḥassān ibn Thābit
A fatwā of the caliph ʿUmar
xsr-015.e: The Ṣaḥīfa is a document attributed to the early period in Madīna that defines the Emigrants, the Anṣār and the Jews of Madīna as an ummah in terms of mutual defence and responsibilities. It is transmitted in Ibn Isḥāq (in Ibn Hishām) without a full chain and in Abū ʿUbayd’s al-Amwāl with a chain. Modern scholars dispute its dating and whether it was one or several documents.

xsr-016.src: Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-maghāzī (numbers of Badr); Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt
xsr-016.q: What do the early sources report as the number of Muslims and of the Quraysh army at Badr?
o: About 313 Muslims (a number in al-Bukhārī, from al-Barā’) against about 950 to 1,000 Quraysh, with few horses on the Muslim side
xsr-016.e: Al-Bukhārī records from al-Barā’ ibn ʿĀzib that the Companions of Badr numbered a little over three hundred, the number of Ṭālūt’s men. The Quraysh army is reported at about nine hundred and fifty to a thousand. The Muslims had only two or three horses and about seventy camels. Details such as the number of martyrs (fourteen) and of the Quraysh dead (about seventy) are in Ibn Hishām.

xsr-017.src: Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-jihād (ʿUmar’s report on the prisoners of Badr); Aḥmad, Musnad; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on sūrat al-Anfāl
xsr-017.q: What is reported about the dispute over the prisoners of Badr and its link to revelation?
o: The Prophet ﷺ consulted Abū Bakr (who favoured ransom) and ʿUmar (who favoured executing them); ransom was taken, after which verses of sūrat al-Anfāl came down in a tone of reproach, as in ʿUmar’s report in Muslim
All Companions agreed to free them without ransom
All Companions agreed to execute them
The prisoners were sent to Abyssinia
xsr-017.e: ʿUmar’s long report in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Ibn ʿAbbās, relates that after Badr the Prophet ﷺ asked the opinion of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar about the prisoners. Abū Bakr preferred ransom for the sake of mercy and strength; ʿUmar preferred execution. The Prophet ﷺ took Abū Bakr’s view, and the following day the verses of al-Anfāl reproaching the taking of prisoners before dominance were revealed, as the report states.

xsr-018.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-maghāzī (Uḥud, al-Barā’); Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya
xsr-018.q: What does the account in al-Bukhārī say about the archers at Uḥud and the reversal of the battle?
o: The Prophet ﷺ stationed fifty archers on the hill under ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jubayr and told them not to leave; most left to collect spoils, and Khālid ibn al-Walīd struck from behind
The archers were on a ship
The archers left by the Prophet’s order
xsr-018.e: In the report of al-Barā’ ibn ʿĀzib in al-Bukhārī, the Prophet ﷺ placed archers on the hill, ordered them to stay, even if the Muslims were seen taking the lead or being defeated. When the Quraysh broke, most archers left their position to seek the spoils despite their commander’s warning, and Khālid ibn al-Walīd (then a Qurashī) attacked from the rear. Seventy Muslims were killed.

xsr-019.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-maghāzī (al-Khandaq, Banū Qurayẓa); Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī
xsr-019.q: What do the early sources say about the Battle of the Trench and the later affair of Banū Qurayẓa?
o: The Muslims dug a trench, following Salmān’s suggestion in the sources; after the Confederates withdrew, the Prophet ﷺ besieged Banū Qurayẓa for breaking the pact, and Saʿd ibn Muʿādh gave the judgement accepted by the Prophet ﷺ
The trench was dug by the Persians; Banū Qurayẓa were never mentioned
The Muslims fought in open ground without any trench
Banū Qurayẓa were allies who joined the Muslims
xsr-019.e: The sources say the Muslims dug a trench around the north of Madīna on the advice of Salmān al-Fārisī, and the Confederates were turned back by siege, wind and dissension. Banū Qurayẓa had been accused of breaking their pact; after a siege they submitted to the judgement of Saʿd ibn Muʿādh, who ruled according to their own law, as in the reports in al-Bukhārī and Muslim. The affair is discussed by later scholars for its details.

xsr-020.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-shurūṭ and Kitāb al-maghāzī; Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-jihād; Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra
xsr-020.q: Which terms of the Treaty of Ḥudaybiya are named in the sound reports?
o: Ten years of truce, the Muslims to return that year and come for ʿumra the next, return of those who came from Quraysh without permission but not of those who left Muslims, and freedom for tribes to join either side
Payment of tribute by Quraysh, and the Muslims to remain in Makka
A union of the two states under one ruler
xsr-020.e: The reports in al-Bukhārī and Muslim give the terms: a ten-year peace (or two years in some reports), that the Muslims would return without ʿumra that year and come the next, that Quraysh members who came to the Prophet ﷺ without permission would be returned, while those leaving the Muslims would not be returned, and that tribes might ally with either side. Several Companions found the terms hard until the revelation of sūrat al-Fatḥ.

xsr-021.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Bad’ al-waḥy (Heraclius and Abū Sufyān); Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-jihād; Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt; Muḥammad Ḥamīdullāh, Majmūʿat al-Wathāʾiq al-Siyāsiyya
xsr-021.q: What is the best-attested exchange of the Prophet’s letters to rulers in the sound sources?
o: The letter to Heraclius, carried by Diḥya al-Kalbī, and the questions Heraclius put to Abū Sufyān, reported in al-Bukhārī from Ibn ʿAbbās
The letter to the Chinese emperor, reported in Muslim
The letter to the Pope, reported in Abū Dāwūd
The letter to the king of India, reported in al-Tirmidhī
xsr-021.e: Al-Bukhārī opens his book with the account of Heraclius, who summoned Abū Sufyān and asked about the Prophet’s lineage, followers and conduct after receiving the Prophet’s letter, carried by Diḥya al-Kalbī. Letters to the Negus, Khosrow and the Muqawqis are also reported in the sources, although the texts of some come with differing chains and the authenticity of certain versions is debated among historians.

xsr-022.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-maghāzī (fatḥ Makka); Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ; Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra
xsr-022.q: What do the sound reports record about the entry into Makka in 8 AH?
o: The Prophet ﷺ entered with a large army without major fighting, proclaimed security for those who stayed in their houses, in the Kaʿba or in the house of Abū Sufyān, and cleansed the Kaʿba of idols
He entered alone at night and left the same day
He destroyed Makka and took its people as captives
xsr-022.e: The reports (al-Bukhārī, Muslim) tell that after Quraysh’s breach of the Ḥudaybiya terms, the Prophet ﷺ marched in the month of Ramadan with about ten thousand men. Abū Sufyān embraced Islam before the entry, and there was security for those in his house. The Prophet ﷺ entered the sanctuary, circled the Kaʿba and had the idols removed. A few individuals were excepted from the amnesty according to the sources.

xsr-023.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-maghāzī (Ḥunayn, al-Barā’); Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ; Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra
xsr-023.q: What do the sound reports record about the Battle of Ḥunayn and the distribution that followed?
o: The Muslims at first fell back under the ambush of Hawāzin, then rallied around the Prophet ﷺ; afterwards he gave generously to recent converts (al-muʾallafa qulūbuhum), which led to complaints among some Anṣār
The Muslims won without any difficulty
The Muslims were defeated and returned to Madīna
xsr-023.e: In al-Barā’’s report in al-Bukhārī, the Muslims were surprised by Hawāzin’s archers in the valley and many scattered, while the Prophet ﷺ held his ground and called to be rallied. After the victory, spoils were distributed with large shares to new Muslims from Quraysh and others, and some of the Anṣār voiced displeasure, to which the Prophet ﷺ replied with an address (reported in the Ṣaḥīḥayn) reminding them that they returned with the Messenger of God.

xsr-024.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-maghāzī (Kaʿb ibn Mālik’s account); Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-tawba; Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra
xsr-024.q: Which sound report relates the expedition to Tabūk and the three Companions who stayed behind?
o: The long first-person account of Kaʿb ibn Mālik in al-Bukhārī and Muslim, about the boycott of him, Hilāl ibn Umayya and Murāra ibn al-Rabīʿ and their forgiveness
The account of Abū Hurayra on the conquest of Egypt
The account of ʿĀʾisha on the Battle of the Camel
The account of Anas on the Battle of Yarmūk
xsr-024.e: Kaʿb ibn Mālik himself told how he stayed behind from the Tabūk expedition (9 AH) without excuse, was boycotted for fifty days with two others, and was finally forgiven by a verse of sūrat al-Tawba. The account is one of the longest in al-Bukhārī and Muslim and is widely used for lessons on truthfulness.

xsr-025.src: Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-ḥajj (Jābir’s long ḥadīth); al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ; Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra
xsr-025.q: What is the main source for the details of the Farewell Pilgrimage, and what disagreement exists about the manner of ihrām?
o: Jābir’s long ḥadīth in Muslim; scholars differ whether the Prophet ﷺ performed ifrād, qirān or tamattuʿ, with each position having supporters, and the Ḥanafīs favouring qirān
Anas’s ḥadīth on the Night Journey; all agree on tamattuʿ
ʿUmar’s ḥadīth on Ḥudaybiya; all agree on ifrād
The Quran alone; there is no hadith
xsr-025.e: Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh’s account in Muslim describes the ḥajj step by step, in the tenth year. The reports about what ihrām the Prophet ﷺ made differ: some say ifrād, some qirān, some tamattuʿ, and each school reconciled them in its own way. The Ḥanafīs held qirān to be the best, the Shāfiʿīs ifrād, and the Ḥanbalīs generally tamattuʿ.

xsr-026.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb faḍāʾil aṣḥāb al-nabī and Kitāb al-ḥudūd (ʿUmar’s khuṭba); Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; al-Ṭabarī, Taʾrīkh
xsr-026.q: What do the sound reports say about the aftermath of the Prophet’s death and the Saqīfa of Banū Sāʿida?
o: ʿUmar at first denied the death, Abū Bakr recited the verse that Muḥammad is only a messenger, and at the Saqīfa the Anṣār and Emigrants debated; ʿUmar pledged to Abū Bakr and others followed
The Anṣār chose ʿAlī immediately without debate
The Prophet ﷺ named his successor in a written will accepted by all
The matter was settled by Quraysh in Makka
xsr-026.e: In al-Bukhārī’s reports, ʿUmar refused to believe the Prophet ﷺ had died until Abū Bakr arrived, praised God, and recited the verse that Muḥammad is but a messenger. At the Saqīfa, the Anṣār gathered around Saʿd ibn ʿUbāda; Abū Bakr, ʿUmar and Abū ʿUbayda joined, and after discussion ʿUmar pledged to Abū Bakr, followed by others. ʿUmar’s later khuṭba described the pledge as a sudden event (falta) from which God protected the community.

xsr-027.src: Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya; al-Nawawī, Tahdhīb al-Asmāʾ wa-l-Lughāt
xsr-027.q: What is the order and the number of the Prophet’s wives who survived him or were married during his life, according to the common account?
o: Eleven wives are commonly counted in his life with Khadīja and Zaynab bint Khuzayma having died before him, and nine survived him; the first marriage was to Khadīja
He had a single wife throughout his life
He had twenty wives who all survived him
xsr-027.e: The common account is that his first wife was Khadīja, followed (after her death) by Sawda, ʿĀʾisha, Ḥafṣa, Zaynab bint Khuzayma (who died soon), Umm Salama, Zaynab bint Jaḥsh, Juwayriya, Umm Ḥabība, Ṣafiyya and Maymūna. Nine wives survived him. The accounts also mention Māriya al-Qibṭiyya, whose status is discussed as a concubine. The ‘Mothers of the Believers’ is the title given to the wives in sūrat al-Aḥzāb.

xsr-028.src: Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt al-Kubrā; Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ (death of Ibrāhīm and the eclipse)
xsr-028.q: What do the sources say about the Prophet’s children and the death of Ibrāhīm?
o: From Khadīja came al-Qāsim, Zaynab, Ruqayya, Umm Kulthūm, Fāṭima and ʿAbd Allāh; Ibrāhīm was born to Māriya and died in infancy, the day of an eclipse mentioned in a report, to which the Prophet ﷺ said that eclipses are not caused by anyone’s death
He had twelve sons who survived him
He had no children at all
xsr-028.e: The sources agree that all children except Ibrāhīm were from Khadīja; the sons died young, and all daughters except Fāṭima died during his life. Ibrāhīm, son of Māriya al-Qibṭiyya, died aged about a year and a half. Al-Bukhārī relates that a solar eclipse occurred on that day and people linked it to the death, and the Prophet ﷺ stated that the sun and moon are signs of God, and do not eclipse for anyone’s death or life.

xsr-029.src: al-Tirmidhī, Jāmiʿ, Kitāb al-manāqib (ḥadīth Saʿīd ibn Zayd); Abū Dāwūd, Sunan; Ibn Mājah, Sunan
xsr-029.q: Who are the ten promised Paradise (al-ʿashara al-mubashshara) according to the report transmitted in the Sunan?
o: Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, ʿUthmān, ʿAlī, Ṭalḥa, al-Zubayr, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, Saʿīd ibn Zayd and Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ
xsr-029.e: A report in Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah, from Saʿīd ibn Zayd, names the ten Companions given good news of Paradise by the Prophet ﷺ in one sitting. The report is judged ṣaḥīḥ by several scholars, though some scholars discussed variants of its chain. The promise to others is also found in separate reports, so the ten are not the only ones promised.

xsr-030.src: Abū Nuʿaym, Ḥilyat al-Awliyāʾ (Ahl al-Ṣuffa); Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt; Ibn Ḥajar, al-Iṣāba; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ (Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿa)
xsr-030.q: Who were the Ahl al-Ṣuffa, and what is the status of the people of Badr in the reports?
o: The poor Emigrants who lodged in a covered area of the Prophet’s mosque and relied on charity; the Prophet ﷺ said that God may have looked at the people of Badr and forgiven them, as in the report on Ḥāṭib ibn Abī Baltaʿa
A band of poets who recited in the mosque
A group of traders from Syria
xsr-030.e: Ahl al-Ṣuffa were poor Muslims with no home, including Abū Hurayra, who stayed near the Prophet ﷺ in a shaded part of the mosque. The people of Badr hold a special status in the Sunna: in al-Bukhārī’s report on Ḥāṭib, who had written to Quraysh, the Prophet ﷺ declined ʿUmar’s request to execute him by saying that he had been at Badr and God may have looked on the Badr fighters, saying to do what they wish, for they were forgiven.

xsr-031.src: al-Tirmidhī, al-Shamāʾil al-Muḥammadiyya; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ (Kitāb al-manāqib); Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ (Kitāb al-faḍāʾil); al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, al-Shifā bi-Taʿrīf Ḥuqūq al-Muṣṭafā
xsr-031.q: Which classical works are the principal collections on the Prophet’s description and character?
o: al-Tirmidhī’s al-Shamāʾil al-Muḥammadiyya and al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ’s al-Shifā bi-Taʿrīf Ḥuqūq al-Muṣṭafā
xsr-031.e: Al-Tirmidhī’s al-Shamāʾil collects hadith on the Prophet’s appearance, dress, food, walk and manners. Al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ’s al-Shifā (d. 544 AH) treats his rights and virtues and includes description. The other works named belong to uṣūl al-fiqh and Arabic grammar. Both principal works were extensively commented upon, for example the Shamāʾil by al-Bājūrī.

xsr-032.src: al-Bayhaqī, Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa; Abū Nuʿaym, Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa; al-Māwardī, Aʿlām al-Nubuwwa; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya
xsr-032.q: Which authors wrote the best-known works titled 'Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa' (Proofs of Prophethood)?
o: Abū Nuʿaym al-Iṣbahānī (d. 430 AH) and al-Bayhaqī (d. 458 AH), the latter being the most comprehensive and drawing on early maghāzī
xsr-032.e: Abū Nuʿaym’s Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa and al-Bayhaqī’s Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa wa-Maʿrifat Aḥwāl Ṣāḥib al-Sharīʿa collect reports of the Prophet’s signs along with chronology of his life. Al-Bayhaqī’s is the largest and includes chains and critical comments. Works with this title also exist by al-Firyābī, al-Ḥākim (not in print) and others. Al-Māwardī’s Aʿlām al-Nubuwwa takes a more theological approach.

xsr-033.src: Ibn Sayyid al-Nās, ʿUyūn al-Athar; Ibn Kathīr, al-Sīra al-Nabawiyya; al-Suhaylī, al-Rawḍ al-Unuf; Ibn al-Qayyim, Zād al-Maʿād
xsr-033.q: Which statement correctly matches later biographical works with their authors?
o: al-Suhaylī: al-Rawḍ al-Unuf (a commentary on Ibn Hishām); Ibn Sayyid al-Nās: ʿUyūn al-Athar; Ibn al-Qayyim: Zād al-Maʿād
al-Suhaylī: Zād al-Maʿād; Ibn Sayyid al-Nās: al-Rawḍ al-Unuf; Ibn al-Qayyim: ʿUyūn al-Athar
All three wrote the same book
None of them wrote on the sīra
xsr-033.e: Al-Suhaylī (d. 581 AH) wrote al-Rawḍ al-Unuf as a commentary on Ibn Hishām’s Sīra with linguistic, legal and historical notes. Ibn Sayyid al-Nās (d. 734 AH) wrote ʿUyūn al-Athar, a hadith-critical compilation of the sīra, and Ibn al-Qayyim (d. 751 AH) wrote Zād al-Maʿād fī Hady Khayr al-ʿIbād, a work of guidance and rulings drawn from the Prophet’s life.

xsr-034.src: Ibn Rajab, Sharḥ ʿIlal al-Tirmidhī; al-Khaṭīb al-Baghdādī, al-Kifāya; al-Bayhaqī, Dalāʾil al-Nubuwwa (introduction on tasāhul)
xsr-034.q: What method did some hadith scholars attribute to themselves regarding reports on the sīra and maghāzī, as opposed to rulings?
o: They were more lenient with chains in sīra, history and virtues than in reports on halal and haram, while still criticising what was fabricated
They accepted every report without chains
They refused to narrate anything from the maghāzī
They required ten narrators for every historical report
xsr-034.e: Some scholars, including those cited by al-Bayhaqī and Ibn Rajab, were more lenient (tasāhul) in the chains of reports on virtues, sīra and history than in those about rulings. This does not mean fabricated reports were accepted, and scholars warned about reports from known liars. Modern researchers debate how far historical reports should be tested by hadith rules, with many applying hadith criticism together with historical criticism.

xsr-035.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-ṣalāh (bina’ al-masjid); Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; Ibn Saʿd, al-Ṭabaqāt
xsr-035.q: How do the sound reports describe the first building of the Prophet’s Mosque in Madīna?
o: It was built on land bought from two orphans, with walls of mud-brick, palm-trunk pillars and a roof of palm fronds, and the Prophet ﷺ himself worked on it
It was built of marble by Byzantine craftsmen
It was built on the site of the Kaʿba
It was built with a minaret and a dome from the start
xsr-035.e: In al-Bukhārī’s report from Anas, the Prophet ﷺ chose the site where his she-camel knelt, an area owned by two orphans, Sahl and Suhayl, whose price was paid, and the Muslims built it from mud-brick with palm trunks as pillars and palm leaves as roof. The Prophet ﷺ carried bricks with the Companions. The qibla was first facing Jerusalem and later changed. Dome and minarets were later additions.

xsr-036.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-īmān and Kitāb al-ṣalāh (al-Barā’); Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on sūrat al-Baqara
xsr-036.q: What do the reports say about the change of the qibla, including the debated timing?
o: The Prophet ﷺ prayed towards Jerusalem for about sixteen or seventeen months after the Hijra and then was commanded to face the Kaʿba; al-Barā’ says sixteen or seventeen months and other reports mention differing months; the date is debated among historians
It changed on the first day of the Hijra
It changed after the conquest of Makka
xsr-036.e: In al-Barā’’s report in al-Bukhārī, the Muslims prayed towards Bayt al-Maqdis for sixteen or seventeen months before the verse about turning the face to al-Masjid al-Ḥarām. Ibn Ḥajar discusses the differing reports on the month (Rajab, Shaʿbān or others) and the first prayer after the change. The Prophet ﷺ used to love facing the Kaʿba, the report says.

xsr-037.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-maghāzī (Ghazwat Muʾta); Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; al-Ṭabarī, Taʾrīkh
xsr-037.q: What do the sound reports say about the expedition to Muʾta (8 AH), including its three commanders and Khālid ibn al-Walīd?
o: The Prophet ﷺ named Zayd ibn Ḥāritha, then Jaʿfar, then ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa as successive commanders; all three fell, the standard was taken by Khālid, whom the Prophet ﷺ called a sword of God, and the army withdrew
The army was led by Abū Bakr and won a great victory
It was a naval battle against Persia
It was led by the Prophet ﷺ himself
xsr-037.e: In al-Bukhārī, the Prophet ﷺ appointed Zayd ibn Ḥāritha, and if he fell, Jaʿfar, and if he fell, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥa. All three were killed. The Prophet ﷺ informed the people in Madīna of the deaths with tears and said the flag was taken by one of God’s swords (Khālid) until God gave victory. Scholars discuss whether Khālid’s withdrawal was a tactical retreat or an outcome described as a victory in the reports.

xsr-038.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-maghāzī; Ibn Hishām, al-Sīra; Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī
xsr-038.q: What disagreement exists about the date of Banū al-Naḍīr’s expulsion relative to Uḥud?
o: Ibn Isḥāq placed it after Uḥud (in 4 AH), while al-Zuhrī, as reported by ʿUrwa and cited in al-Bukhārī, placed it before Uḥud, six months after Badr
All sources place it after the conquest of Makka
All sources place it before the Hijra
xsr-038.e: Ibn Isḥāq puts the expulsion of Banū al-Naḍīr after the events of Biʾr Maʿūna in Rabīʿ al-Awwal of 4 AH. Mūsā ibn ʿUqba, from al-Zuhrī and ʿUrwa, puts it before Uḥud, around six months after Badr, and al-Bukhārī gives the latter without choosing. Ibn Ḥajar discusses the difference and the placing of the revelation of sūrat al-Ḥashr in connection with it.

xsr-039.src: Ibn al-ʿArabī, ʿĀriḍat al-Aḥwadhī; al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, al-Shifā; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ (Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim: names of the Prophet)
xsr-039.q: Which names of the Prophet ﷺ are given in the hadith of Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim, and what is the status of lists of 'a thousand names'?
o: Muḥammad, Aḥmad, al-Māḥī, al-Ḥāshir and al-ʿĀqib; the long lists of names that later authors produced are not matched by sound reports
xsr-039.e: In the Ṣaḥīḥayn, the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said he has names: Muḥammad, Aḥmad, al-Māḥī (the one by whom disbelief is wiped out), al-Ḥāshir (before whom people are gathered) and al-ʿĀqib (the last of the prophets). Later authors, such as in Dalāʾil al-Khayrāt, gave much longer lists. Ibn al-ʿArabī and al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ discussed the names in the sound reports, with Ibn al-ʿArabī giving a long list from the Quran and Sunna.

xsr-040.src: Ibn Khaldūn, Muqaddima; al-Dhahabī, Siyar Aʿlām al-Nubalāʾ; Akram Ḍiyāʾ al-ʿUmarī, al-Sīra al-Nabawiyya al-Ṣaḥīḥa; Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī
xsr-040.q: Which approach to the sources of the sīra is taken in al-ʿUmarī’s al-Sīra al-Nabawiyya al-Ṣaḥīḥa, and how does it relate to classical practice?
o: It applies hadith criticism to reports of the sīra to write a biography from authenticated reports, following the older distinction between Ṣaḥīḥ-grade reports and the general maghāzī material
It rejects all hadith in favour of poetry
It is a commentary on Ibn Khaldūn’s Muqaddima
xsr-040.e: Akram Ḍiyāʾ al-ʿUmarī (20th century) wrote al-Sīra al-Nabawiyya al-Ṣaḥīḥa to collect authenticated reports on the Prophet’s life using the rules of hadith criticism, building on the classical distinction between works of sīra (such as Ibn Isḥāq’s) and the sound reports in the Ṣaḥīḥayn and other collections. Other modern scholars, in contrast, argue that historical criticism should be used in addition to hadith methods.

xtf-001.src: al-Karmānī, al-Burhān fī Mutashābih al-Qurʾān; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 6:151 and 17:31; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr
xtf-001.q: The verse shown promises provision first to the parents and then to the children, while a similar verse in al-Isrāʾ (17:31) reverses the order. What is the classical explanation?
o: Here the fear is of present poverty, so the parents are mentioned first as the ones in need; in al-Isrāʾ the fear is of future poverty, so the children, whose provision is a concern, come first
The two verses were revealed to different people
The order has no significance and is a matter of rhyme alone
One verse is abrogated by the other
xtf-001.e: In al-Anʿām the phrase is ‘because of poverty’ (min imlāq), referring to a poverty already existing in the parents, so God promises to provide for the parents first. In al-Isrāʾ it is ‘for fear of poverty’ (khashya), a fear of future need, so the children, whom the parents fear to feed, are named first. Al-Karmānī and others give this as a model of how a change in order follows the context.

xtf-002.src: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 2:49 and 14:6; al-Karmānī, al-Burhān fī Mutashābih al-Qurʾān; al-Iskāfī, Durrat al-Tanzīl
xtf-002.q: The highlighted verb in this verse has no conjunction before it, whereas in 14:6 the corresponding verb has wāw. How is the difference explained?
o: Here the slaying is an explanation of the ‘evil of the punishment’, so no wāw; in 14:6 the slaying is mentioned as a separate kind of torment alongside others, so it is joined by wāw
The wāw was dropped by a scribal slip
The verses refer to two different Pharaohs
The difference is only because of the recitation
xtf-002.e: Al-Zamakhsharī explains that without the wāw the clause is an explanation of the suffering (the slaying of sons is the very worst of ‘evil punishment’), while with the wāw in 14:6 the slaying is added as another distinct torment, since the speech there reminds of blessings and lists the types of torment. Al-Karmānī and al-Iskāfī give similar accounts.

xtf-003.src: al-Karmānī, al-Burhān fī Mutashābih al-Qurʾān; Ibn al-Zubayr al-Gharnāṭī, Malāk al-Taʾwīl; Zakariyyā al-Anṣārī, Fatḥ al-Raḥmān
xtf-003.q: The verse shown ends with a description of the human being as very unjust and ungrateful, whereas the similar verse in al-Naḥl (16:18) ends with a name of God. How do the commentators explain the difference?
o: Each ending fits its context: in Ibrāhīm the verse stresses the human failing in the face of countless favours, and in al-Naḥl it stresses God’s mercy in forgiving the shortcoming in thanking Him
The endings are interchangeable and were chosen by the scribes
One of the two verses is Makkan and the other Madinan, so the endings differ
The two endings refer to the same attribute
xtf-003.e: Both verses speak of the impossibility of counting God’s favours. In Ibrāhīm the preceding verses mention the unbelievers’ denial, so the ending highlights the wrong and ingratitude of the human being. In al-Naḥl the surrounding verses deal with God’s power and mercy, so the ending is ‘Forgiving, Merciful’. This is a standard example of how the closing of a verse (fāṣila) fits its context.

xtf-004.src: al-Karmānī, al-Burhān fī Mutashābih al-Qurʾān; al-Iskāfī, Durrat al-Tanzīl wa-Ghurrat al-Taʾwīl; Ibn al-Zubayr al-Gharnāṭī, Malāk al-Taʾwīl; Zakariyyā al-Anṣārī, Fatḥ al-Raḥmān
xtf-004.q: Which of the following is a classical work on the similarity between Quranic verses with slightly different wording (al-mutashābih al-lafẓī)?
o: al-Burhān fī Mutashābih al-Qurʾān by al-Karmānī
xtf-004.e: The literature on al-mutashābih al-lafẓī includes al-Karmānī’s al-Burhān, al-Iskāfī’s Durrat al-Tanzīl, Ibn al-Zubayr’s Malāk al-Taʾwīl and Zakariyyā al-Anṣārī’s Fatḥ al-Raḥmān. The Jazariyya is on tajwīd, the Asbāb on occasions, and al-Ashbāh on grammar and jurisprudence.

xtf-005.src: al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā min ʿIlm al-Uṣūl; al-Juwaynī, al-Burhān fī Uṣūl al-Fiqh
xtf-005.q: Which five necessities does al-Ghazālī say the sharīʿa aims to protect?
o: Religion, life, intellect, lineage and property
Prayer, fasting, zakāt, Ḥajj and testimony
Honour, family, justice, trade and knowledge
Law, kingship, treaties, taxes and war
xtf-005.e: In al-Mustaṣfā, al-Ghazālī names the five as the preservation of dīn, nafs, ʿaql, nasl (offspring) and māl. He treats each as a ‘necessity’ (ḍarūra) whose protection is the basis of public interest (maṣlaḥa). Later, al-Qarāfī and others added the protection of honour (ʿirḍ) as a sixth, after earlier classification by al-Juwaynī.

xtf-006.src: al-Shāṭibī, al-Muwāfaqāt fī Uṣūl al-Sharīʿa, kitāb al-maqāṣid
xtf-006.q: Into which three levels does al-Shāṭibī divide the objectives of the sharīʿa in al-Muwāfaqāt?
xtf-006.e: Al-Shāṭibī (d. 790 AH) ranks the interests by their urgency: ḍarūriyyāt (necessities, without which life and religion collapse), ḥājiyyāt (needs that remove hardship) and taḥsīniyyāt (refinements and fine conduct). Each level is served by the lower ones. His division became the standard framework of maqāṣid thinking.

xtf-007.src: Ibn ʿĀshūr, al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr, muqaddima 4 (maqāṣid al-Qurʾān)
xtf-007.q: In the introduction to al-Taḥrīr wa-l-Tanwīr, Ibn ʿĀshūr lists the principal purposes (maqāṣid) of the Quran. Which of these is among his eight?
o: Reforming belief, refining character, legislation, governing the community, stories of earlier nations, teaching, warnings and promises, and inimitability
Collecting hadith, fixing the recitation, ordering the sūras, copying the muṣḥaf, counting verses, writing commentary, translating, and teaching Arabic
Founding the schools, ordering the army, issuing coins, collecting taxes, building mosques, appointing judges, sending envoys, and ruling the lands
Describing the stars, measuring the earth, dividing the seasons, naming the plants, describing animals, classifying minerals, medicine, and arithmetic
xtf-007.e: Ibn ʿĀshūr (d. 1973) identifies eight chief aims: iṣlāḥ al-iʿtiqād, tahdhīb al-akhlāq, al-tashrīʿ, siyāsat al-umma, al-qaṣaṣ wa-akhbār al-umam, al-taʿlīm, al-mawāʿiẓ wa-l-indhār wa-l-tabshīr, and al-iʿjāz. He uses them as a guide in interpretation, to avoid reading verses outside their purpose.

xtf-008.src: al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salām, Qawāʿid al-Aḥkām fī Maṣāliḥ al-Anām; Ibn ʿĀshūr, Maqāṣid al-Sharīʿa al-Islāmiyya
xtf-008.q: Which classical work by al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salām builds the whole law on obtaining benefits and warding off harm?
xtf-008.e: Al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salām (d. 660 AH), the ‘Sultan of the scholars’, wrote Qawāʿid al-Aḥkām, in which rulings are explained through jalb al-maṣāliḥ and darʾ al-mafāsid. Al-Muwāfaqāt is by al-Shāṭibī, al-Mustaṣfā by al-Ghazālī, and Maqāṣid al-Sharīʿa al-Islāmiyya by Ibn ʿĀshūr.

xtf-009.src: Ibn Taymiyya, Muqaddima fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, introduction
xtf-009.q: In what order does Ibn Taymiyya’s Muqaddima fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr place the sources of the best commentary?
o: The Quran by the Quran, then the Sunna, then the statements of the Companions, then those of the Successors, and then the Arabic language
The reader’s opinion, then poetry, then the Sunna
The Companions, then the Sunna, then the Quran
The language first, then the Quran, then the opinions of the Successors
xtf-009.e: Ibn Taymiyya says that the best way is to interpret the Quran by the Quran, because what is brief in one place is explained in another; then the Sunna, which explains the Quran; then the Companions, who witnessed the revelation; then the leading Successors; and the language as a support. Ibn Kathīr follows the same order in his introduction.

xtf-010.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, introduction (on al-isrāʾīliyyāt); Ibn Taymiyya, Muqaddima fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr
xtf-010.q: How does Ibn Kathīr classify the reports taken from the People of the Book (isrāʾīliyyāt) for the purposes of tafsīr?
o: Three kinds: what our sources confirm as true, what they show to be false, and what is neither (to be neither believed nor denied, and used with caution)
All are valid because they are older scripture
All are forbidden and may never be quoted
Two kinds only: those on law and those on stories
xtf-010.e: Ibn Kathīr, relying on the hadith ‘narrate from the Children of Israel, there is no harm’ and on the warning not to believe or disbelieve them, says that some reports agree with the Quran and Sunna and may be cited as support, some contradict them and are rejected, and the rest, about which the sources are silent, may be narrated for illustration but not believed as a matter of faith or used as a proof.

xtf-011.src: al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn; al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān, naw‘ 41; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 78
xtf-011.q: How do scholars reconcile the hadith that warns against explaining the Quran ‘by one’s own opinion’ with the long tradition of tafsīr bi-l-raʾy?
o: They distinguish praiseworthy raʾy (informed by language, Sunna and the sciences) from blameworthy raʾy (whim, ignorance or support for a prior doctrine)
They hold that all tafsīr bi-l-raʾy is forbidden
They hold that raʾy is allowed to everyone without conditions
They say the hadith was abrogated
xtf-011.e: Scholars say the warning concerns speaking without knowledge or on the basis of whim or sectarian purpose. Ijtihād in tafsīr that is grounded in Arabic, the Sunna, the Companions’ statements, asbāb al-nuzūl and the sciences is praiseworthy, and the reports show that the Companions themselves explained by raʾy. The scholars set conditions for the mufassir, including the language sciences.

xtf-012.src: al-Taftāzānī, Sharḥ al-ʿAqāʾid al-Nasafiyya; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 78; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Fatāwā
xtf-012.q: Under what conditions did Sunni scholars accept ishārī (allusive) interpretation of the Quran?
o: That it does not contradict the apparent meaning, has a supporting proof in the sharīʿa or language, and is not claimed to be the only meaning
That it is accepted whenever the commentator claims inspiration
That it replaces the apparent meaning entirely
It was never accepted by any scholar
xtf-012.e: Scholars such as al-Taftāzānī and al-Suyūṭī accepted allusive readings from the mystics on conditions: no conflict with the literal sense or the sharīʿa, a supporting reason, and no claim that this is the intended meaning to the exclusion of the apparent one. Claims that the apparent meaning has no force were condemned as deviation.

xtf-013.src: Ibn Taymiyya, Muqaddima fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 78
xtf-013.q: What is the scholarly position on the explanations of the Successors (tābiʿūn) as evidence in tafsīr?
o: When they agree, their explanation is a proof; when they differ, one view is not a proof against another and the choice is made by the Quran, Sunna, language and the Companions’ statements
Their explanations are never to be cited
Only the Companions’ statements are cited, never the Successors’
xtf-013.e: Two reports from Aḥmad concern whether the Successors’ tafsīr is a proof. Ibn Taymiyya sums up: where they agree, it is not to be disputed; where they disagree, the view of one is not authoritative against that of another, and one turns to the language, the Quran and the Sunna. In practice classical commentaries cite them heavily.

xtf-014.src: al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 78
xtf-014.q: Which Companion is regarded as the founder of the Makkan school of tafsīr, and which Successors belong to it?
o: Ibn ʿAbbās; Mujāhid, ʿIkrima, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ and Ṭāwūs
Ibn Masʿūd; ʿAlqama, Masrūq and al-Aswad
Ubayy ibn Kaʿb; Zayd ibn Aslam and Abū al-ʿĀliya
ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib; al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and Qatāda
xtf-014.e: Ibn ʿAbbās, called the interpreter of the Quran, taught in Makka, and his students Mujāhid, ʿIkrima, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ and Ṭāwūs formed the Makkan school. Ibn Masʿūd stands at the head of the Iraqi school (ʿAlqama, Masrūq, al-Aswad) and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb at the head of the Madinan one (Zayd ibn Aslam, Abū al-ʿĀliya).

xtf-015.src: al-Jaṣṣāṣ, Aḥkām al-Qurʾān; Ibn al-ʿArabī, Aḥkām al-Qurʾān; al-Kiyā al-Harrāsī, Aḥkām al-Qurʾān; al-Qurṭubī, al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān
xtf-015.q: Which pairing of the classical Aḥkām al-Qurʾān works with their authors’ schools is correct?
o: al-Jaṣṣāṣ: Ḥanafī; Ibn al-ʿArabī: Mālikī; al-Kiyā al-Harrāsī: Shāfiʿī
al-Jaṣṣāṣ: Shāfiʿī; Ibn al-ʿArabī: Ḥanafī; al-Kiyā: Mālikī
al-Jaṣṣāṣ: Mālikī; Ibn al-ʿArabī: Shāfiʿī; al-Kiyā: Ḥanbalī
xtf-015.e: These works group the legal verses and their interpretation by the author’s school: Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ (d. 370 AH) is Ḥanafī, Abū Bakr ibn al-ʿArabī (d. 543 AH) is Mālikī, and al-Kiyā al-Harrāsī (d. 504 AH) is Shāfiʿī. Al-Qurṭubī (d. 671 AH) wrote a broader commentary on legal rulings, in the Mālikī tradition.

xtf-016.src: al-Biqāʿī, Naẓm al-Durar fī Tanāsub al-Āyāt wa-l-Suwar; Ibn al-Zubayr al-Gharnāṭī, al-Burhān fī Munāsabat Tartīb Suwar al-Qurʾān
xtf-016.q: Which commentary is best known for its detailed study of the links (munāsabāt) between verses and between sūras?
o: Naẓm al-Durar fī Tanāsub al-Āyāt wa-l-Suwar by al-Biqāʿī
xtf-016.e: Burhān al-Dīn al-Biqāʿī (d. 885 AH) devoted his commentary to showing the coherence of each verse with what precedes and follows and the order of the sūras. Ibn al-Zubayr al-Gharnāṭī wrote a shorter classical study on the sequence of the sūras. The other commentaries cited are better known for language, brevity and a mix of riwāya and dirāya.

xtf-017.src: Abū Ḥayyān, al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, introduction; al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn
xtf-017.q: Which commentary on the Quran is known for its grammatical and linguistic analysis, by the Andalusian grammarian Abū Ḥayyān?
xtf-017.e: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī (d. 745 AH) wrote al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ, a tafsīr in which he discusses grammar, readings and linguistics at length, and he criticised grammatical errors in earlier tafsīrs. Rūḥ al-Maʿānī is by al-Alūsī, Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb by al-Rāzī and Maʿālim al-Tanzīl by al-Baghawī.

xtf-018.src: al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn; Ibn Khallikān, Wafayāt al-Aʿyān
xtf-018.q: Which commentary is known for its extensive discussion of theology, philosophy and the sciences, and is attributed to Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī?
xtf-018.e: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī (d. 606 AH) wrote Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb, which discusses theology, logic, cosmology and many other topics beside the verses, with attention to the links between verses. It is said to have been completed by his students. Taʾwīlāt Ahl al-Sunna is by al-Māturīdī, and Aḥkām al-Qurʾān is the name of several works on legal verses.

xtf-019.src: al-Māturīdī, Taʾwīlāt Ahl al-Sunna (Taʾwīlāt al-Qurʾān); al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn
xtf-019.q: What is the Taʾwīlāt Ahl al-Sunna (Taʾwīlāt al-Qurʾān) and who wrote it?
o: A commentary by Abū Manṣūr al-Māturīdī (d. 333 AH) of Samarkand, an early work of the Sunni rational tradition that gave rise to the Māturīdī school
A commentary by Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī on creed only
A commentary by al-Ṭabarī on the readings
A collection of the sayings of Ibn ʿAbbās
xtf-019.e: Al-Māturīdī’s commentary explains the Quran with attention to language and reason, defending the positions later identified as Māturīdī in creed, and it often gives several possible interpretations. It is among the earliest surviving Sunni commentaries from Central Asia and is a major source for the school in the Ḥanafī world.

xtf-020.src: al-Baghawī, Maʿālim al-Tanzīl, introduction; al-Thaʿlabī, al-Kashf wa-l-Bayān; al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn
xtf-020.q: How is al-Baghawī’s Maʿālim al-Tanzīl related to al-Thaʿlabī’s al-Kashf wa-l-Bayān?
o: Al-Baghawī abridged it, removing the weak and fabricated reports and adding hadith of the Ṣaḥīḥayn and the Sunan
The two works have no relation
xtf-020.e: Al-Baghawī (d. 516 AH) based Maʿālim al-Tanzīl on the commentary of his teacher al-Thaʿlabī (d. 427 AH), which was rich in reports but also contained weak and invented ones. He retained its benefits while deleting the fabricated material and adding sounder reports, so that the work became a widely used commentary bi-l-maʾthūr.

xtf-021.src: al-Karmānī, al-Burhān fī Mutashābih al-Qurʾān; al-Iskāfī, Durrat al-Tanzīl; Zakariyyā al-Anṣārī, Fatḥ al-Raḥmān
xtf-021.q: In this verse the man comes first (‘a man came from the farthest part of the city’), whereas in 36:20 the place comes first. What is the explanation given by the commentators?
o: In al-Qaṣaṣ the focus is on the man and his warning to Mūsā, while in Yā Sīn the emphasis is on the distance from which he came to support the messengers
The scribes mistakenly transposed the words
The two verses refer to the same man in different languages
The order is for the rhyme alone
xtf-021.e: The two verses describe the arrival of a man who tries to help, but each places its emphasis differently. In 28:20 the man is mentioned first because the interest is in what he says to Mūsā about the plot. In 36:20 the place comes first, showing that even from the farthest part of the city a man came with concern for the messengers, though the leaders had rejected them. Commentators such as al-Karmānī give similar accounts.

xtf-022.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on the wāw al-thamāniya; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 18:22; al-Suhaylī, Nataʾij al-Fikr
xtf-022.q: The group of three and five is described without a conjunction before ‘their dog’, whereas the group of seven has the word ‘eighth’ with a wāw. What do some grammarians call this wāw, and how do others explain it?
o: ‘Wāw of the eight’ (wāw al-thamāniya), a feature some thought the Arabs used for the number eight; others take it as an ordinary wāw of the circumstance that confirms the statement
A wāw that changes the meaning into a question
xtf-022.e: Some grammarians, like Ibn Khālawayh, spoke of a wāw al-thamāniya found with the number eight (here and in 9:112, 39:73, 66:5), but many, including Ibn Hishām, did not accept it as a rule. Al-Zamakhsharī takes it as the wāw of the circumstance that confirms the description of the group, which suits the claim that the seven are those whose count is correct.

xtf-023.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Tafsīr and Kitāb al-Ṣawm (hadith of Sahl ibn Saʿd on 2:187); Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī
xtf-023.q: According to the report from Sahl ibn Saʿd in al-Bukhārī, what happened with the highlighted words about the white thread and the black thread?
o: The verse was first revealed without the words ‘of the dawn’, so some men tied white and black threads to their feet to distinguish them; then those words were revealed to show that the threads mean the light of dawn and the dark of night
The words were revealed before the rest of the verse
The words were later removed from the verse
The words were revealed in Makka
xtf-023.e: Sahl reports that men took two threads, one white and one black, and kept eating until they could tell them apart, until the words ‘of the dawn’ were revealed, so they knew that the threads signify night and day. ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim’s similar story also appears. It is a standard example of a later revelation clarifying an earlier one.

xtf-024.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Ḥajj and Kitāb al-Tafsīr (ʿĀʾisha and ʿUrwa on 2:158); Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Ḥajj
xtf-024.q: The words ‘no blame on him’ about going round al-Ṣafā and al-Marwa seem to make the rite optional. How did ʿĀʾisha explain them to ʿUrwa?
o: They were revealed because the Anṣār hesitated to walk between them, having done so for an idol; the words remove the hesitation and do not make the rite optional, and the Prophet established it
They mean that the rite is optional and may be omitted
They were revealed about the Quraysh in Makka only
xtf-024.e: ʿUrwa asked ʿĀʾisha whether the words meant that going between the two hills was optional. She replied that if that were the meaning the text would read ‘no blame on him not to’; the words were revealed because the Anṣār, who used to hail Manāt, felt uneasy, and the Prophet instituted the walk. Most jurists consider it a pillar or an obligation; the Ḥanafīs consider it an obligation whose omission can be compensated for by an offering.

xtf-025.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Tafsīr (ʿĀʾisha’s explanation of 4:3); Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Tafsīr
xtf-025.q: How did ʿĀʾisha explain, in the report in al-Bukhārī, the link between the fear of being unjust to orphans and permission to marry two, three or four women?
o: The verse concerns a guardian of an orphan girl who wants to marry her for her property without giving her a fair dowry; he is told to marry other women instead
The verse concerns an orphan boy who wishes to marry several women
The verse is only about inheritance of orphans
xtf-025.e: ʿUrwa asked ʿĀʾisha about the verse, and she explained that it concerns an orphan girl under a man’s care, who is attracted to her property and beauty and wants to marry her without giving her the full dower; he was forbidden from doing so unless he does justice, and told to marry other women. This is cited in discussions of how the occasion clarifies a verse’s wording.

xtf-026.src: Ibn ʿĀshūr, Maqāṣid al-Sharīʿa al-Islāmiyya, ch. on the general purposes (al-maqāṣid al-ʿāmma)
xtf-026.q: Which general characteristics (not specific interests) does Ibn ʿĀshūr list in his Maqāṣid al-Sharīʿa al-Islāmiyya as the broader intentions of the sharīʿa?
o: Natural disposition (fiṭra), ease and tolerance (samāḥa), equality, and freedom
xtf-026.e: Ibn ʿĀshūr (d. 1973) goes beyond the five necessities and describes the sharīʿa’s general features: it is consistent with the human natural disposition (fiṭra), is built on ease and tolerance (samāḥa), on equality (musāwāt) among people, and on freedom (ḥurriyya) in what the law does not restrict. These serve as criteria for judging the purpose of rulings.

xtf-027.src: al-Shāṭibī, al-Iʿtiṣām; al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; Ibn Qudāma, Rawḍat al-Nāẓir
xtf-027.q: What is maṣlaḥa mursala, and which school is most associated with using it as a source?
o: An interest that no text confirms or cancels specifically, used as a source of rulings, most associated with the Mālikī school
An interest that a text explicitly cancels, used by the Ḥanafī school
A text of the Sunna transmitted by a single narrator, used by the Shāfiʿīs
A ruling established by consensus, used by the Ḥanbalīs
xtf-027.e: Maṣlaḥa mursala (‘unrestricted interest’) is a benefit that the sharīʿa neither specifically endorses nor rejects. The Mālikīs are the school most associated with it, under conditions (consistency with the sharīʿa’s purposes, rationality, removal of hardship), and al-Shāṭibī defends it in al-Iʿtiṣām. Al-Ghazālī accepted it only when it is a necessity, general and certain.

xtf-028.src: Ibn Taymiyya, Muqaddima fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr, faṣl on the disagreement of the Salaf in tafsīr
xtf-028.q: How does Ibn Taymiyya classify the disagreement of the early commentators in tafsīr?
o: Mostly as ikhtilāf tanawwuʿ (variety), where different expressions or examples refer to the same meaning, and less often as ikhtilāf tadādd (real contradiction)
There was no disagreement among the Salaf in tafsīr
All disagreements are only about the readings
xtf-028.e: Ibn Taymiyya says that the disagreements of the Salaf in tafsīr are few compared to those in rulings, and most are of variety: one gives an example, another a definition or another aspect, as when they name different instances of one description. Real contradictions exist but are fewer. This distinction helps a commentator reconcile reports rather than reject them.

xtf-029.src: al-Ḥākim, al-Mustadrak; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ, Muqaddima fī ʿUlūm al-Ḥadīth; al-Suyūṭī, Tadrīb al-Rāwī
xtf-029.q: What rule did al-Ḥākim state about the explanation of a Companion who witnessed the revelation, and how did later scholars limit it?
o: He said that such a tafsīr has the status of a report from the Prophet; Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ and others limited this to the occasions of revelation and matters not open to opinion
That it always has the status of a hadith in all matters including law
That it is accepted only if repeated by ten Companions
xtf-029.e: Al-Ḥākim said that the commentary of a Companion who witnessed the revelation is considered a raised (marfūʿ) report. Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ restricted this to things that cannot be a matter of opinion, such as the occasion of revelation or the unseen. Other tafsīr from Companions is treated as a statement of a Companion, a proof for many but not on the same level as a statement of the Prophet.

xtf-030.src: al-Suyūṭī, Tafsīr al-Jalālayn, introduction; al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn
xtf-030.q: Who wrote Tafsīr al-Jalālayn, and how was it composed?
o: Jalāl al-Dīn al-Maḥallī wrote the second half (from al-Kahf to the end) and the Fātiḥa, and Jalāl al-Dīn al-Suyūṭī completed the remainder from al-Baqara to al-Isrāʾ
Jalāl al-Dīn al-Suyūṭī alone, in ten volumes
xtf-030.e: Al-Maḥallī (d. 864 AH) began the commentary from Sūrat al-Kahf to the end and then the Fātiḥa, but died before completing it; al-Suyūṭī (d. 911 AH) completed it from al-Baqara to al-Isrāʾ, following al-Maḥallī’s method and brevity. The result is a short, widely used commentary in a single volume, hence the name ‘of the two Jalāls’.

xtf-031.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Durr al-Manthūr fī al-Tafsīr bi-l-Maʾthūr, introduction
xtf-031.q: What is the nature of al-Suyūṭī’s al-Durr al-Manthūr fī al-Tafsīr bi-l-Maʾthūr?
o: A collection of reports from the Prophet, Companions and Successors on each verse, which he gives without their chains
A study of the occasions of revelation only
xtf-031.e: Al-Suyūṭī gathered reports on each verse from a large number of earlier hadith and tafsīr works, giving only the source and omitting the chains, which is why its reports need verification in the original books. His earlier Tarjumān al-Qurʾān contained chains, and the Durr is an abridgement of it.

xtf-032.src: al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān ʿan Taʾwīl Āy al-Qurʾān, introduction; Ibn Taymiyya, Muqaddima fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr
xtf-032.q: How is the method of al-Ṭabarī’s Jāmiʿ al-Bayān characterised?
o: He reports the views of earlier authorities with chains, then weighs them and states his preference, using language, the readings and sometimes grammar
He gives only his own opinion with no chains
He quotes only the Prophet’s explanations
xtf-032.e: Al-Ṭabarī (d. 310 AH) lists the earlier opinions on each verse with chains of transmission, then gives his own preference (tarjīḥ), with reasons from the Arabic language, the readings and the consensus of the interpreters. His commentary is the main source for the early tradition, and many later commentaries depend on it.

xtf-033.src: Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz fī Tafsīr al-Kitāb al-ʿAzīz, introduction; al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn
xtf-033.q: What is Ibn ʿAṭiyya’s al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz known for?
o: An Andalusī Mālikī commentary that condenses the views of al-Ṭabarī and others, with attention to language and readings, and praised by Ibn Taymiyya for being closer to the Sunna than many
A commentary only on legal verses
xtf-033.e: Abū Muḥammad Ibn ʿAṭiyya (d. 541 AH) of Granada abridged and verified earlier opinions, particularly those of al-Ṭabarī, and added linguistic and rhetorical notes. His work is used by al-Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān. Ibn Taymiyya praised it as free of the excess of some other commentaries.

xtf-034.src: al-Shawkānī, Fatḥ al-Qadīr al-Jāmiʿ bayna Fannay al-Riwāya wa-l-Dirāya min ʿIlm al-Tafsīr; al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn
xtf-034.q: Why is al-Shawkānī’s Fatḥ al-Qadīr described as ‘uniting the two arts of riwāya and dirāya’?
o: Because it combines reports (athar) with linguistic and rational analysis (dirāya) in explaining the verses
Because it was written by two authors
xtf-034.e: Muḥammad al-Shawkānī (d. 1250 AH) of Yemen sets in his subtitle that the work joins the two methods: reports from the Prophet, Companions and Successors (riwāya), and analysis of language, grammar and meaning (dirāya). It is widely used, though some find its approach selective.

xtf-035.src: al-Alūsī, Rūḥ al-Maʿānī fī Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm wa-l-Sabʿ al-Mathānī, introduction; al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn
xtf-035.q: What is al-Alūsī’s Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, and what characterises it?
o: A large 19th-century commentary from Baghdad that collects the views of the earlier commentaries, with language, readings, law and allusive (ishārī) remarks
A short commentary in a single volume
A commentary by a student of al-Ṭabarī
xtf-035.e: Shihāb al-Dīn al-Alūsī (d. 1270 AH), a Baghdad scholar of the Ottoman period, compiled an encyclopaedic commentary drawing on al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Bayḍāwī and many others, discussing readings, grammar, law and giving allusive interpretations, and sometimes challenging the opinions he cites.

xtf-036.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 80 (ṭabaqāt al-mufassirīn); Ibn Ḥajar, Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb; al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn
xtf-036.q: What is the scholarly view of the book Tanwīr al-Miqbās min Tafsīr Ibn ʿAbbās that circulates under the name of Ibn ʿAbbās?
o: It is a compilation attributed to him through a weak chain (al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ), so its attribution is not reliable
It is a book written by Ibn ʿAbbās himself, with a perfect chain
It is the commentary of al-Ṭabarī under another name
It was written in the 20th century
xtf-036.e: The compilation Tanwīr al-Miqbās, assembled by al-Fīrūzābādī, is based on a chain from Muḥammad ibn al-Sāʾib al-Kalbī, from Abū Ṣāliḥ, from Ibn ʿAbbās. The hadith critics considered al-Kalbī weak, so the transmission is not reliable. A sounder source from Ibn ʿAbbās is the Ṣaḥīfa of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa, which Aḥmad is reported to have praised.

xtf-037.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 80; Ibn Ḥajar, Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb, on ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa
xtf-037.q: Which transmission of the tafsīr of Ibn ʿAbbās was praised by Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal and used by al-Bukhārī and al-Ṭabarī?
o: The Ṣaḥīfa of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa from Ibn ʿAbbās
The chain of al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ
The book of Muqātil ibn Sulaymān
xtf-037.e: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥa (d. 143 AH) narrated tafsīr from Ibn ʿAbbās, though he did not meet him directly but through intermediaries; Aḥmad is quoted as saying that if a man travelled to Egypt for this ṣaḥīfa, it would not be a waste. Al-Bukhārī cites it in places and al-Ṭabarī relies on it. The transmission is regarded as a good, though not flawless, source.

xtf-038.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, introduction; al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn
xtf-038.q: How is Ibn Kathīr’s Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm generally characterised?
o: As a commentary bi-l-maʾthūr that explains the Quran first by the Quran, then by the Sunna and the early authorities, relying heavily on al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim and criticising weak reports
As a commentary on legal verses only
xtf-038.e: Ibn Kathīr (d. 774 AH) follows the order he describes in his introduction, which is that of Ibn Taymiyya, and adds assessments of the chains of the reports and of the isrāʾīliyyāt. He does not include much grammar or theology. Its concision and use of the reports made it one of the most widely read commentaries.

xtf-039.src: al-Bayḍāwī, Anwār al-Tanzīl wa-Asrār al-Taʾwīl, introduction; Ḥājjī Khalīfa, Kashf al-Ẓunūn
xtf-039.q: What is the relation of al-Bayḍāwī’s Anwār al-Tanzīl to earlier commentaries?
o: It is a concise commentary that draws mainly on al-Zamakhsharī’s al-Kashshāf (leaving out its Muʿtazilī points) and on al-Rāzī, and became a standard text in the madrasas
It is an expansion of al-Ṭabarī’s commentary
It is a verse commentary on the Alfiyya
It is a translation of Ibn Kathīr
xtf-039.e: Al-Bayḍāwī (d. around 685 AH) abridged al-Kashshāf, removing the Muʿtazilī doctrines and adding material from al-Rāzī, al-Rāghib and others, with an emphasis on language and meaning. It was widely taught in the Ottoman and Eastern lands and was the subject of many glosses (ḥawāshī).

xtf-040.src: Ibn al-Jawzī, Zād al-Masīr fī ʿIlm al-Tafsīr, introduction; al-Dhahabī, al-Tafsīr wa-l-Mufassirūn
xtf-040.q: How does Ibn al-Jawzī’s Zād al-Masīr fī ʿIlm al-Tafsīr present the verses?
o: Briefly, listing the different views on each point with their attribution to the early authorities
As a single opinion with no mention of alternatives
xtf-040.e: Ibn al-Jawzī (d. 597 AH), a Ḥanbalī of Baghdad, compiled a medium-length commentary that, for each difficult point, lists the opinions with the names of those who held them, and is noted for ease of use. It is among the standard sources for locating attributions of tafsīr views.

xtj-001.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), bāb al-sakt; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, bāb al-sakt
xtj-001.q: Which list gives the four places where Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim (the transmission in the Shāṭibiyya) makes a sakta?
o: The tanwīn alif of ʿiwajā in 18:1, marqadinā in 36:52, man in 75:27 and bal in 83:14
The word rayb in 2:2, marqadinā in 36:52, man in 75:27 and bal in 83:14
The tanwīn alif of ʿiwajā in 18:1, marqadinā in 36:52, bal in 83:14 and the first word of 112:1
The word ʿiwajā in 18:1, man in 75:27, bal in 83:14 and the last word of 114:6
xtj-001.e: Ḥafṣ pauses without breath at four places: after ʿiwajā (18:1), after marqadinā (36:52), after man (75:27) and after bal (83:14). These are the only obligatory sakatāt in his riwāya; the sakta is a feature that Ḥamza and others extend to many more places, such as before every hamza after a sākin letter. The Shāṭibiyya lists them in its chapter on sakt.

xtj-002.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, bāb al-sakt; Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Kashf ʿan Wujūh al-Qirāʾāt
xtj-002.q: Why is the sakta placed after the highlighted word, according to the classical explanation?
o: To show that the word that follows (‘straight’) is not a description of ‘crookedness’ but a separate state of the Book
To prevent the tanwīn from being turned into a nūn
To mark the end of a verse in the reading of Ḥafṣ
To allow the reader to take a breath before the hamza
xtj-002.e: The sakta separates the two words so that the listener does not take ‘straight’ as qualifying ‘crookedness’, which would be absurd. The Book is meant to be straight, and the word is a ḥāl of the Book. Without the sakta the connection of the tanwīn alif and the following word could suggest the wrong meaning. This reason is given in the books of qirāʾāt such as al-Nashr.

xtj-003.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, bāb al-sakt; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xtj-003.q: What is the purpose of the sakta on the highlighted word in the reading of Ḥafṣ?
o: To separate it from the next word, so that ‘this’ is not taken as a qualifier of ‘our resting place’
To avoid the idghām of dāl into the following letter
To lengthen the madd that precedes the hamza
To mark a stop that is obligatory in all riwāyāt
xtj-003.e: The next word begins a new statement: it is the answer of the angels or believers after the sinners ask who woke them. The sakta stops the voice briefly so that ‘this’ is not read as describing the resting place. Other transmitters link the words and rely on the sense; Ḥafṣ makes the break explicit without a breath.
