xtj-004.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-sakt; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī
xtj-004.q: In Ḥafṣ the sakta after the highlighted word has a second function beyond separating the two words. What does it prevent?
o: The idghām of the nūn into the rāʾ of the next word
The ikhfāʾ of the nūn before a ḥalqī letter
The qalb of the nūn into a mīm
xtj-004.e: A nūn sākina before a rāʾ is normally assimilated with idghām bi-ghayr ghunna, which would turn the two words into something like ‘marrāq’ and hide that ‘man’ is a separate question word (‘who is an enchanter?’). The sakta keeps the nūn distinct. The same reasoning applies to the lām in 83:14 and the rāʾ that follows it.

xtj-005.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-sakt; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Tamhīd fī ʿIlm al-Tajwīd
xtj-005.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the sakta at the highlighted word from a waqf and from a qaṭʿ?
o: The sakta is a brief stop of the voice without taking breath, shorter than a waqf, after which the reading continues at once
The sakta is a stop with breath of about six ḥarakāt, followed by a new beginning
The sakta is a prolongation of the lām for two ḥarakāt with continued voice
The sakta is the same as a waqf, but only done at the end of a verse
xtj-005.e: In the terminology of the qurrāʾ, the sakt is a cutting of the sound for a short time (about two ḥarakāt, as is commonly said) without breathing; a waqf includes breathing and is longer, and a qaṭʿ ends the reading altogether. It is therefore also a different thing from a ‘pause sign’ in the muṣḥaf. That is why the sakta here does not allow the reader to take a breath.

xtj-006.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, bāb al-waqf; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xtj-006.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes rawm from ishmām at waqf on a final letter?
o: Rawm pronounces part of the vowel so that a near listener hears it; ishmām is a rounding of the lips for ḍamma after the sukūn, heard by no one
Rawm is a rounding of the lips and ishmām is a whisper of the vowel
Both are heard by the listener but ishmām is longer
Rawm is for sukūn and ishmām is for the tanwīn
xtj-006.e: Rawm is the pronunciation of a part (traditionally a third) of the vowel in a low voice, so that it is audible to someone close by. Ishmām is only a visible gesture of the lips for ḍamma after the letter has been made sākin, with no sound, so a blind person cannot perceive it. The classical books give these definitions in the chapter on waqf.

xtj-007.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-waqf ʿalā ākhir al-kalima
xtj-007.q: On which vowels is rawm permitted at waqf, and on which is ishmām?
o: Rawm on ḍamma and kasra; ishmām only on ḍamma
Rawm on fatḥa and ḍamma; ishmām on kasra
Rawm on all three vowels; ishmām on ḍamma only
Rawm only on kasra; ishmām on all three vowels
xtj-007.e: Rawm can be done on ḍamma and kasra, because these vowels can be partly pronounced; fatḥa is too light and is excluded by most. Ishmām is possible only for ḍamma, because the lips are rounded to show it, and fatḥa and kasra have no corresponding lip gesture.

xtj-008.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-waqf ʿalā ākhir al-kalima; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xtj-008.q: If a reader stops on the highlighted word, which of these statements is correct?
o: Rawm or ishmām is allowed, because the last letter carries an original ḍamma
Neither is allowed, because the word has no tanwīn
Only rawm is allowed, because the verb is imperfect
Only ishmām is allowed, because the word is a verb
xtj-008.e: The final dāl has an original ḍamma that is dropped at waqf, so both rawm and ishmām are permitted. Neither is allowed for fatḥa, for the hāʾ of feminine nouns that is changed from tāʾ, for the mīm of the plural, or for a vowel that is only temporary. A verb does not change the rule.

xtj-009.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, bāb ishmām al-sīn; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-idghām
xtj-009.q: How does Ḥafṣ read the highlighted word, in which a nūn sākina and a following nūn meet?
o: Idghām of the first nūn into the second, together with ishmām (a rounding of the lips for ḍamma before the idghām)
Complete iẓhār of both nūns with ghunna
Plain ikhfāʾ without any sign of the vowel
Ishmām with a full audible ḍamma and no idghām
xtj-009.e: The word is written with a single nūn plus a mark; its original form had two nūns, the first with ḍamma. Ḥafṣ gives the first nūn an ishmām (the lips round for the ḍamma) and then assimilates it, so that the vowel is hinted but not sounded. Some transmitters read plain ikhfāʾ or iẓhār; Abū Jaʿfar reads a complete idghām without the lip gesture.

xtj-010.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, bāb hāʾ al-kināya; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb hāʾ al-kināya
xtj-010.q: The rule is that the pronoun hāʾ has no silā (lengthening) after a sākin letter. What does Ḥafṣ do at the highlighted word, which breaks the rule?
o: He gives the hāʾ a silā of two ḥarakāt, although it follows the sākin yāʾ
He drops the silā and reads the hāʾ with sukūn
He reads the hāʾ with ḍamma and no silā
He reads a silā of six ḥarakāt
xtj-010.e: The general rule for Ḥafṣ is that a pronoun hāʾ between two vowelled letters gets silā, and one after a sākin letter does not. In this word he makes an exception and reads a silā ṣughrā (two ḥarakāt) after the sākin yāʾ, a unique case in his riwāya. The Shāṭibiyya treats it as a deliberate exception.

xtj-011.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, bāb hāʾ al-kināya; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr
xtj-011.q: The highlighted pronoun hāʾ stands between two vowelled letters. What is the reading of Ḥafṣ?
o: Ḍamma on the hāʾ without silā
Ḍamma on the hāʾ with a silā of two ḥarakāt
Kasra on the hāʾ with silā
xtj-011.e: By the general rule a pronoun hāʾ between two vowelled letters takes silā. Here Ḥafṣ reads the ḍamma without the silā (the hāʾ is short), another exception noted by the books on the hāʾ al-kināya. Other transmitters read it with silā, and others with sukūn.

xtj-012.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, bāb hāʾ al-kināya; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr
xtj-012.q: How does Ḥafṣ read the highlighted word?
o: With sukūn on the qāf and kasra on the hāʾ, without silā
With kasra on the qāf and a silā on the hāʾ
With sukūn on both the qāf and the hāʾ
With fatḥa on the qāf and ḍamma on the hāʾ
xtj-012.e: Ḥafṣ silences the qāf and gives the hāʾ a kasra without silā, so the word is shortened. Other transmitters read the qāf with kasra and give the hāʾ a silā, or use other vocalisations. This word is a standard example in the chapter on the pronoun hāʾ.

xtj-013.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, bāb hāʾ al-kināya; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xtj-013.q: How does Ḥafṣ read the hāʾ of the highlighted imperative (the same word occurs in 26:36)?
xtj-013.e: Ḥafṣ reads the hāʾ sākina, whereas other transmitters read it with a vowel, with silā, or with a hamza. The word is a notable example of the rule that pronoun hāʾ may be read with sukūn for lightness, and it must be learned as an exception.

xtj-014.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, bāb hāʾ al-kināya; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr
xtj-014.q: The highlighted verb ends in the pronoun hāʾ. Which of these statements about Ḥafṣ is correct?
o: The hāʾ is read with sukūn, as in the verb of 7:111
The hāʾ takes kasra and a silā because it follows a kasra
The hāʾ takes ḍamma without silā
xtj-014.e: By the general rule a pronoun hāʾ after a vowelled letter takes silā, but Ḥafṣ reads the sukūn, as in 7:111 and 26:36. Other transmitters read a vowel or a silā. Readers must therefore learn the three verbs together.

xtj-015.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, bāb hāʾ al-kināya; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr
xtj-015.q: The pronoun hāʾ of the highlighted word follows a yāʾ. What does Ḥafṣ read?
o: Ḍamma on the hāʾ, the original vowel, instead of the usual kasra
Kasra on the hāʾ, as the pronoun usually takes after yāʾ
xtj-015.e: The general rule is that a hāʾ after yāʾ or kasra takes a kasra. Ḥafṣ keeps the original ḍamma of the pronoun in this word (and in 18:63), where others change it to a kasra. The result also affects the next word: the lām of the name of God, following a ḍamma, is read heavy.

xtj-016.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-lāmāt; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya
xtj-016.q: In the reading of Ḥafṣ, how is the lām of the highlighted name of God pronounced when read continuously from the previous word (which ends in hāʾ with ḍamma)?
o: Heavy (tafkhīm), because it follows a ḍamma
Light (tarqīq), because the hāʾ is a soft letter
Light, because the previous word contains a yāʾ
Heavy only if one stops on the previous word
xtj-016.e: The lām of Allāh is heavy after fatḥa or ḍamma and light after kasra. Because Ḥafṣ reads the hāʾ of the previous word with ḍamma, the lām is heavy. A reader who read the previous hāʾ with kasra, as most transmitters do, would make the lām light. This is why such questions link the hāʾ rule to the rules of the lām.

xtj-017.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, bāb hāʾ al-kināya; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr
xtj-017.q: What is unusual about the highlighted word in the reading of Ḥafṣ?
o: The hāʾ keeps its original ḍamma although it follows a kasra and yāʾ
The word has a silā of six ḥarakāt
The word is read with imāla
The word is read with tashīl of its hamza
xtj-017.e: The pronoun hāʾ of this word follows a yāʾ, and the rule would give it a kasra. Ḥafṣ keeps the ḍamma, as in 48:10, because this is how his transmission is established. This is one of the very few places where the vowel of a pronoun hāʾ against the usual rule is a matter of transmission.

xtj-018.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, bāb al-hamzatayn min kalima; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr
xtj-018.q: How does Ḥafṣ read the double hamza of the highlighted word?
o: The second hamza is made easy (tashīl, between hamza and alif) without a lengthening alif between the two
Both hamzas are pronounced fully with an intervening alif
The second hamza is replaced by a full alif
xtj-018.e: In this word Ḥafṣ is exceptional: he reads tashīl of the second hamza without ādkhāl (the alif of separation), whereas other riwāyāt either read both hamzas (taḥqīq) or insert an alif. The muṣḥaf shows it with a small sign. It is the only place in his riwāya where two hamzas of one word are treated like this.

xtj-019.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, bāb al-fatḥ wa-l-imāla; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-imāla
xtj-019.q: What is special about the highlighted word in the riwāya of Ḥafṣ ʿan ʿĀṣim?
o: It is the only word where Ḥafṣ makes imāla (inclining the fatḥa and the alif toward kasra and yāʾ)
It is the only word where he reads madd of 6 ḥarakāt
It is the only word where he reads a sakta
It is the only word where he reads ishmām
xtj-019.e: In the riwāya of Ḥafṣ there is no imāla in the whole Quran except in this word, in the form of an imāla kubrā in the rāʾ and the alif after it. The muṣḥaf shows the imāla with a special mark below the rāʾ. Other readers (Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Khalaf) make imāla in many more words.

xtj-020.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, bāb al-nūn al-sākina; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī
xtj-020.q: The highlighted word contains a nūn sākina followed by yāʾ in the same word. How is it read?
o: With iẓhār muṭlaq (full clear pronunciation), because both letters are in one word
With idghām bi-ghunna, as for the nūn before yāʾ
xtj-020.e: The nūn before yāʾ, wāw, nūn or mīm is normally merged with ghunna, but not when nūn and yāʾ or wāw are in the same word: then the nūn is clearly pronounced so that the word does not become something else (‘buyyān’). Only four words are like this (dunyā, ṣinwān, qinwān, bunyān). The rule is called iẓhār muṭlaq.

xtj-021.src: al-Dānī, al-Taysīr; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb idghām al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa
xtj-021.q: The name of this letter ends in a nūn that is followed by the wāw of the oath. How does Ḥafṣ read it when continuing?
o: With iẓhār of the nūn (clear pronunciation)
With idghām bi-ghunna into the wāw
xtj-021.e: In the riwāya of Ḥafṣ the nūn of the letter-name is pronounced clearly before the wāw (and likewise the nūn of sīn in 36:1). Some other readers merge the nūn into the wāw. The reason given is that the letters are read as separate, spelled-out names, and no merging is allowed in the spelling.

xtj-022.q: How does Ḥafṣ read the nūn at the end of the name of the second letter in the highlighted word when the reading continues into the oath?
o: With iẓhār (the nūn is clearly pronounced)
With a lengthening of the nūn by six ḥarakāt
xtj-022.e: The nūn sākina is followed by a wāw, which would make an idghām by the general rule, but Ḥafṣ keeps it clear because the letters are spelled out separately. This reading is the same as in 68:1. Some other readers have an idghām here.

xtj-023.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-madd wa-l-qaṣr; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Tamhīd fī ʿIlm al-Tajwīd
xtj-023.q: Which order of the madd causes, from the strongest to the weakest, is the usual one in the books of tajwīd?
o: Lāzim, muttaṣil, ʿāriḍ lil-sukūn, munfaṣil, badal
Muttaṣil, lāzim, munfaṣil, ʿāriḍ lil-sukūn, badal
Badal, munfaṣil, ʿāriḍ lil-sukūn, muttaṣil, lāzim
Munfaṣil, muttaṣil, lāzim, badal, ʿāriḍ lil-sukūn
xtj-023.e: Scholars say the strongest cause is a lasting sukūn (madd lāzim), then the hamza in the same word (muttaṣil), then a temporary sukūn at waqf (ʿāriḍ), then the hamza in the next word (munfaṣil), and the weakest the madd badal. When two causes meet in one letter, the stronger prevails; the ranking is used to settle conflicts of length.

xtj-024.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-madd; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xtj-024.q: The highlighted word has a madd muttaṣil. Which lengths are permitted when the reader stops on it?
xtj-024.e: In waṣl Ḥafṣ reads muttaṣil with 4 or 5 ḥarakāt (and 6 in some ṭuruq). At waqf a second cause is added, the temporary sukūn, so the length may rise to 6, but it cannot fall below the length used in continuation, so 2 is not allowed. The three lengths 4, 5 and 6 are therefore the lengths allowed.

xtj-025.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb madd al-līn; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xtj-025.q: If the reader stops on the highlighted word, which lengths are allowed for the madd līn before the final consonant?
xtj-025.e: A sākin wāw or yāʾ after a fatḥa is a letter of līn, not a true madd letter. Before a temporary sukūn at waqf it may be lengthened with the same three lengths that apply to the madd ʿāriḍ lil-sukūn: 2, 4 or 6 ḥarakāt. It has no length in continuation.

xtj-026.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb madd al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī
xtj-026.q: What lengths does Ḥafṣ allow for the first letter of the highlighted group, whose name contains a līn letter followed by a lasting sukūn?
xtj-026.e: The name of this letter has a yāʾ of līn followed by a lasting sukūn on the nūn, so it takes a madd lāzim of the līn type. In the riwāya of Ḥafṣ it may be read with 4 (tawassuṭ) or 6 (ṭūl) ḥarakāt, whereas the other letters with a madd lāzim take 6. Both lengths are established and equally correct.

xtj-027.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb madd al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima
xtj-027.q: How many ḥarakāt does Ḥafṣ give to each of the two letters of the highlighted opening?
o: Two ḥarakāt each, a natural madd, since their names have no sākin letter after the madd
Six ḥarakāt each, a madd lāzim
Six for the first and two for the second
xtj-027.e: The five letters ḥ, y, ṭ, h and r (the group ‘ḥayy ṭuhur’) have names with a madd letter but no sukūn after it, so they are lengthened only two ḥarakāt (madd ṭabīʿī). The letters of the group ‘kam ʿasal naqṣ wa-qaraṣ’ have a madd lāzim of six, with ʿayn at four or six.

xtj-028.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb madd al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa
xtj-028.q: In the five letters of the highlighted opening, which two letters are given exactly two ḥarakāt of madd by Ḥafṣ?
o: The second and the third: hāʾ and yāʾ (letters of ‘ḥayy ṭuhur’)
The first and the fourth: kāf and ʿayn
The first and the last: kāf and ṣād
xtj-028.e: The five letters are kāf, hāʾ, yāʾ, ʿayn, ṣād. Kāf and ṣād have a madd lāzim of six; ʿayn has four or six; hāʾ and yāʾ have a natural madd of two ḥarakāt. The easiest way to learn this is the mnemonic of the groups of letters.

xtj-029.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, bāb al-madd; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xtj-029.q: What is the name of the madd in the highlighted word and how many ḥarakāt does it have?
o: Madd lāzim kalimī muthaqqal, six ḥarakāt
Madd muttaṣil, four or five ḥarakāt
Madd ʿāriḍ lil-sukūn, two, four or six ḥarakāt
Madd lāzim ḥarfī mukhaffaf, six ḥarakāt
xtj-029.e: The alif after the lām is followed by a lām with shadda, i.e. a lasting sukūn in the same word, so the madd is a lāzim kalimī; because the sukūn is a doubled letter, it is muthaqqal (heavy). It is six ḥarakāt by the agreement of the qurrāʾ. A lāzim ḥarfī belongs to the names of the letters at the openings of chapters.

xtj-030.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-madd; al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī
xtj-030.q: The madd letter in the highlighted word follows a hamza in the same word. What is it and how long does Ḥafṣ make it?
xtj-030.e: When the hamza precedes the madd letter in the same word it is a madd badal (so called because the madd letter replaces a second hamza in the original form). Ḥafṣ reads it with two ḥarakāt only, while Warsh may read it with two, four or six. The madd muttaṣil requires the hamza to come after the madd letter.

xtj-031.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-lāmāt; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya
xtj-031.q: When the reader continues from the end of 112:1 into 112:2, how is the lām of the highlighted name of God pronounced?
o: Light (tarqīq), because the preceding tanwīn is resolved with a kasra
Heavy (tafkhīm), because the preceding word ends in ḍamma
Heavy, because the lām follows a sākin letter
Light only if the reader makes a sakta
xtj-031.e: The tanwīn of the previous word meets the hamzat waṣl of the next, and the two sākin letters are resolved by a kasra on the tanwīn. The kasra, even if temporary, makes the lām of Allāh light. The lām is heavy only after a fatḥa or ḍamma.

xtj-032.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Tamhīd
xtj-032.q: The highlighted word ends in tanwīn, and the next verse begins with a hamzat waṣl. What happens to the tanwīn when the reader continues?
o: The tanwīn is resolved with a kasra on the nūn
The tanwīn is merged into the following letter
xtj-032.e: A sākin nūn of tanwīn meets the sākin lām of the article (after the hamza of waṣl is lost in continuation). The general rule is that the first sākin is given kasra to remove the cluster, so the tanwīn nūn is read with kasra. Other letters such as mīm al-jamʿ take ḍamma and min before al takes fatḥa.

xtj-033.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn; Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Ri'āya
xtj-033.q: Why does the nūn of the highlighted preposition take fatḥa before the article, whereas it takes kasra before most other words with hamzat waṣl?
o: Because three kasras in succession would be heavy, so the fatḥa is preferred before the article
Because the article is always preceded by fatḥa
Because the preposition is a noun
Because it follows a vowel letter
xtj-033.e: When min meets al, the nūn is sākin before the sākin lām, and the usual remedy would be a kasra. But the pronunciation would then have repeated kasras in ‘mini l-jinna’, so the Arabs and the qurrāʾ chose fatḥa for lightness. Before other words with hamzat waṣl, such as ibn, the kasra is kept.

xtj-034.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb mīm al-jamʿ; al-Dānī, al-Taysīr
xtj-034.q: How does Ḥafṣ read the mīm of the plural before the sākin lām of the article, as in the highlighted word?
o: With ḍamma on the mīm (in continuation)
With sukūn, merging into the lām
xtj-034.e: The mīm al-jamʿ was originally ḍamma plus a madd wāw (as in ‘ʿalaykumū’). When a sākin follows, the ḍamma is restored in place of the wāw. Some other readers give the mīm a kasra when it follows a kasra or yāʾ.

xtj-035.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn
xtj-035.q: What happens to the wāw of the group at the end of the highlighted verb when the reader continues into the next word, which starts with the article?
o: It is dropped in pronunciation, leaving ḍamma on the preceding letter
It is lengthened by six ḥarakāt
It is changed into a hamza
xtj-035.e: The wāw of the plural is a sākin madd letter and meets the sākin lām of the article after the hamza of waṣl has been dropped. A sākin madd letter is lost in speech when followed by a sākin (ḥadhf li-iltiqāʾ al-sākinayn), so the verb ends with the ḍamma only. In writing it stays, together with the alif that follows.

xtj-036.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, bāb al-rāʾāt; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr
xtj-036.q: If a reader begins at the highlighted word, how is the rāʾ sākina pronounced, and why?
o: Heavy (tafkhīm), because the kasra before it is temporary, belonging to the hamzat waṣl
Light (tarqīq), because it follows a kasra
Light, because it is followed by the letter jīm
Heavy, because it is followed by a letter of istiʿlāʾ
xtj-036.e: A rāʾ sākina after a kasra is normally light, provided that kasra belongs to the word itself and no letter of istiʿlāʾ follows. Here the kasra belongs to the added hamzat waṣl, not to the root; such a ʿāriḍ kasra does not count. The rāʾ is therefore heavy, as in other imperatives of this pattern.

xtj-037.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-idghām; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Tamhīd
xtj-037.q: What is the nature of the idghām in the highlighted word, where qāf meets kāf?
o: An idghām ṣaghīr nāqiṣ of mutaqāribayn: the qāf is merged into the kāf but keeps its elevation (istiʿlāʾ)
A complete idghām kāmil of mutajānisayn
An iẓhār because qāf and kāf are distant letters
xtj-037.e: Qāf and kāf are close in their articulation points (mutaqāribān) and not identical. Ḥafṣ merges the qāf into the kāf, but because qāf has istiʿlāʾ, a strong quality that the kāf lacks, the merge is incomplete and the sound of the qāf's height remains. The mark in the muṣḥaf is the shadda on the kāf.

xtj-038.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-ibtidāʾ; al-Dānī, al-Muktafā fī al-Waqf wa-l-Ibtidāʾ
xtj-038.q: With which vowel does a reader begin the highlighted verb, which starts with a hamzat waṣl?
o: With ḍamma, because the third letter has an original ḍamma
With kasra, as for all hamzat waṣl in verbs
With fatḥa, as for the article
xtj-038.e: In the beginning of a verb with a hamzat waṣl the vowel follows the third letter: if its vowel is ḍamma (original), start with ḍamma; if fatḥa or kasra, start with kasra. Here the third letter has ḍamma, so one starts with ḍamma. The beginning with a ḍamma is not allowed when the ḍamma is temporary.

xtj-039.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-ibtidāʾ; al-Dānī, al-Muktafā
xtj-039.q: With which vowel does a reader begin the highlighted imperative, which starts with a hamzat waṣl?
o: With kasra, because the third letter has kasra
With ḍamma, because the third letter has ḍamma
xtj-039.e: The vowel of the beginning is decided by the third letter of the verb. In this imperative the third letter, the rāʾ, has kasra, so the hamza is begun with kasra. Compare the verb of 12:9, where the third letter has ḍamma and the reader begins with ḍamma.

xtj-040.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, bāb al-ibtidāʾ; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima
xtj-040.q: With which vowel does a reader begin the highlighted imperative of the group, which starts with a hamzat waṣl?
o: With ḍamma, because the original vowel of the third letter is ḍamma
With kasra, because the second letter has a kasra
With fatḥa, because the second letter is sākin
xtj-040.e: The imperative is formed from the imperfect with ḍamma on its middle consonant, hence the third letter has an original ḍamma. The beginner uses ḍamma on the hamza to match, as in 12:9. The nūn and mīm are letters of the root and here the reader counts letters of the verb from the hamza.

xul-001.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, naw‘ 47 (al-nāsikh wa-l-mansūkh); al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān
xul-001.q: Which classification of naskh in the Quran is given by the scholars of the Quranic sciences?
o: Abrogation of the ruling while the wording remains; of the wording while the ruling remains; and of both the wording and the ruling
Abrogation of the Quran by earlier scriptures, by the Sunna, and by consensus alone
Abrogation of a verse by an interpretation, by a reading, or by a sūra
Abrogation only of the wording, since the rulings are never abrogated
xul-001.e: The books list three kinds: naskh al-ḥukm dūn al-tilāwa (the most common, as in the verse about the year’s waiting of widows), naskh al-tilāwa dūn al-ḥukm (as in the verse of stoning mentioned in ʿUmar’s statement, whose wording was lifted but the ruling stands), and naskh al-ḥukm wa-l-tilāwa together, for which reports are cited. The existence and the extent of each kind is discussed by the scholars.

xul-002.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Tafsīr (on 2:240); al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān
xul-002.q: The verse shown prescribes a year for widows, with provision and the right to stay. By which verse is it commonly said to be abrogated?
o: 2:234, which sets four months and ten days for widows
2:228, which sets three monthly courses for divorced women
65:4, which sets three months for women who no longer have courses
xul-002.e: A well-known report in al-Bukhārī has Ibn al-Zubayr asking ʿUthmān why he included this verse, as it had been abrogated by the other; the answer was that he would not change anything from its place. Most commentators say the waiting period was reduced to four months and ten days. Some, like Mujāhid, held that the right to residence remained.

xul-003.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Tafsīr (on 8:65–66); al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān
xul-003.q: The verse shown sets the ratio of twenty believers to two hundred unbelievers. What follows in the next verse, according to Ibn ʿAbbās?
o: A reduction of the ratio, so that a hundred patient believers should face two hundred
An increase to a hundred against one
A cancellation of the duty of fighting
A prohibition of fighting in all circumstances
xul-003.e: A report in al-Bukhārī from Ibn ʿAbbās says that the command to stand against ten times as many was lightened by God, who knew their weakness, to two times. The reduction is commonly cited as an example of naskh al-ḥukm in the Quran, though some scholars speak of takhfīf (alleviation) rather than abrogation.

xul-004.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Tafsīr and Kitāb al-Ṣawm; Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Ṣiyām (hadith of Salama ibn al-Akwaʿ); al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān
xul-004.q: The verse shown mentions a fidya for ‘those who are able to fast’. What is the disagreement, as recorded in the reports?
o: Salama ibn al-Akwaʿ reported that the option to pay fidya instead of fasting was abrogated by the next verse, whereas Ibn ʿAbbās said the verse is not abrogated and applies to the old who cannot fast
All Companions agreed that the verse was fully abrogated
All Companions agreed that the verse remains for everyone
Ibn ʿAbbās held it abrogated and Salama held it permanent
xul-004.e: In the account of Salama, when the verse was revealed, whoever wished could break the fast and feed a poor person until the following verse abrogated it. Ibn ʿAbbās, in al-Bukhārī, said that it was not abrogated but is for the old man and woman who are unable to fast. Both are reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ collections, and the jurists usually combine them by holding that the fidya remains for the permanently unable.

xul-005.src: al-Tirmidhī, Jāmiʿ, Kitāb al-Tafsīr (on Sūrat al-Mujādila); al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān
xul-005.q: The verse shown asks believers who speak privately with the Messenger to give something first. What happened to this rule?
o: It was lifted by the next verse; a report says that ʿAlī was the only one who acted on it before it was abrogated
It was made obligatory for ever
It was moved to the verse on the Hajj
It was never revealed in Madīna
xul-005.e: The following verse relieves the believers of the duty to give charity before speaking with the Prophet, after they hesitated for fear of poverty. A report from ʿAlī in al-Tirmidhī says that he alone acted on the verse. It is a standard example of the abrogation of a ruling with a short life, and of the combination of a command with its relief.

xul-006.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Ḥudūd (ʿUmar’s sermon); Mālik, al-Muwaṭṭaʾ, Kitāb al-Ḥudūd; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān
xul-006.q: What is the classical example of naskh al-tilāwa dūn al-ḥukm (abrogation of the wording with the ruling remaining)?
o: The ‘verse of stoning’, mentioned in ʿUmar’s address, whose wording is not in the muṣḥaf but whose ruling the Prophet carried out
The verse on the year’s waiting for widows
The reduction of the ratio of fighters
xul-006.e: In his address in Madīna, ʿUmar warned that people might say they did not find stoning in the Book, and affirmed that the Prophet and his successors stoned adulterers and that the verse had been recited. Scholars therefore cite it as an example of a wording lifted while the ruling stays. Some scholars, among them some Muʿtazilīs and Khawārij, reject the idea.

xul-007.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 47; Shāh Walī Allāh al-Dihlawī, al-Fawz al-Kabīr fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr; Ibn al-Jawzī, Nawāsikh al-Qurʾān
xul-007.q: How did scholars differ over the number of abrogated verses in the Quran?
o: Earlier writers listed many, sometimes over a hundred verses; al-Suyūṭī accepted about twenty; Shāh Walī Allāh reduced them to about five
All scholars agree there are exactly twenty-one
All scholars agree there are none
xul-007.e: Early authors, using a broad sense of naskh that included restriction, specification and alleviation, counted a large number. Al-Suyūṭī, in al-Itqān, kept only about twenty. Shāh Walī Allāh al-Dihlawī, treating many cases as takhṣīṣ or tafsīr, reduced the list to five. The variation shows that the dispute is about the definition of naskh more than about the verses.

xul-008.src: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī, al-Tafsīr al-Kabīr, on 2:106; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 47
xul-008.q: Which scholar of the 4th century AH is known for denying that abrogation occurs in the Quran, limiting what others call naskh to specification?
xul-008.e: Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī (d. 322 AH), a commentator of Muʿtazilī leanings, argued that nothing in the Quran is abrogated, interpreting the supposed cases as specification (takhṣīṣ) or time-limited rulings. His view is reported and rebutted by al-Rāzī and others, and is a minority position. The other scholars in the options wrote in favour of naskh.

xul-009.src: al-Shāfiʿī, al-Risāla, bāb al-nāsikh wa-l-mansūkh; al-Sarakhsī, Uṣūl al-Sarakhsī; al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā
xul-009.q: Which statement correctly gives the position of al-Shāfiʿī, as contrasted with that of the Ḥanafī school, on abrogation between the Quran and the Sunna?
o: Al-Shāfiʿī held that the Quran is not abrogated by the Sunna, only by the Quran, while the Ḥanafīs allowed an established (mutawātir or mashhūr) Sunna to abrogate the Quran
Al-Shāfiʿī held that the Sunna abrogates the Quran and the Ḥanafīs denied it
Both denied any abrogation across the two sources
Both allowed any single report to abrogate the Quran
xul-009.e: In al-Risāla, al-Shāfiʿī argued that God abrogates His Book only by His Book, and that the Sunna cannot cancel the Quran, since it merely explains it. The Ḥanafīs, who classify the mashhūr Sunna as a strong proof, permitted its abrogating a general Quranic ruling, as an example of the relation of takhṣīṣ. Both agree that a single report (khabar al-wāḥid) does not abrogate the Quran.

xul-010.src: al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān, naw‘ 31 (al-nāsikh wa-l-mansūkh); al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān
xul-010.q: What distinguishes naskh from takhṣīṣ (specification) in the classical works?
o: Naskh removes a ruling for the future after it had been in force for everything it covered; takhṣīṣ shows that part of the general wording was never meant
Naskh applies to reports, takhṣīṣ to commands only
Naskh needs a later date, takhṣīṣ needs a Companion’s statement
xul-010.e: Takhṣīṣ clarifies that a general text never included part of what it seems to cover, and can be done by a text that comes earlier, together with or later than it. Naskh lifts a ruling that applied from a given point and needs a later abrogating text. Naskh is confined to commands and prohibitions, not to reports of facts.

xul-011.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 47; Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Īḍāḥ li-Nāsikh al-Qurʾān wa-Mansūkhih; Ibn Ḥazm, al-Nāsikh wa-l-Mansūkh
xul-011.q: By which means do the scholars say that abrogation may be established?
o: By a clear statement of the Prophet or of a Companion, by knowing which text came later, or by consensus; not by the opinion of a commentator alone
By the preference of the commentator
By the number of verses in a sūra
By the order of the sūras in the muṣḥaf
xul-011.e: Al-Suyūṭī and others say that abrogation is known by report (from the Prophet or a Companion who states that a verse abrogated another), by knowing the chronology of revelation, or by the community’s agreement. It cannot be decided by ijtihād, or by the order of the verses in the muṣḥaf, since the order of the muṣḥaf is not the order of revelation.

xul-012.src: Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Īḍāḥ li-Nāsikh al-Qurʾān wa-Mansūkhih; Abū ʿUbayd, al-Nāsikh wa-l-Mansūkh; Ibn al-Jawzī, Nawāsikh al-Qurʾān
xul-012.q: Which work on abrogation by Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib is a standard classical source, alongside the works of Abū ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Jawzī?
xul-012.e: Makkī (d. 437 AH) of Qayrawān and Córdoba wrote al-Īḍāḥ li-Nāsikh al-Qurʾān wa-Mansūkhih. Several of his other works are on qirāʾāt and tajwīd (al-Kashf, al-Riʿāya) and on tafsīr (al-Hidāya). Abū ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Jawzī (Nawāsikh al-Qurʾān) wrote earlier and later works on the same topic.

xul-013.src: al-Bāqillānī, Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 64 (iʿjāz al-Qurʾān)
xul-013.q: The verse shown challenges the unbelievers to produce ten sūras. What is the usual order of the challenges in the Quran, according to the scholars?
o: The whole Quran (17:88), then ten sūras (11:13), then one sūra (10:38), then one sūra again in Madīna (2:23)
One sūra first, then ten sūras, then the whole Quran
Ten sūras first, then the whole Quran, then one sūra
Only the whole Quran was ever required
xul-013.e: Commentators note a descent in the challenge: first to the whole Quran, with men and jinn together; then ten sūras; then a single sūra in the Meccan period and again in the Madinan period. The sequence is used to argue that the challenge applied to even the smallest portion, a sūra.

xul-014.src: al-Bāqillānī, Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān, refutation of the ṣarfa; al-Khaṭṭābī, Bayān Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān
xul-014.q: What is the view called ṣarfa on the inimitability of the Quran, and who held it?
o: That God turned people away from imitating the Quran though they would otherwise have been able; held by al-Naẓẓām and some Muʿtazilīs and rejected by most scholars
That the Quran is inimitable only for its rhyme; held by al-Bāqillānī
That the Quran can be imitated but no one tried; held by al-Jurjānī
That the Quran is inimitable only for its prophecies; held by al-Khaṭṭābī
xul-014.e: The ṣarfa theory, attributed to Ibrāhīm al-Naẓẓām and later to others, held that the Arabs were able to produce a text like it but God took away their ability. Most scholars, including al-Bāqillānī, al-Khaṭṭābī and al-Jurjānī, rejected it, saying the inimitability is in the Quran itself, in its composition and meanings. They noted that if the Arabs had been merely prevented, the Quran would not have been a miracle in itself.

xul-015.src: al-Rummānī, al-Nukat fī Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 64
xul-015.q: In his al-Nukat fī Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān, how does al-Rummānī describe the aspects of inimitability?
o: He lists seven, including leaving the challenge unanswered, the challenge to all, the ṣarfa, eloquence, true reports of the future, the breaking of the norm, and comparison with other miracles
xul-015.e: Al-Rummānī (d. 384 AH) said that inimitability appears in seven aspects: abandonment of the challenge despite strong motives, the challenge to all people, ṣarfa, balāgha, true reports about the future, breaking of the norm, and comparison with other signs. That he includes the ṣarfa among the aspects, alongside eloquence, was criticised by later scholars who insisted on the Quran’s intrinsic quality.

xul-016.src: al-Suyūṭī, Muʿtarak al-Aqrān fī Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān
xul-016.q: Who wrote Muʿtarak al-Aqrān fī Iʿjāz al-Qurʾān, a large study of the inimitability of the Quran?
xul-016.e: Al-Suyūṭī (d. 911 AH) wrote Muʿtarak al-Aqrān, a work on the inimitability of the Quran, in addition to the encyclopaedic al-Itqān. Al-Zarkashī is the author of al-Burhān, a main source of al-Itqān; Ibn Qutayba wrote Taʾwīl Mushkil al-Qurʾān; and al-Rāghib is the author of al-Mufradāt.

xul-017.src: al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān
xul-017.q: How many branches (anwāʿ) does al-Suyūṭī’s al-Itqān discuss, and how many does al-Zarkashī’s al-Burhān?
o: Eighty in al-Itqān and forty-seven in al-Burhān
Forty-seven in al-Itqān and eighty in al-Burhān
xul-017.e: Al-Zarkashī (d. 794 AH) divided al-Burhān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān into forty-seven types, and al-Suyūṭī (d. 911 AH), building on it and on al-Balqīnī’s work, arranged al-Itqān in eighty types. The latter is the standard textbook in the Quranic sciences.

xul-018.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 9 (asbāb al-nuzūl); al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān; al-Shāṭibī, al-Muwāfaqāt
xul-018.q: Which principle do most scholars follow when a verse was revealed for a specific occasion but is worded generally?
o: The consideration is with the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion
The consideration is with the specificity of the occasion alone
The verse applies only to the persons of the occasion
The verse is abrogated after the occasion
xul-018.e: The majority of uṣūlīs and commentators say that the ruling of a general text applies to all cases it covers, and the cause serves to explain and to show that this case is definitely included. Some scholars, a small group, held that it is limited to the occasion. The principle is cited in the discussion of asbāb al-nuzūl in al-Itqān.

xul-019.src: Ibn Taymiyya, Muqaddima fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 9; al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān
xul-019.q: What caution does Ibn Taymiyya give about the wording ‘this verse was revealed concerning such-and-such’ in the reports of the Companions and Successors?
o: It may mean that the verse includes the case, as an explanation, not necessarily that this was the actual cause that led to its revelation
It always means a precise chronological cause
It always means the verse is abrogated
It always indicates a late addition to the text
xul-019.e: In the Muqaddima fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr, Ibn Taymiyya says that the Companions and Successors often said ‘this verse was revealed about so-and-so’ meaning that the verse covers it, like a tafsīr. A report is therefore treated as a true cause only if it is stated that the event happened and the verse came in reply. This clarifies why some reports of asbāb contradict each other without contradiction.

xul-020.src: al-Wāḥidī, Asbāb al-Nuzūl; al-Suyūṭī, Lubāb al-Nuqūl fī Asbāb al-Nuzūl
xul-020.q: Which pair of authors and works on asbāb al-nuzūl is correct?
o: al-Wāḥidī: Asbāb al-Nuzūl; al-Suyūṭī: Lubāb al-Nuqūl fī Asbāb al-Nuzūl
al-Wāḥidī: Lubāb al-Nuqūl; al-Suyūṭī: Asbāb al-Nuzūl
Ibn Ḥajar: Asbāb al-Nuzūl; al-Wāḥidī: al-Itqān
xul-020.e: Al-Wāḥidī al-Nīsābūrī (d. 468 AH) wrote the best-known classical collection of reports about the occasions of revelation, often criticised for including weak reports; al-Suyūṭī (d. 911 AH) wrote Lubāb al-Nuqūl, a book of sounder reports in an abridged form. Ibn Ḥajar also wrote on the topic in other works.

xul-021.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 1 (al-makkī wa-l-madanī); al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān, naw‘ 3
xul-021.q: By which three criteria do scholars distinguish Makkan from Madinan revelation, and which is most widely used?
o: By time (before or after the Hijra), by place, and by the addressee; the criterion of time is the most widely used
By length, by rhyme and by theme; theme is most used
By the Companion who reported it, by the reader and by the chain; the chain is most used
By the first word, the last word and the middle word; the first word is most used
xul-021.e: The three criteria are the time (Makkan is what was revealed before the Hijra, even if outside Makka), the place (what was revealed in Makka and surroundings) and the addressee (those addressed). The first is most widely accepted because it divides the entire Quran. On the time criterion, verses revealed during the journey of the Hijra or at Ḥudaybiya and the conquest are Madinan.

xul-022.q: Which features do the classical works associate with Makkan sūras rather than Madinan ones, as general tendencies and not strict rules?
o: The call ‘O people’, the word kallā (nay), short verses with strong rhythm, and themes of tawḥīd, resurrection and stories of earlier prophets
Long legal passages about inheritance, fasting and warfare
The call ‘O you who believe’ throughout
Rules on the Hajj and on treaties with the People of the Book
xul-022.e: The scholars identify tendencies: Makkan sūras use ‘O people’ (and not ‘O you who believe’), kallā, oaths and short, rhythmic verses, and deal with belief, afterlife and earlier nations. Madinan sūras have longer verses, legal rulings (inheritance, fasting, jihad, hypocrites) and address the believers and the People of the Book. Exceptions exist, as with 22:77.

xul-023.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 1; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on Sūrat al-Fātiḥa
xul-023.q: Which statement correctly describes the scholarly record on whether Sūrat al-Fātiḥa is Makkan or Madinan?
o: The majority hold it is Makkan; some reports (from Abū Hurayra and Mujāhid) say Madinan; and some say it was revealed twice
All scholars agree it is Madinan
All scholars agree it is Makkan
No scholar has ever discussed it
xul-023.e: Al-Suyūṭī records three views: Makkan (the majority, since prayer was already established with it in Makka), Madinan (a report attributed to Abū Hurayra and Mujāhid), and a view that it was revealed twice, once in each city. The first is preferred because the opening sūra is associated with the early period of prayer.

xul-024.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Tafsīr (on 4:176 and Sūrat Barāʾa); al-Nasāʾī, Sunan; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 3 (ākhir mā nazala)
xul-024.q: Different reports name the last verse or sūra revealed. Which statement correctly pairs the reports with their narrators?
o: Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have named the verse shown (about guarding against a Day of return to God); al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib named the last verse of al-Nisāʾ and Barāʾa as the last complete sūra
ʿUmar named Sūrat al-Fātiḥa and al-Barāʾ named al-Ikhlāṣ
All named Sūrat al-Naṣr as a verse
xul-024.e: The sources preserve several statements. Ibn ʿAbbās is quoted for 2:281 (in one report, the last before the Prophet’s death, about nine nights before); al-Barāʾ for 4:176 as the last verse and Barāʾa as the last complete sūra (al-Bukhārī). Scholars reconcile these by taking each as ‘last’ in a particular subject or by the narrator’s knowledge.

xul-025.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Badʾ al-Waḥy and Kitāb al-Tafsīr; Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 3
xul-025.q: How do most scholars reconcile ʿĀʾisha’s report that the first revelation was ‘Read!’ with Jābir’s report that al-Muddaththir was first?
o: ‘Read!’ was the first revelation overall, and al-Muddaththir the first after the interval (fatra) in revelation, or the first revealed for the call to warn
Al-Muddaththir was the first revelation and ‘Read!’ the second, and ʿĀʾisha’s report is rejected
The two reports describe different prophets
Both refer to the first verse of al-Fātiḥa
xul-025.e: Ibn Ḥajar and others say that Jābir’s narration, which has the Prophet describing the angel appearing again after a pause, refers to what came after the interval, and not the very first revelation, which is the beginning of Sūrat al-ʿAlaq as in ʿĀʾisha’s report. This is the majority harmonisation; other views place al-Fātiḥa or al-Muzzammil first.

xul-026.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 43 (al-muḥkam wa-l-mutashābih); al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān; al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān
xul-026.q: The verse shown calls the whole Quran mutashābih (alike), while 3:7 divides it into muḥkam and mutashābih verses. How do scholars reconcile these?
o: The Quran is muḥkam in the sense of being precise and flawless (11:1), mutashābih in the sense of its parts resembling one another in excellence (39:23), and in 3:7 mutashābih means the verses whose meaning is not immediately clear
They are contradictory and one is abrogated
Both words have exactly the same meaning in all three verses
Only the Torah is muḥkam, the Quran is mutashābih
xul-026.e: Al-Suyūṭī gives three states: the whole Quran is muḥkam (perfected and without flaw), it is wholly mutashābih (the parts agree with each other in beauty and truth), and in 3:7 it is divided into verses that are clear and others that need reference to the clear. The wording in each verse is different, hence no conflict.

xul-027.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 17 (ʿadad suwar al-Qurʾān); al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān; Ibn Manẓūr, Lisān al-ʿArab, entry sūr
xul-027.q: Which two origins do lexicographers and scholars of the Quranic sciences give for the word sūra?
o: From sūr, an enclosure or wall of a city, because the sūra encloses its verses; or from sūra without hamza, meaning rank or high degree
From sawr, a bull, or from sūra, a picture
From Hebrew and from Persian only
From siyāra, a caravan, or from sūd, a flock
xul-027.e: The word may be taken as sūr (like the enclosure of a town), since each sūra encloses a set of verses, or as sūra in the sense of a high rank, since its verses are raised above others. Both senses are listed and one need not exclude the other. The word is used for the sūras of the Quran in the Quran itself (24:1; 10:38).

xul-028.src: Abū Dāwūd, Sunan, Kitāb al-Ṣalāh (the hadith of Aws ibn Ḥudhayfa); Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān
xul-028.q: What are the seven manāzil of the Quran, associated with the mnemonic ‘fa-mī bi-shawq’?
o: Seven divisions beginning with the sūras al-Fātiḥa, al-Māʾida, Yūnus, al-Isrāʾ, al-Shuʿarāʾ, al-Ṣāffāt and Qāf
Seven divisions beginning with al-Baqara, Āl ʿImrān, al-Nisāʾ, al-Māʾida, al-Anʿām, al-Aʿrāf and al-Anfāl
Seven divisions of equal length of 30 sūras each
Seven divisions by the seven readers
xul-028.e: The mnemonic gives the first letters of the opening sūras of the seven daily portions (fā for al-Fātiḥa, mīm for al-Māʾida, yāʾ for Yūnus, bāʾ for Banī Isrāʾīl, shīn for al-Shuʿarāʾ, wāw for al-Ṣāffāt, qāf for Qāf), according to a report from Aws ibn Ḥudhayfa that the Companions divided the Quran this way for a weekly recitation.

xul-029.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 17; Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, Musnad (hadith of Wāthila ibn al-Asqaʿ); al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān
xul-029.q: Which sūras make up the ‘seven long ones’ (al-sabʿ al-ṭiwal), and what is disputed about them?
o: al-Baqara, Āl ʿImrān, al-Nisāʾ, al-Māʾida, al-Anʿām, al-Aʿrāf and a seventh disputed between Yūnus and al-Anfāl with al-Tawba taken together
al-Fātiḥa, al-Baqara, Yūsuf, al-Kahf, Maryam, Ṭā Hā and al-Ikhlāṣ
The seven longest sūras in Makkan revelation only
xul-029.e: A report associated with Wāthila ibn al-Asqaʿ lists the ṭiwāl, the miʾūn, the mathānī and the mufaṣṣal. The first six of the long ones are agreed; the seventh is either Yūnus or al-Anfāl with Barāʾa treated as one (the reason why there is no basmala between them). The division belongs to the early classification of the Quran by length.

xul-030.src: al-Dānī, al-Bayān fī ʿAdd Āy al-Qurʾān; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 17
xul-030.q: Which verse count is followed by the standard Ḥafṣ muṣḥaf, and what total does it give?
o: The Kufan count, with 6,236 verses; it numbers the basmala of al-Fātiḥa as a verse
The Madinan count, with 6,000 verses exactly
xul-030.e: The Kufan count, traced through Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī to ʿAlī, is used in the common Ḥafṣ muṣḥaf and totals 6,236. In this count the basmala is a verse of al-Fātiḥa. Other cities count slightly differently, as the Madinan, Makkan, Syrian and Basran counts. The figure of 6,666 is popular but not a count of any city.

xul-031.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 43 (fawātiḥ al-suwar); al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān, naw‘ 18
xul-031.q: How many sūras begin with the disjointed letters (al-ḥurūf al-muqaṭṭaʿa), and how many different letters occur?
o: Twenty-nine sūras; fourteen different letters, half of the Arabic alphabet
xul-031.e: The classical works count twenty-nine sūras with such openings, using fourteen different letters, which is half of the twenty-eight letters of the alphabet. Some openings are one letter (ṣād, qāf, nūn), others two to five letters. Al-Suyūṭī and al-Zarkashī discuss the many views on their meaning.

xul-032.src: al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on Sūrat al-Baqara; Ibn Taymiyya, Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 43
xul-032.q: Which view on the disjointed letters is associated with al-Zamakhsharī and, in a related form, with Ibn Taymiyya?
o: That they are a pointer to the inimitability: the Quran is made of the same letters as the Arabs’ speech, yet they could not produce the like
That they are the secret known to God alone, so nothing can be said about them
That they are the names of the angels
That they are the initials of the transmitters
xul-032.e: Among the views are: secrets known only to God (Abū Bakr, ʿAlī and Ibn Masʿūd, in reports); names of sūras; oaths; names of God; and an allusion to the challenge. Al-Zamakhsharī, following some earlier grammarians, took them as showing that the Quran is composed of ordinary letters and yet inimitable; Ibn Taymiyya supports this reading for most openings. The scholars of the schools avoid certainty.

xul-033.src: Ibn Qutayba, Taʾwīl Mushkil al-Qurʾān; Ibn Qutayba, Gharīb al-Qurʾān
xul-033.q: What is Ibn Qutayba’s Taʾwīl Mushkil al-Qurʾān?
o: A defence of the Quran against alleged contradictions and difficulties in language and meaning, with a study of figurative usage
A collection of the occasions of revelation
A work of tajwīd for beginners
xul-033.e: Ibn Qutayba (d. 276 AH) wrote this work in reply to those who found contradiction or errors in the Quran, discussing figurative usage, rare words, variant readings and apparent contradictions with the aid of Arabic poetry and usage. It is a foundation for the later literature on mushkil al-Qurʾān. His Gharīb al-Qurʾān is a separate book of rare words.

xul-034.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 16 (kayfiyyat inzāl al-Qurʾān); al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 2:185; al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān
xul-034.q: Which account of the descent of the Quran is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and favoured by many scholars?
o: It came down all at once to the lowest heaven on Laylat al-Qadr, then was revealed in parts to the Prophet over about twenty-three years
It came down in parts only, with no earlier stage
It was first revealed in Madīna
It was revealed all at once to the Prophet on Laylat al-Qadr
xul-034.e: In the reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, the Quran was sent down as a whole to bayt al-ʿizza in the lowest heaven, and then to the Prophet gradually as events required. Al-Shaʿbī and others said the revelation began on Laylat al-Qadr and then continued. Both views explain the verse mentioning the month in which the Quran was sent down.

xul-035.src: Abū Dāwūd, Sunan, Kitāb al-Ṣalāh (bāb man jahara bi-hā); al-Tirmidhī, Jāmiʿ, Kitāb al-Tafsīr (Sūrat al-Tawba); al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 17
xul-035.q: What reason did ʿUthmān give, in the report preserved in Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī, for placing al-Anfāl and Barāʾa together without a basmala between them?
o: Barāʾa resembled al-Anfāl in its subject, and the Prophet died without having said whether it was part of it, so he joined them without a basmala
The Prophet explicitly ordered that no basmala be written
The two sūras had been revealed at the same hour
The scribes ran out of space
xul-035.e: Ibn ʿAbbās asked ʿUthmān why he placed al-Anfāl (among the early Madinan sūras) next to Barāʾa (among the last), without a basmala. He replied that the Prophet died without explaining Barāʾa, and that its story resembled that of al-Anfāl, so he considered it part of it. Others explain that the Companions did not write a basmala at the start of Barāʾa because of its theme of severing treaties.

xul-036.src: Ibn Rushd, Bidāyat al-Mujtahid, Kitāb al-Ṣalāh (basmala in the Fātiḥa); al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 17; al-Nawawī, al-Majmūʿ
xul-036.q: Which statement correctly describes the views of the schools on whether the basmala is a verse of al-Fātiḥa?
o: The Shāfiʿīs count it as a verse of al-Fātiḥa, whereas the Mālikīs do not count it as a verse of al-Fātiḥa or of any sūra other than al-Naml
All schools count it as a verse of every sūra
All schools deny it is a part of any sūra
The Ḥanafīs say it is a part of al-Fātiḥa, the Shāfiʿīs deny it
xul-036.e: The Shāfiʿīs and the Kufan and Makkan counts treat the basmala as a verse of al-Fātiḥa (and, in one view, of every sūra), so they recite it in prayer. The Mālikīs hold it is not a verse of al-Fātiḥa or of the other sūras, but part of al-Naml (27:30); the Ḥanafīs hold it a verse of the Quran revealed to separate the sūras. The difference lies behind their practice of reciting it aloud or silently.

xul-037.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 18 (tartīb al-āyāt wa-l-suwar); al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān; al-Bāqillānī, al-Intiṣār li-l-Qurʾān
xul-037.q: What do the classical works record on whether the order of the verses and of the sūras in the muṣḥaf is divinely fixed (tawqīfī)?
o: The order of the verses within each sūra is tawqīfī by consensus; for the order of the sūras there are three views: tawqīfī, the Companions’ ijtihād, or a mixture
Both orders were decided by ʿUthmān alone with no precedent
Both orders were settled by a vote of the Companions
Both orders follow the order of revelation exactly
xul-037.e: Al-Suyūṭī records that the arrangement of verses is divinely taught and the scholars agree on it. For the sūras, some say the Prophet arranged them, as shown by his reciting several sūras in order; others, such as Mālik and (in one report) al-Bāqillānī, held that the Companions arranged them by ijtihād; and a third view takes some as taught and some as arranged. The muṣḥaf order is not the order of revelation.

xul-038.src: al-Dānī, al-Bayān fī ʿAdd Āy al-Qurʾān; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān
xul-038.q: Who wrote al-Bayān fī ʿAdd Āy al-Qurʾān, the classical work on the counting of the verses by the cities of Islam?
xul-038.e: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī (d. 444 AH) of Dāniya in Spain wrote al-Bayān, which sets out the verse counts transmitted by the people of Madīna, Makka, Kūfa, Baṣra and Shām. Al-Shāṭibī versified other works of his; Ibn al-Jazarī wrote on qirāʾāt, and al-Zarkashī on the sciences of the Quran.

xul-039.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, naw‘ 16; Abū ʿUbayd, Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān; Ibn Qutayba, Taʾwīl Mushkil al-Qurʾān; al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, introduction
xul-039.q: Which scholar is associated with the view that the seven aḥruf are seven dialects of the Arabs, whereas another scholar understood them as seven kinds of difference in the wording?
o: Abū ʿUbayd for the dialects; Ibn Qutayba for the seven kinds of difference
Ibn Qutayba for the dialects; Abū ʿUbayd for the kinds of difference
Al-Ṭabarī for the dialects; al-Bāqillānī for the kinds of difference
Al-Zarkashī for the dialects; al-Suyūṭī for the kinds of difference
xul-039.e: Abū ʿUbayd al-Qāsim ibn Sallām (d. 224 AH) took the aḥruf as seven dialects of the Arabs, such as Quraysh, Hudhayl and Hawāzin. Ibn Qutayba (d. 276 AH) understood them as seven aspects of differences in the readings (in the form of nouns, verbs, iʿrāb, order, substitution and so on). Al-Suyūṭī lists about forty views.

xul-040.src: al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, introduction (on the aḥruf and ʿUthmān’s collection); Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr; Abū Shāma, al-Murshid al-Wajīz
xul-040.q: Which scholar held that ʿUthmān’s copies preserved a single ḥarf of the seven, and who disagreed?
o: Al-Ṭabarī held that the community was united on a single ḥarf; Ibn al-Jazarī and many others held the copies preserve whatever of the aḥruf was established in the final presentation
Ibn al-Jazarī held it was a single ḥarf; al-Ṭabarī held all seven
Abū Shāma held the copies had no ḥarf of the seven
Both held that the seven aḥruf were written in the copies as separate texts
xul-040.e: In his introduction al-Ṭabarī argued that the permission to read in seven aḥruf was a facility that ended when ʿUthmān united the community on the single ḥarf of Quraysh in order to prevent strife. Ibn al-Jazarī, Abū Shāma and many later scholars held that the copies include whatever of the aḥruf was established in the final presentation, with the dotless rasm allowing several readings.

xuf-001.src: al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Āmidī, al-Iḥkām fī Uṣūl al-Aḥkām; al-Shīrāzī, al-Lumaʿ
xuf-001.q: What do most uṣūlīs hold about an unqualified command (amr) such as an imperative with no accompanying indication?
o: That it indicates obligation (wujūb) unless an indication shows otherwise
That it always indicates only recommendation
That it indicates nothing until the Prophet explains it
xuf-001.e: The majority of the Shāfiʿī, Ḥanafī, Mālikī and Ḥanbalī uṣūlīs hold that the bare imperative form indicates obligation by default, shifting to recommendation, permission or other senses only through a contextual indication (qarīna). Some held it indicates recommendation as the certain minimum, and others suspended judgment (waqf), and the discussion appears in all the major manuals.

xuf-002.src: al-Shīrāzī, al-Lumaʿ; al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Zarkashī, al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ
xuf-002.q: What is the majority position on a prohibition (nahy) in the Sharia texts?
o: That it indicates prohibition (taḥrīm) unless an indication shifts it to disapproval (karāha) or another sense
That it indicates the act is valid
xuf-002.e: Most uṣūlīs hold that the form of prohibition by default indicates unlawfulness, as the imperative indicates obligation by default. The debate also covers whether prohibition requires the invalidity of the act (fasād): the majority hold that a prohibition on an act in itself or its essential part indicates invalidity, while the Ḥanafīs distinguish a prohibition based on an extraneous attribute, which makes the act valid but blameworthy.

xuf-003.src: al-Sarakhsī, Uṣūl al-Sarakhsī; al-Bazdawī, Kanz al-Wuṣūl; al-Āmidī, al-Iḥkām
xuf-003.q: How do the Ḥanafīs and the majority differ on a general text (ʿāmm) whose scope has been restricted?
o: The Ḥanafīs held a general text indicates its scope definitively (qaṭʿī) until restricted by a connected indication, while the majority treat it as probable (ẓannī) even before restriction
The Ḥanafīs held a general text is always probable, and the majority held it definitive
Both held the general text has no scope
Both held a general text can never be restricted
xuf-003.e: In Ḥanafī uṣūl the ʿāmm is definitive in what it covers (like the khāṣṣ) unless it has been restricted by an independent text of equal strength which came together with it. For the majority (Shāfiʿī, Mālikī, Ḥanbalī), the ʿāmm is a probable indication because the possibility of restriction (takhṣīṣ) is always present, so a sound single-narrator report can restrict it. This accounts for several branch disagreements.

xuf-004.src: al-Zarkashī, al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ; al-Āmidī, al-Iḥkām; al-Shīrāzī, al-Lumaʿ
xuf-004.q: What is the Shāfiʿī and general position when an unrestricted text (muṭlaq) and a restricted one (muqayyad) concern the same ruling and the same cause?
o: The muṭlaq is read as the muqayyad, by agreement of most
The later text cancels the earlier one in all cases
xuf-004.e: When a text states a ruling without a qualification and another states the same ruling with a qualification, the scholars agree to read the unrestricted one in the light of the restricted when both the ruling and the cause are the same. When the ruling differs, they disagree: the Shāfiʿīs often carry the muṭlaq on the muqayyad through analogical common ground (as in the question of a believing slave in expiation), while the Ḥanafīs generally refuse.

xuf-005.src: al-Āmidī, al-Iḥkām; al-Sarakhsī, Uṣūl; al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Shīrāzī, al-Lumaʿ
xuf-005.q: How do the schools differ on the argument from the converse meaning (mafhūm al-mukhālafa), such as a condition or description restricting a ruling?
o: The Shāfiʿīs, Mālikīs and Ḥanbalīs generally accept it for conditions and descriptions, while the Ḥanafīs generally reject it as evidence in legal texts
All schools accept it for all texts without exception
xuf-005.e: The mafhūm al-mukhālafa infers that what is not mentioned has the opposite ruling of what is mentioned. The Shāfiʿīs, most Mālikīs and Ḥanbalīs accept it in several forms (condition, description, number), with disputes about each form and some conditions of validity. The Ḥanafīs reject it in textual rulings, though they accept the converse in the speech of the people and in some cases, and are known for refusing it.

xuf-006.src: al-Sarakhsī, Uṣūl al-Sarakhsī; al-Bazdawī, Kanz al-Wuṣūl; al-Zuḥaylī, al-Wajīz fī Uṣūl al-Fiqh
xuf-006.q: How does the Ḥanafī school distinguish fard from wājib, in contrast to the majority?
o: Fard is an obligation established by a definitive evidence and wājib by a probable one; the majority treat both as the same category of obligation
Fard is recommended and wājib is obligatory
Fard is a Quranic term only for prayer
The Ḥanafīs treat both as recommended
xuf-006.e: In Ḥanafī terminology, fard is established by decisive proof (a definitive Quranic text or a mutawātir report), with denial being unbelief, while wājib is established by a probable proof (a sound single-narrator report), whose denier is not considered an unbeliever though he is sinful for neglecting it. The majority consider them synonyms. The Ḥanafī distinction yields branch consequences, for instance regarding the Witr prayer and the rites of ḥajj.

xuf-007.src: al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Shīrāzī, al-Lumaʿ; al-Āmidī, al-Iḥkām
xuf-007.q: Which four pillars (arkān) of qiyās do the uṣūlīs state?
o: The original case (aṣl), the new case (farʿ), the ruling of the original (ḥukm al-aṣl) and the effective cause (ʿilla)
The text, the consensus, the custom and the benefit
The caliph, the judge, the witness and the oath
The question, the answer, the proof and the objection
xuf-007.e: The majority list four pillars: the aṣl (the case with a text or consensus), the farʿ (the case without a text), the ḥukm al-aṣl and the ʿilla that connects them. Some, such as the Ḥanafī Abū Zayd al-Dabūsī, speak of the aṣl as the text while others treat the ruling of the aṣl as separate. The ʿilla is the pivotal topic, with rules for how it is discovered (masālik al-ʿilla).

xuf-008.src: al-Ghazālī, Shifāʾ al-Ghalīl; al-Zarkashī, al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ; Ibn Qudāma, Rawḍat al-Nāẓir
xuf-008.q: Which list names classical ways of establishing the effective cause (masālik al-ʿilla)?
o: Text, consensus, inference by suitability (munāsaba), sorting and elimination (sabr wa-taqsīm), concomitance (dawarān) and fitness for the ruling
Dreams, lots, geography, tribal custom and age
The preference of the judge, the market price, the opinion of the physician and the calendar
Analogy to poetry, the length of the verse, rhyme and metre
xuf-008.e: Uṣūlīs list ways to find the ʿilla: by text (naṣṣ) or indication (īmāʾ), consensus, munāsaba (suitability), sabr wa-taqsīm (examining and eliminating the possible causes), dawarān (the ruling goes with the cause present or absent), shabah and others. Their order and acceptance differ, with al-Ghazālī and Ibn Qudāma giving detailed accounts.

xuf-009.src: al-Shāfiʿī, al-Umm and al-Risāla (Ibṭāl al-Istiḥsān); al-Sarakhsī, al-Mabsūṭ; al-Shāṭibī, al-Muwāfaqāt
xuf-009.q: How did the schools treat istiḥsān (juristic preference) as an argument?
o: The Ḥanafīs and Mālikīs used it as a recognised method while al-Shāfiʿī rejected it in the sense of legislating by one’s own taste; later Ḥanbalīs accepted forms of it grounded in texts
All the schools rejected it entirely
All the schools accepted it without conditions
xuf-009.e: Al-Shāfiʿī wrote a chapter on the invalidation of istiḥsān, saying that whoever prefers by taste has legislated. The Ḥanafīs define it as leaving an apparent analogy for a stronger one or for a text, consensus, necessity or custom, and the Mālikīs similarly speak of it as preferring the best of two evidences. Later uṣūlīs observed that the schools differ more in the definition than in practice.

xuf-010.src: al-Shāṭibī, al-Iʿtiṣām and al-Muwāfaqāt; al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Qarāfī, Sharḥ Tanqīḥ al-Fuṣūl
xuf-010.q: Which school is most closely associated with relying on unrestricted public interest (al-maṣlaḥa al-mursala), and how did al-Ghazālī treat it?
o: The Mālikī school; al-Ghazālī accepted it only if it is essential, universal and certain (ḍarūrī, kullī, qaṭʿī)
The Ḥanafī school only; al-Ghazālī rejected it entirely
The Shāfiʿī school only; al-Ghazālī accepted all interests
No school; it was invented in the 20th century
xuf-010.e: Mālik and his school are associated with maṣāliḥ mursala, interests not specifically endorsed or rejected by a text. Al-Ghazālī in al-Mustaṣfā treated it with conditions: the interest must belong to the necessities (protection of religion, life, intellect, lineage and property), be general for the community and be certain. The Ḥanbalīs, especially al-Ṭūfī, discussed it extensively, and al-Shāṭibī built the theory in al-Iʿtiṣām.

xuf-011.src: al-Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ, Tartīb al-Madārik; Ibn Taymiyya, Majmūʿ al-Fatāwā, on ʿamal ahl al-Madīna; Ibn al-Qayyim, Iʿlām al-Muwaqqiʿīn
xuf-011.q: What is the Mālikī doctrine of the practice of the people of Madīna (ʿamal ahl al-Madīna), and how did the other schools react?
o: Mālikīs treated the established practice of Madīna as evidence, strongest when it is transmitted from generation to generation; the Shāfiʿīs and most Ḥanbalīs did not take it as independent proof, and Ibn Taymiyya distinguished degrees of it
The Ḥanafīs made it equal to the Quran
It was a rule that all prayers must be in Madīna
xuf-011.e: Mālik gave weight to the inherited practice of Madīna, especially where it transmits the Prophetic practice (such as the measure of the ṣāʿ and the call to prayer), considering it stronger than a single-narrator report. Al-Shāfiʿī and others held that the evidence is the text, not the practice, and Ibn Taymiyya in his writings distinguished practice that transmits the sunna from practice based on later ijtihād. Opinions within the Mālikī school also vary.

xuf-012.src: al-Qarāfī, al-Furūq; Ibn al-Qayyim, Iʿlām al-Muwaqqiʿīn; al-Shāṭibī, al-Muwāfaqāt
xuf-012.q: What is sadd al-dharāʾiʿ (blocking the means) and which schools use it prominently?
o: Prohibiting a lawful act when it leads, in most cases, to a forbidden one; the Mālikīs and Ḥanbalīs use it prominently, and Ibn al-Qayyim wrote extensively on it
Closing the doors of mosques at night
Permitting an unlawful act by necessity
A prayer performed on a ship
xuf-012.e: Dharāʾiʿ are the means leading to an end; if the end is forbidden and the means usually lead to it, the means are prohibited. The Mālikīs, with al-Qarāfī’s classification, and the Ḥanbalīs apply it prominently, while the Ḥanafīs and Shāfiʿīs apply it in some cases without making it a distinct proof. Ibn al-Qayyim lists ninety-nine proofs for it in Iʿlām al-Muwaqqiʿīn.

xuf-013.src: al-Shāfiʿī, al-Risāla; al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Shīrāzī, al-Lumaʿ; Ibn Qudāma, Rawḍat al-Nāẓir
xuf-013.q: How do the schools define ijmāʿ, and who held that only the consensus of the Companions counts?
o: Agreement of the mujtahids of the Muslim community of an age on a legal ruling after the Prophet; Dāwūd al-Ẓāhirī and, in one report, Aḥmad limited it to the Companions
Agreement of the rulers of the community on taxes; the Ḥanafīs limited it
Agreement of ordinary Muslims on custom; the Mālikīs limited it
Agreement of the poets of an age; the Shāfiʿīs limited it
xuf-013.e: The majority define ijmāʿ as the agreement of all mujtahids of the Muslim community after the Prophet in a given period on a legal ruling. The Ẓāhirīs (Dāwūd and Ibn Ḥazm) limited it to the Companions, and a report from Aḥmad leans the same way. Mālikīs also speak of the consensus of the people of Madīna, and the Shīʿa have their own conception based on the imām.

xuf-014.src: al-Āmidī, al-Iḥkām; al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Sarakhsī, Uṣūl
xuf-014.q: What is the tacit consensus (al-ijmāʿ al-sukūtī), and how do the schools judge it?
o: When some mujtahids state a ruling and the others know of it and stay silent without objection; the Ḥanafīs and many Ḥanbalīs treat it as proof, while al-Shāfiʿī and many Shāfiʿīs do not
When all mujtahids sign a document
When the Quran is recited silently
xuf-014.e: The ijmāʿ sukūtī occurs when a ruling is expressed by some of the mujtahids of an age and the rest, who know of it, remain silent with no sign of approval or disapproval. The Ḥanafīs and some Ḥanbalīs accept it as proof (some as conclusive, some as probable), but al-Shāfiʿī and many of his followers deny that silence indicates agreement. Al-Āmidī and al-Ghazālī lay out the positions.

xuf-015.src: al-Shāfiʿī, al-Risāla; Ibn al-Qayyim, Iʿlām al-Muwaqqiʿīn, on the opinion of the Companion; al-Āmidī, al-Iḥkām
xuf-015.q: How do the schools treat the opinion of a single Companion (qawl al-ṣaḥābī) as an argument?
o: The Ḥanafīs, Mālikīs and Ḥanbalīs generally treat it as evidence in some conditions, while the later position of al-Shāfiʿī and most Shāfiʿīs did not take it as binding proof
All schools treat it as equal to the Quran
xuf-015.e: A Companion’s opinion where there is no known disagreement and which cannot be a matter of ijtihād is widely treated as carrying the weight of a Prophetic report. For other cases, the Ḥanafīs generally prefer it to analogy, the Mālikīs and Ḥanbalīs use it widely (Ibn al-Qayyim gives a long defence), and in his later view al-Shāfiʿī did not consider it binding, with reports of both views in his writings.

xuf-016.src: al-Āmidī, al-Iḥkām; al-Zarkashī, al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ; al-Zuḥaylī, Uṣūl al-Fiqh al-Islāmī
xuf-016.q: What is the question of 'the law of those before us' (sharʿ man qablanā), and what do the schools hold?
o: Whether laws of earlier prophets, reported in the Quran or sound Sunna without abrogation, bind us; most Ḥanafīs, many Mālikīs and Ḥanbalīs hold that they do, while the majority of Shāfiʿīs in the dominant view and Ashʿarīs hold they do not unless confirmed
Whether previous nations had prayer; all agree
Whether we may read their scriptures in prayer; all agree
xuf-016.e: The question concerns rulings narrated in our sources from earlier prophets without being confirmed or abrogated in our Sharia. The Ḥanafīs, many Mālikīs and Ḥanbalīs hold they bind us, as in the case of retaliation (qiṣāṣ) in some applications. Many Shāfiʿīs and Ashʿarīs say they do not bind unless our Sharia confirms them. Agreed is that what our Sharia abrogates does not bind.

xuf-017.src: Ibn Qudāma, Rawḍat al-Nāẓir; al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Zuḥaylī, al-Wajīz fī Uṣūl al-Fiqh
xuf-017.q: Which list names the four sources of law agreed upon by the Sunni majority, in the usual order?
o: The Quran, the Sunna, ijmāʿ and qiyās
The Quran, custom, reason and poetry
The Sunna, qiyās, istiḥsān and dreams
The Quran, the preference of the caliph, ijmāʿ and the market
xuf-017.e: The four agreed sources are the Quran, the Sunna, ijmāʿ and qiyās (with the Ẓāhirīs rejecting qiyās). The disputed sources include istiḥsān, maṣlaḥa mursala, istiṣḥāb, ʿurf, sadd al-dharāʾiʿ, qawl al-ṣaḥābī and sharʿ man qablanā. The Ibn Qudāma and al-Ghazālī manuals treat the sources in this arrangement.

xuf-018.src: Ibn Ḥazm, al-Iḥkām fī Uṣūl al-Aḥkām; Ibn Ḥazm, al-Muḥallā
xuf-018.q: What was Ibn Ḥazm’s approach to legal reasoning in al-Iḥkām?
o: He rejected qiyās, istiḥsān and taqlīd and held to the apparent meaning of the texts and consensus of the Companions
He accepted all analogies without text
He rejected the Sunna as a source
xuf-018.e: The Ẓāhirī school, founded by Dāwūd al-Ẓāhirī and defended by Ibn Ḥazm (d. 456 AH) in al-Iḥkām fī Uṣūl al-Aḥkām and al-Muḥallā, held to the plain meaning of the Quran and Sunna, and denied that analogy, juristic preference and blind following are valid sources. It limited consensus to that of the Companions. His work is argued in a polemic style against the other schools.

xuf-019.src: al-Shāfiʿī, al-Risāla; al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Āmidī, al-Iḥkām
xuf-019.q: According to the uṣūlīs, which of these is NOT an accepted condition of abrogation (naskh)?
o: That the abrogating text be read more often than the abrogated one
That the two texts truly conflict and cannot be reconciled
That the abrogating text be later
That the abrogating text be at least equal in strength to the abrogated one
xuf-019.e: Uṣūlīs require that there is a true conflict that cannot be harmonised, that the abrogating text is later, and that it is at least of equal strength (a probable report cannot abrogate a definitive text in the majority view). Frequency of reading plays no part. Al-Shāfiʿī insisted that a text is abrogated only by a text, and he did not allow the Sunna to abrogate the Quran, a stance debated in the schools.

xuf-020.src: al-Sarakhsī, Uṣūl; al-Āmidī, al-Iḥkām; al-Zuḥaylī, Uṣūl al-Fiqh al-Islāmī
xuf-020.q: How does the Ḥanafī method order the handling of two conflicting texts, as against the majority?
o: The Ḥanafīs order it as abrogation, then preference (tarjīḥ), then harmonisation, then dropping the two; the majority generally start with harmonisation (jamʿ) where possible
The Ḥanafīs start with dropping both texts; the majority drop one
Both start with preferring the more frequent text
Both call a vote among scholars
xuf-020.e: Ḥanafī uṣūl follows the order naskh, tarjīḥ, jamʿ and then tasāquṭ (dropping both), whereas the majority of the Shāfiʿīs, Mālikīs and Ḥanbalīs generally prefer harmonisation first as it gives both texts effect, and then abrogation, then tarjīḥ. The difference stems from their view that harmonisation can reduce the force of a text.

xuf-021.src: al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Zuḥaylī, al-Wajīz fī Uṣūl al-Fiqh; al-Sarakhsī, Uṣūl
xuf-021.q: Which list correctly gives the five rulings (al-aḥkām al-khamsa) used by the majority?
o: Wājib, mandūb, mubāḥ, makrūh and ḥarām
Fard, sunna, wājib, ḥarām and makrūh only
Ḥalāl, ḥarām, ṭāhir, najis and mubāḥ
Aṣl, farʿ, ʿilla, ḥukm and shart
xuf-021.e: The majority list the five categories of the Sharia ruling as wājib (obligatory), mandūb (recommended), mubāḥ (permitted), makrūh (disliked) and ḥarām (forbidden). The Ḥanafīs expand to seven: fard, wājib, sunna (or mandūb), mubāḥ, makrūh tanzīhan, makrūh taḥrīman and ḥarām. The difference reflects their view of degrees of evidence.

xuf-022.src: al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Juwaynī, al-Burhān; al-Zarkashī, al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ
xuf-022.q: What is the debate over the communal obligation (farḍ al-kifāya) among the uṣūlīs?
o: Whether the obligation is addressed to all and removed by some performing it (the majority), or addressed to an unspecified group; they agree that if no one performs it, all are sinful
Whether it applies only to women
Whether it is performed once a year
Whether it applies only to the ruler
xuf-022.e: Farḍ kifāya (like funeral prayer or knowledge needed by the community) is a duty whose goal is that it be done, not who does it. The majority hold the address is to all, which lapses when enough people do it; al-Juwaynī and others discuss alternative explanations (an unspecified group, or those capable). All agree that the community is sinful if it is left undone.

xuf-023.src: al-Shāṭibī, al-Muwāfaqāt; al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Zuḥaylī, al-Wajīz fī Uṣūl al-Fiqh
xuf-023.q: What do ʿazīma and rukhṣa mean in uṣūl al-fiqh?
o: ʿAzīma is the original general ruling; rukhṣa is a concession allowed because of a difficulty or necessity, such as shortening prayer while travelling
ʿAzīma is a recommended act; rukhṣa is a forbidden act
ʿAzīma is a Quranic reading; rukhṣa is a hadith grade
ʿAzīma is the call to prayer; rukhṣa is the sermon
xuf-023.e: ʿAzīma is the ruling as originally legislated for all. Rukhṣa is a ruling changed to ease because of an excuse (hardship, illness, travel, coercion), as in the shortening of prayer, breaking the fast of Ramadan for a traveller or eating carrion under necessity. The schools differ on whether taking the concession is obligatory, recommended or permitted, depending on the case, with the Ḥanafīs usually treating some as obligatory.

xuf-024.src: al-Juwaynī, al-Burhān; al-Ghazālī, al-Mustaṣfā; al-Āmidī, al-Iḥkām; al-Taftāzānī, Sharḥ al-Talwīḥ
xuf-024.q: What is the debate on taklīf mā lā yuṭāq (imposing what is beyond ability)?
o: Whether God could theoretically impose it; Ashʿarīs allowed it in principle without it occurring, while Muʿtazilīs and many Māturīdīs denied it
Whether the Prophet could fast forever
Whether prayer on a mountain is valid
xuf-024.e: The question is whether imposing something impossible is possible for God. Ashʿarīs, based on God’s absolute power, held it is possible rationally, though by the verse affirming that God does not burden a soul beyond its capacity it does not occur. The Muʿtazila and many Māturīdīs say it is not possible as it contradicts God’s justice. The discussion arose from questions such as the command to Abū Lahab to believe.

xuf-025.src: al-Qarāfī, al-Furūq; al-Zuḥaylī, al-Wajīz fī Uṣūl al-Fiqh; al-Shāṭibī, al-Muwāfaqāt
xuf-025.q: What is the distinction between a cause (sabab), a condition (sharṭ) and an impediment (māniʿ) in uṣūl?
o: A cause necessitates the ruling by its presence; a condition must be present but does not itself necessitate; an impediment prevents the ruling even when the cause is present
A cause is a person; a condition is a place; an impediment is a time
They are three names for the same thing
A cause is voluntary; a condition is forbidden; an impediment is permitted
xuf-025.e: A sabab is a sign whose presence indicates the existence of the ruling and absence indicates its absence (the sunset for the sunset prayer). A sharṭ is what the ruling depends on without being a cause (ablution for prayer). A māniʿ prevents the effect even when the cause and the condition are present (such as debt for zakāt, or killing for inheritance). These form the declaratory rulings (al-ḥukm al-waḍʿī).

xuf-026.src: al-Bazdawī, Kanz al-Wuṣūl; al-Sarakhsī, Uṣūl; al-Taftāzānī, Sharḥ al-Talwīḥ
xuf-026.q: What are the two kinds of legal capacity (ahliyya) distinguished in the Ḥanafī uṣūl?
o: Capacity for obligation (ahliyyat al-wujūb), which a person has from birth, and capacity for performance (ahliyyat al-adāʾ), which depends on reason
Capacity for prayer and capacity for fasting
Capacity of men and capacity of women
Capacity of rulers and capacity of judges
