tfs-056.e: The verse makes an exception from the threatened punishment for those who repent, believe and act righteously, and says Allah turns their bad deeds into good ones; the mufassirūn explain this both as a change of character and as a change in the record.

tfs-057.q: In the verse shown, what do the servants of the Most Merciful ask for themselves at the end of their prayer?
o: To be made examples for the God-conscious
To be granted long lives and much wealth
To be made rulers over the unbelievers
To be spared every hardship in this world
tfs-057.e: They ask for spouses and offspring who are a comfort to the eyes and to be made an imām for the muttaqūn, that is, examples in good whom others follow. The mufassirūn note this is a request for leadership in religion, not in worldly power.

tfs-058.q: What lesson does Luqmān teach with the image of a mustard seed in the verse shown?
o: Nothing is hidden from Allah; He will bring every deed forth
A small seed of faith grows into a great and shady tree
Charity should always begin with the smallest of gifts
Even hard rocks can be split by patient, steady effort
tfs-058.e: Even if a deed were the weight of a mustard seed hidden in a rock, in the heavens or the earth, Allah would bring it forth on the Day of Judgement, for He is Subtle and All-Aware. The 'growing seed' image is from the New Testament, not this verse.

tfs-059.q: Why does Luqmān pair the command to enjoin good and forbid evil with patience in the verse shown?
o: Because whoever calls to good will meet harm and must bear it
Because patience replaces the need to speak out
Because forbidding evil is only for rulers
Because patience is needed only in illness
tfs-059.e: Luqmān commands prayer, enjoining good and forbidding evil, then patience over what befalls him; Ibn Kathīr explains that one who commands and forbids will inevitably be harmed by people, so he is told to be patient.

tfs-060.q: In the verse shown, the moon returns at the end of its phases like the ʿurjūn. What is the ʿurjūn according to the mufassirūn?
o: The old, dried, curved stalk of a date cluster
A crescent-shaped lamp made of bronze
The curved stone rim of a desert well
A hunting bow bent ready for the shot
tfs-060.e: Ibn ʿAbbās and others explain al-ʿurjūn al-qadīm as the stalk of a date bunch that has dried, shrivelled and curved; the waning moon becomes thin, yellowish and bent like it.

tfs-061.q: What happens on the Day of Judgement according to the verse shown?
o: Mouths are sealed, and hands speak and feet bear witness
The angels read every deed aloud to all creation
The earth swallows those who denied the Hour
The disbelievers are given a second chance to repent
tfs-061.e: When the deniers reject the testimony against them, Allah seals their mouths and their own limbs testify to what they earned; similar scenes are in 24:24 and 41:20–21.

tfs-062.q: When two groups of believers fight, what does the verse shown command?
o: Make peace, and fight the aggressor until it returns to Allah's command
Stay neutral and leave them to settle the matter themselves
Fight both groups until each of them lays down its arms
Support the larger group so the fighting ends quickly
tfs-062.e: The verse orders peace-making first; if one party continues in aggression, it is fought until it returns to Allah's command, then peace is made with justice. Ibn Kathīr notes that the fighters are still called believers, so the sin does not take them out of faith.

tfs-063.q: Which distinction does the verse shown draw when the Bedouins claim 'we believe'?
o: Outward submission (islām) versus faith settled in the heart (īmān)
The emigrants of Makka versus the helpers of Madīna
Obligatory prayers versus prayers that are only recommended
The hypocrites versus the People of the Book in Madīna
tfs-063.e: They are told to say 'we have submitted', since faith had not yet entered their hearts. Ibn Kathīr uses the verse to show that īmān is a more specific rank than islām, while noting these Bedouins were not hypocrites.

tfs-064.q: In the passage of the verse shown, two seas meet. What is between them?
o: A barrier (barzakh) that neither of them oversteps
A bridge on which the believers will cross over
A range of mountains dividing two lands
A river of fire that appears on the Last Day
tfs-064.e: Allah lets two bodies of water meet, yet a barrier keeps each from overrunning the other; the passage counts this among His favours, followed by pearls and coral brought out from them.

tfs-065.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 56:77–79; al-Qurṭubī, al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān, on 56:79
tfs-065.q: Which statement correctly describes the views on 'the purified' in the verse shown?
o: Many early authorities: the angels; others linked it to touching the muṣḥaf in purity
All mufassirūn agree it means only people who have performed ghusl
It was understood only of the prophets and never of the angels
It refers to the scribes in Madīna who first wrote the muṣḥaf
tfs-065.e: Ibn ʿAbbās and others said only the angels touch the guarded Book in heaven. Others, citing the letter to ʿAmr ibn Ḥazm, take it as indicating that the muṣḥaf is touched only in purity; Ibn Kathīr mentions both lines of interpretation.

tfs-066.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 57:3; Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Dhikr wa-l-Duʿāʾ
tfs-066.q: The four names in the verse shown (the First, the Last, the Manifest, the Hidden) are explained by the Prophet in a supplication in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim. What does 'the First' mean there?
o: He was the first to be worshipped on earth
He is first in rank among the angels
He created the first human being
tfs-066.e: In the bedtime supplication reported by Muslim, the Prophet explained: the First, with nothing before Him; the Last, with nothing after Him; the Manifest, with nothing above Him; the Hidden, with nothing beneath Him.

tfs-067.q: What warning does the verse shown give the believers?
o: Not to become like earlier scripture-holders whose hearts hardened
Not to build their houses higher than the walls of the mosque
Not to keep trading once the call to Friday prayer is made
Not to take spouses from among the People of the Book
tfs-067.e: The verse asks whether it is not time for believers' hearts to humble themselves at Allah's remembrance, and warns against becoming like those given the Book before, whose hearts hardened after a long time.

tfs-068.q: What image does the verse shown use to describe the greatness of the Quran?
o: A mountain would humble itself and split apart in awe of it
The sea would turn to ink and run dry before its words end
The stars would fall from the sky if it were recited
The earth would shake each time it is read
tfs-068.e: If the Quran were sent down upon a mountain, the mountain would be humbled and split from fear of Allah; how then can human hearts remain unmoved? The image of the sea as ink belongs to 18:109.

tfs-069.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 97:4; al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 97:4
tfs-069.q: Who is 'the Spirit' (al-rūḥ) descending with the angels in the verse shown, according to most mufassirūn?
o: Jibrīl, mentioned separately to honour him
The souls of the deceased believers
tfs-069.e: Most mufassirūn hold that al-rūḥ is Jibrīl, singled out after 'the angels' as a specific named after the general (ʿaṭf al-khāṣṣ ʿalā al-ʿāmm) to show his rank. Other views are reported, but this is the majority view.

tfs-070.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 18:83; Ibn Kathīr, al-Bidāya wa-l-Nihāya, account of Dhū al-Qarnayn
tfs-070.q: How does Ibn Kathīr treat the common identification of Dhū al-Qarnayn in the verse shown with Alexander of Macedon?
o: He rejects it: Alexander came much later and was not a believer
He accepts it fully on the authority of the Greek historians
He accepts it, adding that Alexander later embraced tawḥīd
He leaves the question open without discussing Alexander at all
tfs-070.e: Ibn Kathīr distinguishes the Quranic Dhū al-Qarnayn, a righteous believing king of an earlier age, from Alexander the Macedonian, whose minister was Aristotle and who was a polytheist, and warns that confusing the two leads to serious error.

tfs-071.q: What reason does the verse shown give for the killing of the boy?
o: His believing parents might be driven by him to rebellion and disbelief
He had already killed a man in the town the day before
His own parents had asked al-Khiḍr to punish him for his crimes
He was the son of the king who was seizing the boats by force
tfs-071.e: Al-Khiḍr explains that the boy's parents were believers and it was feared he would overwhelm them with rebellion and disbelief; the next verse says Allah would give them in exchange a child purer and more merciful. Ibn Kathīr cites the hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim that the boy was created a disbeliever.

tfs-072.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 19:96; al-Bukhārī and Muslim (hadith of Allah's love for a servant)
tfs-072.q: With which well-known hadith does Ibn Kathīr explain the 'affection' (wudd) promised in the verse shown?
o: Allah loves a servant, informs Jibrīl, the heavens love him, and acceptance is placed for him on earth
Whoever loves to meet Allah, Allah loves to meet him
None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself
A person will be with those whom he loves
tfs-072.e: The verse promises that the Most Merciful will create affection for those who believe and do good. Ibn Kathīr explains it with the hadith in al-Bukhārī and Muslim: when Allah loves a servant He calls Jibrīl, the inhabitants of heaven love him, and acceptance is then placed for him on earth.

tfs-073.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 20:1; al-Qurṭubī, al-Jāmiʿ li-Aḥkām al-Qurʾān, on 20:1
tfs-073.q: Which statement correctly describes the views on the opening of Sūrat Ṭā Hā shown?
o: Many: disjointed letters; Ibn ʿAbbās and others: 'O man' in a dialect
All agree it is a name of the Prophet used only in this surah
All agree it means 'pure guidance' in the classical Arabic tongue
The Companions read it as a command to stand up for prayer
tfs-073.e: Ibn Kathīr discusses it with the other disjointed letters, and also reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr and others that it means 'O man' (in Nabatean or another dialect). Its use as a name of the Prophet is a later popular view, not a consensus.

tfs-074.q: According to Ibn ʿAbbās and most mufassirūn, what are the 'houses' that Allah permitted to be raised in the verse shown?
o: The homes of the Prophet's wives
The houses of the Companions in Madīna
The houses of the People of the Book
tfs-074.e: Directly after the Light Verse, the passage speaks of houses in which His name is remembered and glorified morning and evening by men whom trade does not distract; Ibn Kathīr reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and others that these are the mosques.

tfs-075.q: According to Ibn Kathīr, what does the 'gentle' walk (hawn) of the servants of the Most Merciful in the verse shown mean?
o: Calm dignity without arrogance, not an affected sickly gait
Walking slowly and weakly as a display of humility
Keeping always to the edges of the road when walking
Avoiding the markets and walking only to the mosque
tfs-075.e: Ibn Kathīr explains hawnan as tranquillity and dignity, free of tyranny and pride, and stresses that it does not mean walking like the sick out of affectation and show; he notes the Prophet walked briskly, as if descending a slope.

tfs-076.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 25:72; al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 25:72
tfs-076.q: Which statement correctly describes the views on al-zūr that the servants of the Most Merciful do not witness in the verse shown?
o: Several views (shirk, pagan feasts, lies, false testimony); many read it broadly
All mufassirūn restricted it to false testimony given before a judge
All mufassirūn restricted it to listening to musical instruments
It was explained only as the mosque built by the hypocrites
tfs-076.e: Ibn Kathīr reports that some said al-zūr is shirk and idol worship, others the polytheists' festivals, others lying and sinful gatherings, and others false testimony. Al-Ṭabarī preferred taking it generally as attending every kind of falsehood.

tfs-077.q: The verse shown says Luqmān was given wisdom. What is the majority view of the salaf about his status, as reported by Ibn Kathīr?
o: He was a wise, righteous servant, not a prophet
He was a prophet sent to the people of Egypt
He was a messenger with a revealed book
He was one of the angels sent in human form
tfs-077.e: Ibn Kathīr notes that the salaf differed on whether Luqmān was a prophet, and that most held he was a righteous servant given wisdom without prophethood; the opposite view is reported from ʿIkrima.

tfs-078.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Īmān (hadith of Ibn Masʿūd); Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 31:13
tfs-078.q: According to the hadith of Ibn Masʿūd in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, how did the Prophet use the verse shown?
o: To show that the 'wrong' in 6:82 means shirk
To prove that every sin cancels a person's faith
To show that Luqmān had been sent as a prophet
To permit obeying one's parents in disbelief
tfs-078.e: When 6:82 was revealed (those who do not mix their faith with wrong are safe), the Companions were troubled, since everyone wrongs himself. The Prophet clarified that the wrong meant is shirk, citing Luqmān's words in the verse shown. It is a classic case of tafsīr of Quran by Quran through the Sunna.

tfs-079.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 36:12; Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Masājid (hadith of Banū Salima)
tfs-079.q: How does Ibn Kathīr treat the two explanations of the 'traces' (āthār) that are recorded in the verse shown?
o: He reports both, effects of deeds and footsteps, and sees no conflict
He accepts only the footsteps and rejects the other view as weak
He accepts only the effects and sets aside the Banū Salima report
He says it means the ruins left behind by destroyed nations
tfs-079.e: One view: what people leave behind of good or bad practices that others follow, supported by the hadith on initiating a good or bad sunna. The other: their footsteps, as in the hadith of Banū Salima who wished to move near the mosque. Ibn Kathīr says the second meaning is included in the first, so there is no contradiction.

tfs-080.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 49:2; al-Bukhārī and Muslim (hadith of Anas on Thābit ibn Qays)
tfs-080.q: Which Companion, known for his loud voice, stayed at home in fear after the verse shown was revealed, until the Prophet said he was of the people of Paradise?
tfs-080.e: The verse forbids raising voices above the Prophet's lest one's deeds be nullified unknowingly. Thābit ibn Qays, the orator of the Anṣār, feared it applied to him; the Prophet sent word that he was not of the people of the Fire but of Paradise, as narrated by Anas in the Ṣaḥīḥayn.

tfs-081.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 55:46 and 55:62; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Tafsīr (hadith of Abū Mūsā)
tfs-081.q: Al-Raḥmān mentions two gardens for the one who fears standing before his Lord, then in the verse shown two more. How does Ibn Kathīr relate the two pairs?
o: The second pair ranks below the first (gold versus silver gardens)
The second pair ranks higher and is for the prophets alone
Both pairs are the same gardens, described twice for emphasis
The second pair is reserved for the believing jinn only
tfs-081.e: Ibn Kathīr holds that the gardens in the verse shown are below the first two in virtue and rank, and links this to the hadith of Abū Mūsā in al-Bukhārī about two gardens of silver and two of gold. The first pair is for the ones brought near, the second for the people of the right.

tfs-082.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 56:75–76; al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 56:75
tfs-082.q: Which statement correctly describes the views on the 'positions of the stars' (mawāqiʿ al-nujūm) sworn by in the verse shown?
o: Mujāhid: the stars' setting places; Ibn ʿAbbās: the Quran's instalments
All agreed it means the twelve constellations of the zodiac
All agreed it means the stars that fall at the Resurrection
It was explained only as the stations where angels stand
tfs-082.e: Ibn Kathīr reports Mujāhid's view that it refers to the rising and setting points of the stars, and from Ibn ʿAbbās that it refers to the parts (nujūm) of the Quran sent down gradually, which fits the following verses about the noble Quran. Al-Ḥasan is reported to have referred it to their scattering at the Hour.

tfs-083.q: The verse shown says those who spent and fought before 'the victory' (al-fatḥ) are not equal to those who did so later. Which statement correctly describes the views on this fatḥ?
o: Most: the conquest of Makka; al-Shaʿbī and others: al-Ḥudaybiya
All agreed that it refers to the Battle of Badr
All agreed that it refers to the conquest of Khaybar
Most said the Trench, and none named al-Ḥudaybiya
tfs-083.e: Ibn Kathīr reports that the majority understood al-fatḥ here as the conquest of Makka, while al-Shaʿbī and others said al-Ḥudaybiya, which is also called a clear victory in Sūrat al-Fatḥ. Either way, the verse ranks the earlier believers higher, while promising good to both.

tfs-084.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 19:71–72; al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 19:71
tfs-084.q: Which statement correctly describes the classical views on the 'coming to it' (wurūd) of Hell mentioned in the verse shown?
o: Ibn Masʿūd: passing over the Ṣirāṭ; Ibn ʿAbbās: entering it
All agreed it applies to the disbelievers alone
All agreed it means only seeing Hell from far away
It was understood only of the hypocrites of Madīna
tfs-084.e: Ibn Kathīr reports that Ibn Masʿūd and others explained wurūd as passing over the bridge above Hell, each according to his deeds, while Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said it means entering. On both views, the next verse states that Allah saves the God-fearing and leaves the wrongdoers in it.

tfs-085.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 112:2; al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 112:2
tfs-085.q: Which of the following is among the classical explanations of al-Ṣamad in the verse shown?
o: The Master to whom all creatures turn in their needs
The First, before whom there is nothing
The Light of the heavens and the earth
The One who covers the sins of His servants
tfs-085.e: Ibn ʿAbbās explained al-Ṣamad as the one to whom creatures turn in their needs and the Master perfect in all attributes; others, such as Ibn Masʿūd, said the one who has no hollow (does not eat or drink). The distractors describe other names (al-Awwal, al-Nūr, al-Ghafūr).

tfs-086.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 113:4; al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Ṭibb (hadith of the sorcery of Labīd ibn al-Aʿṣam)
tfs-086.q: Who are 'those who blow on knots' in the verse shown, according to Mujāhid, ʿIkrima, al-Ḥasan and Qatāda?
o: Poets who recite satire against the Prophet
tfs-086.e: These early mufassirūn explain al-naffāthāt as sorceresses who blow while tying knots. The mufassirūn connect the two surahs of refuge with the sorcery of Labīd ibn al-Aʿṣam against the Prophet, reported in al-Bukhārī and Muslim; the explicit link to the surahs is found in other narrations.

tfs-087.q: What is the point of the verse shown, given the occasion reported by Ibn ʿAbbās and others?
o: The enemy who called him 'cut off' is himself cut off
The Prophet would leave no descendants of any kind
The Prophet should break ties with his hostile relatives
Quraysh would soon be cut off from their trade routes
tfs-087.e: When the Prophet's sons died, an opponent (commonly named as al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil) mocked him as abtar, without a male heir. The surah answers that it is his hater who is cut off from good and remembrance, while the Prophet's name and message endure.

tjm-001.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-001.q: Into how many main areas (mawāḍiʿ) are the points of articulation of the Arabic letters grouped?
tjm-001.e: The five areas are the oral and throat cavity (jawf), the throat (ḥalq), the tongue (lisān), the lips (shafatān) and the nasal cavity (khayshūm). The individual makhārij are distributed across these five.

tjm-002.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-002.q: From which of the five areas do hamza, hāʾ, ʿayn, ḥāʾ, ghayn and khāʾ originate?
tjm-002.e: These six are the throat letters (ḥurūf ḥalqiyya). They come from three points of the throat: the deepest part, the middle and the part nearest the mouth.

tjm-003.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, opening verses on makhārij
tjm-003.q: According to the view adopted by Ibn al-Jazarī in his Muqaddima, how many specific makhārij do the letters have?
tjm-003.e: Ibn al-Jazarī follows al-Khalīl and most reciters in counting seventeen makhārij. Sixteen and fourteen are the counts of other grammarians; twenty-nine is the number of letters, not of makhārij.

tjm-004.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on makhārij al-ḥurūf; Sībawayh, al-Kitāb, ch. on idghām
tjm-004.q: Sībawayh counted sixteen makhārij instead of seventeen. Which area did he not count as a separate makhraj?
o: The jawf, distributing the madd letters among other makhārij
The khayshūm: he treated the ghunna as an attribute of nūn and mīm only
The lips: he joined fāʾ with the makhraj of the dental letters
The deepest throat: he joined hamza and hāʾ with ʿayn and ḥāʾ
tjm-004.e: Sībawayh and those who followed him dropped the jawf. He assigned alif to the deepest part of the throat together with hamza and hāʾ, the madd wāw to the lips and the madd yāʾ to the middle of the tongue.

tjm-005.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-005.q: Which grammarian is best known for counting only fourteen makhārij by giving lām, nūn and rāʾ a single makhraj?
tjm-005.e: Ibn al-Jazarī reports that al-Farrāʾ, with Quṭrub, al-Jarmī and Ibn Kaysān, counted fourteen by merging the makhārij of lām, nūn and rāʾ. Sībawayh counted sixteen and al-Khalīl seventeen.

tjm-006.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-006.q: Which letters are pronounced from the jawf (the empty space of the mouth and throat)?
o: The three madd letters: alif, wāw and yāʾ
The throat letters hamza, hāʾ and ʿayn
Mīm and nūn together with their ghunna
The lip letters fāʾ, bāʾ and mīm
tjm-006.e: The jawf letters are the three madd letters: alif, wāw sākina after ḍamma and yāʾ sākina after kasra. Their sound ends when the air ends, not at a fixed point.

tjm-007.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-007.q: Why is the makhraj of the jawf letters called muqaddar (estimated) rather than muḥaqqaq (fixed)?
o: Their sound ends with the air, not at a specific point
They are only written in the muṣḥaf and are not pronounced at all
Their makhraj changes according to the vowel of the next word
They come from the nose and therefore have no point inside the mouth
tjm-007.e: A muḥaqqaq makhraj is a definite point where the sound is cut, such as the lips for bāʾ. The madd letters have no such point: they run through the cavity of mouth and throat and stop when the breath stops.

tjm-008.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-008.q: What method does Ibn al-Jazarī describe for finding the makhraj of a letter?
o: Make it sākin after a voweled hamza and note where the sound stops
Pronounce it with fatḥa and lengthen the vowel for two counts
Pronounce it with tanwīn and observe whether air leaves the nose
Say the letter's name and note where its last sound is produced
tjm-008.e: Ibn al-Jazarī says: make the letter sākin or mushaddad and put a hamzat waṣl with any vowel before it, as in ab or aq; where the sound stops is its makhraj. A vowel after the letter would carry the sound away from it.

tjm-009.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-009.q: Which two letters come from the deepest part of the throat (aqṣā al-ḥalq)?
tjm-009.e: The deepest part of the throat, nearest the chest, produces hamza and hāʾ. ʿAyn and ḥāʾ come from the middle and ghayn and khāʾ from the part nearest the mouth.

tjm-010.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-010.q: Which two letters come from the part of the throat nearest the mouth (adnā al-ḥalq)?
tjm-010.e: Adnā al-ḥalq, the upper part of the throat next to the mouth, produces ghayn and khāʾ. Qāf is already a tongue letter, from the back of the tongue.

tjm-011.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-011.q: Which letter is produced from the furthest back part of the tongue together with the soft palate above it?
tjm-011.e: Qāf comes from aqṣā al-lisān with the soft palate above it. Kāf comes from slightly lower, nearer the mouth; ghayn is a throat letter.

tjm-012.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-012.q: Which three letters come from the middle of the tongue with the hard palate above it?
tjm-012.e: The middle of the tongue with the palate above produces jīm, shīn and the yāʾ that is not a madd letter. The madd yāʾ belongs to the jawf.

tjm-013.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-013.q: What is the makhraj of ḍād?
o: One or both edges of the tongue against the upper molars
The tip of the tongue against the tips of the upper incisors
The middle of the tongue against the hard palate
The back of the tongue against the soft palate
tjm-013.e: Ibn al-Jazarī: ḍād comes from the side of the tongue where it meets the upper molars, from the left or right side or both. The tip of the tongue with the upper incisors is the makhraj of ẓāʾ, dhāl and thāʾ.

tjm-014.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-014.q: How do the books of tajwīd commonly describe the sides from which ḍād is produced?
o: Left side easier and more common, right side harder, both sides hardest
Only from the right side; the left side produces a different letter
From both sides together is obligatory; one side alone is a fault
From the left side only in waqf and from the right side in waṣl
tjm-014.e: Ḍād may be produced from either edge or from both. The commonly stated description is that the left side is easier and more usual, the right side harder and both sides together the hardest; all three are valid.

tjm-015.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-015.q: Which letter is produced from the front part of the tongue's edges against the gums above the front teeth, below the makhraj of ḍād?
tjm-015.e: Lām comes from the edge of the tongue at its front end, running to its tip, against the gums of the upper front teeth. Nūn and rāʾ come from the tip of the tongue just next to it.

tjm-016.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-016.q: How does the makhraj of rāʾ relate to that of nūn?
o: Close to it, but more toward the upper surface of the tongue
Identical to it; they differ only by the ghunna
Rāʾ is produced at the lips, nūn at the tip of the tongue
Rāʾ comes from the middle of the tongue, far behind nūn
tjm-016.e: Ibn al-Jazarī: nūn comes from the tip of the tongue below the place of lām, and rāʾ is near nūn but enters more toward the back (upper surface) of the tongue. Al-Farrāʾ, by contrast, gave the three letters one makhraj.

tjm-017.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-017.q: Which letters come from the tip of the tongue against the roots (gums) of the upper central incisors?
tjm-017.e: The tip of the tongue with the roots of the upper incisors produces ṭāʾ, dāl and tāʾ. With the tips of the incisors it produces ẓāʾ, dhāl and thāʾ.

tjm-018.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-018.q: Where are ṣād, zāy and sīn produced?
o: At the tip of the tongue just above the lower incisors, with a slight gap
At the tip of the tongue against the roots of the upper incisors
Between the inner lower lip and the tips of the upper incisors
At the middle of the tongue against the hard palate
tjm-018.e: Ibn al-Jazarī says the whistling letters come from the tip of the tongue just above the lower incisors. A slight gap remains between tongue and teeth, through which the whistle (ṣafīr) passes.

tjm-019.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-019.q: Which letters are produced with the tip of the tongue against the tips (edges) of the upper incisors?
tjm-019.e: Ẓāʾ, dhāl and thāʾ come from the tip of the tongue with the edges of the upper incisors, so the tongue tip appears slightly. Ṭāʾ, dāl and tāʾ are made further back, at the roots of the incisors.

tjm-020.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-020.q: Which letter comes from the inner part of the lower lip against the tips of the upper incisors?
tjm-020.e: Fāʾ is the only letter made between the lower lip and the upper incisors. Bāʾ and mīm need both lips, and thāʾ is made with the tongue tip.

tjm-021.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-021.q: Which letters are produced with both lips?
tjm-021.e: Both lips produce bāʾ, mīm and the wāw that is not a madd letter. Fāʾ uses only the lower lip with the upper incisors.

tjm-022.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-022.q: How does the lip position of wāw differ from that of bāʾ and mīm?
o: For wāw the lips are rounded without closing; for bāʾ and mīm they close
For wāw the lips close firmly; for bāʾ and mīm they only round
For wāw only the lower lip moves; for bāʾ and mīm only the upper lip
There is no difference; only the attributes distinguish them
tjm-022.e: Wāw is produced by rounding the lips with an opening in the middle, while bāʾ and mīm require the lips to close. That is why they share an area but are not one point.

tjm-023.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-023.q: What is produced from the khayshūm (the nasal cavity)?
o: The whistle of ṣād and sīn
The echo of the qalqala letters
tjm-023.e: Ibn al-Jazarī ends the makhārij with the ghunna, whose makhraj is the khayshūm. The madd letters belong to the jawf.

tjm-024.src: al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, Kitāb al-ʿAyn, introduction; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, ch. on makhārij
tjm-024.q: Which letters are called niṭʿiyya, after the ridge at the front of the palate?
tjm-024.e: Niṭʿ is the hard ridge of the front palate, near which ṭāʾ, dāl and tāʾ are produced. Ẓāʾ, dhāl and thāʾ are lithawiyya and ṣād, zāy and sīn asaliyya.

tjm-025.src: al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, Kitāb al-ʿAyn, introduction; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, ch. on makhārij
tjm-025.q: In al-Khalīl's naming of the letter groups, which letters are called shajariyya?
tjm-025.e: Shajr is the opening of the mouth between the jaws, where jīm, shīn and yāʾ are produced from the middle of the tongue. Qāf and kāf are lahawiyya, ṣād, zāy and sīn asaliyya, and the lip letters shafawiyya.

tjm-026.src: al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, Kitāb al-ʿAyn, introduction
tjm-026.q: Which two letters are called lahawiyya, after the uvula (lahāt)?
tjm-026.e: Qāf and kāf are produced at the back of the tongue near the uvula and are therefore called lahawiyya. Ghayn and khāʾ, though close, are throat letters.

tjm-027.src: al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, Kitāb al-ʿAyn, introduction
tjm-027.q: The names ḥalqiyya, lahawiyya, shajariyya, asaliyya, niṭʿiyya, lithawiyya, dhalqiyya and shafawiyya for the letter groups go back to whom?
tjm-027.e: These group names are from al-Khalīl in the introduction to Kitāb al-ʿAyn, where he ordered the letters by makhraj. Later tajwīd authors such as Ibn al-Jazarī took them over.

tjm-028.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-028.q: Ṭāʾ and tāʾ share the same makhraj. What distinguishes them?
o: The ghunna that one of them carries
tjm-028.e: Letters that share a makhraj are told apart by their ṣifāt. Ṭāʾ has jahr, istiʿlāʾ, iṭbāq and qalqala, while tāʾ has hams, istifāl and infitāḥ.

tjm-029.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-029.q: What is meant by the ṣifa (attribute) of a letter in tajwīd?
o: The manner in which the letter is produced when it reaches its makhraj
The place in the mouth or throat where the letter is produced
The vowel sign written above or below the letter
The rule that applies when the letter meets another letter
tjm-029.e: The makhraj tells where a letter is produced, the ṣifa how it is produced: with or without breath, sound flow, raising of the tongue and so on. Rules between letters (such as idghām) are a separate topic.

tjm-030.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
o: The flow of breath when the letter is pronounced
The trapping of the sound so that it cannot flow
The raising of the back of the tongue to the palate
A whistling sound that accompanies the letter
tjm-030.e: Hams is the audible flow of breath with the letter, because its reliance on the makhraj is weak. Its opposite, jahr, is the holding back of the breath.

tjm-031.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-031.q: Which mnemonic phrase gathers the ten letters of hams?
tjm-031.e: The hams letters are fāʾ, ḥāʾ, thāʾ, hāʾ, shīn, khāʾ, ṣād, sīn, kāf and tāʾ. The other phrases gather the letters of shidda, istiʿlāʾ and qalqala.

tjm-032.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-032.q: Which mnemonic phrase gathers the eight letters of shidda?
tjm-032.e: Shidda letters are hamza, jīm, dāl, qāf, ṭāʾ, bāʾ, kāf and tāʾ. 'Lin ʿumar' gathers the in-between letters (tawassuṭ) and 'farra min lubb' the letters of idhlāq.

tjm-033.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-033.q: Which letters are in-between (tawassuṭ) shidda and rakhāwa?
o: Lām, nūn, ʿayn, mīm and rāʾ
Hamza, jīm, dāl, qāf and ṭāʾ
tjm-033.e: The phrase 'lin ʿumar' gathers lām, nūn, ʿayn, mīm and rāʾ. With these letters the sound neither stops completely as in shidda nor flows freely as in rakhāwa.

tjm-034.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-034.q: How is shidda defined, as opposed to hams?
o: The sound is trapped because the letter rests firmly on its makhraj
The breath flows because the letter rests weakly on its makhraj
The tongue rises to the palate and the sound becomes full
The letter is pronounced with a light echo at the end
tjm-034.e: Shidda concerns the sound (ṣawt): it is held back. Hams concerns the breath (nafas): it flows. That is why kāf and tāʾ can be both shadīd and mahmūs.

tjm-035.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-035.q: Which mnemonic phrase gathers the seven letters of istiʿlāʾ?
tjm-035.e: Istiʿlāʾ letters are khāʾ, ṣād, ḍād, ghayn, ṭāʾ, qāf and ẓāʾ. With them the back of the tongue rises toward the palate, giving them a full (mufakhkham) sound.

tjm-036.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-036.q: Which are the four letters of iṭbāq?
tjm-036.e: Ibn al-Jazarī: ṣād, ḍād, ṭāʾ and ẓāʾ are muṭbaqa. Khāʾ, ghayn and qāf are mustaʿliya but not muṭbaqa.

tjm-037.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-037.q: Which mnemonic phrase gathers the six letters of idhlāq?
tjm-037.e: The idhlāq letters are fāʾ, rāʾ, mīm, nūn, lām and bāʾ. They come from the tip of the tongue or the lips and are light on the tongue; all others are muṣmata.

tjm-038.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-038.q: Which letters carry the attribute of ṣafīr (whistling)?
tjm-038.e: Ibn al-Jazarī: ṣafīruhā ṣādun wa zāyun sīnu. Shīn has tafashshī, not ṣafīr.

tjm-039.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-039.q: Which letter is described with tafashshī (spreading of the air in the mouth)?
tjm-039.e: In the Muqaddima tafashshī is the attribute of shīn. Ḍād has istiṭāla, rāʾ takrīr and sīn ṣafīr.

tjm-040.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-040.q: Which letter has the attribute of istiṭāla (extension)?
tjm-040.e: Ibn al-Jazarī: wa ḍādan istaṭil. Istiṭāla belongs only to ḍād and is one of the features that separate it from ẓāʾ.

tjm-041.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-041.q: Which letter is described with takrīr (repetition)?
tjm-041.e: Takrīr is the readiness of the rāʾ to repeat because the tongue tip trembles. Lām shares inḥirāf with rāʾ, but not takrīr.

tjm-042.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-042.q: Which letters have the attribute of inḥirāf (deviation)?
tjm-042.e: Ibn al-Jazarī: wa-l-inḥirāfu ṣuḥḥiḥā fī al-lāmi wa-l-rā. Their sound deviates from its makhraj toward another; wāw and yāʾ (after fatḥa) have līn.

tjm-043.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-043.q: Which letters carry the attribute of līn (softness)?
o: Wāw and yāʾ when sākin and preceded by a fatḥa
Wāw and yāʾ when sākin and preceded by their matching vowel
Alif, wāw and yāʾ in every position
Lām and nūn when they are mushaddad
tjm-043.e: Līn is wāw sākina or yāʾ sākina after a fatḥa, pronounced easily without strain. After a matching vowel (ḍamma, kasra) they are madd letters, which is a different category.

tjm-044.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-044.q: Which mnemonic phrase gathers the letters that carry the attribute of qalqala?
tjm-044.e: The qalqala letters are qāf, ṭāʾ, bāʾ, jīm and dāl. All five are both majhūr and shadīd, which is why the sound needs a slight release when they are sākin.

tjm-045.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-045.q: Which statement about iṭbāq and istiʿlāʾ is correct?
o: Every muṭbaq letter is mustaʿlī, but not every mustaʿlī letter is muṭbaq
Every mustaʿlī letter is muṭbaq, but not every muṭbaq letter is mustaʿlī
They are two names for the same seven letters
They have no letter in common
tjm-045.e: In istiʿlāʾ the back of the tongue rises; in iṭbāq the tongue also presses against the palate and encloses the sound. The four muṭbaq letters are all among the seven mustaʿliya; khāʾ, ghayn and qāf are mustaʿliya only.

tjm-046.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-046.q: Which two letters combine hams with shidda?
tjm-046.e: Kāf and tāʾ appear in both mnemonics, 'fa-ḥaththahu shakhṣun sakat' and 'ajid qaṭin bakat'. Their sound is cut off, yet a little breath follows it; this breath should be audible but not exaggerated.

tjm-047.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-047.q: What is the reciter's task regarding the takrīr of rāʾ, according to the Muqaddima?
o: To conceal it, especially when the rāʾ is mushaddad
To make it clearly heard so that the rāʾ is recognised
To apply it only when stopping on a rāʾ
To repeat the rāʾ twice when it carries a shadda
tjm-047.e: Ibn al-Jazarī says: wa akhfi takrīran idhā tushaddadu. Takrīr is described so that it can be avoided; the tongue should not tremble repeatedly, above all on a doubled rāʾ.

tjm-048.src: al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad, Kitāb al-ʿAyn, introduction; Ibn Jinnī, Sirr Ṣināʿat al-Iʿrāb
tjm-048.q: What property of Arabic words is linked with the idhlāq letters?
o: Genuine four- or five-letter roots almost always contain one of them
No genuine Arabic word may ever begin with one of them
They never appear twice within one and the same root
They are dropped whenever a word is stopped on
tjm-048.e: Al-Khalīl observed that genuine quadriliteral and quinqueliteral roots contain at least one of the light letters fāʾ, rāʾ, mīm, nūn, lām or bāʾ. The others are called muṣmata ('silenced'), because they do not form such a root on their own.

tjm-049.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
o: An additional sharp sound resembling a whistle that accompanies the letter
The spreading of air across the mouth when the letter is pronounced
A slight trembling of the tongue tip during the letter
A nasal sound that comes from the khayshūm
tjm-049.e: Ṣafīr is an extra sound like the whistle of a bird, produced as the air passes the narrow gap between tongue tip and incisors. Spreading of air is tafashshī, trembling is takrīr, the nasal sound is ghunna.

tjm-050.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-050.q: What is meant by the istiṭāla of ḍād?
o: The sound extends along the tongue's edge through the whole makhraj
The vowel after ḍād is lengthened by two counts
The ḍād is held longer when it is stopped on
The tongue rises to the palate and the ḍād becomes full
tjm-050.e: Istiṭāla is an extension of the sound within the makhraj itself, which is long, from the back of the tongue's edge toward the lām. It has nothing to do with madd or with lengthening the time of the letter; raising the tongue is istiʿlāʾ.

tjm-051.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
o: The spreading of the air in the mouth when the letter is pronounced
The extension of the sound along the edge of the tongue
The flow of breath because the letter rests weakly on its makhraj
The deviation of the sound from its makhraj toward another
tjm-051.e: Tafashshī means the air spreads widely in the mouth, as with shīn. The extension along the tongue's edge is istiṭāla, flow of breath is hams and deviation is inḥirāf.

tjm-052.src: Sībawayh, al-Kitāb, ch. on idghām (makhārij and ṣifāt)
tjm-052.q: Sībawayh remarks that without iṭbāq certain letters would turn into others. Without iṭbāq, ṭāʾ would become which letter?
tjm-052.e: Sībawayh: without iṭbāq ṭāʾ would be dāl, ṣād sīn, ẓāʾ dhāl, and ḍād would leave the language. Ṭāʾ becomes dāl rather than tāʾ because ṭāʾ is majhūr like dāl, whereas tāʾ is mahmūs.

tjm-053.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-053.q: Which letter is commonly cited as carrying seven attributes, the highest number of any letter?
tjm-053.e: Rāʾ has jahr, tawassuṭ, istifāl, infitāḥ and idhlāq from the paired group, plus inḥirāf and takrīr. Ṭāʾ, ḍād and ṣād each have six.

tjm-054.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-054.q: How many attributes from the group of paired opposites does every letter carry?
o: Three, from the first three pairs
tjm-054.e: There are five pairs: hams/jahr, shidda/rakhāwa (with tawassuṭ between them), istiʿlāʾ/istifāl, iṭbāq/infitāḥ and idhlāq/iṣmāt. Every letter takes exactly one side of each pair; the attributes without opposites are added to some letters only.

tjm-055.src: Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Riʿāya li-Tajwīd al-Qirāʾa, section on the attributes of the letters
tjm-055.q: Which of the following attributes is classed among the weak ones?
tjm-055.e: Hams is weak because the breath escapes and the letter rests weakly on its makhraj. Jahr, iṭbāq and ṣafīr are counted among the strong attributes.

tjm-056.src: Makkī ibn Abī Ṭālib, al-Riʿāya li-Tajwīd al-Qirāʾa, section on the attributes of the letters
tjm-056.q: Which letter is commonly described as the strongest letter, and why?
o: Ṭāʾ, because it combines jahr, shidda, istiʿlāʾ, iṭbāq and qalqala
Rāʾ, because it carries the most attributes of any letter
Ḍād, because it is the only letter with istiṭāla
Qāf, because it is the deepest letter of the tongue
tjm-056.e: Strength is judged by the quality of the attributes, not their number. Ṭāʾ gathers almost all strong attributes; rāʾ has more attributes in total, but several of them are not strong.

tjm-057.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-057.q: Sīn and zāy share makhraj, ṣafīr, rakhāwa and istifāl. Which pair of attributes separates them?
o: Hams in sīn and jahr in zāy
Istiʿlāʾ in sīn and istifāl in zāy
Shidda in zāy and rakhāwa in sīn
Iṭbāq in zāy and infitāḥ in sīn
tjm-057.e: Sīn is mahmūs, so breath flows with it, while zāy is majhūr. If a reciter lets the breath run with zāy, it drifts toward sīn.

tjm-058.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-058.q: Ṣād and sīn share makhraj, hams, rakhāwa and ṣafīr. What separates them?
o: Istiʿlāʾ and iṭbāq, found only in ṣād
Jahr in ṣād and hams in sīn
Shidda in ṣād and rakhāwa in sīn
Tafashshī in ṣād and ṣafīr in sīn
tjm-058.e: Ṣād is raised and enclosed, sīn is lowered and open. This is why a weak iṭbāq turns ṣād into sīn, as Sībawayh noted.

tjm-059.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-059.q: Dhāl and ẓāʾ share makhraj, jahr and rakhāwa. What separates them?
o: Istiʿlāʾ and iṭbāq, found only in ẓāʾ
Hams in dhāl and jahr in ẓāʾ
tjm-059.e: Ẓāʾ is raised and enclosed, dhāl lowered and open; otherwise they are alike. Istiṭāla belongs to ḍād, and neither letter has qalqala.

tjm-060.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-060.q: Thāʾ and dhāl share their makhraj. Which attribute separates them?
o: Hams in thāʾ and jahr in dhāl
Shidda in thāʾ and rakhāwa in dhāl
Istiʿlāʾ in dhāl and istifāl in thāʾ
tjm-060.e: Thāʾ is mahmūs and dhāl majhūr; all their other attributes agree. A thāʾ voiced without breath therefore sounds like dhāl.

tjm-061.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-061.q: ʿAyn and ḥāʾ both come from the middle of the throat. Which description of their attributes is correct?
o: ʿAyn has jahr and tawassuṭ; ḥāʾ has hams and rakhāwa
ʿAyn has hams and shidda; ḥāʾ has jahr and rakhāwa
Both have jahr; only ʿayn has tawassuṭ
Both have rakhāwa; only ḥāʾ has istiʿlāʾ
tjm-061.e: ʿAyn is majhūr and one of the 'lin ʿumar' letters; ḥāʾ is mahmūs and rikhw. Both are mustafil, munfatiḥ and muṣmat. If the breath is held with ḥāʾ it drifts toward ʿayn.

tjm-062.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-062.q: Ghayn and khāʾ share makhraj, rakhāwa, istiʿlāʾ, infitāḥ and iṣmāt. What is the only paired attribute that separates them?
o: Jahr in ghayn and hams in khāʾ
Iṭbāq in khāʾ and infitāḥ in ghayn
Shidda in ghayn and rakhāwa in khāʾ
Istifāl in ghayn and istiʿlāʾ in khāʾ
tjm-062.e: Ghayn is majhūr and khāʾ mahmūs; in every other paired attribute they agree. Neither is muṭbaq, and both are mustaʿlī.

tjm-063.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-063.q: Which is the only muṭbaq letter that is also mahmūs?
tjm-063.e: Of the four iṭbāq letters, only ṣād appears in 'fa-ḥaththahu shakhṣun sakat'. Ṭāʾ, ḍād and ẓāʾ are majhūr.

tjm-064.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ
o: Cutting the sound on a word long enough to breathe, intending to go on
Pausing briefly without taking a breath, then continuing
Ending the recitation altogether and turning to something else
Starting the recitation again after a longer break
tjm-064.e: Ibn al-Jazarī defines waqf as cutting off the voice on a word for a time in which one usually breathes, with the intention of resuming. A pause without breath is sakt; ending the recitation is qaṭʿ.

tjm-065.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ
o: A short pause of about two counts without taking a breath
A stop of normal length with a breath
Ending the recitation and seeking refuge again later
Joining the end of a word to the next without any pause
tjm-065.e: Sakt is a brief cut of the voice, usually estimated at two counts, without breathing. It is transmitted at specific places only and is not left to the reciter's choice.

tjm-066.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ
tjm-066.q: A reciter runs out of breath, coughs or sneezes and has to stop. What is this kind of stop called?
tjm-066.e: A stop caused by necessity, such as shortness of breath, a cough, a sneeze or forgetting, is iḍṭirārī. It is allowed on any word, but the reciter then resumes from a place that gives sound meaning.

tjm-067.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ
tjm-067.q: A teacher asks a student to stop on a word that is not normally a place of stopping, to check how it is stopped on according to its written form. What is this stop called?
tjm-067.e: Ikhtibārī comes from ikhtibār (testing): the stop serves teaching or examination, for example to show whether a word ends in tāʾ maftūḥa or marbūṭa. It is not a stop for meaning.

tjm-068.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ
tjm-068.q: In which situation does the intiẓārī stop occur?
o: When a reciter combining several readings stops on a word to complete its other readings
When a reciter waits for the listeners to settle before beginning
When a reciter waits at a sign of muʿānaqa to choose one of the two places
When an imam pauses for the congregation to say āmīn
tjm-068.e: Intiẓārī belongs to jamʿ al-qirāʾāt: the reciter stops on a word where readings differ, then repeats it with the remaining readings before moving on.

tjm-069.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ
tjm-069.q: How is the waqf tāmm (complete stop) defined?
o: A stop where what follows has no connection with what precedes, neither in wording nor in meaning
A stop where what follows is connected in meaning but not in grammar
A stop where what follows is connected in grammar, so one goes back to continue
A stop where the words before it give no useful meaning
tjm-069.e: At a tāmm stop the passage is finished in both structure and sense, often at the end of a story or topic; one stops and begins with what follows. The other descriptions are kāfī, ḥasan and qabīḥ.

tjm-070.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ
tjm-070.q: How is the waqf kāfī (sufficient stop) defined?
o: What follows is linked to it in meaning only, not in grammar
What follows has no connection with it at all
What follows is connected with it in grammatical structure
The stop is only allowed at the end of a verse
tjm-070.e: In the kāfī stop the sentence is grammatically complete, but the next sentence still continues the same subject. One may stop and begin with what follows, as with tāmm.

tjm-071.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ
tjm-071.q: A reciter makes a ḥasan stop in the middle of a verse. How should he resume?
o: Go back to that word or before it and join it with what follows
Begin directly with the next word, as after a tāmm stop
Skip the next word and begin with the following sentence
Repeat only the last letter of the word before continuing
tjm-071.e: A ḥasan stop gives a sound meaning, but what follows is grammatically tied to it, so beginning with it is not good. Except at a verse end, the reciter returns and connects.

tjm-072.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ
tjm-072.q: What is a waqf qabīḥ (repugnant stop)?
o: A stop on words giving no complete meaning or a wrong one
A stop at the end of a verse whose meaning continues
A stop where the next sentence starts a new topic
A stop made because the reciter ran out of breath
tjm-072.e: A stop is qabīḥ when the words before it make no sense on their own, or worse, when they suggest a meaning that is wrong or improper. Such a stop is only excused by necessity, after which the reciter goes back.

tjm-073.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on waqf and ibtidāʾ
tjm-073.q: What does Ibn al-Jazarī state in the Muqaddima about obligatory and forbidden stops in the Quran?
o: No stop is obligatory or forbidden in itself; only a reason, such as distorting the meaning, makes it so
Every stop marked in the muṣḥaf is obligatory and every unmarked one forbidden
Stopping at the end of every verse is obligatory and in the middle forbidden
The mīm sign makes a stop obligatory in the sense of fiqh, so leaving it is sinful
tjm-073.e: Ibn al-Jazarī says there is no stop in the Quran that is wājib, nor one that is ḥarām, except what has a cause. 'Lāzim' in the mīm sign is a technical term of the qurrāʾ; connecting there is not a sin in itself unless one intends the wrong meaning.

tjm-074.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ
tjm-074.q: What view did many scholars, including Ibn al-Jazarī, hold about stopping at the end of a verse whose meaning continues into the next?
o: Permitted, even sunna, based on the hadith of Umm Salama
Stopping there is qabīḥ, so the reciter must always connect
Stopping there is allowed only in prayer, never outside it
Stopping there obliges the reciter to repeat the last word before continuing
tjm-074.e: The hadith of Umm Salama, reported by Abū Dāwūd and al-Tirmidhī, describes the Prophet's recitation as stopping verse by verse. On this basis many held that stopping at verse ends is sunna even where the meaning continues; others preferred to connect where the link is very close.

tjm-075.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ
tjm-075.q: Why do the scholars say that ibtidāʾ (starting) can only be ikhtiyārī?
o: No necessity forces a reciter to start at a given word
Because starting is always at the beginning of a sūra
Because the muṣḥaf signs mark every permitted starting point
Because starting after a stop needs the istiʿādha every time
tjm-075.e: Ibn al-Jazarī notes that a stop may be forced, but a start never is: the reciter can always choose where to begin. Therefore he must begin only where the meaning is sound and complete.

tjm-076.src: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, al-Muktafā fī al-Waqf wa-l-Ibtidāʾ
tjm-076.q: Which work of Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī is devoted to waqf and ibtidāʾ?
tjm-076.e: Al-Muktafā fī al-Waqf wa-l-Ibtidāʾ classifies the stops of the Quran as tāmm, kāfī and ḥasan. Al-Taysīr and Jāmiʿ al-Bayān deal with the readings and al-Muqniʿ with the rasm of the muṣḥaf.

tjm-077.src: al-Sajāwandī, ʿIlal al-Wuqūf; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ
tjm-077.q: The system of stop symbols such as mīm, ṭāʾ, jīm, zāy and ṣād, still used in many South Asian muṣḥafs, goes back to which scholar?
tjm-077.e: Muḥammad ibn Ṭayfūr al-Sajāwandī classified the stops and gave each class a letter symbol. Al-Ashmūnī, Ibn al-Anbārī and al-Naḥḥās also wrote on waqf, but the letter system is his.

tjm-078.src: Madina Muṣḥaf (King Fahd Complex), explanatory note on the stop signs
tjm-078.q: In the Madina Muṣḥaf, what does a small mīm above the text indicate?
o: A necessary stop, as connecting could distort the meaning
A prohibited stop, so the reader must connect
A stop that is allowed, with connecting preferred
A short pause without taking any breath
tjm-078.e: The mīm marks waqf lāzim: connecting there could make the next words seem to belong to the previous sentence and so distort the meaning. The other descriptions belong to lā, ṣilā and the sakt sign.

tjm-079.src: Madina Muṣḥaf (King Fahd Complex), explanatory note on the stop signs
tjm-079.q: In the Madina Muṣḥaf, what does the sign lā above a word indicate?
o: Do not stop here; if forced to stop, go back and connect
Stopping here is necessary to avoid a wrong meaning
Stopping and connecting are equally good here
Stop on one of two nearby places, not both
tjm-079.e: Lā marks a prohibited stop (waqf mamnūʿ): the next words are tied to it. If a reciter stops there out of necessity, he resumes from the word itself or before it.

tjm-080.src: Madina Muṣḥaf (King Fahd Complex), explanatory note on the stop signs
tjm-080.q: What does the sign of three dots appearing at two nearby places (muʿānaqa) mean?
o: One may stop at either place, but not at both
One must stop at both places
One may stop at neither place
One stops at the first place in prayer and at the second outside it
tjm-080.e: Taʿānuq al-waqf (muʿānaqa) means that each of the two places is a valid stop on its own; stopping at one requires passing the other. Stopping at both would cut a phrase off from both sides.

tjm-081.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on stopping according to the rasm
tjm-081.q: How is a word ending in tāʾ marbūṭa (round tāʾ) pronounced when it is stopped on?
o: With the vowel shortened, but kept
tjm-081.e: Tāʾ marbūṭa becomes a hāʾ with sukūn in waqf. In continuous reading it is pronounced as tāʾ with its vowel.

tjm-082.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf
tjm-082.q: How is a tanwīn with fatḥa (not on a tāʾ marbūṭa) treated when stopped on?
o: It is replaced by an alif
It is dropped and the letter takes sukūn
The nūn sound is kept with sukūn
It is replaced by a hāʾ sākina
tjm-082.e: Tanwīn fatḥ turns into an alif of two counts in waqf (ibdāl). Tanwīn with ḍamma or kasra, by contrast, is dropped and the letter takes sukūn.

tjm-083.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, ch. on stopping with rawm and ishmām
tjm-083.q: What is rawm when stopping on a word?
o: Uttering about a third of the final vowel faintly
Rounding the lips after the sukūn without any sound
Replacing the final vowel with a full sukūn
Lengthening the final vowel into a madd letter
tjm-083.e: Rawm lets a weak part of the vowel be heard so that its kind is recognised; it is used with ḍamma and kasra. Rounding the lips without sound is ishmām.

tjm-084.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, ch. on stopping with rawm and ishmām
tjm-084.q: What is ishmām when stopping on a word, and with which vowel is it used?
o: Rounding the lips right after the sukūn without sound; only with ḍamma
Pronouncing a third of the vowel faintly; with ḍamma and kasra
Rounding the lips with a faint sound; with every vowel
Mixing the vowel with a slight kasra; only with fatḥa
tjm-084.e: Ishmām is seen, not heard: the lips round just after the final letter is made sākin, pointing to the ḍamma. It is not used with kasra or fatḥa.

tjm-085.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on rawm and ishmām
tjm-085.q: Which of these word endings allows neither rawm nor ishmām when stopped on?
o: A tāʾ marbūṭa read as hāʾ
tjm-085.e: Rawm and ishmām point to the vowel of the letter actually stopped on. A tāʾ marbūṭa becomes a hāʾ that never had a vowel, so there is nothing to point to. Ḍamma allows both, kasra allows rawm.

tjm-086.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on rawm and ishmām
tjm-086.q: Why do the qurrāʾ not use rawm on a final fatḥa?
o: Because fatḥa is light: once part of it is uttered, all of it comes out
Because fatḥa at the end of a word always turns into an alif
Because rawm is only allowed on a tāʾ marbūṭa
Because the lips cannot round for a fatḥa
tjm-086.e: Ibn al-Jazarī explains that the reciters did not apply rawm to fatḥa because of its lightness: a part of it cannot be separated from the whole. Lip rounding concerns ishmām, which is limited to ḍamma.

tjm-087.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf according to the rasm
tjm-087.q: How do the reciters in the riwāya of Ḥafṣ stop on the particle idhan, written with tanwīn fatḥ?
o: With an alif, like any tanwīn fatḥ
With a nūn sākina, keeping the tanwīn as nūn
With sukūn on the dhāl and no alif
With a hāʾ sākina, like a tāʾ marbūṭa
tjm-087.e: Idhan is written in the muṣḥaf with an alif carrying tanwīn, and the reciters stop on it with an alif. The written form supports this stop.

tjm-088.src: Madina Muṣḥaf (King Fahd Complex), explanatory note on the stop signs
tjm-088.q: The highlighted word and the word after it both carry the three-dot sign. A reciter stops on the highlighted word. What does he do at the next word?
o: Skip it and continue after it
Stop on it with rawm only
tjm-088.e: With muʿānaqa one may stop at either of the two marked places, but not at both. Whoever stops at the first place reads the second without stopping.

tjm-089.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 2:2; Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs
tjm-089.q: If the reciter stops on the highlighted word, the first of the two muʿānaqa places, how is the next word understood?
o: A new sentence: the Book contains guidance for the God-fearing
As completing the negation: there is no doubt in the Book
As referring back to the people who doubt it
As a separate oath before the rest of the verse
tjm-089.e: Stopping on the first place ends the sentence with the negation of doubt, so the next word opens the statement that the Book contains guidance. Stopping on the second place instead gives 'no doubt in it', and 'guidance' then begins anew. Both meanings are sound, which is why both places are marked.

tjm-090.src: al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 5:26; Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs
tjm-090.q: The highlighted word and a word two places later carry the muʿānaqa sign. If the reciter stops on the highlighted word, to what does the period of forty years attach?
o: To their wandering in the land
To the prohibition of the land for them
To the lifetime of Mūsā among them
To the rule of their later kings
tjm-090.e: Stopping on the first place makes the prohibition a statement without time limit, and the forty years describe how long they wandered. Stopping on the second place makes the prohibition itself last forty years. Al-Ṭabarī and other exegetes report both readings of the meaning.

tjm-091.src: Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 6:36
tjm-091.q: Why is the sign of a necessary stop (mīm) placed on the highlighted word?
o: Connecting would suggest the dead respond along with the hearers
Because the verse is too long to read in one breath
Because the next word begins with a hamzat waṣl
Because the highlighted word ends in a madd letter
tjm-091.e: Only those who hear respond; the dead are the subject of a new sentence about their resurrection. Connecting would join them to the hearers and so suggest a meaning that is not intended.

tjm-092.src: Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 36:76
tjm-092.q: The highlighted word carries a mīm (necessary stop). What would connecting it with the next words risk?
o: Allah's next words could sound like the disbelievers' speech
Merging two letters that share the same makhraj
Lengthening a vowel beyond its proper measure
Dropping the ghunna of the nūn that follows
tjm-092.e: The highlighted word ends the mention of their speech. What follows is Allah's statement that He knows what they hide and reveal; connecting would make it sound like their words.

tjm-093.src: Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 3:181
tjm-093.q: The highlighted word ends a quotation and carries a mīm. What would connecting it with what follows risk?
o: The threat that follows could be heard as part of their claim
That the quotation is understood as Allah's own statement about Himself
That the word after it loses its hamzat waṣl
That the reciter has to stop in the middle of the next sentence
tjm-093.e: The highlighted word ends what they claimed. The next sentence is Allah's warning that their words are recorded; the mīm prevents it from being heard as a continuation of their claim.

tjm-094.src: Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs; al-Ashmūnī, Manār al-Hudā, on 4:171
tjm-094.q: The highlighted word carries a mīm. What could connecting it with the following words wrongly suggest?
o: That the following words describe the son whose existence is being denied
That the denial of a son is withdrawn by the next sentence
That the next sentence is addressed to the People of the Book
That the verse ends at the highlighted word
tjm-094.e: The words after the highlighted one affirm that everything in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah. Connected directly, they could be heard as an attribute of the denied son; the necessary stop keeps them a separate statement.

tjm-095.src: Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 5:73
tjm-095.q: The highlighted word ends a statement that the verse condemns, and carries a mīm. What would connecting risk?
o: The affirmation of the One God could sound like part of the claim
That the condemned statement is heard as Allah's own teaching
That the threat at the end of the verse is cut off
That the highlighted word loses its tanwīn
tjm-095.e: The verse first quotes a false claim and then answers it with the affirmation that there is no god but One God. The necessary stop separates the quoted claim from the answer.

tjm-096.src: Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs; al-Ashmūnī, Manār al-Hudā, on 2:26
tjm-096.q: The mīm on the highlighted word separates two speakers. Which?
o: The disbelievers' question ends here; what follows is Allah's answer
The believers' words end here; the disbelievers' words begin
Allah's words end here; the believers' reply begins
The Prophet's words end here; Allah's words begin
tjm-096.e: The disbelievers ask what Allah intends by such a parable; the question ends on the highlighted word. The following words, that He leads many astray by it and guides many, are Allah's reply, so connecting could make them sound like part of the question.

tjm-097.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ (examples of qabīḥ)
tjm-097.q: How is a deliberate stop on the highlighted word classed?
o: Qabīḥ: it suggests an unrestricted negation the verse does not intend
Ḥasan: the meaning is complete and only the next word is tied to it
Kāfī: the sentence is complete and only the subject continues
Tāmm: the verse turns to a new topic after it
tjm-097.e: The verse says Allah does not shy away from striking a parable; the negation is tied to what follows. Stopping on the highlighted word cuts it off and suggests an unrestricted negation, so it is among the examples of a qabīḥ stop.

tjm-098.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ (examples of qabīḥ)
tjm-098.q: Why is stopping on the highlighted word without necessity considered qabīḥ?
o: It implies prayer itself is forbidden, ignoring the condition after it
Because the highlighted word ends in a tāʾ marbūṭa
Because a mīm sign stands on the highlighted word
Because the verse is addressed to the believers alone
tjm-098.e: The verse forbids approaching prayer in a certain state, which is stated right after the highlighted word. Cutting off there turns a conditional prohibition into an unconditional one, a classic example of a qabīḥ stop.

tjm-099.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ (qabīḥ beginnings)
tjm-099.q: After stopping on the word before it, a reciter begins with the highlighted word. How is this start classed?
o: Qabīḥ: the reciter utters the condemned claim as if his own
Ibtidāʾ ḥasan: the highlighted word begins a new sentence
Ibtidāʾ tāmm: the previous sentence is fully complete
Permissible because a sign of necessary stop precedes it
tjm-099.e: The highlighted word opens the content of a false claim that the verse quotes and condemns. Starting there detaches the claim from 'they said' and makes the reciter utter it as a statement, so the scholars count it among the worst beginnings.

tjm-100.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ (example of ḥasan)
tjm-100.q: Stopping on the highlighted word is a standard example of which stop, and why?
o: Ḥasan: sound meaning, but the next word is an attribute tied to it
Tāmm: what follows has no connection with it at all
Qabīḥ: the meaning is incomplete without the next word
Kāfī: what follows is linked to it in meaning only
tjm-100.e: Ibn al-Jazarī gives this as an example of a ḥasan stop: the phrase before it is meaningful, but the next word describes Allah and is grammatically attached. Since this is not the end of the verse, the reciter who stops here goes back and connects.

tjm-101.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf and ibtidāʾ (example of tāmm)
tjm-101.q: The end of this verse is a common example of which kind of stop?
o: Tāmm, because the next verse turns from the believers to the disbelievers
Kāfī, because the next verse continues to describe the believers
Ḥasan, because the next verse is grammatically tied to this one
Qabīḥ, because the description of the believers is incomplete
tjm-101.e: The passage describing the God-fearing ends here, and the next verse begins a new subject, the disbelievers. With no connection in wording or meaning, the stop is tāmm.

tjm-102.src: Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs
tjm-102.q: What does the sign on the highlighted word tell the reciter?
o: Do not stop: the next words describe their state
Stop: connecting would suggest a wrong meaning
Either stop or connect, both are equal
Stop briefly without taking a breath
tjm-102.e: The highlighted word carries lā. What follows describes the angels' greeting to these people at the moment of death and is grammatically tied to the sentence, so the reciter should not stop.

tjm-103.src: Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs
tjm-103.q: Which sign appears on the highlighted word, and what does it mean?
o: Qilā: stopping is permitted and preferred
Ṣilā: stopping is permitted, connecting preferred
Jīm: stopping and connecting are equal
tjm-103.e: The ligature qilā marks a permitted stop where stopping is better. Here the sentence about how few know their number is complete, and a new instruction to the Prophet follows.

tjm-104.src: Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs
tjm-104.q: The highlighted word carries the sign ṣilā. What does it mean?
tjm-104.e: Ṣilā is short for 'al-waṣl awlā': the reader may stop, but continuing is preferred. Qilā is the reverse.

tjm-105.src: Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 3:7; al-Dānī, al-Muktafā, on 3:7
tjm-105.q: The highlighted word carries qilā. Which statement correctly describes this sign and the related discussion?
o: Stopping is preferred, in line with those who hold that only Allah knows its ultimate reality; connecting stays permitted
Stopping is obligatory, because all scholars agree that the firmly grounded know nothing of the interpretation
Connecting is obligatory, because all scholars agree that the firmly grounded share in all knowledge of it
The sign has no link to meaning; it only marks a convenient place to breathe
tjm-105.e: Many of the early scholars stopped here, understanding taʾwīl as the ultimate reality known only to Allah. Others, such as some reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid, connected, understanding taʾwīl as explanation that the firmly grounded also attain. The Madina Muṣḥaf marks the stop as preferred, while connecting remains permitted.

tjm-106.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on stopping according to the rasm
tjm-106.q: The highlighted word is written in the muṣḥaf with an open tāʾ (tāʾ maftūḥa). If it is stopped on, for example in an ikhtibārī stop, how does Ḥafṣ stop?
o: With a tāʾ sākina, following the written form
With a hāʾ sākina, like a tāʾ marbūṭa
With an alif, like a tanwīn fatḥ
With the tāʾ and its full vowel
tjm-106.e: Ḥafṣ follows the rasm: what is written with an open tāʾ is stopped on with tāʾ. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisāʾī stop on such words with hāʾ, which is why this is a classic place for an ikhtibārī stop.

tjm-107.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh of Sūrat al-Kahf; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, ch. on sakt
tjm-107.q: In Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya, what does the reciter do at the end of the highlighted word when he connects it with the next verse?
o: A sakt: a brief pause without breath, then continue
A full stop with a breath, then continue
He connects with tanwīn and no pause at all
He stops and repeats the highlighted word
tjm-107.e: Ḥafṣ has an obligatory sakt here when connecting, with the tanwīn turned into an alif. The usual explanation is that it shows the next word is not an attribute of the highlighted one.

tjm-108.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh of Sūrat al-Qiyāma; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, ch. on sakt
tjm-108.q: In Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya there is a sakt on the highlighted word. What does it prevent?
o: Merging its nūn into the next rāʾ, so the words sound like one
Lengthening a vowel beyond its proper measure
Losing the hamzat waṣl of the following word
A full stop that would cut the question off
tjm-108.e: Without the sakt, the nūn would be merged into the rāʾ and the two words would be heard as a single word. The sakt keeps them apart, so the nūn is pronounced clearly.

tjm-109.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh of Sūrat al-Muṭaffifīn; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, ch. on sakt
tjm-109.q: The highlighted word carries a sakt in Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya. Which consequence does the sakt have for its final letter?
o: The lām is pronounced clearly instead of being merged into the following rāʾ
The lām is merged into the rāʾ, but with a brief pause before it
The lām is pronounced with a short vowel to separate the words
The lām is dropped and the rāʾ is doubled
tjm-109.e: Normally a lām sākina is merged into a following rāʾ. The sakt interrupts the contact, so the merging cannot happen and the lām is heard. This is one of the four sakt places of Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya.

tjm-110.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, farsh of Sūrat Yā Sīn; Madina Muṣḥaf, explanatory note on the stop signs
tjm-110.q: The highlighted word carries both the qilā sign and the sakt sign. How does a reciter of Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya treat it?
o: Stop on it (preferred), or connect with a sakt before the next word
He must stop on it, because the sakt sign forbids connecting
He must connect without pause, because the two signs cancel each other
He makes a sakt and then repeats the highlighted word
tjm-110.e: Both options are valid: a full stop, which the qilā marks as preferable, or connecting with the obligatory sakt. What is not valid in this riwāya is connecting directly without any pause. The sakt shows that what follows is a new sentence, not a description of the highlighted word.

tjm-111.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on stopping according to the rasm
tjm-111.q: How is the last letter of the highlighted word pronounced when stopping at the end of the verse?
tjm-111.e: The word ends in tāʾ marbūṭa with tanwīn. In waqf the tanwīn is dropped and the tāʾ marbūṭa becomes a hāʾ with sukūn.

tjm-112.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf
tjm-112.q: If a reciter stops on the highlighted word, which ends in tāʾ marbūṭa with tanwīn fatḥ, how does he pronounce its end?
o: With a hāʾ sākina, without an alif
With an alif, as for every tanwīn fatḥ
With a tāʾ followed by an alif
tjm-112.e: Tanwīn fatḥ normally becomes an alif in waqf, but not on a tāʾ marbūṭa: there the rule of the tāʾ marbūṭa takes precedence and the word ends in hāʾ sākina. The muṣḥaf accordingly writes no alif after it.

tjm-113.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on waqf
tjm-113.q: How is the end of the highlighted word pronounced when stopping at the end of the verse?
o: The tanwīn becomes an alif of two counts
The tanwīn is kept as a nūn sākina
The last letter takes sukūn with no alif
The tanwīn becomes a hāʾ sākina
tjm-113.e: The highlighted word ends in tanwīn fatḥ, which is replaced by an alif in waqf. That alif is written in the muṣḥaf after the letter.

tjm-114.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, ch. on stopping with rawm and ishmām
tjm-114.q: The highlighted word ends in tanwīn with ḍamma. In which ways may the reciter stop on it?
o: With pure sukūn, with rawm, or with ishmām
With sukūn or rawm, but not ishmām
With an alif replacing the tanwīn
tjm-114.e: A final ḍamma (with or without tanwīn) allows all three: pure sukūn, rawm and ishmām. The tanwīn itself is dropped; only tanwīn fatḥ becomes an alif.

tjm-115.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, ch. on stopping with rawm and ishmām
tjm-115.q: The highlighted word ends in kasra. In which ways may the reciter stop on it?
o: Sukūn or rawm, but not ishmām
Ishmām only, to show the vowel
tjm-115.e: Rawm is used with ḍamma and kasra, ishmām only with ḍamma. So a final kasra allows sukūn or rawm. Rawm here means pronouncing a faint part of the kasra.

tjm-116.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī, ch. on stopping with rawm and ishmām
tjm-116.q: The highlighted word ends in a fatḥa without tanwīn. How is it stopped on?
o: With an alif after the last letter
tjm-116.e: A final fatḥa without tanwīn takes pure sukūn only: rawm is not used with fatḥa, ishmām only with ḍamma, and an alif replaces only tanwīn fatḥ.

tjm-117.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on hāʾ al-kināya and on waqf
tjm-117.q: The highlighted word ends in a pronoun hāʾ (hāʾ al-ḍamīr). How is it pronounced when stopping at the end of the verse?
o: As a hāʾ sākina; its vowel and any ṣila are dropped
With its ḍamma lengthened into a wāw
With its ḍamma kept short and clearly voiced
As a tāʾ sākina instead of hāʾ
tjm-117.e: In waqf the hāʾ al-ḍamīr is made sākin, so the connecting vowel (ṣila) that may appear in continuous reading disappears. Only a tāʾ marbūṭa changes its letter in waqf; a pronoun hāʾ simply loses its vowel.

tjm-118.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on beginning with hamzat al-waṣl
tjm-118.q: If a reciter begins with the highlighted verb, which vowel does its hamzat al-waṣl take, and why?
o: Ḍamma, because the third letter of the verb has an original ḍamma
Kasra, because hamzat al-waṣl in verbs always takes kasra
Fatḥa, because it is the hamza of a command
No vowel: the reciter begins with the sākin letter
tjm-118.e: In a verb, hamzat al-waṣl takes ḍamma when the third letter has an original ḍamma, and kasra when it has fatḥa or kasra. In the highlighted verb the third letter is voweled with ḍamma, so the start is with ḍamma.

tjm-119.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on beginning with hamzat al-waṣl
tjm-119.q: If a reciter begins with the highlighted verb, which vowel does its hamzat al-waṣl take?
o: Kasra, because its third letter has a fatḥa
Ḍamma, because the verb is a command
Fatḥa, as with the definite article
Ḍamma, because the verb ends in a wāw
tjm-119.e: Counting the hamza, the third letter of the highlighted verb has a fatḥa, so hamzat al-waṣl takes kasra. Ḍamma is only used when the third letter has an original ḍamma, regardless of the verb's ending.

tjm-120.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-120.q: The highlighted word contains a doubled ḍād. From where is this letter produced?
o: From the edge of the tongue against the upper molars
From the tip of the tongue against the tips of the upper incisors
From the tip of the tongue against the roots of the upper incisors
From the back of the tongue against the soft palate
tjm-120.e: Ḍād comes from one or both edges of the tongue with the upper molars. Producing it with the tongue tip at the incisors turns it into ẓāʾ or dāl, a common error in this very word.

tjm-121.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-121.q: The first root letter of the highlighted word is ṣād. Which attribute without an opposite does it carry?
tjm-121.e: Ṣād is one of the three whistling letters. It also has istiʿlāʾ and iṭbāq, which give it its full sound; tafashshī belongs to shīn, istiṭāla to ḍād and inḥirāf to lām and rāʾ.

tjm-122.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-122.q: The highlighted word begins with qāf. From where is qāf produced?
o: The back of the tongue with the soft palate above it
From the deepest part of the throat
From the middle of the tongue with the hard palate
