From the part of the throat nearest the mouth
tjm-122.e: Qāf is the deepest of the tongue letters, made at the back of the tongue against the soft palate. Kāf is made slightly further forward; ghayn and khāʾ belong to the throat.

tjm-123.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on makhārij al-ḥurūf
tjm-123.q: The first root letter of the highlighted word is fāʾ. Where is it produced?
o: The inner lower lip with the tips of the upper incisors
Between the two lips, which close completely
Between the tongue tip and the tips of the upper incisors
Between the tongue tip and the roots of the upper incisors
tjm-123.e: Fāʾ is the only letter produced by the lower lip with the upper incisors. Closing both lips gives bāʾ or mīm, and the tongue tip at the incisors gives thāʾ.

tjm-124.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-124.q: The highlighted word begins with shīn. Which attribute is particular to this letter?
o: Tafashshī, the spreading of air in the mouth
Ṣafīr, a whistle at the incisors
Istiṭāla, extension along the edge of the tongue
Takrīr, a trembling of the tongue tip
tjm-124.e: Shīn is the letter of tafashshī: the air spreads in the mouth. Ṣafīr belongs to ṣād, zāy and sīn, istiṭāla to ḍād and takrīr to rāʾ.

tjm-125.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-125.q: The highlighted word contains a yāʾ sākina after a fatḥa. Which attribute does this yāʾ carry?
tjm-125.e: A yāʾ or wāw that is sākin after a fatḥa is a letter of līn, pronounced easily. It is a madd letter of the jawf only after a kasra (for yāʾ) or ḍamma (for wāw).

tjm-126.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, sections on makhārij and on ḍād and ẓāʾ
tjm-126.q: The highlighted word begins with ẓāʾ. What must the reciter keep in mind to avoid confusing it with ḍād?
o: A different makhraj (tongue tip at the incisors) and no istiṭāla
Ẓāʾ is mahmūs while ḍād is majhūr, so only the breath separates them
Ẓāʾ has istifāl while ḍād has istiʿlāʾ
Ẓāʾ is a throat letter while ḍād is a tongue letter
tjm-126.e: Both letters are majhūr, rikhw, mustaʿlī and muṭbaq, so their attributes nearly coincide. They differ in makhraj and in the istiṭāla of ḍād; Ibn al-Jazarī devotes a passage of the Muqaddima to distinguishing them.

tjm-127.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on ṣifāt al-ḥurūf
tjm-127.q: The highlighted word contains a zāy sākina. Which attribute must the reciter preserve so that it does not drift toward sīn?
o: Jahr: the breath must not flow with the zāy
Istiʿlāʾ: the back of the tongue must rise
Iṭbāq: the tongue must press against the palate
Shidda: the sound must be cut off completely
tjm-127.e: Zāy and sīn share makhraj, ṣafīr, rakhāwa and istifāl; only jahr separates them. A sākin zāy whose breath is released easily sounds like sīn, so its jahr must be kept.

tjr-001.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-001.q: How many rules apply to nūn sākina and tanwīn?
tjr-001.e: They are iẓhār, idghām, iqlāb and ikhfāʾ. Which one applies depends on the letter that follows the nūn sākina or tanwīn.

tjr-002.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-002.q: Before which letters is nūn sākina or tanwīn pronounced with clear iẓhār ḥalqī?
tjr-002.e: Iẓhār ḥalqī applies before the throat letters: hamza, hāʾ, ʿayn, ḥāʾ, ghayn and khāʾ. Their point of articulation is far from that of the nūn, so the nūn is pronounced clearly.

tjr-003.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-003.q: Which single letter causes iqlāb of nūn sākina and tanwīn?
tjr-003.e: Iqlāb has one letter only, the bāʾ: the nūn is turned into a concealed mīm with ghunna. Mīm and wāw are idghām letters, fāʾ is an ikhfāʾ letter.

tjr-004.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-004.q: In which mnemonic word are the six letters of idghām for nūn sākina and tanwīn gathered?
tjr-004.e: The idghām letters are yāʾ, rāʾ, mīm, lām, wāw and nūn, gathered in yarmalūn. Quṭbu jad gathers the qalqala letters, khuṣṣa ḍaghṭin qiẓ the heavy letters, and ibghi ḥajjaka begins the list of the lām qamariyya letters.

tjr-005.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-005.q: How many letters cause ikhfāʾ ḥaqīqī of nūn sākina and tanwīn?
tjr-005.e: Of the 28 letters, six are for iẓhār, six for idghām and one for iqlāb; the remaining fifteen are the letters of ikhfāʾ.

tjr-006.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-006.q: Which four letters cause idghām WITH ghunna of nūn sākina and tanwīn?
tjr-006.e: Idghām with ghunna occurs before the letters of yanmū: yāʾ, nūn, mīm and wāw. Lām and rāʾ take idghām without ghunna.

tjr-007.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-007.q: Before which letters is nūn sākina or tanwīn merged WITHOUT ghunna in Ḥafṣ?
tjr-007.e: Before lām and rāʾ the nūn is merged completely, letter and ghunna, so no nasal sound remains. Before mīm, nūn, wāw and yāʾ the ghunna is kept.

tjr-008.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-008.q: Which rule applies to the tanwīn at the end of the highlighted word when it is read continuously with the next word?
tjr-008.e: The next word begins with ʿayn, a throat letter, so the tanwīn is pronounced clearly without prolonged ghunna.

tjr-009.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-009.q: Which rule applies to the tanwīn of the highlighted word when it is joined to the next word?
tjr-009.e: The next word begins with lām. Before lām and rāʾ the tanwīn is merged completely without ghunna.

tjr-010.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-010.q: Which rule applies to the tanwīn of the highlighted word when it is joined to the next word?
tjr-010.e: The next word begins with bāʾ, so the tanwīn is turned into a concealed mīm with ghunna. Ikhfāʾ shafawī is the name for a mīm sākina before bāʾ, not for tanwīn.

tjr-011.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-011.q: Which rule applies to the nūn sākina of the highlighted word, read together with the next word?
tjr-011.e: The next word begins with shīn, one of the fifteen ikhfāʾ letters. The nūn is hidden with a ghunna of two counts.

tjr-012.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-012.q: Which rule applies to the tanwīn of the highlighted word when it is joined to the next word?
tjr-012.e: The next word begins with mīm, a letter of yanmū, so the tanwīn is merged into the mīm with ghunna.

tjr-013.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-013.q: Which rule applies to the nūn sākina of the highlighted word when it is joined to the next word?
tjr-013.e: The next word begins with rāʾ. Nūn sākina before rāʾ is merged completely, and the rāʾ is pronounced doubled without ghunna.

tjr-014.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on nūn and tanwīn
tjr-014.q: The highlighted word contains a nūn sākina followed by ʿayn inside the same word. Which rule applies?
tjr-014.e: Iẓhār ḥalqī applies whether the throat letter comes in the same word or in the next word. Iẓhār muṭlaq is the term for nūn before wāw or yāʾ inside one word.

tjr-015.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-015.q: The highlighted word has a nūn sākina followed by bāʾ within the same word. How is it read?
o: Iqlāb: a concealed mīm with ghunna
Clear iẓhār, as it is inside one word
Ikhfāʾ of the nūn with light ghunna
tjr-015.e: Iqlāb applies before bāʾ both within a word and across two words. The nūn becomes a mīm, which is then concealed with ghunna.

tjr-016.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-016.q: Which rule applies to the tanwīn of the highlighted word when it is joined to the next word?
tjr-016.e: The next word begins with wāw, a letter of yanmū, so the tanwīn is merged with ghunna. This idghām is incomplete (nāqiṣ), as the ghunna of the nūn remains.

tjr-017.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-017.q: Which rule applies to the tanwīn at the end of the highlighted word when it is joined to the next word?
tjr-017.e: The next word begins with yāʾ, a letter of yanmū, so the tanwīn is merged with ghunna.

tjr-018.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on nūn and tanwīn
tjr-018.q: Which rule applies to the nūn sākina of the highlighted word when it is joined to the next word?
tjr-018.e: The next word begins with khāʾ. In Ḥafṣ, ghayn and khāʾ are throat letters of iẓhār; reading them with ikhfāʾ is a frequent mistake.

tjr-019.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-019.q: Which rule applies to the nūn sākina of the highlighted word when it is joined to the next word?
tjr-019.e: The next word begins with jīm, one of the fifteen ikhfāʾ letters, so the nūn is concealed with ghunna.

tjr-020.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-020.q: The highlighted word contains a nūn sākina followed by kāf in the same word. Which rule applies?
tjr-020.e: Ikhfāʾ applies within a word as well as across words. Kāf is an ikhfāʾ letter, so the nūn is concealed with ghunna.

tjr-021.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-021.q: Why is the idghām of nūn sākina into wāw and yāʾ called incomplete (nāqiṣ)?
o: The ghunna of the nūn remains audible
The wāw and yāʾ lose their vowel
The nūn is pronounced half clearly
It only occurs within a single word
tjr-021.e: In idghām nāqiṣ the letter disappears but its attribute, the ghunna, remains. Before nūn and mīm the idghām is complete (kāmil), since the ghunna heard belongs to the doubled following letter.

tjr-022.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-022.q: In how many Quranic words does a nūn sākina meet a wāw or yāʾ within the same word, so that iẓhār muṭlaq applies?
tjr-022.e: Idghām requires the nūn to end one word and the idghām letter to begin the next. The four words in which nūn sākina meets wāw or yāʾ inside one word are read with iẓhār (al-Jamzūrī names them).

tjr-023.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-023.q: The highlighted word has a nūn sākina followed by yāʾ in the same word. How is the nūn read?
tjr-023.e: This is one of the four words with nūn sākina before wāw or yāʾ inside one word. Idghām is not applied, so the nūn is pronounced clearly; this is called iẓhār muṭlaq.

tjr-024.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-024.q: Why is the nūn sākina before wāw in the highlighted word not merged?
o: So the word is not mistaken for a doubled root
Because wāw is not a letter of idghām
Because the nūn there is really a tanwīn
Because Ḥafṣ makes a brief pause on it
tjr-024.e: If the nūn were merged, the word would sound like one from a doubled (muḍāʿaf) root, and its form would be obscured. Wāw is an idghām letter, but only across two words.

tjr-025.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), ch. on letters with close points of articulation
tjr-025.q: How does Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya read the nūn at the end of the letter name that opens the verse shown, when joined to the following wāw?
tjr-025.e: In the letter names nūn (68:1) and yā-sīn (36:1) before the following wāw, Ḥafṣ reads iẓhār, while several other readers merge. Al-Shāṭibī records both cases in the chapter on letters close in articulation.

tjr-026.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh of Sūrat al-Kahf (the sakt of Ḥafṣ)
tjr-026.q: The highlighted word ends in a nūn sākina and the next word begins with rāʾ. How does Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya read it?
o: A short pause (sakt) on the nūn, so no idghām
Idghām without ghunna, as usual before rāʾ
Idghām with ghunna into the rāʾ
Ikhfāʾ of the nūn with ghunna
tjr-026.e: Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya makes a brief sakt without breath here, which prevents the usual idghām into rāʾ. The same sakt occurs in 83:14 between lām and rāʾ.

tjr-027.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-027.q: When is the ghunna of an ikhfāʾ pronounced heavy (with tafkhīm)?
o: When the following letter is a heavy letter such as ṭāʾ or qāf
When the following letter is a throat letter
When the nūn is a tanwīn rather than a nūn
When the ikhfāʾ falls inside a single word
tjr-027.e: The ghunna of ikhfāʾ follows the next letter: it is heavy before the istiʿlāʾ letters among the ikhfāʾ letters (ṣād, ḍād, ṭāʾ, ẓāʾ, qāf) and light before the others.

tjr-028.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-028.q: The ikhfāʾ of nūn sākina has three levels. Before which letters is it closest to iẓhār?
tjr-028.e: The farther the letter's point of articulation from the nūn, the closer the ikhfāʾ is to iẓhār: this is the case with qāf and kāf. With ṭāʾ, dāl and tāʾ, which are closest to the nūn, it is nearest to idghām.

tjr-029.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on meeting of two sākins
tjr-029.q: The tanwīn at the end of the highlighted word is followed by a hamzat al-waṣl. How is it read in continuous recitation?
o: The tanwīn's nūn is pronounced with a kasra
The tanwīn is read with ikhfāʾ
The tanwīn is merged into the next letter
tjr-029.e: The tanwīn and the sākin letter after the dropped hamzat al-waṣl would form two sākins in a row, so the nūn of the tanwīn takes a kasra to connect them.

tjr-030.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on nūn sākina and tanwīn
tjr-030.q: How is ikhfāʾ ḥaqīqī correctly defined?
o: A state between iẓhār and idghām, without doubling, keeping the ghunna
Full merging of the nūn into the next letter with ghunna
Changing the nūn into a mīm before bāʾ
Pronouncing the nūn clearly from its own point of articulation
tjr-030.e: In ikhfāʾ the nūn is neither shown nor merged: the next letter is not doubled, and only the ghunna of the nūn remains. Full merging is idghām, changing into mīm is iqlāb.

tjr-031.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on mīm sākina
tjr-031.q: How many rules apply to mīm sākina?
tjr-031.e: They are ikhfāʾ shafawī (before bāʾ), idghām mithlayn ṣaghīr (before mīm) and iẓhār shafawī (before all other letters).

tjr-032.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on mīm sākina
tjr-032.q: Before which letter does mīm sākina take ikhfāʾ shafawī?
tjr-032.e: Ikhfāʾ shafawī has one letter, the bāʾ, which shares the lips with the mīm. Before mīm it is idghām, before fāʾ and wāw clear iẓhār.

tjr-033.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on mīm sākina
tjr-033.q: What is it called when a mīm sākina is followed by a vowelled mīm?
tjr-033.e: Two identical letters meet, the first sākin, so the first mīm is merged into the second with ghunna. It is also called idghām shafawī.

tjr-034.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on mīm sākina
tjr-034.q: Which rule applies to the mīm sākina at the end of the highlighted word when it is joined to the next word?
tjr-034.e: The next word begins with bāʾ, so the mīm sākina is concealed with ghunna. Iqlāb concerns nūn sākina and tanwīn, not mīm.

tjr-035.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on mīm sākina
tjr-035.q: Which rule applies to the mīm sākina at the end of the highlighted word when it is joined to the next word?
o: Idghām with ghunna of the nūn
tjr-035.e: The next word begins with a vowelled mīm, so the two mīms merge into one doubled mīm with ghunna.

tjr-036.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on mīm sākina
tjr-036.q: Which rule applies to the mīm sākina at the end of the highlighted word when it is joined to the next word?
tjr-036.e: The next word begins with ʿayn, which is neither bāʾ nor mīm, so the mīm is pronounced clearly. Iẓhār ḥalqī is the term used for nūn sākina and tanwīn.

tjr-037.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on mīm sākina
tjr-037.q: The mīm sākina of the highlighted word is followed by wāw. Why do teachers insist on special care with its iẓhār here?
o: Before wāw and fāʾ the mīm is easily concealed
Wāw is an idghām letter for mīm sākina
The mīm turns into a nūn before wāw
A madd follows, so the mīm must be lengthened
tjr-037.e: Ibn al-Jazarī warns against concealing the mīm before wāw and fāʾ: wāw shares the lips with mīm, and fāʾ is close to them, so the mīm tends to be hidden.

tjr-038.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on mīm sākina
tjr-038.q: Which statement correctly describes how the experts of performance treated mīm sākina before bāʾ?
o: Most chose ikhfāʾ with ghunna; a group read clear iẓhār
All agreed on complete idghām of the mīm into the bāʾ
All agreed on clear iẓhār without any ghunna
Most applied iqlāb, exactly as with nūn sākina
tjr-038.e: Ibn al-Jazarī reports that ikhfāʾ with ghunna is the choice of al-Dānī and most experts of performance, while a group, among them experts in Iraq, read full iẓhār. Ikhfāʾ is the common practice today.

tjr-039.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on mīm sākina
tjr-039.q: Why are the rules of mīm sākina described as shafawī?
o: Because the mīm is pronounced with the lips
Because they apply only at the end of a verse
Because they were transmitted orally only
Because the mīm comes from the nasal cavity alone
tjr-039.e: Shafawī means labial: the mīm is articulated by closing the lips, so its iẓhār, ikhfāʾ and idghām are called labial.

tjr-040.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn and mīm mushaddad
tjr-040.q: What is required for the doubled nūn in the highlighted word?
tjr-040.e: Every nūn or mīm with shadda is a letter of ghunna, held for about two counts (ḥarakatān).

tjr-041.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on nūn and mīm mushaddad
tjr-041.q: In which two letters is ghunna an inherent quality?
tjr-041.e: Ghunna is a nasal sound from the nasal cavity (khayshūm) and belongs to nūn and mīm. It is strongest when they are doubled.

tjr-042.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on ghunna
tjr-042.q: In which case is the ghunna most complete?
o: Nūn sākina before a throat letter
A vowelled mīm at the start of a word
tjr-042.e: The ghunna is at its fullest in the doubled nūn and mīm. Before a throat letter the nūn is shown clearly, and before lām the ghunna disappears entirely.

tjr-043.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on ghunna
tjr-043.q: What happens to the ghunna of nūn sākina in iẓhār ḥalqī?
o: It is not prolonged; only its minimal inherent trace remains
It is held for two counts like ikhfāʾ
It is held for four counts before hamza
It is transferred to the following throat letter instead
tjr-043.e: In iẓhār the nūn is pronounced from its own point of articulation and the ghunna is not lengthened; prolonging it is an error. The two-count ghunna belongs to ikhfāʾ, idghām with ghunna, iqlāb and the doubled letters.

tjr-044.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on the levels of ghunna
tjr-044.q: Which order of the levels of ghunna, from most complete to least, is the one commonly taught?
o: Doubled, merged, concealed, sākin shown, vowelled
Merged, doubled, sākin shown, concealed, vowelled
Concealed, doubled, merged, vowelled, sākin shown
Doubled, concealed, merged, vowelled, sākin shown
tjr-044.e: Al-Marṣafī and others rank the ghunna: most complete in the doubled letter, then the merged one, then the concealed one, then the sākin letter pronounced clearly, and least in the vowelled letter.

tjr-045.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on madd
tjr-045.q: Which are the three letters of madd?
tjr-045.e: The madd letters are alif after fatḥa, wāw sākina after ḍamma and yāʾ sākina after kasra.

tjr-046.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on madd
tjr-046.q: How long is the natural madd (madd ṭabīʿī)?
tjr-046.e: The natural madd is the basic length of a madd letter that is not followed by a hamza or a sukūn: two counts (ḥarakatān).

tjr-047.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on madd
o: A madd letter followed by hamza in the same word
A madd letter at the end of a word, hamza at the start of the next
A hamza followed by a madd letter
A madd letter followed by a permanent sukūn
tjr-047.e: In madd muttaṣil (connected) the hamza is in the same word as the madd letter. Across two words it is munfaṣil, hamza before the madd is badal, and permanent sukūn makes it lāzim.

tjr-048.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on madd
tjr-048.q: Which kind of madd occurs in the highlighted word?
tjr-048.e: The alif is followed by a hamza in the same word, so it is a connected madd, read with 4 or 5 counts in Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya.

tjr-049.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on madd
tjr-049.q: Which madd occurs at the end of the highlighted word when it is joined to the next word?
tjr-049.e: The word ends in an alif and the next word begins with hamza, so the madd is separated (munfaṣil). If one stopped on the word, only a natural madd would remain.

tjr-050.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), ch. on madd and qaṣr
tjr-050.q: How long is madd muttaṣil in continuous reading for Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya?
tjr-050.e: Madd muttaṣil is obligatory (wājib) and may not be shortened to two counts; Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya reads it with 4 or 5 counts. Six counts are added only when stopping on a hamza at the end of a word.

tjr-051.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on madd and qaṣr
tjr-051.q: Which statement about madd munfaṣil in the narration of Ḥafṣ is correct?
o: Via al-Shāṭibiyya it is 4 or 5; shortening comes only via other routes of the Ṭayyiba
Via al-Shāṭibiyya it may be shortened to 2 counts
It is always 6 counts, like madd lāzim
It has the same fixed length in every route of Ḥafṣ
tjr-051.e: Al-Shāṭibiyya gives Ḥafṣ only lengthening in munfaṣil (4 or 5 counts). Shortening it to two counts (qaṣr) is valid for Ḥafṣ only via certain routes of Ibn al-Jazarī's Ṭayyibat al-Nashr.

tjr-052.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on madd lāzim
tjr-052.q: The alif in the highlighted word is followed by a doubled lām. Which madd is this, and how long is it?
o: Madd ʿāriḍ, two to six counts
Madd muttaṣil, four or five counts
tjr-052.e: A madd letter followed by a permanent sukūn (here the first part of a doubled letter) in the same word is madd lāzim kalimī muthaqqal, read with six counts by all readers.

tjr-053.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on madd lāzim
o: Its sukūn stays in both continuing and stopping
It occurs only at the end of a verse
It is the only madd the reciter may shorten
It always comes before a hamza
tjr-053.e: The sukūn after the madd letter is permanent, present whether one continues or stops, and all readers agree on lengthening it to six counts.

tjr-054.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on the kinds of madd lāzim
tjr-054.q: Into which four kinds is madd lāzim divided?
o: Kalimī and ḥarfī, each muthaqqal or mukhaffaf
Muttaṣil and munfaṣil, each long or short
Aṣlī and farʿī, each in waṣl or waqf
Ṣila and līn, each kubrā or ṣughrā
tjr-054.e: Madd lāzim is kalimī (in a word) or ḥarfī (in an opening letter name), and each is muthaqqal (the sukūn is followed by a doubled letter) or mukhaffaf (plain sukūn).

tjr-055.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), ch. on two hamzas in one word
tjr-055.q: In the highlighted word the hamza of the question meets the hamzat al-waṣl of the article. With the preferred way of ibdāl, which madd results?
tjr-055.e: The hamzat al-waṣl is changed into an alif and lengthened six counts before the plain sākin lām, so it is kalimī mukhaffaf. Tashīl of the second hamza without madd is also valid.

tjr-056.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on madd al-farq
tjr-056.q: The long madd in the highlighted word is also called madd al-farq. Why?
o: It distinguishes a question from a statement
It separates two words of different roots
It marks the difference between two readers
It separates this verse from the next one
tjr-056.e: Without the madd, the hamza of the question would be lost and the phrase would sound like a statement. Here the lām is merged into the dhāl, so the madd is kalimī muthaqqal.

tjr-057.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), ch. on two hamzas in one word
tjr-057.q: How often does a hamza of question enter the hamzat al-waṣl of the definite article in the Quran (the case of madd al-farq)?
tjr-057.e: The cases are found in al-Anʿām (twice, 6:143–144), Yūnus (10:51, 10:59, 10:91) and al-Naml (27:59): three words, each occurring twice, six places in all.

tjr-058.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on the kinds of madd lāzim
tjr-058.q: In the opening letters of the verse shown, which madd is in the name of the letter lām?
tjr-058.e: The name lām has a madd letter followed by a sākin mīm, which merges into the mīm of the next letter name. Sukūn plus idghām in a letter name makes it ḥarfī muthaqqal, six counts.

tjr-059.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on the kinds of madd lāzim
tjr-059.q: Which madd is in the opening letter name highlighted in the verse shown?
tjr-059.e: The name qāf is spelled with three letters, the middle one a madd letter, followed by a sākin that is not merged. That is ḥarfī mukhaffaf, six counts.

tjr-060.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on the kinds of madd lāzim
tjr-060.q: Which opening (disjointed) letters are read with only two counts?
tjr-060.e: The letters gathered in ḥayy ṭahur have names of two letters ending in a madd letter, so they take a natural madd. The letters of naqaṣa ʿasalukum take six counts.

tjr-061.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on the kinds of madd lāzim
tjr-061.q: Which of the disjointed opening letters has no madd at all?
tjr-061.e: The name alif has no madd letter in its middle, so it is not lengthened. Ḥāʾ and rāʾ take two counts, ʿayn four or six.

tjr-062.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), ch. on madd and qaṣr
tjr-062.q: How long may the name of the letter ʿayn among the opening letters shown be read, according to al-Shāṭibiyya?
tjr-062.e: The middle letter of ʿayn is a yāʾ of līn (sākin after fatḥa), not a true madd letter, so two ways are allowed: four and six counts. Al-Shāṭibī states that the longer one is preferred.

tjr-063.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on madd
tjr-063.q: When stopping on the highlighted word, which madd occurs and what lengths are permitted?
tjr-063.e: Stopping makes the last letter sākin, so a temporary sukūn follows the madd letter. The reader may choose two, four or six counts.

tjr-064.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on madd
tjr-064.q: When stopping on the highlighted word, which madd occurs on its yāʾ?
tjr-064.e: The yāʾ is sākin after a fatḥa, a letter of līn. When the next letter becomes sākin by stopping, it is madd līn with 2, 4 or 6 counts; in continuous reading it is not lengthened.

tjr-065.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on madd
tjr-065.q: What are the letters of līn?
o: Wāw or yāʾ sākina after a fatḥa
Wāw or yāʾ sākina after a kasra
Wāw or yāʾ with a shadda
tjr-065.e: Līn means softness: wāw and yāʾ that are sākin after a fatḥa are pronounced softly. After a matching vowel (ḍamma, kasra) they are madd letters instead.

tjr-066.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on madd
tjr-066.q: The highlighted word begins with a hamza followed by a madd letter. Which madd is this, and how long is it in Ḥafṣ?
o: Madd muttaṣil, four or five counts
Madd badal, four or six counts
tjr-066.e: When the hamza comes before the madd letter, the madd is badal. Ḥafṣ reads it like a natural madd, two counts; longer lengths belong to Warsh via al-Azraq.

tjr-067.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), ch. on madd and qaṣr
tjr-067.q: In which narration and route is madd badal read with 2, 4 or 6 counts?
tjr-067.e: Al-Shāṭibiyya gives Warsh via al-Azraq three ways in badal: shortening, middle length and full length. All other readers read badal with two counts.

tjr-068.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on madd al-ṣila
tjr-068.q: The pronoun hāʾ at the end of the highlighted word lies between two vowelled letters, and the next word begins with hamza. How long is it?
tjr-068.e: The hāʾ is lengthened with a wāw sound (ṣila). Because a hamza follows, it is ṣila kubrā and takes the length of munfaṣil, 4 or 5 counts for Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya.

tjr-069.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on madd al-ṣila
tjr-069.q: The pronoun hāʾ at the end of the highlighted word lies between two vowelled letters, and the next word does not begin with hamza. How is it read?
o: Ṣila kubrā: four or five counts
tjr-069.e: A pronoun hāʾ between two vowelled letters is joined with a wāw sound. Without a following hamza this is ṣila ṣughrā, a natural length of two counts.

tjr-070.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), ch. on hāʾ al-kināya
tjr-070.q: In Ḥafṣ, when is the pronoun hāʾ normally NOT lengthened with ṣila?
o: When the letter before it is sākin
When the letter after it is vowelled
When it has a kasra rather than a ḍamma
tjr-070.e: The rule of Ḥafṣ is ṣila only when the hāʾ lies between two vowelled letters. If the letter before it is sākin, it is read short; the known exception in Ḥafṣ is 25:69.

tjr-071.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), ch. on hāʾ al-kināya
tjr-071.q: The pronoun hāʾ of the highlighted word comes after a sākin yāʾ. How does Ḥafṣ read it?
o: With ṣila, despite the sākin before it
tjr-071.e: This is the one place where Ḥafṣ lengthens the pronoun hāʾ although the letter before it is sākin, in agreement with Ibn Kathīr. Elsewhere Ḥafṣ reads such a hāʾ short.

tjr-072.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), ch. on hāʾ al-kināya
tjr-072.q: The pronoun hāʾ in the highlighted word lies between two vowelled letters. How does Ḥafṣ read it?
o: With a short ḍamma, without ṣila
With ṣila ṣughrā of two counts
With ṣila kubrā of four or five counts
tjr-072.e: Although the hāʾ is between two vowelled letters, Ḥafṣ reads it with a short ḍamma here, because the original letter before it (an alif) was dropped for the jussive. Other readers have sukūn or ṣila.

tjr-073.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh of Sūrat al-Kahf
tjr-073.q: How does Ḥafṣ read the hāʾ of the highlighted word, and what follows for the lām of the Divine Name after it?
o: With ḍamma, so the lām is heavy
With kasra, so the lām is light
With ḍamma, yet the lām stays light
With kasra, yet the lām is heavy
tjr-073.e: Ḥafṣ reads the hāʾ with ḍamma here (as in 18:63), while others read kasra. After a ḍamma the lām of the Divine Name is pronounced heavy (tafkhīm).

tjr-074.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on madd al-ʿiwaḍ
tjr-074.q: When a reciter stops on a word ending in tanwīn with fatḥa (not on tāʾ marbūṭa), what happens?
o: The tanwīn becomes an alif of two counts
The tanwīn is kept with ghunna
The last letter takes a kasra
The word is lengthened six counts
tjr-074.e: This is madd al-ʿiwaḍ (madd of compensation): the tanwīn fatḥ is replaced by an alif of two counts. On tāʾ marbūṭa one stops with a sākin hāʾ instead.

tjr-075.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on madd
tjr-075.q: For Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya, which lengths are allowed when stopping on a word that ends in a madd letter followed by hamza?
tjr-075.e: The madd is muttaṣil and also meets a sukūn from stopping. The shortest length of muttaṣil (4) remains the minimum, and stopping adds the option of six: 4, 5 or 6.

tjr-076.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on the strength of the madds
tjr-076.q: What is the commonly taught order of the madds from strongest to weakest?
tjr-076.e: The order decides which madd prevails when two causes meet in one letter. Lāzim is strongest (its cause is permanent), badal weakest (its hamza comes before the madd).

tjr-077.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on madd and qaṣr
tjr-077.q: A reciter of Ḥafṣ chooses 4 counts for madd munfaṣil at the start of a recitation. What applies to the rest of that recitation?
o: The same length for every munfaṣil
Free choice between 4 and 5 at each place
4 in Meccan surahs, 5 in Medinan ones
Only the first munfaṣil of each verse counts
tjr-077.e: The principle of equality (taswiya) requires like madds to be read with the same length within one recitation; switching between lengths is considered a fault.

tjr-078.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on madd and qaṣr
tjr-078.q: For Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya, which combination of lengths in one recitation is NOT permitted?
tjr-078.e: Muttaṣil is stronger than munfaṣil, so it may never be shorter than it. Equal lengths, or muttaṣil longer than munfaṣil, are acceptable.

tjr-079.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on the attributes of letters
tjr-079.q: Which letters are the letters of qalqala?
tjr-079.e: The qalqala letters are gathered in quṭbu jad. When sākin, they are released with a slight echo so that they are heard clearly.

tjr-080.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on qalqala
tjr-080.q: When stopping on the highlighted word, how is its last letter pronounced?
o: With a ghunna of two counts
tjr-080.e: The dāl is a qalqala letter, and stopping makes it sākin at the end of the word. Qalqala at a stop is stronger than qalqala in the middle of a word.

tjr-081.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on qalqala
tjr-081.q: The highlighted word has a sākin dāl in its middle. How is it pronounced?
o: Without qalqala, as it is in the middle
tjr-081.e: A qalqala letter with an original sukūn in the middle of a word has the lightest level of qalqala, but it must still be released clearly.

tjr-082.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on qalqala
tjr-082.q: In which case is the qalqala at its strongest?
o: Stopping on a doubled qalqala letter
Stopping on a single qalqala letter
A sākin qalqala letter in mid-word
tjr-082.e: The levels are: strongest when stopping on a doubled qalqala letter, then stopping on an undoubled one, then a sākin one in mid-word. A vowelled letter has no qalqala.

tjr-083.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on the lām of al
tjr-083.q: How is the lām of the definite article in the highlighted word pronounced?
tjr-083.e: The lām is followed by shīn, a 'sun letter', so it is not pronounced and the shīn is doubled.

tjr-084.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on the lām of al
tjr-084.q: How is the lām of the definite article in the highlighted word pronounced?
tjr-084.e: The lām is followed by qāf, a 'moon letter', so the lām is pronounced clearly with sukūn.

tjr-085.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on the lām of al
tjr-085.q: How many letters cause the lām of the definite article to be merged (lām shamsiyya)?
tjr-085.e: The 28 letters divide evenly: fourteen sun letters, before which the lām is merged, and fourteen moon letters, before which it is pronounced.

tjr-086.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on the lām of al
tjr-086.q: In which phrase are the letters of lām qamariyya gathered?
tjr-086.e: Al-Jamzūrī gathers the moon letters in ibghi ḥajjaka wa-khaf ʿaqīmah. The phrase beginning ṭib thumma ṣil opens his verse listing the sun letters.

tjr-087.src: al-Jamzūrī, Tuḥfat al-Aṭfāl, section on lām of the verb
tjr-087.q: The highlighted word contains the sākin lām of a verb followed by tāʾ. How is the lām pronounced?
tjr-087.e: The sākin lām of a verb is pronounced clearly before all letters except lām and rāʾ. The rule of the sun letters belongs only to the definite article.

tjr-088.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on idghām
tjr-088.q: The highlighted word ends in a sākin lām and the next word begins with rāʾ. How is it read?
o: The lām is merged into the rāʾ
The lām is concealed with ghunna
A short pause is made on the lām
tjr-088.e: Lām and rāʾ are close in articulation (mutaqāribayn). A sākin lām before rāʾ is merged completely, and the rāʾ is pronounced doubled.

tjr-089.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on the lām of the Divine Name
tjr-089.q: How is the lām of the Divine Name in the highlighted word pronounced?
o: Light (tarqīq), because a kasra precedes it
Light, because it is at the start of a verse
Heavy, because a sukūn precedes it
tjr-089.e: The lām of the Divine Name is light after a kasra and heavy after a fatḥa or ḍamma. Here the preceding letter has a kasra.

tjr-090.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on the lām of the Divine Name
tjr-090.q: Read continuously from the previous word, how is the lām of the Divine Name in the highlighted word pronounced?
o: Heavy, because of the qalqala after it
Light, because the word is a predicate
tjr-090.e: The word before ends in a ḍamma, so the lām of the Divine Name is pronounced heavy.

tjr-091.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on the lām of the Divine Name
tjr-091.q: The word before the highlighted Divine Name is an imperative whose last letter takes a kasra to avoid two sākins. How is the lām of the Divine Name read?
o: Light, since any kasra before it counts
Heavy, since the kasra is only accidental
Heavy, since the imperative ends in sukūn
Either way, at the reciter's choice
tjr-091.e: The lām of the Divine Name is made light after any kasra, whether original or added to avoid two sākins. So here it is light, although the same word would end in sukūn on its own.

tjr-092.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on the lām of the Divine Name
tjr-092.q: If a reciter begins with the Divine Name itself, how is its lām pronounced?
o: Heavy, because one begins with a hamza with fatḥa
Light, because the hamza is a throat letter
Either way, at the reciter's choice
tjr-092.e: When beginning with the Divine Name, its hamzat al-waṣl is pronounced with fatḥa, so the lām follows a fatḥa and is heavy.

tjr-093.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on rāʾ
tjr-093.q: How is a rāʾ with kasra pronounced?
o: Heavy if a heavy letter follows
tjr-093.e: A rāʾ that carries a kasra is always light, whatever comes after it. Rāʾ with fatḥa or ḍamma is heavy.

tjr-094.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on rāʾ
tjr-094.q: When beginning with the highlighted word, its sākin rāʾ follows the kasra of the hamzat al-waṣl. How is the rāʾ pronounced?
o: Heavy, because the kasra is not original
Light, because a kasra precedes it
Light, because a yāʾ comes later in the word
Either way, at the reciter's choice
tjr-094.e: A sākin rāʾ is light only after an original kasra in the same word. The kasra of a hamzat al-waṣl is not original, so the rāʾ stays heavy.

tjr-095.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on rāʾ
tjr-095.q: The sākin rāʾ in the highlighted word follows an original kasra. Why is it nevertheless pronounced heavy?
o: A heavy letter without kasra follows in the same word
The kasra before it is accidental
The rāʾ is at the end of the word
The word is read with imāla
tjr-095.e: A sākin rāʾ after an original kasra is light unless a heavy (istiʿlāʾ) letter that is not vowelled with kasra follows it in the same word, as the qāf does here.

tjr-096.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), ch. on rāʾāt
tjr-096.q: The sākin rāʾ of the highlighted word follows an original kasra and precedes a qāf with kasra. What is the ruling?
o: Both tafkhīm and tarqīq are reported
Only tafkhīm, because of the qāf
Only tarqīq, because of the two kasras
Tafkhīm when continuing, tarqīq when stopping
tjr-096.e: Because the heavy letter after the rāʾ itself carries a kasra, its heaviness is weakened. Al-Shāṭibī and Ibn al-Jazarī report both ways for this word.

tjr-097.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on rāʾāt
tjr-097.q: When stopping on the highlighted word, its rāʾ follows a sākin heavy letter preceded by a kasra. Which way did Ibn al-Jazarī prefer?
o: Tafkhīm, because of the heavy ṭāʾ
Tafkhīm, the only way reported for this word
Tarqīq, the only way reported for this word
tjr-097.e: Both ways are valid. Ibn al-Jazarī preferred tarqīq in this word and tafkhīm in Miṣr, in each case following how the rāʾ is read in continuous recitation.

tjr-098.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on rāʾ
tjr-098.q: When stopping on a word ending in rāʾ that is preceded by a sākin yāʾ (as in khabīr), how is the rāʾ pronounced?
o: Either way, at the reciter's choice
tjr-098.e: When stopping, a rāʾ preceded by a sākin yāʾ is light, whether the yāʾ is a madd letter or a letter of līn.

tjr-099.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on rāʾ
tjr-099.q: When stopping on a rāʾ preceded by a sākin light letter, which is itself preceded by a kasra (as in ḥijr or dhikr), how is the rāʾ pronounced?
o: Heavy, because the rāʾ is sākin
tjr-099.e: The sākin letter between them does not count as a barrier, so the rāʾ is treated as if it followed the kasra directly and is light. If the sākin letter is heavy, as in miṣr or qiṭr, both ways are reported.

tjr-100.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh of Sūrat Hūd
tjr-100.q: In the narration of Ḥafṣ, how is the rāʾ with alif in the highlighted word pronounced?
o: With major imāla, so the rāʾ is light
With full fatḥa, so the rāʾ is heavy
With minor imāla, the rāʾ semi-heavy
With fatḥa or imāla, at the reciter's choice
tjr-100.e: This is the only place in which Ḥafṣ reads a major imāla, leaning the fatḥa toward kasra and the alif toward yāʾ. A rāʾ with imāla is pronounced light.

tjr-101.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on tafkhīm and tarqīq
tjr-101.q: Which letters are always pronounced heavy (mufakhkham)?
o: The seven letters of khuṣṣa ḍaghṭin qiẓ
The five letters of quṭbu jad
tjr-101.e: The istiʿlāʾ letters, khāʾ, ṣād, ḍād, ghayn, ṭāʾ, qāf and ẓāʾ, are always heavy, to different degrees. The other letters are light, except alif, rāʾ and the lām of the Divine Name, which vary.

tjr-102.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on tafkhīm and tarqīq
tjr-102.q: In which state is a heavy letter at its heaviest, according to the common ranking?
o: With fatḥa not followed by alif
tjr-102.e: Heaviness is strongest with fatḥa followed by alif, then fatḥa alone, then ḍamma, then sukūn, and weakest with kasra.

tjr-103.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on tafkhīm and tarqīq
tjr-103.q: Is the alif (of madd) heavy or light?
o: It follows the letter before it
It follows the letter after it
tjr-103.e: The alif has no quality of its own here: after a heavy letter it is heavy, after a light letter it is light.

tjr-104.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on tafkhīm and tarqīq
tjr-104.q: Which letters are sometimes heavy and sometimes light, depending on their context?
o: Alif, rāʾ, and the lām of the Divine Name
Qāf, kāf, and the lām of the article
Nūn, mīm, and the tāʾ marbūṭa
tjr-104.e: These three change: the alif follows the letter before it, the rāʾ depends on its own vowel and its surroundings, and the lām of the Divine Name depends on the vowel before it.

tjr-105.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on mithlayn, mutajānisayn and mutaqāribayn
tjr-105.q: What are two letters called that are identical in point of articulation and attributes, i.e. the same letter twice?
tjr-105.e: Mutamāthilayn are the same letter, such as bāʾ and bāʾ. Mutajānisayn share the point of articulation but differ in attributes; mutaqāribayn are close in articulation or attributes.

tjr-106.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on mithlayn, mutajānisayn and mutaqāribayn
o: Same point of articulation, different attributes
Same attributes, different point of articulation
Close in point of articulation only
tjr-106.e: Mutajānisayn share one point of articulation but differ in some attributes, like dāl and tāʾ, or ṭāʾ and tāʾ.

tjr-107.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on mithlayn, mutajānisayn and mutaqāribayn
tjr-107.q: Lām and rāʾ, or qāf and kāf, are classed as which kind of letter pair?
tjr-107.e: They have neighbouring, not identical, points of articulation, so they are mutaqāribayn. A sākin lām before rāʾ, or a sākin qāf before kāf, is merged.

tjr-108.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on mithlayn, mutajānisayn and mutaqāribayn
tjr-108.q: The highlighted word ends in a sākin bāʾ and the next word begins with bāʾ. How is it read?
o: Qalqala on the first bāʾ, then the second
tjr-108.e: When the first of two identical letters is sākin and the second vowelled (mithlayn ṣaghīr), the first must be merged into the second.

tjr-109.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on idghām
tjr-109.q: The highlighted word ends in a sākin dāl and the next word begins with tāʾ. How is it read?
o: Complete idghām of the dāl into the tāʾ
Incomplete idghām, keeping the dāl's voice
tjr-109.e: Dāl and tāʾ share a point of articulation (mutajānisayn). A sākin dāl before tāʾ is merged completely, so a doubled tāʾ is heard.

tjr-110.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on idghām
tjr-110.q: In the highlighted word a sākin ṭāʾ meets a tāʾ. How is it read?
o: Incomplete idghām: the ṭāʾ's heaviness remains
Complete idghām into a plain doubled tāʾ
Clear ṭāʾ with qalqala, then the tāʾ
Ikhfāʾ of the ṭāʾ with ghunna
tjr-110.e: Ṭāʾ and tāʾ are mutajānisayn. The ṭāʾ is merged, but its attributes of itbāq and istiʿlāʾ remain, so the idghām is incomplete (nāqiṣ) and there is no qalqala.

tjr-111.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on idghām
tjr-111.q: The highlighted word ends in a sākin tāʾ and the next word begins with ṭāʾ. How is it read?
o: Complete idghām into a heavy doubled ṭāʾ
tjr-111.e: Tāʾ and ṭāʾ are mutajānisayn. Here the lighter letter is merged into the heavier one, so the idghām is complete and a doubled, heavy ṭāʾ is heard.

tjr-112.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, ch. on idghām of sākin letters
tjr-112.q: In the highlighted word a sākin qāf meets a kāf. What is reported for its idghām?
o: Complete idghām, preferred; incomplete also reported
Only incomplete idghām, keeping the qāf's heaviness
Only clear iẓhār of the qāf with qalqala
Ikhfāʾ of the qāf with ghunna
tjr-112.e: All agree that the qāf is merged into the kāf; they differ on whether its istiʿlāʾ remains. Ibn al-Jazarī judges the complete idghām sounder in transmission and analogy, while the incomplete one is also read.

tjr-113.src: Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Muqaddima al-Jazariyya, section on idghām
tjr-113.q: The highlighted word ends in a sākin dhāl and the next word begins with ẓāʾ. How is it read?
o: Complete idghām into a doubled ẓāʾ
tjr-113.e: Dhāl and ẓāʾ come from the same point of articulation (mutajānisayn). A sākin dhāl before ẓāʾ is merged completely into a heavy doubled ẓāʾ.

tjr-114.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), ch. on letters with close points of articulation
tjr-114.q: The highlighted word ends in a sākin thāʾ and the next word begins with dhāl. How does Ḥafṣ read the two when joined?
o: With idghām of the thāʾ into the dhāl
With clear iẓhār of the thāʾ
With a short pause (sakt) on the thāʾ
tjr-114.e: Thāʾ and dhāl are mutajānisayn. Ḥafṣ merges here, while some other readers read iẓhār, as al-Shāṭibī records.

tjr-115.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), ch. on letters with close points of articulation
tjr-115.q: The highlighted word ends in a sākin bāʾ and the next word begins with mīm. How does Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya read it?
o: With idghām of the bāʾ into the mīm, with ghunna
With a clear bāʾ released with qalqala
With ikhfāʾ shafawī of the bāʾ before the mīm
With iqlāb of the bāʾ into a concealed nūn
tjr-115.e: Bāʾ and mīm are both labial. Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya merges the bāʾ into the mīm, producing a doubled mīm with ghunna, while some other readers keep the bāʾ.

tjr-116.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on mithlayn, mutajānisayn and mutaqāribayn
tjr-116.q: The highlighted word ends in a wāw of madd and the next word begins with wāw. Why is there no idghām?
o: A madd letter is never merged into its like
Wāw is not a letter of idghām
The second wāw carries a sukūn
Ḥafṣ makes a sakt between the words
tjr-116.e: Mithlayn ṣaghīr is normally merged, but if the first letter is a madd letter, merging would destroy the madd, so both are pronounced with the madd kept.

tjr-117.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh of Sūrat al-Kahf (the sakt of Ḥafṣ)
tjr-117.q: The highlighted word ends in a sākin lām and the next word begins with rāʾ. How does Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya read it?
o: A short sakt on the lām, so no idghām
Complete idghām of the lām into the rāʾ
tjr-117.e: Normally a sākin lām before rāʾ is merged, but Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya makes a brief sakt here, which keeps the lām clear. The same applies to the nūn in 75:27.

tjr-118.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on mithlayn, mutajānisayn and mutaqāribayn
tjr-118.q: When two meeting letters are classed as ṣaghīr, what is the case?
o: The first is sākin and the second vowelled
The first is vowelled and the second sākin
tjr-118.e: Ṣaghīr: first sākin, second vowelled (this is where idghām mostly applies). Kabīr: both vowelled. Muṭlaq: first vowelled, second sākin.

tjr-119.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on hamzat al-waṣl
o: Pronounced when beginning, dropped when joining
Dropped when beginning, pronounced when joining
tjr-119.e: Hamzat al-waṣl lets the reader begin on a word whose first letter is sākin. In continuous reading it falls away. Hamzat al-qaṭʿ, by contrast, is pronounced in every position.

tjr-120.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on hamzat al-waṣl
tjr-120.q: When beginning a verb that starts with hamzat al-waṣl, and its third letter has an original ḍamma, which vowel does the hamza take?
tjr-120.e: In verbs the hamzat al-waṣl takes ḍamma if the third letter has an original (lāzim) ḍamma, and kasra if the third letter has fatḥa or kasra.

tjr-121.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on hamzat al-waṣl
tjr-121.q: Which list consists only of nouns that begin with hamzat al-waṣl?
tjr-121.e: Hamzat al-waṣl occurs in a small number of nouns such as ibn, ibna, ism, imruʾ, imraʾa, ithnān and ithnatān; one begins them with kasra. Insān, imām, arḍ and amr begin with hamzat al-qaṭʿ.

tjr-122.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on hamzat al-waṣl
tjr-122.q: If a reciter begins with the highlighted imperative, whose third letter is heard with ḍamma, how does he pronounce the hamzat al-waṣl?
o: With kasra, as the ḍamma is not original
With ḍamma, following the third letter
With fatḥa, as in the definite article
With ḍamma or kasra, at his choice
tjr-122.e: The ḍamma on the third letter here is not original: the original vowel is a kasra, changed because of the plural wāw. So one begins with kasra. This applies to a small group of imperatives of this pattern.

tjr-123.src: al-Shāṭibī, Ḥirz al-Amānī (al-Shāṭibiyya), farsh of Sūrat Fuṣṣilat
tjr-123.q: The highlighted word begins with two hamzas of qaṭʿ. How does Ḥafṣ read the second one?
o: With tashīl, between hamza and alif
Changed into a long alif of six counts
tjr-123.e: This is the only place in which Ḥafṣ via al-Shāṭibiyya reads tashīl: the second hamza is pronounced between a hamza and an alif, without inserting an alif between the two.

tjr-124.src: al-Marṣafī, Hidāyat al-Qārī, ch. on hamzat al-waṣl
tjr-124.q: In which verb form is the initial hamza a hamzat al-qaṭʿ?
o: Form IV (afʿala), its past, imperative and verbal noun
Form VIII (iftaʿala), its past, imperative and verbal noun
Form X (istafʿala), its past, imperative and verbal noun
Form VII (infaʿala), its past, imperative and verbal noun
tjr-124.e: The hamza of form IV is part of the pattern and is always pronounced. The hamzas of forms VII, VIII and X are hamzat al-waṣl, dropped in continuous reading.

ulc-001.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb jamʿ al-Qurʾān
ulc-001.q: Whom did Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq charge with collecting the Quran into one compilation?
ulc-001.e: According to the report of Zayd himself in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Abū Bakr chose Zayd ibn Thābit, who had been a scribe of the revelation for the Prophet. Ubayy, Ibn Masʿūd and Muʿādh were famous reciters, but the task was given to Zayd.

ulc-002.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb jamʿ al-Qurʾān
ulc-002.q: Which event prompted the compilation of the Quran under Abū Bakr?
o: The death of many reciters at the Battle of al-Yamāma
The death of many reciters at the Battle of Uḥud
The death of many reciters at Biʾr Maʿūna
The death of many reciters at the Battle of Muʾta
ulc-002.e: Many memorisers of the Quran were killed at al-Yamāma, fought against Musaylima after the Prophet's death, and ʿUmar feared that parts of the Quran could be lost. Biʾr Maʿūna and Uḥud were also tragic losses, but they happened during the Prophet's lifetime.

ulc-003.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb jamʿ al-Qurʾān
ulc-003.q: After the death of ʿUmar, with whom were the sheets (ṣuḥuf) compiled under Abū Bakr kept?
ulc-003.e: The report in al-Bukhārī states that the sheets stayed with Abū Bakr until his death, then with ʿUmar, then with his daughter Ḥafṣa, the Mother of the Believers. ʿUthmān later borrowed them from her to make his copies.

ulc-004.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb jamʿ al-Qurʾān
ulc-004.q: Which caliph had standardised copies of the Quran made and sent to the main regions?
ulc-004.e: ʿUthmān had copies made from the sheets kept by Ḥafṣa and sent them to the regions so that people would unite on them. Abū Bakr's compilation was a single set of sheets that was not distributed.

ulc-005.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb jamʿ al-Qurʾān; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on collection and arrangement
ulc-005.q: On what kinds of materials was the Quran written down during the Prophet's lifetime?
o: Palm stalks, thin flat stones and pieces of parchment
Bound paper volumes produced in the workshops of Medina
Papyrus scrolls imported from Egypt for the scribes
Wax tablets kept in the Prophet's mosque for copying
ulc-005.e: Zayd ibn Thābit reports that he gathered the Quran from palm stalks (ʿusub), thin white stones (likhāf) and the memories of men; other reports add parchment and shoulder blades. Bound paper volumes did not exist in Medina at that time.

ulc-006.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb jamʿ al-Qurʾān
ulc-006.q: Which Companion came to ʿUthmān alarmed by the differences in recitation among the troops and urged him to act?
ulc-006.e: Al-Bukhārī reports that Ḥudhayfa ibn al-Yamān, alarmed by how the people of Syria and Iraq differed in recitation, told ʿUthmān to save the community before it differed over its Book as earlier communities had.

ulc-007.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb jamʿ al-Qurʾān
ulc-007.q: During which campaign did Ḥudhayfa notice the disputes over recitation that led to ʿUthmān's copies?
o: The conquest of Armenia and Azerbaijan
The conquest of Egypt and Barqa
The Battle of al-Qādisiyya in Iraq
The siege of Jerusalem in Palestine
ulc-007.e: The report in al-Bukhārī places it in the campaign of Armenia and Azerbaijan, where troops from Syria and Iraq fought together and their differing recitations clashed.

ulc-008.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb jamʿ al-Qurʾān
ulc-008.q: What did ʿUthmān instruct the committee to do if they differed with Zayd ibn Thābit on how to write something?
o: Write it in the dialect of Quraysh
Write it in the dialect of Hudhayl
Write it in the dialect of Tamīm
Write it in the dialect of the Anṣār
ulc-008.e: ʿUthmān said that the Quran was revealed in the tongue of Quraysh, so in case of difference they should write it in their dialect. Zayd was from the Anṣār, while the other three members were Qurashī.

ulc-009.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb jamʿ al-Qurʾān
ulc-009.q: According to al-Bukhārī, which group formed ʿUthmān's committee for copying the muṣḥaf?
o: Zayd ibn Thābit, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith
Zayd ibn Thābit, Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ, ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās
Zayd ibn Thābit, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd, ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, Muʿādh ibn Jabal
Zayd ibn Thābit, Abū al-Dardāʾ, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf, Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ
ulc-009.e: The report names Zayd ibn Thābit together with three Qurashīs: ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr, Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Hishām. Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd were great reciters but are not named in this report.

ulc-010.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on collection and arrangement
ulc-010.q: Which statement best describes the difference in purpose between the compilation of Abū Bakr and that of ʿUthmān?
o: Abū Bakr: gather it lest it be lost; ʿUthmān: unite people on one standard
Abū Bakr: write it in Quraysh's dialect; ʿUthmān: add the other dialects
Abū Bakr: gather the Meccan surahs; ʿUthmān: add the Medinan surahs
Abū Bakr: fix the dotting; ʿUthmān: fix the order of the verses
ulc-010.e: Al-Suyūṭī cites scholars who explain that Abū Bakr's aim was to secure the Quran in one written compilation for fear of loss, while ʿUthmān's aim was to unite the community on standard copies and end disputes over recitation.

ulc-011.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb jamʿ al-Qurʾān; Ibn Ḥajar, Fatḥ al-Bārī, on the same chapter
ulc-011.q: Zayd reported that he found the end of Sūrat al-Tawba (the verse shown and the next) only with Abū Khuzayma al-Anṣārī. How do scholars understand this?
o: He found it in written form with no one else, though many had memorised it
Only one Companion had memorised it, so it rests on a single report
No other Companion had heard these verses before
All other written copies had lost it through abrogation
ulc-011.e: Ibn Ḥajar and others explain that Zayd sought every verse in writing as well as from memory; these verses were known and memorised by many, but the written piece was found only with Abū Khuzayma. The Quran's transmission therefore did not rest on one person.

ulc-012.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb Faḍāʾil al-Qurʾān, bāb jamʿ al-Qurʾān
ulc-012.q: According to al-Bukhārī, with whom did Zayd find the verse shown (from al-Aḥzāb) in writing while copying the muṣḥaf under ʿUthmān?
ulc-012.e: Zayd said he missed a verse of al-Aḥzāb that he had heard the Prophet recite and found it with Khuzayma ibn Thābit, whose testimony the Prophet had counted as that of two men. The end of al-Tawba, by contrast, was found with Abū Khuzayma during Abū Bakr's compilation.

ulc-013.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on collection and arrangement
ulc-013.q: Which of these cities is commonly listed among the destinations of the copies sent by ʿUthmān?
ulc-013.e: The reports commonly name Kufa, Basra, Syria and Mecca besides the copy kept in Medina, though the exact number of copies is disputed. Baghdad, Cairo and Qayrawān were all founded after ʿUthmān's death.

ulc-014.src: al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on collection; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on collection and arrangement
ulc-014.q: Why, according to scholars such as al-Khaṭṭābī, was the Quran not bound into a single volume during the Prophet's lifetime?
o: Revelation was still ongoing and abrogation was still possible
Writing materials were forbidden for recording the revelation
The Companions disliked writing down anything besides hadith
The Prophet ordered that it be preserved only in memory
ulc-014.e: Al-Suyūṭī quotes al-Khaṭṭābī: the Prophet did not gather it in one muṣḥaf because he expected further revelation or abrogation. Once revelation ended with his death, the Companions gathered it.

ulc-015.src: al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, introduction; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr fī al-Qirāʾāt al-ʿAshr, introduction
ulc-015.q: Which scholar is known for the view that the ʿUthmānic copies preserve only one of the seven aḥruf?
ulc-015.e: Al-Ṭabarī held that ʿUthmān united the community on a single ḥarf and the others were left. Ibn al-Jazarī reports the majority view that the copies contain whatever of the aḥruf their script can bear; Ibn Qutayba and Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī explained the aḥruf as types of variation found within the readings.

ulc-016.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on the script of the muṣḥaf
ulc-016.q: What does the term al-rasm al-ʿuthmānī refer to?
o: The spelling conventions of the copies made under ʿUthmān
The rules of pausing that ʿUthmān followed in the prayer
The order of the surahs as fixed by ʿUthmān's committee
A style of calligraphy that was invented in ʿUthmān's era
ulc-016.e: Al-rasm al-ʿuthmānī is the way words are spelled in the copies written by ʿUthmān's committee, which sometimes differs from ordinary Arabic spelling. It concerns spelling, not a particular calligraphic hand.

ulc-017.src: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, al-Muḥkam fī Naqṭ al-Maṣāḥif, introduction
ulc-017.q: Who is commonly credited with first marking the vowels of the muṣḥaf with dots?
ulc-017.e: Most accounts credit Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī with the first vowel marks, coloured dots placed around the letters. Al-Khalīl later replaced these dots with the signs used today.

ulc-018.src: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, al-Muḥkam fī Naqṭ al-Maṣāḥif
ulc-018.q: Who replaced the vowel dots with the vowel signs used in the muṣḥaf today?
ulc-018.e: Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad derived the signs from letters: a small alif for fatḥa, a small wāw for ḍamma and a small yāʾ for kasra, together with signs for shadda and sukūn. Abū al-Aswad had used dots, and Naṣr worked on the dots that distinguish letters.

ulc-019.src: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, al-Muḥkam fī Naqṭ al-Maṣāḥif; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on the script of the muṣḥaf
ulc-019.q: What contribution is attributed to Naṣr ibn ʿĀṣim and Yaḥyā ibn Yaʿmar?
o: The dots that tell apart letters of the same shape
The first coloured dots that marked the vowels
The division of the muṣḥaf into thirty parts
The signs for shadda and sukūn above letters
ulc-019.e: They are credited with naqṭ al-iʿjām, the dots that distinguish letters of the same shape. Vowel dots (naqṭ al-iʿrāb) are attributed to Abū al-Aswad, and the shadda and sukūn signs to al-Khalīl.

ulc-020.src: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, al-Muḥkam fī Naqṭ al-Maṣāḥif
ulc-020.q: In the vowel-dot system of Abū al-Aswad al-Duʾalī, what did a dot placed above the letter indicate?
ulc-020.e: Abū al-Aswad told his scribe to put a dot above the letter when he opened his mouth (fatḥa), below it when he lowered it (kasra), and in front of it when he rounded his lips (ḍamma); two dots marked tanwīn.

ulc-021.src: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, al-Muḥkam fī Naqṭ al-Maṣāḥif
ulc-021.q: In al-Khalīl's system of signs, from what is the shadda sign derived?
o: The head of the letter shīn
The head of the letter khāʾ
The head of the letter ʿayn
ulc-021.e: Al-Khalīl took the shadda from the head of shīn (for shadīd), the sukūn in one form from the head of khāʾ (for khafīf), and the hamza from the head of ʿayn, because of the closeness of their points of articulation.

ulc-022.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on the script of the muṣḥaf
ulc-022.q: Al-Suyūṭī groups the rules of the ʿUthmānic script under six headings. Which set matches them?
o: Omission, addition, hamza, substitution, joining and separating, variant words
Clear pronunciation, assimilation, conversion, concealment, lengthening, echo
Dotting, vowelling, pausing, starting, verse counting and dividing into parts
The vowel signs fatḥa, kasra and ḍamma, with sukūn, shadda and tanwīn
ulc-022.e: In al-Itqān the rasm is treated under ḥadhf, ziyāda, hamz, badal, waṣl and faṣl, and words read in two ways but written according to one of them. The other sets are tajwīd rules, other muṣḥaf sciences or vowel signs.

ulc-023.src: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Rasm Maṣāḥif al-Amṣār; Ibn al-Jazarī, al-Nashr, introduction
ulc-023.q: In the ʿUthmānic rasm the highlighted word has no full alif after the mīm (the small alif is a later reading sign). What is the significance of this?
o: The spelling carries both readings, māliki and maliki
It marks a compulsory pause at this word in recitation
It shows that the word may only be read with a short vowel
It reflects a dialect form used by the tribe of Hudhayl
ulc-023.e: Writing the word without the alif allows both established readings, māliki (with a long ā) and maliki. This is one of the ways the rasm was able to carry more than one reading.

ulc-024.src: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Rasm Maṣāḥif al-Amṣār; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on the script of the muṣḥaf
ulc-024.q: Asked whether a muṣḥaf may be written in the spelling that people had newly devised, which imam answered that it should be written according to the first writing?
ulc-024.e: Al-Dānī reports through Ashhab that Mālik was asked this and replied that it should be written only according to the first writing. Al-Dānī adds that no scholar opposed him; many later scholars held following the rasm to be obligatory.

ulc-025.src: al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on the script of the muṣḥaf
ulc-025.q: Which scholar, as reported by al-Zarkashī, held that copies for the general public should be written in the familiar spelling so that the uneducated would not misread them?
ulc-025.e: Al-Zarkashī quotes al-ʿIzz ibn ʿAbd al-Salām saying that the muṣḥaf should not now be written in the first spelling for fear that the ignorant would alter it; al-Zarkashī adds that the old rasm must still be preserved by scholars. Mālik, Aḥmad and al-Dānī are associated with holding to the first writing.

ulc-026.src: Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ fī Rasm Maṣāḥif al-Amṣār
ulc-026.q: Which work by Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī is a foundational reference on the spelling of the ʿUthmānic copies?
ulc-026.e: Al-Muqniʿ collects the spellings of the copies of the various cities. Al-Taysīr is al-Dānī's work on the seven readings, al-Nashr is by Ibn al-Jazarī and Ḥirz al-Amānī is al-Shāṭibī's poem on the readings.

ulc-027.src: al-Shāṭibī, ʿAqīlat Atrāb al-Qaṣāʾid; Abū ʿAmr al-Dānī, al-Muqniʿ
ulc-027.q: Which poem by al-Shāṭibī versifies the content of al-Dānī's al-Muqniʿ on the rasm?
ulc-027.e: Al-Shāṭibī put al-Muqniʿ into verse in ʿAqīlat Atrāb al-Qaṣāʾid (often called al-Rāʾiyya). Ḥirz al-Amānī versifies al-Taysīr on the readings, Nāẓimat al-Zuhr deals with verse counting, and al-Durra al-Muḍīʾa is Ibn al-Jazarī's poem on the three additional readings.

ulc-028.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on the number of surahs
ulc-028.q: How many surahs does the Quran contain?
ulc-028.e: The muṣḥaf contains 114 surahs, beginning with al-Fātiḥa and ending with al-Nās.

ulc-029.src: al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān, ch. on the order of verses; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on collection and arrangement
ulc-029.q: What is the established position on the order of the verses within each surah?
o: It was fixed by the Prophet's instruction, by consensus
It was arranged by the ijtihād of Zayd ibn Thābit
It follows the chronological order of revelation
It was decided by vote in ʿUthmān's committee
ulc-029.e: Al-Zarkashī and al-Suyūṭī report consensus that the order of verses is tawqīfī: the Prophet told the scribes where to place each verse. Revelation order and verse order often differ.

ulc-030.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on collection and arrangement; al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān, ch. on the order of surahs
ulc-030.q: Which statement correctly describes the scholars' views on the order of the surahs?
o: Views differ: tawqīfī, Companions' ijtihād, or mostly tawqīfī with exceptions
All scholars agree it was by ijtihād, unlike the order of verses within surahs
All scholars agree it follows the chronological order of revelation
All scholars agree Jibrīl fixed it in the final review in Ramaḍān
ulc-030.e: Unlike verse order, the order of surahs is disputed: one view holds it was fixed by the Prophet, another (attributed to Mālik and, in one statement, al-Bāqillānī) that the Companions arranged it by ijtihād, and a third that most was fixed with a few surahs left to them.

ulc-031.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on collection and arrangement
ulc-031.q: What evidence did those who held that the order of surahs was set by the Companions' ijtihād cite?
o: Personal copies of Ibn Masʿūd and Ubayy had different surah orders
The Companions disagreed on the order of verses in al-Baqara
The Prophet never recited more than one surah in a single prayer
Zayd ibn Thābit stated that he had arranged the surahs himself
ulc-031.e: Al-Suyūṭī notes that the private copies of Companions such as ʿAlī, Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd had different surah orders before ʿUthmān's copies, which suggests the order was not fixed by explicit instruction.

ulc-032.src: al-Tirmidhī, Jāmiʿ, Abwāb al-Tafsīr, on Sūrat al-Tawba; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on collection and arrangement
ulc-032.q: In the report in which Ibn ʿAbbās asked ʿUthmān why he had placed two surahs side by side without a basmala line between them, which surahs were meant?
ulc-032.e: ʿUthmān answered that the Prophet died without making clear whether al-Tawba belonged to al-Anfāl, and because their contents were similar he put them together without writing a basmala line. Scholars cite this report in the debate on whether surah order is tawqīfī.

ulc-033.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on the number of surahs, verses and words
ulc-033.q: Into how many parts (ajzāʾ) is the muṣḥaf commonly divided for recitation?
ulc-033.e: The common division is into thirty ajzāʾ, each of which is made of two aḥzāb, giving sixty aḥzāb. This makes it easy to complete the Quran in a month.

ulc-034.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on the number of surahs, verses and words; al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān
ulc-034.q: What name is given to the group of shorter surahs at the end of the muṣḥaf?
ulc-034.e: Al-Mufaṣṣal is the last group, so called because of the many separations between its surahs by the basmala. Al-Sabʿ al-Ṭiwāl are the long surahs at the beginning, al-Miʾūn those of about a hundred verses, and al-Mathānī those after them.

ulc-035.src: Abū Dāwūd, Sunan, Kitāb al-Ṣalāt, on dividing the recitation (report of Aws ibn Ḥudhayfa); al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān
ulc-035.q: In the report of Aws ibn Ḥudhayfa (Sunan Abī Dāwūd), the Companions divided their recitation into groups of 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 13 surahs, then the mufaṣṣal. Counting from al-Baqara, with which surah does the final portion begin?
ulc-035.e: Three, five, seven, nine, eleven and thirteen surahs make 48 surahs after al-Fātiḥa, ending with al-Ḥujurāt (49), so the last portion starts with Qāf (50). Al-Ḥujurāt and other surahs are named in other views on where the mufaṣṣal begins.

ulc-036.src: al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on abrogation
ulc-036.q: What does the word naskh mean linguistically?
ulc-036.e: Linguistically, naskh is used for removal (as the sun removes the shade) and for transferring or copying (as in copying a book). The technical meaning in uṣūl builds on the sense of removal.

ulc-037.src: al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān, ch. on abrogation; al-Zurqānī, Manāhil al-ʿIrfān, ch. on abrogation
ulc-037.q: Which is the standard technical definition of naskh?
o: Lifting a sharʿī ruling by a later sharʿī proof
Limiting a general word to some of its individuals
Explaining an ambiguous verse by a clearer one
Restricting an unrestricted word by a description
ulc-037.e: Naskh is the lifting of a sharʿī ruling by a sharʿī proof that comes later. Limiting a general word is takhṣīṣ, restricting an unrestricted word is taqyīd, and explaining an ambiguous text is bayān.

ulc-038.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, on 2:106
ulc-038.q: The verse shown is a principal proof for which concept in ʿulūm al-Qurʾān?
ulc-038.e: The verse speaks of God replacing a verse with one better or like it, and scholars such as Ibn Kathīr cite it as a main proof that abrogation occurs in the Sharīʿa.

ulc-039.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on abrogating and abrogated
ulc-039.q: What is the name of the category in which the text of a verse is still recited but its ruling no longer applies?
o: Abrogation of the ruling without the recitation
Abrogation of the recitation without the ruling
Abrogation of both ruling and recitation
Specification of the ruling without abrogation
ulc-039.e: Al-Suyūṭī lists three kinds: ruling and recitation both abrogated, ruling abrogated while recitation remains, and recitation abrogated while the ruling remains. The described case is the second, and most books on naskh deal mainly with it.

ulc-040.src: al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān, ch. on abrogation; al-Zurqānī, Manāhil al-ʿIrfān, ch. on abrogation
ulc-040.q: According to the majority, which kind of text cannot be subject to abrogation?
o: A pure report of a past event or a matter of belief
A command addressed to the believers to perform an act
A prohibition of an act that was previously allowed
A permission granted for a limited period of time
ulc-040.e: Naskh applies to rulings (commands, prohibitions, permissions). A pure report cannot be abrogated, because abrogating it would mean declaring a true report false; matters of belief likewise do not change.

ulc-041.src: al-Zurqānī, Manāhil al-ʿIrfān, ch. on abrogation; al-Shawkānī, Irshād al-Fuḥūl, ch. on abrogation
ulc-041.q: When may a scholar judge one text to be abrogated by another?
o: When they truly conflict, cannot be reconciled and the later one is known
Whenever a later verse gives a more detailed ruling on the matter
Whenever the earlier verse was revealed in Mecca before the Hijra
Whenever a later scholar finds the earlier ruling hard to apply
ulc-041.e: Abrogation is not presumed: the two texts must genuinely conflict, reconciliation must be impossible, and which came later must be known from a reliable proof. A more detailed later text is usually explanation or specification, not abrogation.

ulc-042.src: Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, on 58:12–13; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on abrogating and abrogated
ulc-042.q: The command in the verse shown (giving charity before a private consultation with the Prophet) is commonly cited by scholars as an example of what?
o: A ruling lifted by the next verse while its recitation remains
A recitation removed from the muṣḥaf while its ruling remains
A general ruling that was later specified by the Sunna
An unrestricted ruling that was restricted by a description
ulc-042.e: Most mufassirūn hold that the duty of charity before consultation was lifted by the following verse (58:13), while the verse is still recited. It is among the examples al-Suyūṭī accepts in his short list of abrogated verses.

ulc-043.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Tafsīr, on 2:240; Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm, on 2:240
ulc-043.q: Which statement correctly describes the scholars' positions on the verse shown, about provision for a widow for a full year?
o: Most: abrogated by 2:234; some, such as Mujāhid, reconciled the two verses
All scholars agree that 2:234 was itself abrogated by this verse
All scholars agree that it was never part of the recited Quran
Most: it abrogated the waiting period of four months and ten days
ulc-043.e: The majority held that the year's provision was abrogated by the waiting period of four months and ten days in 2:234 (and the shares of inheritance). Al-Bukhārī reports that Mujāhid instead saw the year as a recommended bequest beyond the obligatory waiting period, so the verses do not conflict.

ulc-044.q: Ibn al-Zubayr asked ʿUthmān why he still wrote the verse shown in the muṣḥaf although another verse had abrogated it. What did ʿUthmān answer?
o: That he would not move anything of the Quran from its place
That the verse had in fact never been abrogated at all
That the Prophet had ordered it to be written down twice
That Zayd ibn Thābit had insisted on including it there
ulc-044.e: Al-Bukhārī reports ʿUthmān's reply that he would not change anything of it from its place. The report shows that abrogated rulings could remain in the recited text and that the placement of verses was not a matter of personal choice.

ulc-045.src: al-Bukhārī, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Ḥudūd, report of ʿUmar on stoning; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on abrogating and abrogated
ulc-045.q: Which example do scholars commonly give for abrogation of the recitation while the ruling remains?
o: The verse of stoning mentioned by ʿUmar in his sermon
The verse of the widow's provision for a full year
The verse requiring charity before consultation
The verse on the ratio of fighters in al-Anfāl
ulc-045.e: ʿUmar stated in a sermon reported by al-Bukhārī and Muslim that a verse on stoning had been revealed and acted upon; its wording is not in the muṣḥaf but the ruling remained. The other three are examples given for abrogation of a ruling while the recitation remains.

ulc-046.src: Muslim, Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb al-Raḍāʿ, report of ʿĀʾisha; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on abrogating and abrogated
ulc-046.q: In ʿĀʾisha's report in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim about the number of sucklings, the 'ten known sucklings' are commonly cited as an example of which kind of abrogation?
o: Abrogation of both the recitation and the ruling
Abrogation of the ruling while the recitation remains
Abrogation of the recitation while the ruling remains
Abrogation of the Sunna by the Quran
ulc-046.e: ʿĀʾisha reported that ten sucklings had been revealed and were then abrogated by five; the ten are no longer recited nor acted upon, so they serve as the standard example of both being abrogated. How to treat the five is a separate fiqh discussion in which the schools differ.

ulc-047.src: al-Shāfiʿī, al-Risāla, chapter on abrogation; al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān, ch. on abrogation
ulc-047.q: Which imam is best known for holding that the Quran is abrogated only by the Quran and the Sunna only by the Sunna, a view many later uṣūlīs did not share?
ulc-047.e: Al-Shāfiʿī argued in al-Risāla that only the Quran abrogates the Quran, with the Sunna explaining rather than abrogating it. The Ḥanafīs and many others permitted abrogation of the Quran by mutawātir Sunna in principle.

ulc-048.src: al-Rāzī, Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb, on 2:106; al-Zurqānī, Manāhil al-ʿIrfān, ch. on abrogation
ulc-048.q: Which early scholar is known for denying that any verse of the Quran is abrogated, explaining the usual examples as specification instead?
ulc-048.e: Abū Muslim al-Iṣfahānī, a Muʿtazilī mufassir, is regularly cited (for example by al-Rāzī) for denying abrogation within the Quran; the majority rejected his view. Al-Naḥḥās, Abū ʿUbayd and Ibn al-Jawzī all wrote books listing abrogated verses.

ulc-049.src: Shāh Walī Allāh al-Dihlawī, al-Fawz al-Kabīr fī Uṣūl al-Tafsīr; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on abrogating and abrogated
ulc-049.q: Al-Suyūṭī reduced the genuinely abrogated verses to about twenty. To how many did Shāh Walī Allāh al-Dihlawī reduce them in al-Fawz al-Kabīr?
ulc-049.e: Shāh Walī Allāh examined al-Suyūṭī's list and accepted abrogation in only five cases, reconciling the rest. Earlier works counted far more because they used naskh in a broader sense.

ulc-050.src: al-Shāṭibī, al-Muwāfaqāt, Kitāb al-Adilla, on abrogation; Ibn al-Qayyim, Iʿlām al-Muwaqqiʿīn
ulc-050.q: Why do early lists of 'abrogated' verses contain far more verses than the lists of later scholars?
o: Early scholars also called specification and restriction naskh
Later scholars lost many of the earlier reports on abrogation
Early scholars held every Meccan verse abrogated by Medinan ones
Later scholars rejected abrogation in the Quran entirely
ulc-050.e: Al-Shāṭibī and Ibn al-Qayyim explain that the Salaf called any lifting or modification of an apparent meaning naskh, including takhṣīṣ, taqyīd and bayān. Later uṣūlīs reserved the term for lifting a ruling, so their lists are much shorter.

ulc-051.src: al-Zarkashī, al-Burhān, ch. on abrogation; al-Zurqānī, Manāhil al-ʿIrfān, ch. on abrogation
ulc-051.q: What is the key difference between naskh and takhṣīṣ?
