o: Baʾsāʾ is poverty and hardship, ḍarrāʾ is illness and physical harm
Baʾsāʾ is illness and bodily harm, while ḍarrāʾ is poverty and hardship
They are exact synonyms in every context and cannot be told apart
Baʾsāʾ is a time of joy and plenty, while ḍarrāʾ is a time of grief
vc-083.e: Commentators such as Ibn Masʿūd explain baʾsāʾ as poverty and hardship and ḍarrāʾ as illness and bodily affliction; both stand for trials that befell earlier believers.

vc-084.src: Ibn Qutayba, Gharīb al-Qurʾān, on Sūrat al-Baqara
vc-084.q: What does the highlighted verb mean here?
vc-084.e: Ikhtāna means to act dishonestly or betray; Ibn ʿAbbās and others said they used to break the restriction secretly after the night prayer. God pardons this in the verse.

vc-085.q: What does the highlighted word mean, said of the hearts of some people?
vc-085.e: Zaygh is inclining away from the straight path. The verse says that those with it follow the ambiguous verses out of a desire for discord and for their own interpretation.

vc-086.q: What does the highlighted word, said of Ibrāhīm, mean?
o: One who turns away from falsehood towards the truth
One who is a scholar of law
One who lives in the desert
vc-086.e: Ḥanīf comes from ḥanaf, an inclining of the foot, and became used for one who inclines from all falsehood to the pure worship of God, as Ibn ʿAbbās and others explained.

vc-087.q: What is the basic meaning of the highlighted intensive form?
o: Those who stand in charge and maintain
vc-087.e: Qawwāmūn is an intensive from qāma, to stand, and means those who stand in charge, taking responsibility to maintain and protect. Commentators relate it to the duty of financial support stated in the same verse.

vc-088.q: What is the basic meaning of the highlighted word?
o: Rising up in disobedience or arrogance
vc-088.e: Nushūz comes from a root meaning to rise above or stand out; in the verse it is used for rising up in disobedience. The verse then sets out graded steps of response.

vc-089.q: What does the highlighted word mean?
o: The sacred rites and signs of God
vc-089.e: Shaʿāʾir (singular shaʿīra) are the marks and rites of God's religion, especially the rites of Ḥajj. The verse forbids treating them as lawful to violate.

vc-090.src: Ibn Qutayba, Gharīb al-Qurʾān, on Sūrat al-Māʾida
vc-090.q: What does the highlighted word refer to?
vc-090.e: Al-qalāʾid are animals for sacrifice wearing a garland or sandal mark, which shows they are dedicated to the sanctuary and protected.

vc-091.q: What does the highlighted word mean?
vc-091.e: Shanaʾān is strong hatred. The verse says that hatred for a people must not lead believers to transgress against them.

vc-092.q: What does the highlighted word mean, in what the Prophet removes from them?
o: Their heavy burden (of covenants and strict laws)
vc-092.e: Iṣr is a heavy burden or binding obligation. The verse says the Prophet removes the burdens and shackles that lay on them, referring to harsh laws of earlier communities.

vc-093.q: What does the highlighted verb mean here, used with ‘to the earth’?
o: He clung to the worldly life and inclined to it
vc-093.e: Akhlada ilā al-arḍ means to cling to the earth, that is to give himself to the pleasures of this world and follow his desires.

vc-094.q: Who are the people described by the highlighted phrase?
o: Those whose hearts are to be reconciled (won over)
vc-094.e: Al-muʾallafa qulūbuhum are people whose hearts are to be won over to Islam or kept firm in it, one of the eight categories of zakāt recipients. Its present application is discussed in the schools.

vc-095.q: What does the highlighted command, addressed to the earth, mean?
vc-095.e: Ibliʿī is an imperative of balaʿa, to swallow. The earth is told to swallow its water and the sky to hold back, ending the flood.

vc-096.src: Ibn Qutayba, Gharīb al-Qurʾān, on Sūrat Yūsuf
vc-096.q: What does the highlighted word mean, said of the price?
vc-096.e: Bakhs is a diminished value, a price below the true worth, hence unfair. The verse adds that the sum was a few dirhams that were counted out.

vc-097.src: Muqātil ibn Sulaymān, al-Ashbāh wa-l-Naẓāʾir fī al-Qurʾān al-Karīm; Ibn Qutayba, Gharīb al-Qurʾān
vc-097.q: The highlighted word often means ‘a community of people’. What does it mean in this verse?
vc-097.e: The word is polysemous. Here, as Ibn ʿAbbās and others explained, it means a span of time (the one who was saved remembered after some years). Other verses use it for a people or a religious community.

vc-098.src: Ibn Qutayba, Gharīb al-Qurʾān, on Sūrat al-Kahf
vc-098.q: What does the highlighted word mean in Mūsā's words to his servant?
vc-098.e: Ḥuqub (plural of ḥuqb) means long spans of time, said in Mūsā's determination to continue the journey however long it took.

vc-099.src: Ibn Qutayba, Gharīb al-Qurʾān, on Sūrat al-Kahf
vc-099.q: What does the highlighted word mean in the parable of worldly life?
vc-099.e: Hashīm is dried and broken plants that the wind scatters, an image of how quickly this life fades.

vc-100.q: What does the highlighted verb mean, said of the soul?
vc-100.e: Sawwalat is from sawl, a wish or temptation; it means that his soul embellished the act and made it seem good to him.

vc-101.src: Ibn Qutayba, Gharīb al-Qurʾān, on Sūrat Fāṭir
vc-101.q: What does the highlighted word name, as an image of something tiny?
o: The thin skin over a date stone
vc-101.e: Qiṭmīr is the thin membrane covering a date stone. The verse says those called upon besides God do not own even that.

vc-102.src: Ibn Qutayba, Gharīb al-Qurʾān, on Sūrat Fuṣṣilat
vc-102.q: What does the highlighted word mean, said of the ears of those who do not believe?
vc-102.e: Waqr is a heaviness in the ears that prevents hearing. The verse speaks of a spiritual deafness to the Quran.

vc-103.q: What does the highlighted verb mean?
o: Do not slander or find fault with one another
vc-103.e: Lamz is defaming or finding fault with someone; the verse uses it with ‘yourselves’ because believers are like one body.

vc-104.q: What does the highlighted word mean?
vc-104.e: Khaṣāṣa is severe poverty or want. The verse praises the Anṣār for giving preference to others even when they themselves were in such need.

vc-105.q: What does the highlighted word mean?
vc-105.e: Shuḥḥ is the miserliness that goes with covetousness. The verse says that whoever is protected from the shuḥḥ of his own soul is successful.

vc-106.src: Ibn al-Jawzī, Nuzhat al-Aʿyun al-Nawāẓir fī ʿIlm al-Wujūh wa-l-Naẓāʾir; al-Rāghib, al-Mufradāt
vc-106.q: What does the highlighted command mean here, from the same root as ‘prayer’?
o: Pray for them (make supplication for them)
Lead them in the ritual prayer
vc-106.e: In its linguistic sense ṣalāt means supplication. The Prophet is told to take their charity and to pray for them, and the verse adds that his prayer is a source of calm for them.

vc-107.src: Ibn Qutayba, Gharīb al-Qurʾān, on Sūrat al-Raḥmān
vc-107.q: What does the highlighted verb mean, said of the two seas?
o: He let them flow freely so that they meet
vc-107.e: Maraja means to let loose and release; the two seas are allowed to flow and meet. The next verse mentions a barrier between them which they do not cross.

vc-108.src: Ibn Qutayba, Gharīb al-Qurʾān, on Sūrat Muḥammad
vc-108.q: What does the highlighted word mean, said of captives?
vc-108.e: Wathāq is what binds, here the bonds with which captives are secured. The verse then says to release them as a favour or for ransom.

vc-109.q: What does the highlighted word mean in ‘until the war lays down its …’?
vc-109.e: Awzār (singular wizr) means burdens; war is imagined carrying a load of arms which it puts down when it ends.

vc-110.q: Which statement about the highlighted verb is correct, from the root ṣ-l-w?
o: When said of God it means mercy and praise, of the angels it means asking forgiveness, of people it means supplication
It always means the ritual prayer with bowing and prostration, whoever the subject is
It always means to wash or to purify, whether the subject is God or a person
It means to build or to repair when the subject is a person
vc-110.e: Al-Bukhārī relates from Abū al-ʿĀliya that God's ṣalāt on the Prophet is His praising him before the angels, and that of the angels is their supplication. The root is thus polysemous, depending on the subject.

vc-111.q: What does the highlighted verb mean, said of those who believe in the Prophet?
vc-111.e: Taʿzīr combines support and respect; ʿazzarūhu means they defended and honoured him. It is not simple helping or following, which are expressed by other verbs in the same verse.

vc-112.src: Ibn al-Anbārī, Kitāb al-Aḍdād; al-Suyūṭī, al-Muzhir, on words with opposite meanings
vc-112.q: The root of the highlighted verb can mean both ‘to buy’ and ‘to sell’ (a word with opposite senses, ḍidd). What does it mean here?
vc-112.e: Sharā is one of the aḍdād: it can mean to buy or to sell. Here the subject is the brothers' side who took Yūsuf from the well and sold him for a low price, as Mujāhid and others explained.

vc-113.src: Abū Hilāl al-ʿAskarī, al-Furūq al-Lughawiyya; al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt
vc-113.q: The verse calls the sun ḍiyāʾ and the moon nūr. What distinction is commonly drawn between the two words?
o: Ḍiyāʾ is light that comes from the thing itself and is intense; nūr is more general, including light that is received or reflected
Ḍiyāʾ is the light of the day only, while nūr is the light of the night only and never of the day
Ḍiyāʾ is light perceived by the eye, while nūr is only a light perceived by the heart
They are strict synonyms that never differ in any verse or in any lexicon
vc-113.e: Lexicographers and commentators often say ḍiyāʾ is the self-generated, stronger light and nūr the more general and gentler light, which fits the sun and the moon. Some scholars, however, treat the two as close in meaning in other contexts.

vc-114.src: al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt, entries laʿiba and lahā
vc-114.q: The verse names worldly life as laʿib and lahw. What distinction between the two is commonly given?
o: Laʿib is activity without a serious aim; lahw is a diversion that distracts from what matters
Laʿib is wealth, lahw is power
Laʿib is grief, lahw is joy
Laʿib is prayer, lahw is fasting
vc-114.e: Lexicons describe laʿib as purposeless play and lahw as what occupies and turns the heart away from more important concerns. The verse lists them first among the things that make worldly life deceptive.

vc-115.src: Ibn al-Qayyim, Madārij al-Sālikīn, on shukr; al-Jurjānī, al-Taʿrīfāt
vc-115.q: Which statement correctly states the classical distinction between ḥamd (the highlighted word) and shukr?
o: Ḥamd is wider in its object (praise of any perfection) but only by the tongue; shukr is wider in means (heart, tongue, limbs) but only for a favour received
Ḥamd is carried out by actions of the limbs, while shukr is by the tongue only and never by the heart
Ḥamd may be directed only to human beings, while shukr is directed to God alone
They are identical in object and in means, differing only in the letters used
vc-115.e: The classical formula is that each is ‘general from one side and particular from another’: ḥamd covers praise for any attribute, even without benefit, but is verbal; shukr is gratitude for a benefit and can be expressed by heart, tongue and limbs.

vc-116.src: al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt, entry khashiya; Abū Hilāl al-ʿAskarī, al-Furūq al-Lughawiyya
vc-116.q: The verse says that only the knowledgeable among God's servants have this feeling. What distinguishes khashya (the highlighted verb) from khawf?
o: Khashya is fear that comes from knowledge of the greatness of the one feared and mixes with reverence
Khashya is fear of creatures only
Khashya is fear of the grave only
Khashya is a sudden fright that does not last
vc-116.e: Lexicographers describe khawf as the general fear of harm, while khashya is fear based on knowledge and awe of the one feared. This fits the verse, which links it to knowledge.

vc-117.src: Ibn Manẓūr, Lisān al-ʿArab, entry ayada; al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 51:47
vc-117.q: The highlighted word looks like the plural of ‘hand’. What does it mean in this verse?
o: Might and power (a singular noun, ayd)
Hands, as the plural of yad
vc-117.e: Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and others explained it as strength: ayd is a noun meaning power, not the plural of yad, which is aydī. The verse says the heaven was built with might.

vc-118.q: What does the highlighted verb mean?
o: You have overpowered them with heavy slaughter
vc-118.e: Ithkhān is the thorough subduing of an enemy through much killing, from thakhīn (thick, heavy). Only after that, the verse says, are captives to be bound.

vc-119.src: al-Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-Bayān, on 39:23; al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān
vc-119.q: Which explanation of the highlighted word, a description of the Book, is commonly given?
o: Repeated: its stories, rulings and warnings are repeated and paired
vc-119.e: Mathānī is often explained as ‘repeated’ because the Quran returns to its themes and pairs promise with warning. The same word is used for al-Fātiḥa in another verse (the seven oft-repeated), with a related sense.

vc-120.src: Ibn Hishām, Mughnī al-Labīb, on lāta; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Kashshāf, on 38:3
vc-120.q: The highlighted word is made of a particle and a feminine ending. What is it?
o: Lāta: a negative particle working like laysa, used with words of time
vc-120.e: Lāta is lā with a feminine tāʾ; it negates like laysa and is used with words denoting time such as ḥīn (the following noun). The sense is ‘it was no time of escape’.

vc-121.q: What does the highlighted verb mean here?
o: He multiplies you (creates you in numbers) by this arrangement
vc-121.e: Dharaʾa means to create and to multiply; the verse says God multiplies humankind through the pairing He made. It is a different verb from dharā, which means to scatter.

vc-122.src: Ibn Qutayba, Gharīb al-Qurʾān, on Sūrat al-Ḥadīd
vc-122.q: What does the highlighted verb describe in the parable?
o: The plant dries up and turns yellow
vc-122.e: Hāja means to dry and wither; in the parable the green growth that pleased the farmers dries, turns yellow and becomes crumbled stubble.

vc-123.src: Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha, entry waqā
vc-123.q: What is the root letter set of the highlighted word?
vc-123.e: Muttaqīn comes from ittaqā, whose initial tāʾ is the result of a wāw turned into tāʾ and assimilated: the root is w-q-y, to guard oneself. It is not from y-q-n (certainty).

vc-124.src: Ibn Fāris, Maqāyīs al-Lugha, entry warada
vc-124.q: What is the root of the highlighted word, which names the one sent by the caravan to the well?
vc-124.e: Wārid is the active participle of warada, to arrive at a water source. The caravan's scout who goes to fetch water is called wārid.

vc-125.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on the names of the Quran
vc-125.q: Which scholar is reported to have held that the word Qurʾān is a proper name, not derived from any root and pronounced without hamza?
vc-125.e: Al-Suyūṭī reports several views on the word: al-Zajjāj derived it from qarʾ (gathering), al-Farrāʾ from qarāʾin (signs), al-Ashʿarī from qarana (joining), and the majority from qaraʾa (to recite). Al-Shāfiʿī is reported to have said it is a name with no derivation.

vc-126.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān, ch. on non-Arabic words in the Quran (al-muʿarrab); al-Shāfiʿī, al-Risāla
vc-126.q: Some reports from early authorities say the highlighted word is of Roman (Greek) origin. Which statement correctly describes the scholarly disagreement on foreign words in the Quran?
o: Al-Shāfiʿī, Abū ʿUbayda and al-Ṭabarī rejected non-Arabic words in the Quran, while reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and others name some; many reconcile by calling them Arabicised words
All scholars agree that most words of the Quran were borrowed from Persian and Greek and later Arabicised
All scholars agree that foreign words occur in the Quran and that al-Shāfiʿī was the first to list them
The question was never discussed in the classical works and arose only in the modern period
vc-126.e: The matter is discussed in the classical works. Al-Shāfiʿī, Abū ʿUbayda and al-Ṭabarī held that the Quran has no non-Arabic words, while others cited reports from Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid; al-Suyūṭī and many reconcile the two by saying such words were Arabicised by the Arabs before revelation.

vc-127.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on al-wujūh wa-l-naẓāʾir
vc-127.q: What does the genre called al-wujūh wa-l-naẓāʾir study?
o: Words that carry several meanings in different verses, and different words with the same sense
The wording of the Quran in different dialects
The occasions of revelation of each verse
vc-127.e: In this genre authors collect one Quranic word and its different senses in different verses (wujūh) and group verses that use the same word in the same sense (naẓāʾir). Early works include Muqātil's al-Ashbāh wa-l-Naẓāʾir.

vc-128.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on the gharīb of the Quran
vc-128.q: Which Companion's answers to the questions of Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq, citing Arabic poetry for the meaning of Quranic words, are quoted in al-Itqān?
vc-128.e: Ibn ʿAbbās answered Nāfiʿ ibn al-Azraq and Najda ibn ʿUwaymir by quoting pre-Islamic poetry for the senses of the unusual words; al-Suyūṭī reports these as a model of using poetry to explain gharīb al-Qurʾān.

vc-129.src: al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī, al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, introduction
vc-129.q: Which scholar wrote al-Mufradāt fī Gharīb al-Qurʾān, a dictionary of Quranic words?
vc-129.e: Al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī (5th century AH) compiled al-Mufradāt, arranging the Quranic vocabulary by root and giving the basic sense of each. Ibn Manẓūr wrote the general dictionary Lisān al-ʿArab.

vc-130.src: al-Suyūṭī, al-Itqān fī ʿUlūm al-Qurʾān, ch. on works of gharīb al-Qurʾān
vc-130.q: Which work, by Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar ibn al-Muthannā, explains the Quran through the idiom and figurative usage of Arabic?
vc-130.e: Abū ʿUbayda's Majāz al-Qurʾān explains the wording by Arab usage; ‘majāz’ there means the way the language takes the expression, not figurative language in the later technical sense. Al-Farrāʾ wrote Maʿānī al-Qurʾān and Ibn Qutayba wrote Taʾwīl Mushkil al-Qurʾān.
